text:
Do Drafters Work on Small Models? Gemma 4 E2B and E4B on Two Small GPUs

---
title: "Do Drafters Work on Small Models? Gemma 4 E2B and E4B on Two Small GPUs"
published: true
description: "Yes. Speculative decoding with Google's 59 MB QAT multi-token prediction (MTP) drafters speeds up Gemma 4 E4B 1.72x and E2B 1.40x on an 8 GB RTX 3050, and 1.49x and 1.18x on a 4 GB laptop GTX 1650 Ti, served by llama.cpp one request at a time, with unchanged GSM8K and BFCL scores."
tags: gemma, llamacpp, cuda, benchmarking
cover_image: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/main/docs/drafter-3050-vs-1650ti/devto-cover.7d054a5b.jpg
---

This article provides a step by step guide to serving Gemma 4 E2B and E4B with Google's QAT assistant drafters through llama.cpp's speculative decoding, and measuring what the drafter is worth on two small NVIDIA cards: a desktop RTX 3050 OEM and a laptop GTX 1650 Ti. A suite of Python MCP tools is built to simplify management of the llama.cpp hosted deployment.

This is the second part of a short series. [Part 1, Gemma 4's MTP Drafter, Explained](https://dev.to/gde/gemma-4s-mtp-drafter-explained-speculative-decoding-and-a-4-bit-drafter-at-60-of-the-size-1oc0), covers how speculative decoding and Gemma 4's multi-token prediction (MTP) drafter work and how the exact Q4_0 repack is built. This part has the measurements.

https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev

A drafter is the guesser in speculative decoding: it proposes the next few tokens, and the main model checks them all in one pass.

**Do drafters work on small models? Yes.** Gemma 4 E2B and E4B are already small, and their drafter is a 4-layer model of 59 MB. Served one request at a time, it makes both models faster on both cards, and GSM8K and BFCL scores stay the same:

| one request at a time | RTX 3050 | GTX 1650 Ti |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| E4B | **1.72x** | **1.49x** |
| E2B | **1.40x** | **1.18x** |
| Answer quality | unchanged | unchanged |

The smaller model gains less. E2B is already fast per token, so each drafted step costs a larger share of what it saves (inferred from the draft-length results below, not measured directly). Both cards keep the same share of the drafted tokens, within 0.03, so the gap between the cards comes from the cards.

The gain has limits. With several requests at once it shrinks on both cards, and on the 1650 Ti it turns into a loss from 4 requests (E4B) or 8 (E2B). On the 1650 Ti, E2B's gain is gone by about 32k tokens of conversation. Too many drafted tokens also cost speed on the slower card.

The drafter here is an exact Q4_0 repack of Google's weights. It matches the converter's Q8_0 file on speed and answers at 60% of its size, and beats Google's bf16 weights on speed on every card and model.

---

#### What Is Being Measured?

A language model writes one token per forward pass, and every pass reads every weight. For one user on a small GPU, each pass spends most of its time moving weights, which leaves compute to spare. Speculative decoding uses it: a small drafter guesses the next few tokens, and the main model checks all of them in one pass. It keeps the guesses up to the first one it disagrees with and adds one token of its own, so the output is the main model's either way. When most guesses are kept, one pass yields several tokens instead of one.

Gemma 4's drafter uses multi-token prediction (MTP). It is a 4-layer model that reads the main model's hidden state and reuses its KV cache, so it keeps no cache of its own and costs little more than its weights.

MTP is one of several ways to do speculative decoding. llama.cpp `77c4540ce` offers ten through `--spec-type`: a separate small draft model (`draft-simple`), `draft-eagle3`, `draft-mtp`, `draft-dflash`, `draft-dspark`, and five n-gram methods. MTP is the one Google builds drafters for: E2B, E4B, 12B, 26B-A4B and 31B each have a published assistant checkpoint (E2B's config names it `Gemma4AssistantForCausalLM`), which llama.cpp runs as `draft-mtp` and vLLM as `"method":"mtp"`. This article measures MTP only. [Part 1](https://dev.to/gde/gemma-4s-mtp-drafter-explained-speculative-decoding-and-a-4-bit-drafter-at-60-of-the-size-1oc0) explains this in full.

Google publishes an assistant drafter for each Gemma 4 QAT checkpoint. Both cards here serve the exact Q4_0 GGUFs of `gemma-4-E2B-it` and `gemma-4-E4B-it` with the drafters stored back as Q4_0 on their trained 4-bit grid, 59 MB each. The question is what the drafter is worth on each card, and why the two cards differ.

---

#### At This Point You Should Have…

- An NVIDIA GPU with a CUDA driver — here an RTX 3050 OEM (driver 615.78.08) and a GTX 1650 Ti with Max-Q Design (driver 615.71.09)
- The CUDA toolkit, 13.4 here, and `cmake`
- llama.cpp at a commit with `--spec-type draft-mtp` — both cards ran `77c4540ce` for every comparison below
- Python 3.10 or newer, the system `python3`, no virtualenv
- The repository cloned, with the four rigs `local-llamacpp-{3050oem,1650ti}-{2b,4b}-q4_0/`
- Claude Code, or any MCP client that speaks stdio

---

#### The Two Cards

| | RTX 3050 OEM | GTX 1650 Ti Max-Q |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Host | i7-5820K desktop, 46 GiB | i7-10750H laptop (Lenovo Yoga 9), 15 GiB |
| Memory | 8192 MiB | 4096 MiB |
| Architecture | Ampere, compute capability 8.6, tensor cores | Turing TU117, compute capability 7.5, no tensor cores |
| Power limit | 120 W | about 40 W |
| E2B, no drafter | 108.2 tok/s | 76.5 tok/s |
| E4B, no drafter | 58.3 tok/s | 38.0 tok/s |

Without a drafter the 3050 generates 1.41x faster on E2B and 1.53x on E4B. Different hosts, so treat ratios between the cards as indicative.

---

#### Step 1 — Repack the Drafter on Its Trained Grid

Google publishes the QAT assistant drafters as [google/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized-assistant](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized-assistant) and [google/gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized-assistant](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized-assistant). Each is a 4-layer model that reads the main model's KV cache, stored as bf16 safetensors.

Quantization-aware training already put the weights on a 4-bit grid: in every group of 32 values there are at most 16 distinct levels, evenly spaced. bf16 spends 16 bits storing each of those levels.

llama.cpp's `convert_hf_to_gguf.py` has no way to know that, so it writes Q8_0: 8.5 bits per weight, re-rounded onto an 8-bit grid of its own. The file shrinks, and the values move. Only 11.7% of the drafter's weights come back bit-identical.

Q4_0 is 4.5 bits per weight: one fp16 step per group of 32, and a 4-bit level for each value. That is enough to hold the trained grid, provided each group's step is read off its own values. `gguf_exact.py` does this for each group:

```python
amax = np.abs(g).max(-1, keepdims=True)
for m in range(1, 9):                      # try steps amax/1 .. amax/8
    cand = amax / m
    q = np.clip(np.rint(g / cand), -8, 7)
    good = np.abs(g - q * cand).max(-1, keepdims=True) <= amax * 2**-7
```

The first step that puts every value in the group on an integer level wins. A least-squares fit then refines it, and it is rounded to fp16, Q4_0's step type. A group that fits no step stops the build, since nothing is re-rounded. On both drafters no group was off the grid.

The script takes Google's safetensors and the converter's Q8_0 file, copies the Q8_0 file's metadata byte for byte (tokenizer, chat template, settings), and writes every weight matrix as Q4_0. That covers 23 tensors per drafter, including the token embedding, which holds 86–87% of the values rewritten:

```shell
python3 gguf_exact.py <google-snapshot-dir> gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-assistant-q8_0.gguf gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-assistant-q4_0-exact.gguf
python3 gguf_exact.py <google-snapshot-dir> gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-assistant-q8_0.gguf gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-assistant-bf16.gguf --bf16
```

`--bf16` writes Google's weights unchanged into the same layout, so all three formats can be compared with identical metadata.

| E2B drafter | Q8_0 (converter) | exact Q4_0 (repack) | bf16 (Google's weights) |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| File size | 97.8 MB | **59.2 MB** | 170.2 MB |
| Bits per weight | 8.5 | **4.5** | 16 |
| Error against Google's weights | 0.00494 | **0.00138** | 0 |
| Values bit-identical, read back in fp32 | 11.7% | **29.4%** | 100% |
| Values bit-identical, rounded to bf16 | — | **96.5–97.0% per tensor** | 100% |

The repack is 60% of the Q8_0 file and its error is 3.6x lower. Rounded back to bf16, the format Google stored, 97% of its values match Google's bit for bit. The E4B drafter gives the same picture: 59.7 MB, error 0.00138, 96.4–97.1% per tensor.

#### Is the Repack Worth It?

Yes, as the drafter file to ship. Against the two files a user would otherwise serve:

| exact Q4_0 repack against | Q8_0 (converter) | bf16 (Google's weights) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Speed | level on both cards | faster on every card and model |
| Share of drafted tokens kept | level, within 0.012 | level, within 0.012 |
| GSM8K and BFCL | level | not scored |
| File size | 60% | 35% |
| Card memory | 38–40 MiB less | 106–108 MiB less |
| Match to Google's weights | 3.6x lower error | 97% bit-identical in bf16 |

- 🟢 **Against bf16 it is the clear choice.** It is faster everywhere, and on the 1650 Ti bf16 makes E2B slower than serving without a drafter.
- 🟢 **Against Q8_0 it is a free improvement**: smaller, closer to the trained weights, and level on speed and answers.
- ⚠️ **The memory it saves over Q8_0 is under 1% of either card.** It counts only on a 4 GB card running near its limit.
- ⚠️ **Speed stays level with Q8_0** because the drafter's precision leaves the kept tokens unchanged. Every format keeps the same share, so a more exact drafter guesses as well as a rounded one and gains its speed from size alone.

The drafter adds four flags to the rig's normal command line:

#### 🔎 Tip: The Shared KV Cache Has a Price on Both Cards

llama-server gives each slot its own KV cache by default. On llama.cpp `77c4540ce` that layout halved generation speed at random with several requests in flight, on both cards: per-slot repeats spread 28–36% at 2 requests on the 1650 Ti. `-kvu` gives all slots one shared cache and the spread drops to about 1%. It also costs output as the total text held grows. At 16 requests in `sweep.py` the shared cache delivered 0.86–0.94x of per-slot output on the 3050 and 0.59–0.81x on the 1650 Ti. The drafter's ratio is nearly the same under either layout. With 1,000–3,500-token prompts on the 3050 the per-slot cache is the faster layout and showed no random slowdown: it beat the shared cache in 204 of 232 paired batches, and the shared cache gave 0.68–0.82x of its output at 16 requests and 0.49–0.66x at 32. All four rigs serve one request at a time, where the two layouts are identical.

#### So, Which One?

Drafters work on small models. Turn the drafter on for both cards when they serve one user. It costs no answers and 72–84 MiB of memory, and E4B gains the most on both: 1.72x on the 3050 and 1.49x on the 1650 Ti. Set the draft length per card, 2 tokens on the 3050 and 1 on the 1650 Ti.

On the 1650 Ti, leave E2B's drafter off for long conversations past about 32k tokens and for several users at once. On the 3050, the drafter keeps paying with long text ahead, and with long prompts it pays up to 16 users at once and breaks even at 32.

#### Summary

The goal of this article was to find out whether Google's Gemma 4 assistant drafters speed up small models on small NVIDIA cards served by llama.cpp. They do. The key to the solution was running the same llama.cpp build, scripts, prompts and drafter files on both cards, one setting per server, and checking answer quality alongside speed. The results were:

- 🟢 One request at a time the drafter speeds up E4B 1.72x on the RTX 3050 and 1.49x on the GTX 1650 Ti, and E2B 1.40x and 1.18x
- 🟢 Both cards keep the same share of drafted tokens, within 0.03 at every draft length
- 🟢 GSM8K and BFCL scores are unchanged with the drafter on both cards
- 🟢 The exact Q4_0 repack of the drafter is 60% of the Q8_0 file and level with it on speed on both cards; Google's bf16 weights are slowest on both
- ⚠️ The best draft length differs: 2 tokens on the 3050, 1 on the 1650 Ti
- ⚠️ With long text ahead, E2B's gain on the 1650 Ti is gone by 32k tokens; on the 3050 it holds at 1.23x at 120k
- 🟢 With 1,000–3,500-token prompts on the 3050 the drafter pays at every level up to 16 requests at once
- ❌ With 4–8 or more requests at once the drafter costs output on the 1650 Ti

Scope: Gemma 4 E2B and E4B only, MTP speculative decoding only, two cards on two hosts, llama.cpp `77c4540ce` on both, the exact Q4_0 E2B and E4B GGUFs with Google's QAT assistant drafters as exact Q4_0 (plus Q8_0 and bf16 for the format comparison), six short prompts for speed, one 120k-token document for long text, `sweep.py` at 1–16 requests with a shared KV cache, six long-prompt tasks at 1–32 requests on the 3050 with both cache layouts, GSM8K and BFCL simple one request at a time, each setting run once with a repeat check. The T4 tip comes from a separate vLLM run.

The strategy for using MCP for local accelerator comparison was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

🌑 Blue October TLDR: A brief summary of how I got here. ![divider](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/gmwxs2h211kfqgpurpop.png) ## The Mindset For the last 3 years, I have been learning tech. It started with feeling tired of working at dead end jobs. The trigger was asking myself "How bad could it be if I just tried to learn programming?" This mindset was around 2023 when I was working at a printing company doing graphic mock-ups for clients and reviewing installer plans, among other things. I was good at this but it was very boring and the smell from acrylic being cut by lasers periodically gave me frequent headaches and made me feel nauseous. I had additional stresses going on in my life that made me feel, to put it lightly, not so great. I ended up quitting that job because my performance started to tank, and I knew it. I would be sitting at my desk and trying very hard to hold back my emotions. I quit, and a month later I had an emergency surgery. While laying on the couch post-surgery and unable to basically walk around for a month, I decided my laptop was my new best friend. 💻 ![divider](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/i07u2cvwbvaacaxfnwd9.png) ## The Student I approached programming like an academic - researching schools, bootcamps, salaries, potential wages, life-work balance, and job outlook. Making the conscious decision to learn programming in the post-pandemic landscape was not a venture for money, but of personal curiosity. If I must work, I want to do something I actually like and find interesting. A long, long time ago, in a galaxy far away, I had taken an interest in the programming classes offered at my high school. Of course, back in 2005 with myspace near its peak, I thought I was some king s*** styling my page with HTML and CSS. I wanted to have what all the other cool people had, so I figured out how to do it myself. IT WAS SO COOL 😂
### Unique Experiences Anyways, I got away from all that. I pursued art and nutrition at the university. I was inspired to become a video game creator/3D model artist after taking some not-for-credit classes at the Academy of Art in San Francisco as a teenager. I absolutely loved that experience. I remember the game design teacher, a large man with a ponytail. He commented on my stature since I was in wrestling in high school for a while and had continued to maintain physical fitness in the years the followed. For a large chunk of my teenage and younger adult life, I was very physically fit, and unafraid of humans in general. That same summer, living with my sister, I got to experience san-fran through teenager eyes. I visited amazing restaurants, like "The Stinking Rose" - a garlic based restaurant where I had probably the best roasted garlic I will ever eat in my life. My sister was also into wellness, and she took me to some edgy meditation classes. I'll never forget seeing the people sitting around me, covered in tattoos and piercings, the most metal-head looking people you ever saw, sitting peacefully on cushions on the ground leading a meditation. This group is still around, they are called Dharma Punx. I highly recommend checking them out Dharma Punx. I am far removed but it's on my agenda at some point to visit them again.
### High School Frustrations I think it was probably that same year returning to the high school where I had another interesting experience. There was a girl at the high school that would always, always, ALWAYS make fun of me and she would get her friends on board making fun of me. I was never sure why, I never did anything to her. She didn't like me when I made my move from the nerd table to the goth table after obtaining a boyfriend. Retrospectively she may have been jealous. But I didn't see that. I saw hate, accusations, lies, and repeated embarrassment. She was pretty bad. Everyday, I couldn't sit at that table without getting hated on. Of course I did it for love. A cute boy liked me, I must persevere. What stupidity. After months of this, one day at the lunch table she said something that totally triggered me. I think it had to do with my boyfriend pretending to like me or repeated name calling. Whatever the case, a storm was brewing inside my hormone-fueled teenage body. Something inside of me snapped. I quite literally hunted her down in the hallway. She had no idea I was coming for her. I found her, slammed her to the ground and drew back a fist. I looked her straight in the eye pinning her down with the other hand. I said absolutely nothing. I thought with every cell in my body I was going to knock her out. A tiny voice inside me held my fist back: "She is weak, and she is not actually trying to kill you." Frustrated, I let her go. I think the knowledge of knowing what I could do was enough for me. But as soon as let her go, I picked her up and literally threw her in a garbage can. (She remained physically unharmed.) Everyone was watching at this point. I was generally quiet, and probably shocked a few people. I was suspended for a week. It was awesome. I felt like I had proven a point after years of bullying. I was high on pride and my mom bought me DDR and some of those flexible dance pads, and I played DDR the whole week staying home "suspended". My dad told me he was proud of me after I explained myself. That meant a lot. Those were not words I heard a lot. He is an engineer, and is very intelligent. I never felt the need to do such a thing ever again. ### Trying Things Let me circle back. I tried a few things at the university, with interests in illustration, green engineering, meteorology, graphic design, and nutrition. I changed my major so many times I was lucky I graduated at all. My problem is that I like everything, because everything is interesting. It has been a real problem. Top that with a people pleasing personality for many years and I was basically lost and confused. After I graduated I discovered electronic dance music and got heavy into the festival scene. So much so that I started a vending business called Ever Fluorescent where I would sell my art and clothing at festivals around the nation. This was a main stream of income for a while. It's still alive, but on the back burner at the moment. The unpredictable nature of income generated from festivals makes it extremely difficult for a solo artist to budget life expenses. So, needing structure, I started working regular full time jobs. Starting with that printing factory I mentioned earlier. That's a whole lot of life summarization compacted very small. Now that you know I didn't just randomly arrive here, I can continue. ![divider](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/yzyne4bp5e7xs6uktzis.png) ## Recent Timeline I think a timeline would work here. 📈 - Late 2023 - Started relearning HTML and CSS - Very early 2024 - Explored JavaScript - Spring 2024 - Found and Applied to Full Stack Web Dev Apprenticeship - Summer 2024 - Studied Ruby/Rails - Fall 2024 - Started Apprenticeship - Winter 2024 - Completed Apprenticeship - Early 2025- Completed Google IT Support Cert - Spring 2025 - Worked temporarily as TA at University of Chicago, then got first part-time IT job - Winter 2025 - Received an offer for fulltime work doing IT elsewhere - Early 2026 - Hired full time as building tech for a middle school - Currently - Unemployed ![divider](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/3yf22rlhjc2o2tqnbr1i.png) ## Current Status Through all of these changes I have also been pursuing classes for a second bachelors in computer science. I have even taken a few masters level classes. This would be my second bachelors. I have also been studying CCNA topics on the side. After being let go from my previous job after nearly a year, I have been left feeling defeated despite trying my hardest. I started this tech journey wanting to simply be a web developer. With the current state of things - post pandemic layoffs, AI, fierce competition - I sometimes feel like I waste my time. Frustrated, I try to reframe my thinking. That is part of the reason why I thought studying CCNA topics would be a good idea. This way, I can have a deeper general understanding of things and why they are the way they are. I went so far as to buy multiple books and networking equipment to aid the journey, as I am a fan of tangible items. The news of losing my job that I was trying so hard at has left me in a turbulent emotional state. I did the only thing I know I could do - find a distraction. This time, that distraction is HTB. Why this choice, you may ask. Well, as any developer would likely do, I ran to Google for some counseling. I simply asked it: "Would knowledge of penetration testing help me find a job as a developer?" I'll let you hypothesize what the answer was. As someone who appreciates a good rabbit hole, this is both a blessing and a curse. I cannot say for sure where I am going, but I can tell you that I will get there in an unrelenting manner, persevering in the darkness with no compass, and no flashlight. Yesterday I learned what a .ko file was after asking "What is ELF>?" There is a humongous unexplored world hiding right in front of me. 😮 ![divider](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/pthw4extm3xmud6w9dw7.png)

Small Apache-2.0 Models Against Gemma 4 E2B on One TPU v5e: Which Ones Keep Up?

---
title: "Small Apache-2.0 Models Against Gemma 4 E2B on One TPU v5e: Which Ones Keep Up?"
published: true
description: "Fourteen Apache-2.0 and MIT open-weight models that fit one TPU v5e chip, served one after another through vLLM on the same pinned image and scored on GSM8K and BFCL against Gemma 4 E2B. Qwen3-4B matches Gemma's accuracy at 0.57x its output, SmolLM3-3B and Granite 3.3 2B match it on tool calls, and Gemma keeps the lead on long prompts."
tags: tpu, vllm, gemma, llm
cover_image: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xbill9/model-sweep/main/article/devto-cover.a42e27c5.jpg
---

This article provides a step by step guide to surveying small open-weight models on one Google Cloud TPU v5e chip through vLLM, with Gemma 4 E2B as the baseline. Every model is Apache-2.0 or MIT licensed, so any of them can be repacked and redistributed, and every one is served on the same pinned image with the same settings, then timed and scored by code.

Gemma 4 E2B is small and workable on a v5e-1, but its attention is unusual: two head sizes, 256 for sliding-window layers and 512 for full-attention layers, one KV head, and 20 of its 35 layers reading another layer's KV cache. The question here is which plainer model can stand in for it. Qwen3-4B matches Gemma on both accuracy tests at 0.57x the output. SmolLM3-3B and Granite 3.3 2B match it on tool calls at 0.76x and 0.93x. With long prompts, Gemma stays ahead of every model of comparable accuracy.

https://github.com/xbill9/model-sweep

---

#### Why One v5e Chip?

A `v5litepod-1` is the cheapest TPU Google Cloud rents and is usually available as flex-start capacity in `us-west4-a`. It has 15.75 GiB of HBM, and vLLM gets 0.9 of that, so a bf16 model has to leave room for its KV cache in about 14 GiB.

That rules the field down to roughly 4B parameters. Gemma 4 E2B loads in 8.97 GiB on this chip, which makes it one of the larger models in the lineup.

---

#### At This Point You Should Have…

- A Google Cloud project with the Cloud TPU API enabled and flex-start TPU v5e quota in `us-west4-a`
- A GCS bucket for results, and a Hugging Face token saved in Secret Manager as `hf-token`
- `gcloud` with the alpha components, and Python 3 with no extra packages
- A clone: `git clone https://github.com/xbill9/model-sweep`

---

#### Step 1 — Build the Lineup From the Hub

`survey.py` reads each candidate's license, architecture and weight size from the Hugging Face API and decides whether it fits the chip. A model is in when its license is Apache-2.0 or MIT and at least 2 GiB is left for the KV cache. vLLM on TPU runs some architectures as native JAX models and the rest through a PyTorch fallback, so the survey splits the lineup into two tiers:

```bash
python3 survey.py
```

```text
| `tpu-vllm-v5e1-qwen3_4b` | `Qwen/Qwen3-4B` | apache-2.0 | Qwen3ForCausalLM | 4.02 | 7.49 | 6.68 | JAX | ✅ | 1 |
| `tpu-vllm-v5e1-gemma4_2b` | `google/gemma-4-E2B-it` | apache-2.0 | Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration | 5.12 | 9.54 | 4.63 | JAX | ✅ | 1 |
| `tpu-vllm-v5e1-smollm3_3b` | `HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM3-3B` | apache-2.0 | SmolLM3ForCausalLM | 3.08 | 5.73 | 8.45 | torchax |  | 2 |
| `tpu-vllm-v5e1-qwen25_3b` | `Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct` | other | Qwen2ForCausalLM | 3.09 | 5.75 | 8.43 | JAX |  | excluded: license |
| `tpu-vllm-v5e1-qwen3_8b` | `Qwen/Qwen3-8B` | apache-2.0 | Qwen3ForCausalLM | 8.19 | 15.26 | -1.08 | JAX |  | excluded: memory |

Tier 1: 8 models. Tier 2: 7 models. Excluded: 2.
```

Qwen2.5-3B is out on its license and Qwen3-8B on memory. Everything else goes into two arms files, one per tier.

---

#### Step 2 — Describe Each Model in One Line

An arms file lists one model per line: the checkpoint, its rig name, what to measure, and any serving flags it needs. The tool-call parser and the thinking switch differ by family:

```text
google/gemma-4-E2B-it=gemma4_2b=load+long+gen=parser=gemma4,mm=image+audio+video
Qwen/Qwen3-4B=qwen3_4b=load+long+gen=parser=hermes,nothink
HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM3-3B=smollm3_3b=load+long+gen=parser=hermes,nothink
ibm-granite/granite-3.3-2b-instruct=granite33_2b=load+long+gen=parser=granite
```

`nothink` sends `chat_template_kwargs {"enable_thinking": false}` with every request, so Qwen3 and SmolLM3 answer directly like the others. `mm=` turns off the image, audio and video inputs of multimodal checkpoints. A unit test checks every line against the lineup and against the tool-call parsers registered in the pinned vLLM build.

---

#### Step 3 — Launch One Chip per Tier

`tpu/launch.sh` bundles the committed tree, uploads it, and creates a flex-start queued resource whose startup script serves every arm in turn, uploads results after each one, and deletes the TPU at the end:

```bash
tpu/launch.sh arms-v5e1-tier2.txt --go
```

```text
arms:    tpu/arms-v5e1-tier2.txt (7 arms)
bundle:  gs://aisprint-491218-bucket/model-sweep/inputs/sweep-86d97ba02-0837b648.tgz
results: gs://aisprint-491218-bucket/model-sweep/2026-10-12-v5e1-tier2/
Created queued_resource [ms-2026-10-12-v5e1-tier2-1349].
created ms-2026-10-12-v5e1-tier2-1349; it deletes itself when the last arm finishes, or at 4h
```

Both tiers ran on `vllm/vllm-tpu@sha256:19a1a0526476f902eb83e1057f3d8938f35b457dd7716a30e9ab4f7bee90d507`, vLLM `0.29.1rc1.dev468+g0b7f11a1e`, so the tier 2 models pair with tier 1's Gemma run:

```text
[sweep 2026-10-11T17:14:28Z] start 2026-10-11-v5e1-tier1 on us-west4-a, arms arms-v5e1-tier1.txt
[sweep 2026-10-11T18:24:30Z] DONE: all arms attempted
[sweep 2026-10-12T13:51:26Z] start 2026-10-12-v5e1-tier2 on us-west4-a, arms arms-v5e1-tier2.txt
[sweep 2026-10-12T16:02:12Z] DONE: all arms attempted
```

---

#### Step 4 — Measure Speed and Accuracy the Same Way

Every model is served with `--max-model-len 4096 --max-num-seqs 16` and prefix caching on. Each one gets three measurements:

- **Output speed:** 256 output tokens per request at 1, 4 and 16 requests at once, median of three passes
- **Long prompts:** the same with 1,024- and 3,072-token prompts that never repeat, so the prefix cache cannot help
- **Accuracy:** all 1,319 GSM8K problems, greedy, with a 2,048-token answer limit, and the 400 BFCL simple tool-call records for models with a tool-call parser

Answers are scored in code. Differences against Gemma are paired on the same problems, with a 95% range from 10,000 resamples; a range that includes zero means no measured difference.

---

#### Step 5 — File the Results and Build the Report

```bash
python3 sweep_report.py file 2026-10-12-v5e1-tier2
python3 sweep_report.py report 2026-10-12-v5e1-tier2 --baseline-run 2026-10-11-v5e1-tier1
```

```text
filed smollm3_3b -> tpu-vllm-v5e1-smollm3_3b/benchmarks/runs/2026-10-12-v5e1-tier2
wrote results/2026-10-12-v5e1-tier2/REPORT.md (6 served, 1 failed)
```

`file` moves each model's logs and scored answers into its own directory. `report` refuses to pair two runs that served different image digests.

---

#### How Accurate Is Each Model?

Against Gemma 4 E2B, in percentage points, with the 95% range:

| Model | GSM8K | vs Gemma | BFCL | vs Gemma |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gemma 4 E2B | 0.911 | — | 0.927 | — |
| Qwen3-4B | 0.915 | +0.4 (-1.2 to +2.0) | 0.940 | +1.2 (-1.8 to +4.2) |
| Phi-4-mini | 0.895 | -1.6 (-3.2 to -0.1) | not scored | — |
| SmolLM3-3B | 0.858 | -5.3 (-7.2 to -3.5) | 0.945 | +1.7 (-1.0 to +4.8) |
| Qwen3-1.7B | 0.827 | -8.4 (-10.5 to -6.4) | 0.935 | +0.8 (-2.2 to +3.8) |
| Granite 3.3 2B | 0.817 | -9.5 (-11.6 to -7.4) | 0.920 | -0.7 (-3.8 to +2.2) |
| Qwen2.5-1.5B | 0.729 | -18.2 (-20.6 to -15.8) | 0.910 | -1.7 (-5.2 to +1.8) |
| Qwen3-0.6B | 0.599 | -31.2 (-34.0 to -28.5) | 0.825 | -10.3 (-14.2 to -6.5) |
| Qwen2.5-0.5B | 0.469 | -44.3 (-47.0 to -41.4) | 0.818 | -11.0 (-14.8 to -7.2) |
| SmolLM2-1.7B | 0.461 | -45.0 (-47.8 to -42.2) | no parser | — |

Five models are level with Gemma on BFCL tool calls, down to Qwen2.5-1.5B. Only Qwen3-4B is level on GSM8K, and from 1.7B down, Qwen3-1.7B aside, the score falls by 18 to 45 points.

---

#### How Fast Is Each Model?

Output tokens per second with 16 requests at once, and against Gemma:

| Model | Weights GiB | 16 requests | vs Gemma | 16 × 3,072-token prompts | vs Gemma |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen2.5-0.5B | 0.92 | 4176 | 2.21x | 2596 | 2.48x |
| Qwen3-0.6B | 1.40 | 3210 | 1.70x | 1301 | 1.24x |
| Qwen2.5-1.5B | 2.88 | 2780 | 1.47x | 1570 | 1.50x |
| Qwen3-1.7B | 3.78 | 2049 | 1.09x | 926 | 0.88x |
| Gemma 4 E2B | 8.97 | 1887 | 1.00x | 1049 | 1.00x |
| Granite 3.3 2B | 4.92 | 1761 | 0.93x | 732 | 0.70x |
| SmolLM3-3B | 6.22 | 1440 | 0.76x | 725 | 0.69x |
| Phi-4-mini | 8.31 | 1136 | 0.60x | 404 | 0.39x |
| Qwen3-4B | 7.49 | 1080 | 0.57x | 373 | 0.36x |

Gemma carries the largest weights in the table and still out-serves every model with more than 4 GiB of weights. With 3,072-token prompts the gap widens: Granite and SmolLM3 drop to about 0.7x, and Qwen3-4B to 0.36x.

---

#### Why Does Gemma Hold Up on Long Prompts?

The KV cache. Each model's boot log reports how many tokens of cache fit in the HBM left after its weights:

| Model | KV heads | Head size | Layers | KV cache tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gemma 4 E2B | 1 | 256 / 512 | 35, 20 sharing | 321,280 |
| Granite 3.3 2B | 8 | 64 | 40 | 125,184 |
| SmolLM3-3B | 4 | 128 | 36 | 120,320 |
| Qwen3-1.7B | 8 | 128 | 28 | 100,096 |
| Qwen3-4B | 8 | 128 | 36 | 50,688 |

Gemma stores one KV head per layer, 28 of its 35 layers keep only a 512-token sliding window, and 20 layers reuse an earlier layer's cache. That leaves it 2.6 to 6.3 times the cache of the four models below it, even though its weights are the largest.

The same features that make Gemma awkward to port are the ones paying for its long-prompt speed on this chip.

---

#### 🔎 Tip: Turn Thinking Off Per Request

Qwen3 and SmolLM3 think by default, which spends the GSM8K answer budget on reasoning text. Passing the chat template switch with each request turns it off without a different checkpoint:

```json
{"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}}
```

With it, Qwen3-4B leaves no GSM8K answer at the 2,048-token limit, and SmolLM3-3B leaves 16 of 1,319.

---

#### 🔎 Tip: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B Needs a One-Line Fix on TPU

The MIT-licensed R1 distill stops at load on this image:

```text
FAILED deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (exited) after 75s: AttributeError: 'Qwen2Config' object has no attribute 'text_config'. Did you mean: 'get_text_config'?
```

`tpu_inference/models/jax/qwen2.py` builds an untied `lm_head` with `getattr(hf_config, 'hidden_size', hf_config.text_config.hidden_size)`. Python evaluates the default argument first, so any Qwen2 checkpoint with `tie_word_embeddings: false` fails. The Qwen2.5 Instruct checkpoints tie their embeddings and load.

---

#### Compare and Contrast

| Model | Size | GSM8K | BFCL | 16 requests | Long prompts |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gemma 4 E2B | 5.12B | 0.911 | 0.927 | 1.00x | 1.00x |
| Qwen3-4B | 4.02B | 0.915 | 0.940 | 0.57x | 0.36x |
| SmolLM3-3B | 3.08B | 0.858 | 0.945 | 0.76x | 0.69x |
| Qwen3-1.7B | 2.03B | 0.827 | 0.935 | 1.09x | 0.88x |
| Granite 3.3 2B | 2.53B | 0.817 | 0.920 | 0.93x | 0.70x |

Long prompts are 16 requests of 3,072 tokens; every ratio is against Gemma on the same image.

---

#### So, Which One?

For the best accuracy per chip, Gemma 4 E2B: no other model matches both its scores and its speed on a v5e-1. For accuracy with standard attention, Qwen3-4B, level with Gemma on both tests at a bit over half the output. For tool calling at Gemma's size with the plainest architecture, SmolLM3-3B: level on BFCL, 5.3 points lower on math, three quarters of the speed. For tool calling at close to Gemma's speed, Granite 3.3 2B or Qwen3-1.7B, if math matters less. The models from 1.7B down run faster than Gemma but, apart from Qwen3-1.7B, give up 18 to 45 points of GSM8K.

---

#### Teardown

Each queued resource deletes itself after its last model. Confirm nothing is left:

```bash
gcloud alpha compute tpus queued-resources list --zone us-west4-a
```

---

#### Summary

The goal of this article was to find which small Apache-2.0 or MIT model can stand in for Gemma 4 E2B on one TPU v5e chip. The key to the solution was serving every model on one pinned vLLM image with identical settings, scoring every answer in code, and pairing each model against Gemma on the same problems. The results were:

- 🟢 Qwen3-4B is level with Gemma on GSM8K and BFCL, at 0.57x the output
- 🟢 SmolLM3-3B, Granite 3.3 2B, Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen2.5-1.5B are level with Gemma on BFCL tool calls
- 🟢 Gemma has the largest weights in the lineup and still out-serves every model with more than 4 GiB of weights
- ⚠️ Gemma's shared, single-head, sliding-window KV cache holds 2.6 to 6.3 times the tokens of Granite, SmolLM3, Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B, and keeps its lead with 3,072-token prompts
- ⚠️ Every model under 2B parameters except Qwen3-1.7B scores 18 to 45 points below Gemma on GSM8K
- ❌ DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and OLMo 2 1B do not load on this image

Scope: one TPU v5e chip (`v5litepod-1`) in `us-west4-a`, flex-start, two runs on 2026-10-11 and 2026-10-12 on the same image digest, vLLM `0.29.1rc1.dev468+g0b7f11a1e`. Speed is the median of three passes; accuracy is one greedy pass. Gemma's figures come from the first run and pair with the second through the shared image. OLMo 2 1B fails to compile (it asks for 133.56 MB of the chip's 128 MB vector memory). Ministral 3 3B and Qwen3.5 0.8B and 2B served but are left out of the tables: on this image Ministral returned server errors on part of each test and Qwen3.5 returned unusable text, so their scores describe the serving path. Phi-4-mini produced no parsed tool calls with the `phi4_mini_json` parser and is reported on GSM8K and speed only. Parts of the analysis and writing were done with AI assistance (Claude); every figure comes from the committed report files.

The strategy for surveying small open models against Gemma 4 on a TPU v5e was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

Why you still need a Website Portfolio, even though everyone can Vibe Code it. If you have been following me for a long time, you already know that I have been holding off on my Portfolio review for several months. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/55r34irqjs415ihk0o1e.gif)   **Before you ask, yes, I will finally show my portfolio website.** First, I want to write about something we all may have been thinking about at some point.   **Everyone needs a developer portfolio.** It's one of the big ways to stand out in the tech market because it shows your work and experience to recruiters in a friendly UI format. Some may say it's a great alternative to review a candidate's work **(Source: Trust me bro).** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/7h8pveibft5pc28guc01.png) However, in the age of AI, it seems that it's almost impossible to create a portfolio that stands out. **Why is that the case?**   ## AI Can do...anything? We all (probably) have tried using AI at some point and even still use AI in our daily lives. Whether how much you have used it, you probably already know its capabilities. **AI is trained so well that it can potentially one-shot a website portfolio.** Even better, if the person decides, it can add features and other stuff to make the website look like it was built in months (even though it was built in minutes). We even got to the point where **Claude was able to merge two games into one in a matter of a few weeks!** {% embed https://www.youtube.com/shorts/xo3vpvbA8p8 %} **It's crazy isn't it.** AI development has been rapidly growing in the last few years to the point where it is accomplishing tasks that may have taken months to do. With that said, I thought to myself: **"Why consider building a portfolio if everyone can vibe code their way into making their perfect portfolio?"** To be honest, it's a valid question. The market has been difficult because **everyone is using AI to their advantage to stand out from the market.** I have seen a lot of Website Portfolios and Resumes that have been assisted with AI. **As a result, the bar has never been higher.** However, I still believe having a portfolio still matters, even in this age where it seems impossible. **Here's my reasoning.**   ---   ## AI Portfolios may look different, but they are the same. **What do I mean by this?** I am talking about **"style".** If you try to vibe code a portfolio, people can tell that the portfolio is vibe coded. Sure, it's not the EXACT replica compare to 100 portfolios out there, but you can easily tell by seeing some UI features that are defaulted if you vaguely prompt it. A small example is this: ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/1floz2r2trb7qglvp6l7.png) I have reviewed a lot of portfolios that has this (or something similar). Sure this may be a coincidence, but I want you to try to vibe code a sample website portfolio. Most of the time, they will add this feature. This matters because if you think about it, a lot of portfolios out there are simply the same, **even though it may not look like it.** You have to have good "attention to detail" to see this for sure. However, at this point, coming from a person who has reviewed candidates before, it tends to be **really repetitive.** Hence, making it harder in the hiring process since everyone is doing the same thing and more research needs to be accounted for. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/otitvym1xxhlr917bsuf.png) This leads to the next point.   ## "New Mask, Same Task" ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/iyhst5tknfvs08r0i8wn.png) **Yes, I took this straight up from RDJ.** Though the whole point is that even though he plays a different character, **he is still RDJ.** **What does this mean in this context?** Just because you have pretty portfolio, **it does not mean your work reflects that.** You can create many different portfolios under your name. At the end of the day, **it's still you that needs to improve and not the portfolio.** **Portfolio is used as a presentation.** If you are presenting your portfolio and it looks good, I would assume you have a lot of work experience and projects that are noticeable based on your portfolio design and how you are selling yourself. For example, you have a front-end developer portfolio, **but if I were to investigate further into your GitHub, I may see the following things:** - You just joined as of this year on GitHub. - You claimed you did Open-Source, but there is no PR that reflects that. - Your Portfolio has good UI, your project doesn't. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/hqqedl0o60hmgy3vmbwq.png) I can list a lot of things, but the main point is that if you have a good portfolio with a good list of projects you have done, **you better hope that your projects and work reflects on how you built this portfolio.** This is **ESPECIALLY** true if you tried to become a front-end developer. If your UI is good, you better hope your projects reflects that. It's something to keep in mind when building your portfolio. Of course, if you are applying for a back-end developer role, having a good UI on your website portfolio isn't really required, but it's a nice to have. **The whole point is to not misrepresent yourself. Be careful on what you add on your portfolio. Always assume people will have questions on your work.**     Those are the two main things. Though you may be asking **"How do I make my portfolio stand out"?** **Here are some key things that you can do (and yes, I am now showing my portfolio lol).**   ---   ## 1. Start with a basic portfolio template, then use AI to add onto it. ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/nl747eyej271ayfn2iit.png) For my case, I have used an existing portfolio from **"brittanychiang.com and meikopoulos.com"**. From there, I grab existing features using AI and put them together into a portfolio I am proud of. Additionally, I added some new features that are not distracting, but is something I want to add onto my portfolio to make it unique to me: ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/y6mihaafktq4gfkff5ut.png) **Instead of building it from scratch, I encourage you to find a portfolio that already exists (Bonus points: Proven that it stands out in the tech market) and build it on top of it.** This allows the portfolio to be unique and that **reflects you.** Additionally, building on to of a template is a good starting point because it already has the fundamentals on what makes a portfolio "good". In this case, I added a feature where the "Skills" section reveals Pokemon in each Skill Card, though I am not sharing how it works. **Can you find the Easter egg that does that?** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/vvvd3q57f49bbfmctdxz.png)   ## 2. Usability and Accessibility! ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/kqbmxzxpo3fhlxop36kf.png) **This is the most OVERLOOK aspect of making a portfolio.** Even though you can make your portfolio look nice, it's most likely that it's **not accessible.** **For example, it can be very laggy on low-end devices, not responsive on mobile, not following best practices, etc.** There are a lot of things that is overlooked because we focus on building the best looking portfolio where we should be focusing on making our website portfolio optimized. I would recommend spending time using AI to optimize your portfolio. In other words: **"Boil the lake to make the portfolio, but boil the ocean for website optimization and accessibility".** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/shabozho5fs63ftadpah.png) **For mine, I spend countless prompts where I tell the AI to make sure my portfolio is less "laggy" and being able to run on mobile.** This will allow to make a much cleaner portfolio and being able to be used by many people such as people who have disabilities, devices that are not powerful, etc.   ## 3. Simplicity beats Complexity! ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/3jdxudp8a03vvlni8jvj.png) **A lot of portfolios we have seen tends to be very complex where there are a lot of animations and such.** However, the more you think about it, the more you realized that you can **stand out easily.** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/8pa5pdohs07xc78ycnsv.png) I have seen a lot of portfolios that are REALLY complex and have a lot of animations, but what people fail to realized is that: **You are doing what everyone else is doing.** **At the end of the day, you are not standing out, even if you THINK that you are.** If I see a portfolio that is heavily designed using AI, I can guarantee that I can find the exact same person who can one-up that. **The best advice is making it simple.** Yes, it's boring and yes it's common. But..that's the whole point. I rarely see any portfolio that is simply built. **Usually the ones that are simple tends to stand out because it shows a lot of information really quickly.** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/yprh442j56lfeei9e71u.png) **This is huge because recruiters tends to review portfolios and resumes in seconds.** They will not have time to look over your awesome UI and animation you have Vibe Coded. The UI should be the icing on the cake, not the whole cake. **The most important parts is your work and experience.** Then why design your portfolio? It makes it much easier for people to navigate your work and experience than reading your resume line-by-line of course lol. The point is not spending time making the UI look nice, but **spending more time on making sure they are able to access your work and experience within a small amount of clicks.**   ## 4. Networking (AKA show your portfolio) This is the biggest thing. **SHOW YOUR PORTFOLIO.** ![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/k81pc52mdsl6gld3udrp.gif)
Don't know what your talking about lol
  **What's the point of making a portfolio if no one is going to see it.** You can share it to your family, friends, your LinkedIn connections, and even on DEV! **With that said, here is my portfolio. Give it a review and let me know what you think!** {% embed https://francistrdev.github.io/ %}   ---   **Speaking of, if you have a portfolio that has been sitting around, feel free to share your portfolio in the comments. I would love to see your portfolio and review them!** **That is all! Cya :D**

Building Production-Ready Open-Weights AI Agents with Gemma, Google ADK, and Cloud Run GPUs

---
title: "Building Production-Ready Open-Weights AI Agents with Gemma, Google ADK, and Cloud Run GPUs"
published: true
description: "How I designed, connected, scaled, governed, evaluated, and QLoRA fine-tuned an enterprise SecOps & FinOps agent on Google Cloud."
tags: googlecloud, ai, python, opensource
cover_image: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent/main/assets/article_cover_cloudguard_gemma.jpg
---

![Figure 1: The 4 Architectural Pillars of the Gemma Enterprise Agent Platform on Google Cloud](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent/main/assets/series_architecture_pillars.jpg)
*Figure 1: The four foundational pillars I used to take an open-weights Gemma agent from a local prototype to governed enterprise production on Google Cloud.*

---

Most AI tutorials stop at a basic "Hello World" chatbot running on a laptop. However, when engineering teams try to move **open-weights models like Google’s Gemma 3 (`gemma-3-4b-it`, `gemma-3-12b-it`, `gemma-3-27b-it`)** into real enterprise production, they immediately hit four hard engineering questions:

1. **Grounding:** *How do I connect Gemma to live enterprise data (like Cloud Firestore) so it doesn't hallucinate?*
2. **Serverless GPU Scaling:** *How do I serve Gemma on GPUs (Cloud Run + vLLM + Cloud Storage FUSE) so it scales to zero when idle instead of burning thousands of dollars a month?*
3. **Security & Governance:** *How do I guarantee the agent cannot leak API keys, fall for prompt injections, or accidentally take down a production service?*
4. **Testing & Optimization:** *How do I unit-test an AI agent's tool calls in CI/CD, and how do I fine-tune a small, fast Gemma 4B model with LoRA on Vertex AI so it performs like a 27B model?*

I wrote this article to serve as a complete, end-to-end **Enterprise Reference Blueprint** that answers all four questions using a single, working project (**CloudGuard**) verified in Google Cloud Shell (all working code is available in my [**cloudguard-gemma-agent GitHub repository**](https://github.com/RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent)).

### Where This Blueprint Is Useful in Production

* **DevOps, SRE & Automated Incident Response:** On-call engineers often waste 20–30 minutes during an outage manually querying logs, searching old postmortems, and finding remediation runbooks. CloudGuard automatically pulls live incident telemetry from Cloud Firestore (`get_service_incident`), matches symptoms against historical postmortems in its **Long-Term Memory Bank** (`MEM-2026-014`), and executes approved mitigations in staging (`mitigate_runaway_workload`).
* **Cloud FinOps & GPU Quota Governance:** A single misconfigured ML batch job or unthrottled retry loop can spin up dozens of GPUs overnight. CloudGuard checks real-time regional GPU utilization (`NVIDIA L4` and `RTX PRO 6000`) and monthly budget burn (`check_gpu_quota_and_cost`), immediately scaling down runaway staging workloads and calculating hourly dollar savings (`$36.12/hr`).
* **Regulated Enterprises Requiring Data Sovereignty (Banking, Healthcare, Government, SecOps):** Organizations prohibited from sending internal incident logs, credentials, or infrastructure schemas to external third-party APIs can deploy open-weights Gemma inside their own Google Cloud project behind `--no-allow-unauthenticated` IAM and **Model Armor** guardrails (`cloudguard_agent/guardrails.py`), where accidentally pasted GCP API keys (`AIza...`) are redacted *before* reaching the model.
* **AI Engineering & MLOps CI/CD Pipelines:** Instead of relying on manual "vibe checks" when prompts or tools change, my **ADK Eval** harness (`scripts/run_eval.py`) scores **Tool Trajectory Accuracy (`1.00`)** and **Response Factuality (`1.00`)** on every build, while my **Vertex AI QLoRA** pipeline (`scripts/prepare_and_verify_lora.py`) lets teams replace a 54 GB VRAM model (`Gemma 27B`) with an 8.9 GB VRAM model (`Gemma 4B + LoRA`) running in ~51ms on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU.

Here are the six stages of the production lifecycle I will walk through:

1. **Build:** Scaffolding a model-agnostic **Google ADK** agent in Python that runs against local Gemma weights (via Ollama) during development and seamlessly switches to **Cloud Run GPUs** or **Vertex AI Model Garden** in production.
2. **Connect:** Authoring native Python function-calling tools backed by **Cloud Firestore** to inspect live production incidents and regional GPU FinOps quotas.
3. **Scale:** Deploying **vLLM** on **Cloud Run Serverless GPUs (`NVIDIA L4` / `RTX PRO 6000`)** with **Cloud Storage FUSE** for zero-download weight streaming, paired with **Short-Term Session State** and a **Long-Term Memory Bank**.
4. **Govern:** Enforcing defense-in-depth security with private Cloud Run IAM service accounts, **Model Armor** secret redaction (`before_model_callback`), and deterministic RBAC tool policies (`before_tool_callback`).
5. **Optimize:** Automating CI/CD release gates with **ADK Eval** (`tool_trajectory_avg_score` and `response_match_score`) and **OpenTelemetry** tracing for **Google Cloud Trace**.
6. **Specialize:** Fine-tuning a compact **`google/gemma-3-4b-it`** model using **QLoRA on Vertex AI** so it matches **`gemma-3-27b-it`** tool-calling accuracy (`1.00`) at **2.8x faster latency and 6x lower GPU memory**.

![Figure 2: CloudGuard End-to-End Request Flow Architecture](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent/main/assets/end_to_end_request_flow.jpg)
*Figure 2: End-to-end request lifecycle for my CloudGuard Incident & FinOps Agent across Cloud Run, vLLM, Cloud Firestore, Model Armor guardrails, and Cloud Trace.*

---

## Part 1: Platform Foundations & Scaffolding the First Gemma Agent

### Prerequisites & Google Cloud Setup

To follow along with my setup, you will need:

* A **Google Cloud Project** with billing enabled.
* The **Google Cloud SDK (`gcloud`)** installed and authenticated.
* **Python 3.10+** and **[`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)** (the fast Python package and virtual environment manager I use across this project).
* **Ollama** installed locally (`ollama pull gemma3:4b` or `ollama pull gemma3:27b`) for zero-cost local prototyping before deploying to Google Cloud GPUs.

First, I set my project and region environment variables and enabled the required Google Cloud APIs:

```bash
export PROJECT_ID="your-gcp-project-id"
export REGION="us-central1"

gcloud config set project $PROJECT_ID
gcloud config set compute/region $REGION

gcloud services enable \
  aiplatform.googleapis.com \
  run.googleapis.com \
  artifactregistry.googleapis.com \
  firestore.googleapis.com \
  cloudtrace.googleapis.com \
  iam.googleapis.com
```

Next, I configured Application Default Credentials (ADC) so my local Python environment can authenticate with Google Cloud services:

```bash
gcloud auth application-default login
```

### Scaffolding the Project (Local or 1-Click in Google Cloud Shell)

You can either clone and run this project directly inside **Google Cloud Shell** (which comes pre-authenticated with `gcloud` and Python in your browser) by clicking [**Open in Google Cloud Shell**](https://shell.cloud.google.com/?cloudshell_git_repo=https://github.com/RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent), or initialize the workspace locally with `uv`:

![Cloning the CloudGuard Gemma Agent repository directly into Google Cloud Shell](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent/main/assets/open_in_cloud_shell.png)
*Step 1: Launching the [`RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent`](https://github.com/RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent) repository directly inside Google Cloud Shell.*

![Authorizing Google Cloud Shell to access Google Cloud API credentials](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent/main/assets/cloud_shell_authorize.png)
*Step 2: Authorizing Google Cloud Shell credentials while the repository clones into the Cloud Shell workspace.*

![Running the CloudGuard setup and verification commands inside Google Cloud Shell Editor](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent/main/assets/cloud_shell_terminal_clone.png)
*Step 3: Executing the CloudGuard environment setup, database seeding, and ADK evaluation commands inside the Google Cloud Shell terminal.*

```bash
mkdir cloudguard-gemma-agent && cd cloudguard-gemma-agent
uv init
```

I structured the repository so that agent orchestration, native tools, memory management, security guardrails, and evaluation suites are cleanly separated (and runnable offline via a deterministic local simulation harness before touching cloud GPUs):

```text
cloudguard-gemma-agent/
├── pyproject.toml
├── .env.example
├── cloudguard_agent/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── agent.py          # Core ADK LlmAgent & Gemma LiteLLM configuration
│   ├── tools.py          # Native Python tools backed by Cloud Firestore
│   ├── memory.py         # Short-Term Session & Long-Term Memory Bank
│   ├── guardrails.py     # Model Armor & RBAC policy callbacks
│   └── finetuning.py     # Vertex AI QLoRA dataset & job spec builder
├── deploy/
│   ├── Dockerfile.vllm
│   ├── Dockerfile.vllm.lora
│   └── deploy_cloud_run_gpu.sh
├── scripts/
│   ├── seed_firestore.py
│   ├── simulate_parts.py
│   ├── run_eval.py
│   └── prepare_and_verify_lora.py
└── tests/
    └── eval_dataset.json
```

![Repository structure of cloudguard-gemma-agent on GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent/main/assets/github_repo_structure.png)
*Repository structure of [`RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent`](https://github.com/RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent) showing the modular separation across agent orchestration, Firestore tools, memory, guardrails, deployment manifests, and evaluation scripts.*

In `pyproject.toml`, I declared `google-adk`, `litellm`, `google-cloud-firestore`, and `opentelemetry-sdk`:

```toml
[project]
name = "cloudguard-gemma-agent"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Enterprise SecOps & FinOps Triage Agent powered by Open-Weights Gemma & Google ADK on Cloud Run GPUs"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = [
    "google-adk>=1.0.0",
    "google-genai>=1.0.0",
    "google-cloud-firestore>=2.19.0",
    "litellm>=1.60.0",
    "pydantic>=2.10.0",
    "python-dotenv>=1.0.1",
    "opentelemetry-api>=1.29.0",
    "opentelemetry-sdk>=1.29.0",
]
```

Then I locked and installed the dependencies:

```bash
uv sync
```

### Decoupling Local vs. Cloud GPU Inference (`.env.example`)

One of the strongest architectural benefits of **Google ADK** is its model-agnostic `LiteLlm` integration. By defining a `.env` configuration file, I can point my agent to a local Ollama server on `localhost:11434` during development and switch to a self-hosted **vLLM** endpoint on **Cloud Run GPUs** (or **Vertex AI Model Garden**) in production without changing a single line of agent orchestration code:

```ini
# Google Cloud Project Settings
GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT="cloudguard-enterprise-demo"
GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION="us-central1"

# Gemma Inference Backend Mode: "local_ollama" | "cloud_run_vllm"
GEMMA_BACKEND_MODE="local_ollama"

# Local Prototyping via Ollama
OLLAMA_API_BASE="http://localhost:11434"
GEMMA_MODEL_NAME="ollama_chat/gemma3:27b"

# Production Cloud Run GPU vLLM Endpoint
GEMMA_VLLM_ENDPOINT_URL="https://gemma-vllm-service-xyz-uc.a.run.app/v1"
GEMMA_VLLM_MODEL_ID="google/gemma-3-27b-it"

# Firestore Configuration
FIRESTORE_DATABASE="(default)"
USE_LOCAL_MOCK_DB="true"
```

### Defining the CloudGuard Agent Persona (`cloudguard_agent/agent.py`)

When building agents with open-weights models like Gemma, **explicit, numbered system instructions** are essential. Here is how I defined the agent's identity, tool bindings, and strict operational constraints in `cloudguard_agent/agent.py`:

```python
import os
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent
from google.adk.models.lite_llm import LiteLlm
from .tools import (
    check_gpu_quota_and_cost,
    get_service_incident,
    list_active_alerts,
    mitigate_runaway_workload,
)

CLOUDGUARD_SYSTEM_INSTRUCTION = """You are CloudGuard, an Enterprise SecOps & FinOps Incident Response Agent running on Google Cloud and powered by open-weights Gemma.

Your primary responsibilities:
1. Incident Triage: Retrieve real-time operational and FinOps telemetry using `get_service_incident` and `list_active_alerts`.
2. GPU FinOps & Capacity: Verify regional NVIDIA L4 and RTX PRO 6000 GPU availability and monthly budget burn using `check_gpu_quota_and_cost`.
3. Safe Remediation: When authorized, mitigate runaway staging workloads using `mitigate_runaway_workload`.
4. Enterprise Governance Compliance:
   - NEVER execute automated scaling or termination in `production` without explicit `sre-incident-commander` escalation.
   - Always cite the exact Incident ID, affected service name, hourly USD burn rate, and recommended runbook ID in your response.
"""

def build_adk_root_agent() -> LlmAgent:
    backend_mode = os.getenv("GEMMA_BACKEND_MODE", "local_ollama")
    if backend_mode == "cloud_run_vllm":
        model_id = f"openai/{os.getenv('GEMMA_VLLM_MODEL_ID', 'google/gemma-3-27b-it')}"
        api_base = os.getenv("GEMMA_VLLM_ENDPOINT_URL")
    else:
        model_id = os.getenv("GEMMA_MODEL_NAME", "ollama_chat/gemma3:27b")
        api_base = os.getenv("OLLAMA_API_BASE", "http://localhost:11434")

    gemma_model = LiteLlm(model=model_id, api_base=api_base)

    return LlmAgent(
        name="cloudguard_gemma_agent",
        model=gemma_model,
        description="Enterprise SecOps and FinOps incident triage agent powered by Gemma.",
        instruction=CLOUDGUARD_SYSTEM_INSTRUCTION,
        tools=[
            get_service_incident,
            list_active_alerts,
            check_gpu_quota_and_cost,
            mitigate_runaway_workload,
        ],
    )

root_agent = build_adk_root_agent()
```

---

## Part 2: Native Python Tools & Connecting to Cloud Firestore

![Figure 3: Part 2 — ADK Native Function Calling & Cloud Firestore Integration](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent/main/assets/part2_native_tools_firestore.jpg)
*Figure 3: How Google ADK introspects my Python type hints and docstrings to drive structured Gemma tool calls against Cloud Firestore.*

An isolated LLM knows nothing about active Cloud Run services, internal SRE runbooks, or current monthly GPU FinOps burn rates. To bridge that gap, **Google ADK** automatically converts standard Python functions into JSON Schema tool definitions for Gemma.

> **My Engineering Rule for Open-Weights Gemma:** Compact open-weights models (`Gemma 4B`, `12B`, `27B`) rely heavily on explicit `Args:` descriptions and concrete format examples (such as `'INC-YYYY-NNNN'`) in Python docstrings to construct valid JSON tool arguments. I treat Python docstrings as first-class prompt engineering.

### Implementing the Operational Tools (`cloudguard_agent/tools.py`)

I built four native Python tools backed by **Cloud Firestore** (plus a zero-config local JSON schema mirror (`USE_LOCAL_MOCK_DB="true"`) so the entire test suite can be verified locally before provisioning cloud resources):

* `get_service_incident(incident_id: str)`: Retrieves severity, symptom, GPU type, hourly USD burn rate, and remediation runbook for a specific incident ticket.
* `list_active_alerts(environment: str = "all")`: Lists open incidents filtered by `production`, `staging`, or `all`.
* `check_gpu_quota_and_cost(region: str)`: Checks regional NVIDIA L4 and RTX PRO 6000 quota limits, active usage, and monthly FinOps budget percentage.
* `mitigate_runaway_workload(...)`: Scales down a runaway Cloud Run service or batch job and records the hourly cost savings.

```python
def get_service_incident(incident_id: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Retrieves full operational and FinOps telemetry for a specific incident ID.

    Use this tool whenever a user asks about a specific incident ticket (e.g.,
    'INC-2026-0891' or 'INC-2026-0904'), its symptoms, severity, or recommended runbook.

    Args:
        incident_id: The unique incident identifier formatted as 'INC-YYYY-NNNN'.

    Returns:
        A dictionary containing the incident status, severity, affected service,
        GPU usage, hourly burn rate, and recommended remediation runbook.
    """
    use_mock = os.getenv("USE_LOCAL_MOCK_DB", "true").lower() == "true"
    normalized_id = incident_id.strip().upper()

    if not use_mock:
        from google.cloud import firestore

        db = firestore.Client(project=os.getenv("GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT"))
        doc = db.collection("incidents").document(normalized_id).get()
        if not doc.exists:
            return {"status": "error", "message": f"Incident {normalized_id} not found in Firestore."}
        return {"status": "success", "incident": doc.to_dict()}

    db_data = _load_db()
    incident = db_data.get("incidents", {}).get(normalized_id)
    if not incident:
        return {
            "status": "error",
            "message": f"Incident '{normalized_id}' not found. Valid IDs: {list(db_data.get('incidents', {}).keys())}",
        }
    return {"status": "success", "incident": incident}


def check_gpu_quota_and_cost(region: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Checks current Cloud Run GPU quota utilization and monthly FinOps spend for a GCP region.

    Use this tool when evaluating whether a region has available NVIDIA L4 or
    RTX PRO 6000 GPUs or when checking monthly budget consumption.

    Args:
        region: The Google Cloud region identifier (e.g., 'us-central1', 'europe-west4').

    Returns:
        A dictionary with GPU quota limits, active usage, and budget utilization metrics.
    """
    db_data = _load_db()
    clean_region = region.strip().lower()
    quota_info = db_data.get("quotas", {}).get(clean_region)
    if not quota_info:
        return {
            "status": "error",
            "message": f"No quota telemetry found for region '{clean_region}'. Supported: us-central1, europe-west4.",
        }

    l4_free = quota_info["nvidia_l4_limit"] - quota_info["nvidia_l4_in_use"]
    budget_pct = round(
        (quota_info["current_month_spend_usd"] / quota_info["monthly_budget_usd"]) * 100, 1
    )
    return {
        "status": "success",
        "region": clean_region,
        "available_nvidia_l4_gpus": l4_free,
        "budget_utilization_percent": budget_pct,
        "details": quota_info,
    }
```

Moving an open-weights Gemma model from a developer laptop into enterprise production on Google Cloud offers two primary deployment patterns: **[Cloud Run Serverless GPUs](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/services/gpu) with vLLM** (for scale-to-zero serverless containers) or **[Vertex AI Model Garden](https://cloud.google.com/model-garden)** (for one-call managed GPU endpoints).

### Option A: Serverless GPU Serving on Cloud Run with vLLM & Cloud Storage FUSE

Instead of baking multi-gigabyte model weights into a container image — or downloading them from Hugging Face on every cold start — I stage the Gemma weights in a regional **[Google Cloud Storage (GCS)](https://cloud.google.com/storage)** bucket and mount that bucket at `/mnt/models` using **[Cloud Storage FUSE](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/services/cloud-storage-volume-mounts)**.

> **VRAM Sizing Note on Google Cloud Run GPUs:** A single **NVIDIA L4 GPU** on Cloud Run provides **24 GB of VRAM**, which easily fits `google/gemma-3-4b-it` (~8.4 GB in `bfloat16`), `google/gemma-3-12b-it`, or a 4-bit AWQ quantized `google/gemma-3-27b-it`. To run unquantized `bfloat16` `google/gemma-3-27b-it` (~54 GB VRAM) on a single serverless instance, use `--gpu-type=nvidia-rtx-pro-6000` on Cloud Run or deploy on [Vertex AI Model Garden](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/open-models/use-gemma).

Here is my `deploy/Dockerfile.vllm` configuration:

```dockerfile

ENV HF_HOME=/mnt/models \
    VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn \
    PORT=8080

ENV MODEL_PATH="/mnt/models/gemma-3-27b-it"

EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["python3", "-m", "vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server"]
CMD ["--model", "/mnt/models/gemma-3-27b-it", \
     "--served-model-name", "google/gemma-3-27b-it", \
     "--host", "0.0.0.0", \
     "--port", "8080", \
     "--dtype", "bfloat16", \
     "--max-model-len", "8192", \
     "--gpu-memory-utilization", "0.92", \
     "--enable-auto-tool-choice", \
     "--tool-call-parser", "pythonic"]
```

### Dual-Tier Memory: Short-Term Session State vs. Long-Term Memory Bank

In `cloudguard_agent/memory.py`, I equipped the agent with two distinct memory layers:

1. **Short-Term Conversational Session (`AgentSessionState`):** Tracks the active incident ID (`active_incident_id`) within the current troubleshooting thread. When an engineer inspects `INC-2026-0891` in Turn 2 and says *"Go ahead and mitigate that runaway staging workload"* in Turn 4, the agent resolves the reference automatically.
2. **Long-Term Organizational Memory (`EnterpriseMemoryBank`):** Stores verified postmortem learnings across all sessions. When `INC-2026-0891` triggers on `ml-batch-indexer-dev`, the agent automatically searches historical postmortems and retrieves `MEM-2026-014`.

## Part 4: Enterprise Governance, IAM Isolation & Model Armor Guardrails

![Figure 5: Part 4 — Defense-in-Depth Security with IAM, Model Armor & RBAC Callbacks](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RobinaMirbahar/cloudguard-gemma-agent/main/assets/part4_zero_trust_governance.jpg)
*Figure 5: Three sequential security gates I implemented to protect the CloudGuard agent: Cloud Run IAM isolation, Before-Model secret redaction & injection blocking, and Before-Tool RBAC enforcement.*

Giving an AI agent write-access to infrastructure requires deterministic security boundaries. Telling an LLM *"Never scale down production"* inside a system prompt is a probabilistic guideline — not an enterprise security control.

I implemented defense-in-depth across three sequential gates:

* **Gate 1 — Zero-Trust Cloud Run IAM Isolation:** The `gemma-vllm-service` is configured with `--no-allow-unauthenticated`. Only the ADK orchestrator's service account (`cloudguard-agent-sa`) holds `roles/run.invoker` permission.
* **Gate 2 — Before-Model Input Sanitization (`inspect_and_sanitize_prompt`):** Modeled on **Google Cloud Model Armor**, this interceptor scans every incoming prompt for adversarial jailbreak signatures and automatically redacts live credentials (such as `AIza...` GCP API keys or `ya29...` bearer tokens) *before* they reach the Gemma model or telemetry logs.
* **Gate 3 — Before-Tool Deterministic RBAC (`validate_tool_invocation`):** Intercepts every `mitigate_runaway_workload` call before Python executes it, blocking any `production` mutation unless the caller holds `sre-incident-commander` privileges (`POL-PROD-MUTATION-001`).

### Guardrail Implementation (`cloudguard_agent/guardrails.py`)

```python
SENSITIVE_PATTERNS: list[tuple[str, re.Pattern[str]]] = [
    ("GCP_API_KEY", re.compile(r"AIza[0-9A-Za-z\-_]{35}")),
    ("BEARER_TOKEN", re.compile(r"ya29\.[0-9A-Za-z\-_]+")),
    ("PRIVATE_KEY_HEADER", re.compile(r"-----BEGIN (?:RSA )?PRIVATE KEY-----")),
]

PROMPT_INJECTION_SIGNATURES: list[str] = [
    "ignore all previous instructions",
    "bypass governance policy",
    "override system prompt",
]

def validate_tool_invocation(
    tool_name: str,
    tool_args: dict[str, Any],
    caller_role: str = "sre-tier1-operator",
) -> tuple[bool, dict[str, Any] | None, dict[str, Any]]:
    """Enforces deterministic policy checks before any ADK tool executes."""
    if tool_name == "mitigate_runaway_workload":
        target_env = str(tool_args.get("target_environment", "")).lower()
        action = str(tool_args.get("action", "")).lower()

        if target_env == "production" and caller_role != "sre-incident-commander":
            block_payload = {
                "status": "blocked_by_governance_policy",
                "policy_id": "POL-PROD-MUTATION-001",
                "reason": (
                    f"Automated '{action}' on environment='production' is prohibited for role "
                    f"'{caller_role}'. Escalate to an 'sre-incident-commander' or execute "
                    "manual runbook verification first."
                ),
            }
            entry = audit_log.record(
                event_type="BEFORE_TOOL_GUARDRAIL",
                decision="DENIED",
                details={
                    "tool_name": tool_name,
                    "environment": target_env,
                    "caller_role": caller_role,
                    "policy_id": "POL-PROD-MUTATION-001",
                },
            )
            return False, block_payload, entry

    entry = audit_log.record(
        event_type="BEFORE_TOOL_GUARDRAIL",
        decision="ALLOWED",
        details={"tool_name": tool_name, "caller_role": caller_role},
    )
    return True, None, entry
```
