Your AI Agent Just Got a Passport: Agent Identity on Google Cloud and the Redeploy Trap Nobody Talks About

## Why your agents need their own identity

Most teams run every AI agent under one shared service account. That works until an agent does something it should not, and the audit log only says "the service account did it." You cannot tell which agent acted, and you cannot cut off one agent without breaking the rest.

Google Cloud now has a fix for this called Agent Identity, part of the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (the new name for Vertex AI). Each agent gets its own verifiable identity, so you can grant, deny and audit access per agent, just like you do for people.

In this post I walk through how it works, how to deploy an ADK agent with it, and one production trap I think every SRE should know about before they wire this into a CI/CD pipeline: **every redeploy gives your agent a brand new identity, and its old permissions do not follow it.**

## What Agent Identity actually is

Think of it as a passport for each agent. When you deploy an agent to Agent Runtime with this feature turned on, Google Cloud gives it a unique identity based on the open SPIFFE standard, plus an X.509 certificate that Google creates and manages for you.

In IAM, that identity shows up as a principal you can bind roles to:

```plaintext
principal://agents.global.org-ORGANIZATION_ID.system.id.goog/resources/aiplatform/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/reasoningEngines/AGENT_ENGINE_ID
```

A few details worth knowing:

- The trust domain is created for you when you enable the Agent Platform API. With an organization it lives at the org level (`agents.global.org-...`). Without one it lives at the project level (`agents.global.proj-...`).
- The identity is tied to the agent's resource ID, not to the framework you built it with. ADK, LangGraph and others all work the same way.
- Out of the box the agent gets two default roles, `roles/aiplatform.agentContextEditor` and `roles/aiplatform.agentDefaultAccess`, so it can reach its own logs, metrics, model access, sessions and memory.
- The part I like most as an SRE: tokens are locked to the runtime by a Google-managed Context-Aware Access policy using mTLS certificate binding. If someone steals the token and tries to use it from outside the agent's runtime, it fails with a 401. Stolen credentials cannot be replayed.

One gotcha: in IAM bindings you must use the `principal://` format, not the raw `spiffe://` string. Using the SPIFFE string returns an INVALID_ARGUMENT error.

## Hands-on: deploy an ADK agent with its own identity

You have three ways to turn it on. Pick the one that fits how you work.

**Option 1: Python SDK.** Define a normal ADK agent, wrap it, and pass `identity_type` when you deploy:

```python
from google.adk.agents import Agent
import agentplatform
from agentplatform import types
from agentplatform.frameworks import AdkApp

agent = Agent(
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",
    name="minimal_agent",
    instruction="You are a helpful assistant.",
)

client = agentplatform.Client(
    project=PROJECT_ID,
    location=LOCATION,
    http_options=dict(api_version="v1beta1"),
)

remote_app = client.runtimes.create(
    agent=AdkApp(agent=agent),
    config={
        "display_name": "running-agent-with-identity",
        "identity_type": types.IdentityType.AGENT_IDENTITY,
        "requirements": ["google-cloud-agentplatform[adk,runtimes]"],
        "staging_bucket": f"gs://{BUCKET_NAME}",
    },
)

print(remote_app.api_resource.spec.effective_identity)
```

Note the `v1beta1` API version. Agent Identity needs it.

**Option 2: `adk deploy`.** Drop a small config file in your agent folder before deploying:

```bash
echo '{ "identity_type": "AGENT_IDENTITY" }' > .agent_engine_config.json
```

**Option 3: Agents CLI.** Good for quick tests and prototypes:

```bash
agents-cli deploy --agent-identity
```

A tip I recommend: you can create the Agent Runtime instance with only `identity_type` and no code. That gives you the identity first, so you can set up IAM before the agent ever runs. Then add the code later with `client.runtimes.update(...)`.

If you skip the identity flag, the agent keeps using service accounts as before, so existing pipelines do not break.

## Least privilege in two layers

The pattern that works best is to split permissions into a shared floor and a narrow ceiling.

**Layer 1: a baseline for every agent in the project.** Use a `principalSet` so one binding covers all agents, now and in the future. Put only boring, low-risk roles here:

```bash
AGENTS="principalSet://agents.global.org-ORGANIZATION_ID.system.id.goog/attribute.platformContainer/aiplatform/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER"

for ROLE in roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageConsumer roles/browser \
            roles/aiplatform.expressUser roles/logging.logWriter \
            roles/monitoring.metricWriter; do
  gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID \
    --member="$AGENTS" --role="$ROLE"
done
```

**Layer 2: narrow grants per agent.** Anything sensitive, like a BigQuery dataset or a Cloud Storage bucket with customer data, goes to one specific agent's `principal://` only:

```bash
gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://orders-data \
  --member="principal://agents.global.org-ORGANIZATION_ID.system.id.goog/resources/aiplatform/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/us-central1/reasoningEngines/AGENT_ENGINE_ID" \
  --role="roles/storage.objectViewer"
```

**Multi-agent bonus (A2A).** If a parent agent calls a subagent registered in Agent Registry, the *parent agent's identity* needs two roles: `roles/agentregistry.viewer` to look the subagent up, and `roles/aiplatform.user` on the subagent's reasoning engine to call it. Grant these to the parent agent, not to your own user account. This is an easy mistake that shows up as confusing permission errors.

## The redeploy trap nobody talks about

This is the part that will bite SRE and platform teams. **Every time a pipeline deletes and recreates an agent, the agent gets a new `reasoningEngines` ID, which means a brand new principal.** Permissions granted to the old principal do not carry over.

Picture a normal day:

1. Your agent runs fine with read access to `gs://orders-data`.
2. A blue-green deploy, an ephemeral test environment or a `terraform apply` with a replace recreates the agent.
3. The new agent starts, passes its health check, and then quietly gets 403 errors the first time it touches the bucket.

No deploy failure, no alert, just an agent that suddenly "can't find" data. That is a silent outage.

It gets worse in the other direction. Deleting an agent does **not** remove the IAM bindings that point to it. Those dead bindings stay in your policies until someone cleans them up by hand. Over time that is policy clutter and an audit headache.

### How to fix it

**Fix 1: grant access as a post-deploy step.** Read the new identity right after deploy and bind roles to it:

```bash
IDENTITY=$(gcloud ai reasoning-engines describe RESOURCE_ID \
  --project=PROJECT_ID --location=LOCATION \
  --format="value(spec.effectiveIdentity)")

gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://orders-data \
  --member="principal://${IDENTITY}" \
  --role="roles/storage.objectViewer"
```

**Fix 2: let Terraform build the principal for you.** Derive it from the deployed resource so bindings are always recreated with the agent:

```hcl
resource "google_vertex_ai_reasoning_engine" "agent" {
  provider     = google-beta
  project      = var.project_id
  region       = var.region
  display_name = "orders-agent"

  spec {
    agent_framework = "google-adk"
    identity_type   = "AGENT_IDENTITY"
    # source_code_spec and deployment_spec here
  }
}

locals {
  agent_id        = element(split("/", google_vertex_ai_reasoning_engine.agent.id), -1)
  agent_principal = "principal://agents.global.org-${data.google_organization.org.org_id}.system.id.goog/resources/aiplatform/projects/${data.google_project.project.number}/locations/${var.region}/reasoningEngines/${local.agent_id}"
}

resource "google_storage_bucket_iam_member" "orders_reader" {
  bucket = "orders-data"
  role   = "roles/storage.objectViewer"
  member = local.agent_principal
}
```

Because the binding depends on the agent resource, Terraform replaces both together, and destroying the agent removes its binding too. That also solves the orphaned binding problem.

**Fix 3: lean on the baseline layer.** Project-level `principalSet` bindings survive delete and recreate, so the agent still has quota, logging and model access right after a redeploy. Keep per-agent bindings only for sensitive data.

**Fix 4: add a smoke test.** After deploy, have the pipeline send one real request that touches each protected resource. A 403 here fails the pipeline instead of failing in front of users.

## Guardrails: what agents must never do

Allow policies say what an agent can do. For agents that act on their own, you also want hard limits that no allow policy can override. Agent Identity works with two IAM tools for this.

**IAM deny policies.** Block specific permissions for all agent identities across the org, no matter what roles someone grants later. Good candidates are destructive actions like deleting buckets or creating IAM roles. The official docs include a ready deny policy example you can adapt (link in Sources).

**Principal Access Boundary (PAB).** This limits *where* an agent can operate at all. For example, you can say agents in your org may only touch resources inside one folder. Even if someone accidentally grants an agent a role on a production project outside that folder, PAB blocks it.

My rule of thumb: allow policies are for daily work, deny policies are for "never, ever", and PAB is the fence around the whole yard. Agent Identity also plugs into VPC Service Controls if you need a network-level perimeter on top.

## Audit: finally knowing which agent did what

With Cloud Logging turned on, every access shows the agent's own identity instead of a shared service account. Two cases matter:

- When the agent acts on its own, the log shows only the agent's identity.
- When the agent acts on behalf of a user, the log shows both the agent and the user.

That second case is a big deal for compliance reviews. You can answer "which agent read this data, and for whom?" without guessing.

To see all your agents and their identities in one place, open the Agent Platform **Deployments** page in the console and look at the **Identity** column, or read `spec.effectiveIdentity` from the API.

## Limitations and caveats

Be honest with your team about these before you roll it out:

- It needs the `v1beta1` API version, so treat it as a moving target and check the docs before each upgrade.
- Agent identities cannot be granted the legacy Cloud Storage bucket roles (`legacyBucketReader`, `legacyBucketWriter`, `legacyBucketOwner`). If your buckets still depend on those, plan a cleanup.
- The redeploy trap above is by design, not a bug. Your pipeline has to handle it.
- Deleted agents leave orphaned IAM bindings unless your tooling removes them.
- You can turn off the Context-Aware Access token binding for special token-sharing cases, but Google strongly discourages it because it reopens the door to credential theft. I would not.
- Identity controls *what an agent can reach*, not *what it decides to do*. A prompt injection can still trick an agent into misusing access it legitimately has. Pair this with content safety controls like Model Armor and keep a human in the loop for risky actions.

## Wrap-up: a production checklist

Agent Identity turns agents into first-class citizens in IAM. The feature is easy to turn on. The real work is in the pipeline around it. Here is the checklist I would use:

- [ ] Deploy every agent with `identity_type = AGENT_IDENTITY`
- [ ] Put low-risk shared roles on a project `principalSet`
- [ ] Grant sensitive data access per agent only
- [ ] Rebind per-agent roles automatically after every redeploy (Terraform or a post-deploy step)
- [ ] Clean up IAM bindings when an agent is deleted
- [ ] Add a post-deploy smoke test that touches each protected resource
- [ ] Add deny policies for destructive permissions
- [ ] Fence agents in with Principal Access Boundary
- [ ] Turn on Cloud Logging so every action is traceable to one agent

If you are running agents in production on Google Cloud, I would love to hear how you are handling identity today. Shared service accounts, or something better?

### Sources

- [Use Agent Identity with Agent Runtime](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/scale/runtime/agent-identity) (Google Cloud docs)
- [Agent Identity overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/agent-identity-overview) (IAM docs)
- [Agent Registry: identity and identifiers](https://docs.cloud.google.com/agent-registry/identity-and-identifiers)
- [Introducing Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/introducing-gemini-enterprise-agent-platform) (Google Cloud blog)

published: true
description: "Descubre cómo diseñar una interfaz TUI en Go con marcos Unicode (┌─┐ / ╔═╗), auto-descubrimiento de clusters Oracle RAC y flujos de mantenimiento guiados por flechas sin depender de Oracle Instant Client."
tags: go, oracle, linux, database
---

Son las 3:15 AM de una guardia de producción. Te conectas por SSH a un nodo de **Oracle RAC** en Oracle Linux porque ha saltado una alerta crítica. En cuestión de segundos tienes que:

1. Comprobar si los demonios del cluster (`CRS`, `CSSD`, `EVMD`, `ASM`) están `ONLINE` en todos los nodos (`crsctl check cluster -all` y `crsctl status resource -t`).
2. Cambiar del usuario `grid` al usuario `oracle` para abrir `sqlplus / as sysdba`.
3. Averiguar qué sesión está bloqueando una tabla crítica en `gv$session` (`enq: TX - row lock contention`) o qué tablespace acaba de lanzar un `ORA-01654` porque llegó al 93% sin `AUTOEXTEND`.
4. Si toca mantenimiento de sistema operativo en un nodo, reubicar todos los servicios RAC (`srvctl relocate service`), parar la instancia local y detener la pila CRS sin provocar ni un segundo de caída en las aplicaciones.

Después de repetir este ritual cientos de veces, decidí construir **`ora-tui`**: una herramienta interactiva de terminal (**TUI**) escrita en **Go**, empaquetada como un único binario estático (`CGO_ENABLED=0`) e instalable vía `dnf install ora-tui`.

En este artículo te cuento cómo funciona por dentro, cómo resolví los retos de arquitectura en servidores Oracle y cómo puedes probar su modo simulador (`--mock`) en tu propio portátil.

---

## 🖥️ El Diseño: Marcos Unicode (`┌─┐` y `╔═╗`) y Navegación con Flechas

Uno de los objetivos principales era que la herramienta se sintiera rápida y clara sobre cualquier sesión SSH, utilizando una jerarquía visual de **marcos Unicode**:

* **Borde Simple (`┌ ─ ┐ │ └ ┘`)** para los paneles secundarios y tablas de datos.
* **Borde Doble (`╔ ═ ╗ ║ ╚ ╝`)** para la cabecera principal, el panel que tiene el foco activo, las **ventanas emergentes de mantenimiento** y los diálogos de confirmación.
* **Barras de progreso por bloques (`[█████████░] 93.0%`)** coloreadas según criticidad (verde $<80\%$, amarillo $80\text{–}90\%$, rojo $>90\%$).

---

## ⚙️ Decisiones Clave de Arquitectura

### 1. ¿Por qué `CGO_ENABLED=0` y cero librerías de cliente C?
La mayoría de los drivers de Oracle requieren `CGO` y enlazar dinámicamente contra `libclntsh.so` (Oracle Instant Client). En entornos empresariales con RHEL / Oracle Linux 7, 8 y 9 y distintas versiones de `glibc`, distribuir binarios con dependencias dinámicas es una fuente constante de problemas.

En `ora-tui`, el binario se compila 100% estático (`CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64`) y se comunica directamente con las herramientas nativas que ya residen en `$ORACLE_HOME/bin` y `$GRID_HOME/bin` (`sqlplus -s / as sysdba`, `srvctl`, `crsctl`, `olsnodes`, `lsnrctl`, `rman`, `adrci`).

### 2. Auto-Descubrimiento sin Archivos de Configuración
Nada más ejecutarse, `ora-tui` descubre qué tipo de instalación Oracle tiene delante sin pedir un solo archivo `.yaml` o `.env`:

1. **Topología del Servidor:**
   Lee `/etc/oracle/ocr.loc` y `/etc/oracle/olr.loc`:
   * `local_only=false` $\rightarrow$ **ORACLE RAC**
   * `local_only=true` $\rightarrow$ **ORACLE RESTART (Standalone Grid)**
   * No existe $\rightarrow$ **SINGLE INSTANCE**
2. **Homes e Instancias Vivas en `/proc`:**
   Además de leer `/etc/oratab` e `inventory.xml`, escanea `/proc/[0-9]*/cmdline` para localizar procesos `ora_pmon_<SID>`, `db_pmon_<SID>` (Oracle 21c/23ai) y `asm_pmon_+ASM*`. Así detecta bases de datos levantadas aunque nadie las haya registrado en `/etc/oratab`.

```go
func ExtractSIDFromPMON(cmdline string) (sid string, isASM bool) {
	fields := strings.Fields(cmdline)
	if len(fields) == 0 {
		return "", false
	}
	proc := filepath.Base(fields[0])
	switch {
	case strings.HasPrefix(proc, "ora_pmon_"):
		return strings.TrimPrefix(proc, "ora_pmon_"), false
	case strings.HasPrefix(proc, "db_pmon_"):
		return strings.TrimPrefix(proc, "db_pmon_"), false
	case strings.HasPrefix(proc, "asm_pmon_"):
		return strings.TrimPrefix(proc, "asm_pmon_"), true
	}
	return "", false
}
```

### 3. Cambio Dinámico de Usuario UNIX (`root` $\rightarrow$ `oracle` / `grid`)
En un cluster RAC con separación de roles, `grid` es dueño de `$GRID_HOME` y `oracle` es dueño de `$ORACLE_HOME`. Ejecutar `sqlplus` o `srvctl` como `root` falla o ensucia permisos.

`ora-tui` lee el `uid` y `gid` propietarios de cada directorio con `os.Stat` y lanza cada subproceso con las credenciales exactas de ese usuario mediante `syscall.Credential`, reservando `root` **únicamente** para `crsctl start/stop crs`:

```go
if !asRoot && targetOwner != nil && targetOwner.UID != 0 && currentUID == 0 {
	cmd.SysProcAttr = &syscall.SysProcAttr{
		Credential: &syscall.Credential{
			Uid: targetOwner.UID,
			Gid: targetOwner.GID,
		},
	}
}
```

### 4. Marcos Simples (`┌─┐`) y Dobles (`╔═╗`) en `tview`
La librería [`rivo/tview`](https://github.com/rivo/tview) permite definir globalmente los runas de dibujo de cajas, distinguiendo entre ventanas normales y ventanas con foco activo. Configurando `tview.Borders`, conseguimos que cualquier tabla o menú emergente resalte automáticamente con borde doble cuando el usuario lo selecciona con las flechas:

```go
// Borde simple (┌ ─ ┐ │ └ ┘) para contenedores y tablas estándar
tview.Borders.Horizontal = '─'
tview.Borders.Vertical = '│'
tview.Borders.TopLeft = '┌'
tview.Borders.TopRight = '┐'
tview.Borders.BottomLeft = '└'
tview.Borders.BottomRight = '┘'

// Borde doble (╔ ═ ╗ ║ ╚ ╝) para la ventana con foco y modales emergentes
tview.Borders.HorizontalFocus = '═'
tview.Borders.VerticalFocus = '║'
tview.Borders.TopLeftFocus = '╔'
tview.Borders.TopRightFocus = '╗'
tview.Borders.BottomLeftFocus = '╚'
tview.Borders.BottomRightFocus = '╝'
```

Además, pulsando la tecla **`b`** en cualquier momento, puedes alternar en caliente entre el modo mixto (`┌─┐` + `╔═╗`), todo borde doble (`╔═╗`), todo borde simple (`┌─┐`) o ASCII clásico de 7 bits (`+ - = |`) si entras desde una consola serie antigua.

---

## 🛠️ Los 8 Módulos de Diagnóstico y Mantenimiento Guiado

En lugar de memorizar comandos, te mueves con las **flechas del teclado (`↑`/`↓`)** por las 8 vistas y pulsas **`Enter`** sobre cualquier fila para abrir su menú contextual de mantenimiento:

1. **Cluster & DB Estado:** Salud de demonios (`CRS`, `CSSD`, `EVMD`, `ASM`), VIPs, instancias, PDBs y **Drenado Seguro de Nodo (Graceful Node Drain)** en 4 pasos:
   * *Paso 1:* Pre-chequeo de nodos failover `ONLINE`.
   * *Paso 2:* Reubicación en caliente de servicios (`srvctl relocate service`).
   * *Paso 3:* Parada limpia de la instancia local (`srvctl stop instance -stopoption IMMEDIATE`).
   * *Paso 4:* Parada opcional de la pila de clusterware (`crsctl stop crs`).
2. **Usuarios Conectados (`gv$session`):** Detección instantánea de bloqueos `TX/TM`, `SQL_ID`, evento de espera y texto SQL actual, con opción para ejecutar `KILL SESSION IMMEDIATE` o `DISCONNECT SESSION POST_TRANSACTION`.
3. **Tablespaces & Datafiles:** Barras visuales de llenado y asistente para añadir datafiles en ASM (`+DATA`), activar `AUTOEXTEND ON` o hacer `COALESCE`.
4. **Tablas, Segmentos & Objetos Inválidos:** Identificación de tablas con estadísticas `STALE` o alta fragmentación para lanzar `DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS`, `SHRINK SPACE CASCADE`, `REBUILD ONLINE` de índices o recompilar objetos inválidos con `UTL_RECOMP`.
5. **ASM & Red Listeners:** Monitorización de diskgroups (`v$asm_diskgroup`) y control de listeners locales y SCAN (`lsnrctl start/stop/reload`).
6. **RMAN, Flashback & Data Guard:** Estado de backups RMAN, creación de *Guaranteed Restore Points (GRP)* antes de un cambio crítico y verificación de lag en réplicas *Data Guard Standby*.
7. **Alert Log & Errores `ORA-`:** Lectura directa sobre `v$diag_alert_ext` con salto automático al módulo que resuelve el error y purgado de trazas con `adrci`.
8. **Centro de Mantenimiento:** Catálogo guiado de operaciones DBA con confirmación de seguridad y consola de auditoría en tiempo real.

---

## 🚀 Pruébalo en 30 Segundos (Modo Simulación `--mock`)

No necesitas tener un cluster Oracle RAC instalado en tu máquina para probar la interfaz. `ora-tui` incluye un modo simulador (`--mock`) con datos realistas de un cluster RAC en producción (incluyendo sesiones bloqueadas, un tablespace al 93% y alertas `ORA-01654`):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/mario/ora-tui.git
cd ora-tui

# Compilar y lanzar el simulador interactivo en modo Oracle RAC:
make mock

# O ver la captura estática directamente en tu terminal:
make preview
```

¿Qué otra tarea repetitiva de administración Oracle te gustaría automatizar desde un menú de consola? ¡Te leo en los comentarios!

For Agents, Waiting is the Hardest Part

Many engineers rightfully view every step in a financial workflow as a potential point of failure, because services go down and networks go offline. Yet there's often an even bigger danger lurking at the spaces in between those steps, because waiting is often where problems accumulate. As the application waits for account verification or settlements, it might restart when a new version is deployed, or its container may crash, or the hardware it's running on might fail. The longer the process runs, the more likely that these or other problems will occur.

AI agents introduce another source of delay: people. Some approvals may arrive in seconds, while others may take hours or days. The agent must track the current state, and to keep the business moving, may escalate if a deadline passes, choose an authorized alternative, or cancel the operation by compensating for previously completed steps.

How can a system wait reliably for as long as required and act immediately when a deadline expires? How can it recover from software or hardware failures without losing known progress or needlessly repeating model calls? How can engineers see what the agent is doing right now? How can the compliance team see what it did last week?

Durable Execution is the foundation that makes all of this possible. A Durable Execution platform, such as Temporal (MIT-licensed open source), records an application's progress and detailed results of every important step. If the application is interrupted, it uses that information to automatically recover the complete application state and then continue from where it left off. Model and tool results become part of that recorded progress, allowing the agent to resume without repeating completed work or wasting tokens unnecessarily. Durable timers allow the agent to wait reliably for any duration, whether seconds or months. The application can also await a specified condition, optionally with a defined time limit, and take action when it receives a message from an external system. These applications are written using normal code, in a standard language such as Python or TypeScript, and can run on standard infrastructure.

If you'd like to find out more about how Durable Execution can help you build reliable agents, stop by the Temporal booth in the Expo Hall for a whiteboarding session with technical staff.

A Data Company in an AI World

**Anekha Sokhal** spent nearly a decade trading energy derivatives at JP Morgan, then came to the US on a Fulbright to study data science at Rice University. Today she's the founder and CEO of Moshi, a Houston-based, VC-backed real-time quant platform for institutional finance. Ahead of her talk at AIE New York, we talked about why she calls Moshi a data company, what it's like to build in Houston, and the growing gap between how easy it is to build with AI and how hard it is to run what you've built.

## Moshi, Anekha, and building in Houston

**Tell me about Moshi.**

> Moshi is a real-time quant for institutional finance. We provide real-time analytics for financial traders. Every time you open Moshi, you're going to learn something new because of the volume and quality of data that we watch.
>
> A fun fact about Moshi: it takes a human four seconds to read a sentence. In that same amount of time, Moshi has learned 300 new things. We watch more than 2.5 billion data points, and we grow our internal database every minute.
>
> The value we add is that you're going to learn something new about your market every time you look at Moshi, and you're going to be so much more efficient. The problem traders have is that they're trying to keep up with everything, and everything is changing constantly. When you're a financial investor or trader, what you knew this morning is no longer true by lunchtime. The news is changing, Twitter is changing, Instagram is changing. People are flooded with data. And the problem with that is: What is true? What is relevant to me? What can I trust? That's where we come in. We are that one-source platform.
>
> Typically, you would hire a team of analysts to do that for you. I used to be a trader at JP Morgan, and I could never even hire an intern, so I was doing all of this myself. So I built the platform I wish I had when I was trading. Because I'm also a data scientist, a lot of machine learning and statistics has gone into it. We've built all of our own models.

**And tell me about yourself.**

> I'm Anekha, the founder and CEO of Moshi. I've grown Moshi myself. We're a VC-backed startup based in Houston, and the reason we're based in Houston is that I used to be a trader at JP Morgan. I was there for nearly a decade, trading energy derivatives.
>
> I really just love data. I'm obsessed with data. I got a Fulbright scholarship (England has one Fulbright scholarship for data analytics) and came to Rice University to do my master's in data science. I got really into machine learning there and was published at conferences like ICLR.
>
> When I was interviewing for jobs, a bunch of hedge funds reached out, and they all had this same problem of data synthesis. Instead of building it for one hedge fund and doing very similar work to what I did before my master's, I thought: I'm in the US. There's a huge venture industry. It's such an entrepreneurial country. That's why I came to the US. I really wanted to be part of that ecosystem.
>
> I did an accelerator program while I was at university, then happened to meet a venture capital fund that loved the idea of building Moshi for everyone. And that's where we are today. My story is very intertwined with the company's story.

**That sounds like a wild ride. What is it like to build in Houston?**

> The straightforward answer is that you get to be a big fish in a small pond. But I do feel like you have to keep your connections with other cities alive.
>
> We're backed by one of the biggest venture capital funds in Texas. If someone is coming to Houston and wants to know which AI companies or finance companies are there, we're top of mind for everyone, which is great.
>
> However, we can't ignore that, at least in our situation, AI and finance have other cities that are very important. San Francisco is one. New York is one. London is huge in finance, and so is Singapore. Houston is a very good city, especially for energy. I used to be an energy trader, and a lot of energy clients are here, so it's great in that way. But you also need to be connected to the other cities, because the hype is happening there too. San Francisco for the venture environment and the people. Austin has a great ecosystem. London has a fantastic finance community. And New York, I feel like, is coming up a little more in startups now, and it's obviously huge in finance.
>
> So what is it like building here? There's a fantastic community. Some of the nicest people I've ever met in my life are here, so many helpful people. You can really make a difference here. But there aren't always going to be as many events, and it's not as easy to meet people because it's a very spread-out city. You don't have those shoulder-to-shoulder conversations you'd have in a walking city.

## A data company in an AI world

**So, what is your personal relationship to AI?**

> For my undergrad, which was a very long time ago now, I studied MORS (mathematics, operational research, statistics and economics) at the University of Warwick, and it was not a sexy degree. If I told anyone I was studying MORS at Warwick, they were just like, "Oh my God."
>
> Because I loved statistics and data, I went on to trading. It was a very natural transition. Trading is just data and machine learning. And when I was doing it, no one cared. No one thought what I was doing was interesting or sexy.
>
> I remember once meeting a family friend with my best friend, who was studying law. I'd gotten my internship at JP Morgan at the time. The family friend asked me, "What about you? Do you want to be a tutor or a teacher?" Then I looked at my friend and said, "Wow, you're incredible. You're going to be a lawyer."
>
> It's so different now. I graduated in 2014, and now if you say "machine learning" to people, you're blowing their minds.
>
> So my connection is that I was in it before it was cool to be in it. Now we have this separation between machine learning and generative AI. I call Moshi a data company because I love data. We have data scientists. I'm obsessed with data. One thing we do that's very different from most companies is that we do so much data engineering and machine learning, and then generative AI sits on top of all of that. So my relationship is: I want to understand the data, and generative AI is how we communicate it to people in a more human way.

**The bar for calling a company an AI company has gotten way higher. It's not a differentiator anymore.**

> I finished work super late last night, and to decompress I went on Instagram, because it's the most mindless scrolling. Embarrassingly, I was on it for 40 minutes, until I got the timer notification. This was at 1 a.m. In that time, I got 25 ads for AI.
>
> I screenshotted every single one and sent them to Rick, my head of growth, and said, "Rick, we cannot advertise on Instagram." Twenty-five companies in 40 minutes calling themselves AI, AI for finance. It's so easy to generate. How can I trust them? I think that says everything about what it's like to build today.

**I'll never forget driving in from the San Francisco airport earlier this year. There was nothing but AI billboards.**

> There was a time when our investor told us we needed a .ai domain. I don't really believe in all of that, but we got the .ai domain, and now I don't even call us an AI company. I say we're providing a solution, and part of it does have generative AI, as you'd expect. That's an expectation now. If you have an LLM, it's not cool. It's the expectation.

**It's the same in media relations. Five years ago AI was unique. Now the best way to get a company coverage is to not talk about its AI.**

> It's definitely different. Before Moshi, while I was at university, I tried to start another company, which I closed down, called Jewel Vision. My parents are in the jewelry business, and I wanted to give people the ability to try on jewelry in 3D without even needing models.
>
> It was too early. The technology didn't exist. It was 3D computer vision. To this day, I have recruiters asking, "Can you come to Apple's recruiting events? Can you come to Tesla's?" because it's not a skill people have. I tried to build a company doing it for a year.
>
> That was super cool AI. That is pure 3D computer vision. But if you have an LLM agent, to me, that is not AI. There's a difference.

## Prompt fatigue and where humans come in

**Where are you seeing prompt fatigue show up?**

> I want to explore how our work is changing and where humans actually play a part. One thing I've found is that people are now just copy-pasting Claude output to each other. So where does that stop?
>
> If I think about the whole workflow of where we are today: people want solutions that make them more efficient, make them better decision makers and integrate their workflows, and they're using generative tools to do that. The questions that come up a lot for us are: How can I trust the output? How can I connect everything? And what about the data? Where are you getting the data from?
>
> The biggest thing we've realized is that the foundational companies are making it feel like it's so easy to build. And it is easy to build. You can get a $200 subscription to any of them and build a dashboard for yourself, and it will be fantastic. I do it for my wedding planning. I have my little dashboard. Now try to make that production-ready. Try to make it run for more than one person. If I want to send that dashboard to my mom, who doesn't have a Claude account, that's the problem I want to talk about.

**What happens when you try to take that into an enterprise?**

> When you try to implement that in an enterprise, you actually need to run the system. And when you need to run the system, you need DevOps, you need error handling, you need to pay other people to run it. That's the bit no LLM is going to tell you upfront.
>
> So yes, you can spend weeks building a dashboard on Claude. Now try to make that dashboard available to the public. Now you need DDoS protection when you host it on a website. Now you have to make sure your API keys are hidden and not in the code. You have to make sure you're not showing your code on the website. You have to get a database. You can't just host it locally. Those are the things that end up wasting people's time.
>
> Instead of managing it yourself, giving that job to a human, or even doing it the old-fashioned way, you've built it yourself on Claude. But now you have to run it. So you're dealing with prompt management, because every time you want to make a change, you wanted to change one thing and you've gone and changed 50 other things. That's what I wanted to talk about: the prompt fatigue, and the realization that I can build really easily, but I cannot run a system as easily.

**So where do people come into all of that?**

> I think companies are still figuring that out. CEOs and CTOs are constantly posting about how, oh, let's fire everyone, because now we only need two or three people to do that job. And I'm sure you've seen the AWS outages and all these other outages. This never used to happen.
>
> What we're seeing now is a confidence everyone has been given by these AI tools: I can build anything I want. But the thing people are forgetting is that every single person has access to the same tool. Now you're going to tell me, "But I've got a different skills.md file, or a different Claude connector, or a different MCP." Yes, I agree, those are different. But you are still pulling and pushing the same data. It's still the same model. If my engineer asks Claude a question, they're going to get the exact same answer, even if the prompt changes a little.
>
> So where do humans come into this? It's the judgment piece. Claude can't build Moshi. Why? Because I had to take 10 years of derivatives trading, and I'm a data scientist as well, so I knew how to build the system. I had people sitting with me when I was 19 or 20 years old at JP Morgan, spending three hours explaining systems to me. I took all of that, and that's what I'm bringing to my agents. A lot of people are not doing that.
>
> I think one thing we're going to come across is that things are going to break more easily, because of the trust people have in these systems. One tool says, give it all your bank details, your credit card details and your email details, and it will go and run everything for you. We don't do any of that internally, and we have engineers from Microsoft and Meta. No one on our team does that. You can ask them to, and they won't. It's similar to the CEOs of all these tech companies who won't let their kids use social media.
>
> I think there's going to be a sort of awakening. We have big enterprise clients who come to us and say, "Why do I need you? I've got an Anthropic subscription." And I say, try to run that same thing for more than one person. You're going to have security issues. You're not going to want to manage it. You're supposed to be trading and watching the markets. You're not supposed to be telling Claude that FOMC is today, not tomorrow.
>
> There's going to be friction for a while. It's like a purge. People will do all the AI, and then they're going to realize: actually, I want to see a spreadsheet that I have to use my brain to check. I want to remember someone's phone number. I want to see a PDF that isn't perfect. I think you just have to let it happen.
>
> The interesting thing for us is that enterprise software is changing. We have clients sending us their prompts. We had a client today who said, "Hey, can you just run this for us?" And I said, that's not what we do. And they said, "Yeah, but I don't want to run it anymore. You guys do a better job. You do all the trust, you do all the things." People are interacting with us like that now.

**Did you do it?**

> We had to build that, because we didn't know we needed to before.
>
> For us, having been a trader for so long, the human brain is so much more advanced than machine learning. The number of connections we can make in real time, the power of the human brain: there is no data analytics that powerful. We're trying to get closer and closer to that human way of thinking, but machines are not there yet. So why would you want a machine to make such important decisions?
>
> Claude is an incredible tool, but it's incredible at summarizing what you tell it to do and explaining the prompt. What it's not great at is making those second- and third-order connections, which is what humans are great at. It's seeing around the corner, being able to say, "This is what I think I should do," or "This is what I don't see." Those gut feelings, those human interactions.

**Can you give an example?**

> A simple one is hiring. So many times LinkedIn will ask, "Do you want us to AI-interview this person?" And I'm like, no. I want to interview this person.
>
> When I was hiring a couple of weeks ago, I ran a simple experiment. I ran every résumé through Claude, because I wanted to see who Claude would hire versus who I would hire. It was so different. Claude came up with a scoring system and said: based on these people's answers, how they use AI and everything else, these are the numbers one, two and three you should hire. I thought, okay, that's really interesting.
>
> Then I brought everyone to the office. One thing I do is spend three to four hours with each person, because I want to see how you think. Each candidate met me, our team members and our investor. Every person agreed on the ranking, and it was not the same as Claude's. The person Claude ranked first wasn't even in our top five.
>
> There's a company that raised a ridiculous amount of money, something like $30 million, and they're a one-person company. Their whole thing is, "We are a one-person company." On social media they're doing incredibly. But you look at the reviews, and every single person says, "I just want to speak to a human. There's 99% I can do myself, but for this 1%, I just want to speak to someone." You can't replace that.
>
> That's what we're trying not to do at Moshi. We give you the data and the information. We do all the data engineering you wouldn't know how to do, because most people are not trained data scientists, data engineers and quants. But ultimately, you have to decide what trade you want to put on and how you want to manage it. We can give you the conviction and the data. That's what we're selling: you are going to be so much more confident in your trades, because you have blind spots. Why do you have blind spots? Because we watch way more data than is humanly possible. We'll tell you the connections, but ultimately you're the one who's going to put on the trade and sleep with that risk.
>
> I think it's a really interesting time. Social media makes people see things a certain way, but the reality is that AI needs to be a tool for certain things, not a tool to replace everything.

**So much of this resonates with me. I can't tell you how many times I've gone to a brainstorm or a workshop and people have shown up with the same ideas, because they all used the same system. It's like everyone shopped at the same stores and showed up in the same gray top and jeans.**

> It really is. And one funny thing about what you just said, everyone coming up with the same thing: we gave about 20 people a hiring assessment, and we told them to use whatever AI tools they wanted. We asked them to come up with a list of 10 target people we should speak to. Real people at real companies, from LinkedIn.
>
> Bear in mind we interviewed people across the US, and LinkedIn has hundreds of millions of people. Can you believe that 90% came up with the same 10 companies?
>
> I'm not putting anyone down, but we were hiring salespeople and a head of growth. If you're doing outreach to clients, think about that. Yes, I agree AI can help you. But think about what your difference is.

**There's an idea I keep coming back to: the iPhone moment that Major League Hacking (MLH) CEO Swift has written about. Suddenly everyone thought they could be a photographer, but you still wouldn't let someone with an iPhone shoot your wedding, you know?**

> There's a lot we can do with AI, and there's a lot we don't have to do with it. It's simple: if I can get Claude to do something, then I will get Claude to do it. I'll get Claude to do the 90%. But that 10% is exactly where you don't want Claude.
>
> You don't want AI there, because at the end of the day, if something goes wrong, you want to go talk to someone. You want to be able to say, "Hey, let's figure this out." You don't want to just talk to your chat model.

Building Better Agents through End-to-End Evals

## Deeply understand the task at hand

The biggest mistake teams make with agents is automating a process they don’t understand. Before writing one line of code, you should be able to describe exactly how a human does the job.

To build Ramp Stack, we wanted to automate bookkeeping tasks. Before thinking about code, we thought about the jobs to be done. There are four primary categories of work: reconciliation, data entry, variance analysis, and schedules and accruals. Categories keep the eval balanced across the real job and later show you where the agent is weak.

Next, we break each task into its steps. Take an accounts payable reconciliation: an accountant pulls unpaid bills and the AP ledger, lines them up in a spreadsheet, and investigates anything that doesn’t match. If the bills total $3,500 and the ledger shows $3,000, the job is to find the missing $500 bill and record the correction. Each step is something the agent must do and something your eval must check.

## Data is the bottleneck

An end-to-end eval has the same shape at every stage: business data populates a database, the agent works with that state through tools, and you grade what it produces. Before launch, you have no data to work with, so you must simulate it.

Our answer was synthetic businesses, which we call worlds. One is a DTC home goods brand selling through Shopify, Amazon, and wholesale, with a full set of books, realistic transactions, and messy Excel files. The mess matters; too often, teams build data that is too clean. This means things look good offline, but do not survive once confronted with real users.

## Anatomy of an eval

Each eval case combines four parts:

- **Task:** the request, such as “Reconcile our AP payables and bills for Q4 2025.”
- **World:** the synthetic ERP and business data the agent can access.
- **Trajectory:** the steps the agent takes, like reading bills, matching payments, and investigating differences.
- **Score:** a rubric of accountant-written criteria, graded by an LLM judge on the final output.

The rubric is what makes the eval useful. Pass/fail hides partial progress; six criteria such as “Q4 AP balance correct” and “duplicates flagged” tell you the agent scored 4 of 6 and exactly which two it missed. Have domain experts write the criteria, since they know what a reviewer would actually reject.

## Using the eval to make changes

An eval earns its keep when it changes decisions. The first decision was model choice, but the biggest alpha is tuning your harness: optimizing skills, tools, and infrastructure to produce good results at low cost and latency. Several popular ideas didn’t hold up:

- **Auto-tuned skills (GEPA-style autoresearch):** training gains didn’t generalize. We have yet to see good evidence that automated prompt optimization works.
- **High reasoning effort:** same accuracy, higher cost.

What did work was treating the agent like an ML model and its context like features:

- **Skill ablation:** we benchmarked one skill at a time against a no-skill baseline, then trimmed eight skills to four, gaining 2.8 points of mean score across six worlds. Several skills actively hurt, and none was best everywhere.
- **Skill compression:** cutting our largest skill, a spreadsheet skill, by 61% left quality essentially unchanged and saved about $30k a month.

The pattern: measure every change against a fixed baseline, across many worlds, and keep only what moves the score.

## Test what others skip: memory

Memory is rarely evaluated because it requires time to pass. We built roll-forward worlds: the same business, advanced one month. The agent completes this month’s close, writes down what it learned, and is graded on next month’s tasks.

The rule we learned: remember how the business works, but use fresh numbers. Memory distilled from prior trajectories, with period-specific amounts removed, improved mean score by 5.7 points over skills alone. A memory that captured a reusable workflow took one task from 0% to 100%. One that smuggled in last month’s specific recipe dropped another from 75% to 25%.

## The takeaway

Agent development needs the same discipline as ML development. Understand the process, build a dataset hard enough to be meaningful and stable enough to compare runs, and let it, not intuition, decide what ships.
