Frontier AI models outperform human experts on earnings prediction for the first time

*Does the progress in frontier AI capabilities lead to superhuman performance in finance?*

Finance is arguably the largest and hardest area of knowledge work. Accurate predictions of the global financial market drive trillions of dollars of value, and take the best experts many years to hone, and even then imperfectly.

A couple of months back, we created a research effort at Samaya to study AI’s predictive capabilities in finance. Making accurate financial predictions requires access to a large set of high quality, real-time financial information — finance’s “open-world” equivalent of a codebase. We built a finance-specific prediction harness and environment to give AI models comprehensive, point-in-time financial information at parity with human experts so that we could push their capabilities to the limit.

Our results show that we have reached a critical inflection point. **For the first time, we see that the latest frontier AI models working with Samaya’s finance harness outperform human experts in financial prediction.** Specifically, we find that the latest AI models outperform expert analysts in predicting earnings surprises.

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/5ylajvu0dxd00952o43i.jpg)

**Figure 1. Recent AI models are able to predict earnings better than human experts.** The plot shows prediction error of company revenue as reported in earnings compared to (i) raw analyst consensus (the unadjusted human baseline) and (ii) bias-corrected consensus (a stronger baseline) across 456 Q2 earnings releases. We observe a clear trend of prediction error decreasing with more capable models, and the most recent models outperforming even the strong, bias-corrected consensus baseline. Errors are adjusted for each company’s surprise volatility (σ).

## Earnings predictions and surprises

Global stock markets are worth more than **$150 trillion** and are the most closely watched asset class in the world, for professionals and individual investors alike. More than ten thousand public companies make up the investable universe across global markets, and most of them report earnings results every quarter, sharing metrics such as **revenue**, **gross margin**, **operating income** and **adjusted EPS**, also referred to as *actuals*. These metrics are the foundation for investment decisions into these companies and so an enormous amount of analyst time is spent on modelling, predicting and publishing these metrics ahead of earnings. The average of these predictions is called the **consensus estimate**.


![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/8802aydx09jrugpjd01e.jpg)

**Figure 2.** How an earnings surprise forms. Analysts forecast the next quarter, their average forecast is the consensus, and the gap between the reported actual and the consensus is the surprise the market reacts to.

Consensus estimates form a market baseline for the expectation of a company’s performance. When the company reports, the actual is either a “beat” (above consensus) or a “miss” (below consensus) with the gap being the **earnings surprise**. Because predicting earnings is extremely challenging, and even the best consensus estimates miss, the market can react strongly to earnings surprises. So consensus estimates provide a **strong “feasible” expert baseline** to evaluate AI’s ability to predict earnings and earnings surprises.

## Building the environment and harness

Besides being a very important task for investing, earnings prediction is also a great task for AI. Not only do we have ground-truth actuals and a consensus human baseline, we also have surprise drivers revealed by the company management which can help us understand if the models’ reasoning process was correct. The earnings prediction task advances financial reasoning: it tests the ability to understand company fundamentals, do deep search and retrieval on competitors, supply chain and macro factors, identify key drivers, make the right assumptions and account for them appropriately.

### 1. Task environment

In the earnings prediction task, we run the models under Samaya’s harness and make predictions one week before earnings. Through our harness, we provide access to all financial sources available until that point in time. We ask the models to predict four headline metrics: revenue, gross margin, operating income and adjusted EPS. These metrics track the flow of money through the income statement and capture essential aspects important for financial analysis (described in Appendix B). We call each such prediction task, predicting all four metrics for one company ahead of one earnings release, an **instance**.


![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/n0o90d8dr6xfub2c6ll7.jpg)

**Figure 3.** The prediction setting: five trading sessions before earnings, the agent under Samaya’s harness researches the quarter using only information published up to that day and makes predictions for the headline metrics. Nothing after the cutoff is visible; the predictions are scored once the company reports.

To compare the AI models, we calculate three performance metrics (precise definitions in Appendix C):

- **Prediction error** measures how far the predicted numbers are from the actuals.
- **Surprise correlation** measures if the surprise (i.e. actual − consensus) is correlated with the predicted surprise (prediction − consensus). This is an overall metric that measures the ability of models to predict big beats and misses correctly.
- **Hit rate** measures if the prediction and actual are on the same side of consensus.

**Normalizing for volatility:** Because some companies’ financials vary more than others, we normalize by each company’s historical surprise volatility to make the predictions comparable across companies.

**Building a harder expert baseline:** We found the consensus baseline relatively easy for AI models to outperform. This is because analysts systematically lower their estimates ahead of earnings,<sup>1</sup> so actuals beat the consensus more often than not. We wanted to measure the ability of AI models beyond simple corrections like this, so we created a harder bias-corrected consensus baseline by adding each company’s historical median surprise.

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/ei5b04zpmp4mvgemdquv.jpg)

### 2. Samaya’s prediction harness

To evaluate models on this task, we needed to be able to run multiple experiments by rewinding time and restricting access to future information. To build Samaya’s prediction harness, we started with our production harness and modified it for this environment.

1. **Production harness.** To begin with, Samaya’s production harness provides context-efficient financial retrieval over unstructured and structured data sources used for real-world investment decision-making.
2. **Point-in-time gate.** Then, we introduce a point-in-time gate enforced at the harness layer. This gate is enforced programmatically with an authentication token that prevents any possible hacking or cheating by the model.
3. **Time-aware retrieval and data tools.** We modify our retrieval stack to respect the time-based cutoff, and we re-create some of our structured data tools to support this gate as well.
4. **Substituted web access.** We remove web access because it is very difficult to apply a point-in-time gate to it. Instead, we add essential news sources behind the gate, which are a reasonable proxy for web access for this task.
5. **Expert guidance.** Finally, we modified our harness to increase context efficiency and added expert-guided instructions to improve predictive reasoning.

In our experiments, we tested seven frontier models: GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.8 Flash and Kimi K3. We chose companies that reported from July 14th onward (after the knowledge cutoff for all models) with more than $5 billion in market cap and more than 8 brokers providing estimates, leading to 456 companies that cover all sectors.

## AI outperforms consensus in predicting earnings surprises

Our main results show that frontier AI models using Samaya’s harness are able to outperform consensus. Even older, smaller models such as Sonnet 5 and Kimi K3 outperform raw consensus, but only the most recent models (Fable 5.1; Opus 5.5; GPT-6 Astra) are able to outperform the harder, bias-corrected consensus baseline — highlighting a key inflection point in AI capabilities. We find GPT-6 Astra to be the highest performing model across the most metrics (prediction error for revenue (Figure 1), overall prediction error, hit rate), but we see some variation in model performance (Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 best performing on surprise correlation).


![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/4pjgeuazb2sjbr4w9o4v.jpg)

**Figure 4. Surprise correlation for AI models is increasing with more capable models**, with the latest models significantly outperforming the bias-corrected consensus. The figure shows how well each model’s predicted surprises line up with the actual surprises (Spearman ρ, across revenue, gross margin, operating income and adjusted EPS), compared to the bias-corrected consensus scored the same way. † significantly better than the bias-corrected consensus (one-sided paired company-cluster bootstrap, p<0.05).


![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/8guakizmbr81nmixeqmz.jpg)
**Figure 5. Earnings prediction error for AI models is decreasing with more capable models**, with all models outperforming consensus and the best model, GPT-6 Astra, outperforming even the bias-corrected consensus. The figure shows average prediction error across revenue, gross margin, operating income and adjusted EPS for each model compared to consensus and bias-corrected consensus.


![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/06gtu8uzl7dz49734vtw.jpg)

**Figure 6. The best AI predictions have hit rates above baselines from historical results and show a substantial gain on below-consensus calls.** We compute the hit rate (whether the AI prediction called the direction of the actual correctly) and compare to a per company historical majority: for each company and metric, predict a beat or miss based on the majority result over the past 8 quarters, and a coin flip on ties. We find that the best AI models outperform this historical majority, most strongly so on below-consensus calls.

We looked at some of the traces produced by Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra (the top two models) under Samaya’s prediction harness and analyzed the reasoning process they followed. We find that the models are able to calculate the financial impact of world events and news the way we expect from a strong human analyst. **In fact, anecdotally, the models’ ability to gather new evidence and willingness to adjust their view away from the consensus drive their wins over consensus.**


![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/u0yiyu8gc0jqcmv1yy3v.jpg)

**Figure 7. Examples of model wins and misses.** Each card shows the evidence the model found before the earnings release, the arithmetic it applied, and where its forecast landed against the actual. The bottom strip shows the consensus (filled red), the bias-corrected consensus (open red, dashed), the model’s forecast (blue) and the actual (black). All quotes are verbatim from documents the agent retrieved before the earnings release. *All six cases are in the [interactive version of this figure](https://samaya.ai/blog/frontier-ai-models-outperform-human-experts-on-earnings-prediction#fig-cases) on the original post.*

## Disentangling the impact of the data, harness and model

We carried out an ablation study to understand the individual components of our system and their contribution to model performance.

### Access to live data is the most important factor in accurate financial predictions

Here we compare three settings: (1) no data, i.e. the model relies purely on parametric memory; (2) stale data, by asking the models to make the same prediction 11 weeks in advance, i.e. within a couple of weeks of the previous earnings call; and (3) the latest data.


![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/e3v92sucotcd4kocj7f2.jpg)

**Figure 8.** Surprise correlation, all four metrics pooled, surprises measured against the consensus. Each bar is one run of the model over the same instances: no data (parametric knowledge only); stale data, with the clock rewound to 55 trading sessions before the earnings release; and the latest data, five sessions before. Grey dotted line: the bias-corrected consensus scored as if it were a prediction.

- As expected, even the best models struggle without access to any data. In particular, we see that Claude Fable 5.1 (knowledge cutoff June 26) is unable to utilize publicly available information in its parametric memory.
- Giving models access to the data at the beginning of the quarter raises performance by 25pp, underscoring the importance of having access to real data.
- But there is still a 12–16pp gap with the full data setting, roughly equivalent to the difference between Claude Sonnet 5 and Kimi K3 vs the frontier models. This also corroborates the observational evidence in the previous section that models do well by finding timely information and updating their estimates.

### Expert guidance strengthens search and reasoning

We also ablate the effect of expert guidance, finding that with expert-guided instructions models research roughly 1.6–2.7× more (in time spent and context used), leading to reductions in model error.


![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/kt3eya2brh4z39yp7cvc.jpg)

**Figure 9.** Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra without and with expert guidance. Left: median time per forecast and median context used (tokens in the final model call), on the same companies; arrows point from without to with guidance. Right: mean prediction error, in units of each company’s surprise volatility σ, on the same instances; † significantly lower with guidance (one-sided paired company-cluster bootstrap, p<0.05). Claude Fable 5.1’s drop is borderline (p ≈ 0.05).

### The best models do well even when the consensus is taken away

While using consensus and improving upon it is standard practice for traders and portfolio managers, we also wanted to measure AI performance when it cannot see the consensus at all. We created a new set of tools that eliminate all structured sources of estimates and redact any sentences in the retrieved documents that give away consensus figures.


![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/btfw2p41n50evtgr1ng4.jpg)

**Figure 10.** Overall surprise correlation (Spearman ρ, all four metrics pooled, surprises measured against the consensus) without access to consensus estimates (light) vs with access (dark), on the same instances. † consensus access significantly better (one-sided paired company-cluster bootstrap, p<0.05).

We found that the weaker models benefit a lot from having access to consensus, whereas the gap narrows with better models. In particular, GPT-6 Astra achieves nearly identical performance, possibly reconstructing the consensus from publicly available information.

## What’s next?

Our results show an exciting advance in AI for finance: frontier AI models, given the right harness integrated with financial data, are able to outperform experts at prediction tasks such as earnings surprises.

- **Try out the predictions and adapt them to internal data.** We have an alpha version of the earnings prediction agent within the Samaya product available for users and clients. We’re also working with clients on adapting these predictions to internal data to generate firm-specific insights. Get in touch to try it out and collaborate!
- **Further research on modeling reasoning.** How do these models make the predictions? Are they able to identify the actual drivers reliably? Are they less biased compared to human analysts? Can we complement human reasoning with AI reasoning mechanisms? We’re researching these and other related questions.
- **RL post-training and continual learning.** The earnings prediction environment provides high quality signal for RL training and we’re working on training AI models to learn from their past mistakes on this and other predictive tasks.


![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/wt0ya7a0jnvwl61huboe.jpg)

**Figure 11.** Company revenue, 100-company cohort, five runs per model. For each instance we pick the trace with the lowest error (dark) or the highest error (lightest); medium is the error of those predictions averaged. The rollouts show significant variance and the best rollouts have significantly lower error compared to the average.

## Acknowledgements

We thank Richard Diehl Martinez and Rajul Bothra for their contributions to designing the environment, and Yuhao Zhang, Ozan Koyluoglu and Thejas Venkatesh for their feedback on this work.

## Appendix A. Additional results

**Frontier models outperform on bigger surprises.** The revenue error split by how far the actual landed from the consensus, six models, the three frontier models in colour and the rest in grey. In the two outer groups the bars are sorted by height; the line in each group is the raw consensus.

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/0vqf52hbenlpyzv2ztzb.jpg)

**Figure 12.** Average revenue prediction error in σ, split by how far the actual landed from the raw consensus. Black dashed line: the raw consensus scored as a prediction in each group. Company counts under each group.

**Understanding the stochasticity of models.** We ran GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 five times each on a cohort of 100 companies. We found that while there is variation from run to run, averaging across multiple runs does not lead to significant improvements.


![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/km5f93omijf407wvzd4k.jpg)

**Figure 13. Company revenue**, 100-company cohort, five runs per model.

**Some metrics are harder to get right than others.** The models did better relative to the street on revenue and gross margin than on operating income and adjusted EPS. There are two possible explanations: (1) operating income and EPS are downstream of the other two metrics and can have compounding errors; (2) these are adjusted numbers and different companies have different conventions on accounting for one-off items.


![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/mq2ywencdcx007kc4tei.jpg)

**Figure 14.** Vol-adjusted mean absolute error: the error on each metric of each instance, |prediction − actual|, is expressed in units of the company’s own historical surprise volatility σ (capped at 10σ), so metrics and companies are directly comparable. Grey dotted line = error of the bias-corrected consensus used as the prediction.

## Appendix B. Why we chose the 4 headline metrics

**The four metrics follow the flow of money through the income statement.** The flow begins with revenue, the goods or services sold by the company. Gross margin is the share of each sales dollar left after the direct cost of making the product. Then we take out the cost of running the business, leaving us with operating income. Finally, adjusted EPS is the per-share profit that ultimately accrues to shareholders, after financing and taxes.

| Metric | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| Revenue | Total value of what the company sold. The starting point: what the business sells. |
| Gross margin | Share of each sales dollar left after the direct cost of making the product. Revenue minus the direct cost of making the product, as a share of revenue. |
| Operating income | Profit from the core business after the cost of running it. Gross profit minus the cost of running the business. |
| Adjusted EPS | Per-share profit after financing and taxes, one-time items excluded. The number the market reacts to most. Operating income minus interest and taxes, divided by shares outstanding. |

## Appendix C. How we score the models

Each {% katex inline %}i{% endkatex %} is one metric of one instance (one company and one earnings release), with the model’s prediction {% katex inline %}\hat{y}_i{% endkatex %} and the actual reported value {% katex inline %}y_i{% endkatex %}.

**Consensus.** On the prediction day, every broker covering the company has a published estimate for the metric. We take the **median broker estimate** at the close of that day as the consensus, to prevent skew due to outliers:

{% katex %}
r_i = \operatorname{median}(\text{broker estimates on the prediction day}).
{% endkatex %}

**Past surprises.** For each of the company’s previous eight quarters {% katex inline %}q{% endkatex %}, the **surprise** is how far the actual landed from the consensus a week before that quarter’s earnings release, as a percentage of the consensus for revenue and operating income and as a plain difference for gross margin (in points) and adjusted EPS (in dollars):

{% katex %}
s_{i,q} = \frac{\text{actual}_q - \text{consensus}_q}{\text{consensus}_q} \quad \text{or} \quad s_{i,q} = \text{actual}_q - \text{consensus}_q.
{% endkatex %}

**Bias-corrected consensus.** The company’s typical surprise is the **median of its past surprises**, {% katex inline %}b_i = \operatorname{median}_q \, s_{i,q}{% endkatex %}. We add it to this quarter’s consensus, but only when it is positive, so the correction can lift the consensus and never lowers it:

{% katex %}
c_i = r_i \,\bigl(1 + \max(0, b_i)\bigr) \quad \text{or} \quad c_i = r_i + \max(0, b_i),
{% endkatex %}

the first form for revenue and operating income, the second for gross margin and adjusted EPS.

**Surprise volatility.** Some companies surprise by much more than others. Their **surprise volatility** {% katex inline %}\sigma_i{% endkatex %} is the standard deviation of the same eight past surprises, floored at a quarter of the median {% katex inline %}\bar{\sigma}{% endkatex %} across companies for that metric,

{% katex %}
\sigma_i = \max\Bigl(\operatorname{std}_q \, s_{i,q},\; \tfrac{1}{4}\,\bar{\sigma}\Bigr),
{% endkatex %}

so that a company with an unusually steady history cannot turn an ordinary miss into a huge error.

**Prediction error** is the distance between the prediction and the actual, in units of the surprise volatility, averaged over all metrics of all instances, with a single metric capped at 10 so it cannot dominate the average:

{% katex %}
\text{Prediction error} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i \min\left( \frac{|\hat{y}_i - y_i|}{a_i \, \sigma_i},\; 10 \right),
{% endkatex %}

where the scale {% katex inline %}a_i{% endkatex %} puts the error in the same units as {% katex inline %}\sigma_i{% endkatex %}: the reported revenue for revenue and operating income (a percentage error), and 1 for gross margin and adjusted EPS.

**Hit rate** is the share of predicted metrics where the prediction and the actual land on the same side of the consensus,

{% katex %}
\text{Hit rate} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i \mathbf{1}\bigl[\, \operatorname{sign}(\hat{y}_i - r_i) = \operatorname{sign}(y_i - r_i) \,\bigr],
{% endkatex %}

leaving out metrics where either equals the consensus exactly.

**Surprise correlation** first turns the predicted and the actual surprise of each metric into units of the company’s surprise volatility, so that all companies and metrics sit on one scale (both clipped at ±10),

{% katex %}
\hat{z}_i = \frac{\hat{y}_i - r_i}{k_i \, \sigma_i}, \qquad z_i = \frac{y_i - r_i}{k_i \, \sigma_i},
{% endkatex %}

where {% katex inline %}k_i = |r_i|{% endkatex %} for revenue and operating income and 1 otherwise. It is then the rank correlation between the two across all metrics of all instances, high when bigger predicted surprises go with bigger actual surprises, in direction and size:

{% katex %}
\text{Surprise correlation} = \rho_{\text{Spearman}}\bigl(\hat{z}_i,\; z_i\bigr).
{% endkatex %}

This is a standardised unexpected earnings measure in the spirit of Livnat and Mendenhall (2006),<sup>2</sup> scaled by the company’s own surprise volatility rather than by analyst dispersion.

**Significance.** Significance marks (†) use a one-sided paired company-cluster bootstrap (companies resampled with replacement, 2,000 draws).

---

1. B. Baik and G. Jiang (2006), [“The use of management forecasts to dampen analysts’ expectations”](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0278425406000664), *Journal of Accounting and Public Policy* 25(5), 531–553.
2. J. Livnat and R. R. Mendenhall (2006), “Comparing the post–earnings announcement drift for surprises calculated from analyst and time series forecasts”, *Journal of Accounting Research* 44(1), 177–205. Our version is scaled by the company’s own past-surprise volatility rather than by analyst dispersion.

Brakes Let You Go Fast: Balancing Acceleration and Safety for AI Agents

_Written by John Feminella_

We now inhabit a world where agents can execute operations in production environments and at the speed of light. The question many are now grappling with: How can we ensure safety for agentic systems with access to powerful operations, without handcuffing what they can accomplish?

## The problem

I think about this a lot in the context of the controls we’ve introduced at Two Sigma to limit risks from agents. At a regulated firm, too little safety is an existential risk, and too little innovation is a slow death.

If we want to reap the benefits of agents, we must do so in a way that gives us both safety and freedom to innovate. As John Shedd wrote, “A ship in harbor is safe — but that is not what ships are for.”

For us, we started with five essential ingredients. What’s right for your enterprise will depend on your own exposure to risks and what you want to allow agents to do.

## 1. Registering agents

To tap the vast potential of our teams to innovate, we need a way for them to share those ideas with each other and for their agents to communicate and work together. An agent registry that allows them to connect to each other is the first, most important step. Without a way for agents (and humans) to understand what’s already been written, we run the risk of wasting a lot of duplicated time, energy, and tokens.

In our case, the registry records each agent’s tools, endpoints, owner, and associated products. One of our goals is to be minimally invasive. We’ve designed our approved templates so that agents built from those templates register themselves, while the bespoke ones are detected heuristically and auto-registered with their owners notified.

## 2. Risk scoring

Popular agentic harnesses work differently from the way most deployed enterprise agents operate. In general, when you start interacting with a harness like Claude Code, Codex, or Pi, it doesn’t know what kind of request it might get or what purpose it is about to be imbued with — it’s open-ended by design. This presents a challenge for risk evaluation because it could do practically anything.

That’s in contrast to enterprise agents, which almost always have a specific and dedicated purpose. This means that it’s much clearer how we might evaluate and understand these agents. For example, a ticket summarizer differs from an agent reading production market signals.

The registry scores each agent’s risk profile from its declared tools, purpose, and systems, on every update. If an agent is approved for use, the declaration also circumscribes the agent by limiting through policy what it’s allowed to do. The risk scores are based on observed factors like which tools the agent uses, but also qualitative ones like the nature of the agent’s purpose.

Low-risk agents with limited capabilities and access publish without humans involved, and high-risk agents get flagged. This discernment process lets us spend review effort where it matters the most.

## 3. Egress controls

Agents derive value in part from how they’re allowed to combine and remix information to produce output. But by default, the environments in which our agent processes run don’t trust agents. Instead, agents run behind a proxy that allows only approved destinations. The proxy does not trust agent code, fails closed, and takes the policy for each agent from the registry directly. No one needs to file firewall tickets or maintain brittle configuration.

## 4. Evaluations

Without a consistent way to do evaluations, teams will have to construct bespoke approaches to understanding model performance against their agent. To us, this would be like asking each team to invent their own unit-testing framework — it’s a wasteful and unnecessary distraction that might be necessary, but ultimately detracts from their ability to innovate.

Instead of bespoke approaches in each team, we aim to have shared evaluations, so that each team writing agents has a consistent way to compare performance. These individual performances against individual models can then be aggregated across teams to understand model performance in the firm’s context. Without this, we’d only have public benchmark numbers, and our experience has taught us that public benchmarks generally don’t have a great correspondence to individual, specific firms.

Our shared framework also handles trace collection and pipeline work, so authors only need to write their usual agent logic and test cases. This means that evals run on every change, just like a CI/CD pipeline.

## 5. Auto-mode classifiers

If humans need to manually review and approve every agent action, this both slows down the agent and makes the human careless through complacency and alert fatigue. To combat this, we implement a model familiar to folks who use agentic harnesses: “auto mode” classifiers.

If an agent wants to do something that is not expressly forbidden, a two-stage classifier decides what should happen: quick triage that leans toward blocking, then deeper review for unclear cases.

## Conclusion

Taken together, these are five of the controls that we’ve put into place for our platform and agentic workloads. This is an evolving space, and what’s right today may not be in six months; we’re constantly engineering our platforms to be ahead of where we need to be to meet internal demand for these capabilities. Our agents will run at machine speed, whether or not their controls do. Successful enterprises build controls that keep up, so nobody has to slow down.

How Anthropic’s Dynamic Workflows Coordinate Claude Agents

_At AI Engineer New York, Anthropic drew on lessons from Unix and Linux to explain how agents can tackle bigger projects without overwhelming developers._

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/2av24lfhx2h1hw0w5zxo.jpeg)
<figcaption>CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, at AI Engineer NYC today</figcaption>

The AI Engineer New York 2026 conference kicked off this morning with a series of workshops, including Anthropic discussing how to orchestrate its Claude Managed Agents. Of particular interest was a brand new feature, announced on Friday, called dynamic workflows — or simply “flows,” as the presenters repeatedly called it.

Flows are defined as “a new type of multiagent orchestration, built for your most ambitious workloads.”

CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, both Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, began by invoking some operating system projects of the past — from Ken Thompson building the original Unix operating system, through to Linux evolving from one person (Linus Torvalds) to layers of trusted maintainers. The lesson: agents need the same level of organization in order to do the types of big, ambitious projects Anthropic envisions for dynamic workflows.

“I think a lot of us who are orchestrating and managing lots of agents now might start to feel this feeling of being the bottleneck and being the breaking point as we have lots of agents contributing tons and tons of PRs,” Avilla said. “And we’re sitting there in our GitHub trying to approve PRs and make sure that everything works as expected.”
<!-- IMAGE 02 (CHECK): 02-likely-unionai-sponsor-photo-long-running-slide.png sits here in the original, with no caption.
Its slide matches the Union.ai sponsor copy, so it may belong to the sponsor block. Drop it if you drop the sponsor block. -->

From agent rosters to dynamic workflows
The pair noted that dynamic workflows began in Claude Code as the “a harness for every task” concept. But flows can run longer than a single agent or a roster. The basic idea is that Claude chooses the organization of agents.

“Flows are essentially the next version of multi-agent orchestration,” said Stall, “where you can let Claude fully orchestrate the entirety of its own multi-agent topology.”

The way this works is that the lead agent creates a plan for how it wants to accomplish tasks. Claude then writes an orchestration program, which launches agents, collects results, and manages information flow.

Previously, Claude Managed Agents required developers to configure a coordinator and a roster of subagents. With dynamic workflows, Claude itself determines how to divide and orchestrate the work.

“Across multiple different phases of the multi-agent orchestration, it’s able to accomplish discrete, verifiable units of work without you having to manage any of the interconnections between these things,” Stall said.

That said, Avilla noted that the user can introduce specialist sub-agents if they wish.

“It’s also possible in the agent config to pass in pre-configured sub-agents,” he said.

All of this is available in Claude Console, the interface used by developers accessing Claude through API — the whole point of Claude Managed Agents.

The presenters then showed a relatively simple workflow of a stock watchlist scanner. Although this was far removed from the big, ambitious projects Anthropic is encouraging, it did illustrate the basic pattern: a scan phase distributed individual tickers to agents with isolated contexts, and a later review phase examined the findings before producing a report.

Q&A: Budgets and the limits of self-improvement
The audience Q&A surfaced a number of potential problems. One audience member asked how Claude decides how many agents a task needs, and could a simple ticker scan trigger hundreds of sub-agents?

“The answer really is evals and lower defaults,” Stall replied, noting that ambitious tasks generally require explicitly encouraging greater parallelization.

One enduring concern with agent orchestration is maintaining control over your token budget. Someone asked whether the lead agent knows how much money it has available?

Stall replied that the model does not know its budget while running, but that developers can set a session budget. He added that informing models of their budgets could make the agents “a little bit anxious,” which elicited chuckles from the audience.

A related question was how can developers make repeated flows cheaper and more efficient over time?

Outside of asking Claude to examine the costs incurred, Avilla suggested another relatively new feature be used: dreaming. In the documentation, “dreaming” is defined as a research preview feature. A dream “reads an existing memory store alongside past session transcripts, then produces a new, reorganized memory store,” with duplicates merged, “stale or contradicted entries” replaced, and “new insights surfaced.”

Avilla described dreaming in the flow context as being able to “crystallize and basically improve the memory store that is related to those sessions.”

For the stock watchlist example, someone asked whether the watchlist flow can improve itself? For example, recognize that its scanning model is inadequate and change the next scheduled run?

Stall said this wasn’t built in, but he and Avilla suggested hill-climbing and dreaming could be used to improve the loop.

What about visibility into the actions of the sub-agents, another audience member asked.

Avilla replied that yes, developers can always inspect that through graphing functionality inside Claude Console.

“You can tell, what did the lead agent actually pass to the sub-agent? You can look at that payload here to deeply understand what is actually happening for every transition in this entire graph.”

Another interesting question was whether the subagents can communicate with each other?

Stall said the agents share a filesystem and can use it to exchange information, but developers cannot directly instruct one workflow subagent to message another through the API.

Flows cost much more, but are designed for big tasks
In the watchlist-scanner comparison, Avilla said flows cost “much more” than a single-agent approach, but were also “much more effective at finding all of the details.”

The bigger question is how ambitious can flows be, really? One audience member asked whether dynamic workflows can power large scientific research projects, referencing OpenAI’s recently announced proof concerning the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem.

While Stall wouldn’t be drawn on specifics about how Anthropic computes large scientific problems, he said it is their goal to enable general users to tackle those problems too.

“Flows are basically a way to throw test-time compute at hard problems and get more capability faster out of the models,” he said. “We think, especially as an API service, that unlocking the power of this is the first step for us making these types of discoveries, or scientific progress, broadly doable by the general public.”

What 1,368 Real-World AI Incidents Teach Us About Evaluation

AI evaluation has become increasingly sophisticated at testing individual models. We measure accuracy, test hallucinations, run fairness checks, evaluate robustness, and compare systems against increasingly demanding benchmarks.

Yet when we studied real-world AI failures, one pattern kept appearing: many of the failures that mattered most were not really model failures alone. They emerged after the model entered a real operational environment.

A model can perform well during testing and still create problems because the data is incomplete, the workflow is poorly designed, monitoring is weak, or nobody can realistically intervene once something goes wrong.

To understand whether this pattern was random or systematic, we examined 1,368 documented real-world AI incidents and asked whether these failures had recurring features.

## Failures rarely stay inside the model

A technical problem might begin with poor data, weak predictive performance, or an overlooked failure mode, but whether that weakness became harmful often depended on what happened after deployment.

The consequences depended on AI authority, meaningful human intervention, business usage, and whether anyone noticed the problem early enough.

That distinction also appeared in our analysis. Severe monitoring-and-detection failures were associated with a 4.7-times lift in fatal outcomes, while high AI decision authority was associated with a 2.8-times lift. These are associations within reported incidents, not causal estimates, and the underlying data is subject to reporting bias. Even so, they raise an important question: what if consequential AI risks are shaped not only by what a model gets wrong, but by what the surrounding system allows to happen afterward?

## What this looks like in practice

Consider Michigan's MiDAS unemployment system, which automatically issued fraud findings and penalties. Michigan's unemployment agency later reviewed 40,195 fraud findings resolved by computer program alone and reversed 85 percent of them. It also reviewed 22,589 cases initiated by computer and then referred to an investigator, reversing 44 percent of those findings.

The lesson is not simply that automation made mistakes; human involvement alone did not make the problem disappear either. The better question is whether the process provides a meaningful opportunity to detect and correct errors before consequences reach people.

A similar pattern appeared in a South Australian aged-care monitoring pilot. An independent review found that the system generated more than 12,000 alerts that were not verified as true events. During the final months, staff could no longer respond to every alert, and at least one unanswered alert involved an actual resident fall.

A related question arises in an ongoing U.S. class action involving UnitedHealth. Plaintiffs allege that staff were expected to remain within one percent of the care duration predicted by an algorithm. The defendants dispute the allegations, the litigation remains ongoing, and no liability has been established.

Regardless of how that case is resolved, it illustrates a broader question: when an AI system is wrong, can a human realistically disagree with it and change the outcome?

## Evaluation needs a second question

Traditional evaluation still needs to ask whether the model works under expected conditions. That question remains essential, but real-world incidents suggest it cannot be the only question we ask.

We also need to ask: under what conditions can the system fail, and what happens when that failure reaches the real world? That question shifts evaluation toward actively searching for conditions where our confidence might break.

What happens when the underlying data changes over time? What happens when thousands of alerts arrive faster than humans can meaningfully review them? What happens when a human can technically override the AI, but organizational pressures make that override difficult in practice?

## From model evals to system evals

Model evaluation is not becoming less important. It is becoming one layer of a larger evaluation problem.

We think about that problem through three connected questions. Where can the system break across data, design, predictive validity, fairness, explainability, and failure modes? Can that failure reach the real world through excessive authority, weak oversight, limited reversibility, or inadequate monitoring? How much does the failure matter in financial, legal, operational, safety, reputational, or human terms?

Not every technical weakness deserves equal attention. The goal should not simply be to identify more possible failures. The more important goal is to identify the failures that matter, understand how they can travel through a system, and determine whether enough controls exist to stop them before they become real harm.

That becomes increasingly important as AI systems move from recommending what people should do toward taking more consequential actions themselves.

The next generation of AI evaluation will require better benchmarks and stronger model-level measurement. It will also require something broader: the ability to evaluate the entire system around the model and discover how it can fail before the real world discovers those failures for us.

Workshop Day Opens AI Engineer NYC

AI Engineer NYC kicked off yesterday with a day devoted to workshops: 18 hands-on sessions built for learning by doing. You can watch someone demo an eval framework and nod along. Running it against your own agent is different, especially when it fails on a case you never thought to test and there’s an expert a few feet away who can tell you why. That kind of learning sticks. The Expo floor opened at 4:00pm, and a welcome reception sponsored by Sonar closed out the evening.

Opening days at conferences tend to be about listening. This one put people at their keyboards from the first session, and the lineup ended up doubling as a snapshot of the problems engineering teams are wrestling with right now. Three came up again and again.

**Evals take center stage.** Seven of the 18 workshops focused on proving an agent actually works. Plenty of teams have learned the hard way that getting an agent to run is easy and knowing whether to trust it is not. Laurie Voss taught Evaluations with Phoenix 101, SallyAnn DeLucia led AI Evaluation 101, and Xander Song’s Harbor intro covered shipping agents “on evidence, not vibes.” Sessions from Sonar and Langfuse, plus Nick Nisi and Zack Proser’s workshop on verification loops, pushed the same message: “done” needs a definition. Evals used to be something teams added after a demo impressed someone. In these sessions, they were treated as part of the build itself, written early and run constantly, the way software engineers treat unit tests.

**Finance is a proving ground.** Six workshops targeted financial services and other regulated industries, from a wealth management concierge built in ChatGPT to an anti-money-laundering agent for financial crime detection to insurance programs running on unstructured data. Regulated industries make a demanding test case for agents. Every decision needs an audit trail, mistakes carry legal and financial consequences, and the data rarely arrives in a clean format. An agent that holds up under compliance review and messy policy documents has cleared a much higher bar than one answering questions in a sandbox. It was a fitting focus for a New York crowd, in a city where so many banks, insurers, and fintechs are headquartered.

**The harness matters as much as the model.** A third group of workshops looked at everything surrounding the model: orchestration, permissions, reliability, and cost. Attendees could orchestrate Claude Managed Agents, build agents that self-improve overnight, secure long-running agents with Keycard and Temporal, and dig into Lance Martin’s Unhobbling the Frontier. Eugene Cheah’s Tokenomics 101 tackled the bill that comes after. Model capability keeps climbing, but what users actually experience depends just as heavily on the system wrapped around it: how an agent is scheduled, what it’s allowed to access, how it recovers when something fails halfway through a task, and what each run costs. An agent that works on its own for hours needs guardrails a chatbot never did, and its spend can grow faster than anyone budgeted.

For builders coming off Sunday’s AI Engineer New York Hackathon with MLH, Monday was a natural next step. The hackathon rewarded speed: pick an idea, ship something that works, demo it before time runs out. The workshops asked people to slow down and learn the parts a weekend sprint skips, like testing, security, and cost control. Less sprinting, more depth, and real hands-on time with the tools shaping how agents get built and trusted.

Gemma 4 on a Used 8 GB RTX 3050: 116 Tokens/s for One User, 618 for 64

---
title: "Gemma 4 on a Used 8 GB RTX 3050: 116 Tokens/s for One User, 618 for 64"
published: true
description: "Gemma 4 E2B and E4B on a used RTX 3050 OEM in an old desktop, step by step: single-user speed, the full 131k context, concurrency, answer quality, and how it compares on price with laptop GPUs, ARM laptops, a T4 and a TPU v5e."
tags: gemma, llamacpp, cuda, localllm
cover_image: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/main/local-llamacpp-3050oem-2b-q4_0/docs/first-light-3050oem/devto-cover.c84e6ee4.jpg
---

This article provides a step by step deployment guide for Gemma 4 E2B and E4B to a local, desktop hosted GPU enabled system: an RTX 3050 OEM with 8 GB, in a 2014-era Haswell-E desktop. A suite of Python MCP tools is built to simplify management of the llama.cpp hosted deployment.

https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/tree/main/local-llamacpp-3050oem-2b-q4_0

**A used RTX 3050 OEM, listed at $179.97, serves Gemma 4 E2B at 116 tokens per second for one user and 618 tokens per second across 64 users, with the model's full 131,072-token context in 3.6 GB of its 8 GB. Against an AWS T4 on demand, the card costs as much as 342 hours of rental.**

---

#### What is this project trying to Do?

Earlier rigs in this repository served Gemma 4 from rented TPUs and GPUs, and from hardware already on the desk: a 2021 laptop with a 4 GB GTX 1650 Ti, its CPU, and two Snapdragon ARM laptops. This rig asks what the cheapest dedicated card adds. The RTX 3050 OEM is an 8 GB Ampere card with tensor cores, and used ones were listed on eBay at about $145 to $210 on 2026-10-14.

The rig serves the same model file as the 1650 Ti rig, byte for byte, with the same server flags. The questions are single-user speed, how much context fits, how many users one card carries, whether the bigger E4B model is worth its cost, and what all of it costs against the alternatives.

Speculative decoding with Google's drafter models is a separate article. Every figure here was measured without it.

---

#### At This Point You Should Have…

- An Nvidia GPU with 8 GB of memory. This one is an RTX 3050 OEM: GA106, compute capability 8.6, tensor cores, 120 W power limit.
- The CUDA toolkit (13.4 here) and `cmake`.
- About 7 GB of disk for both model files.
- A clone of `xbill9/gemma4-dev`.

---

#### The Hardware

```text
power.limit [W], clocks.max.sm [MHz], clocks.max.memory [MHz]
120.00 W, 2100 MHz, 7001 MHz
```

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| GPU | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 OEM, PCI `10de:2508` (GA106), compute capability 8.6, 8192 MiB |
| Driver | 615.78.08 |
| CPU | Intel i7-5820K, 6 cores / 12 threads, AVX2 |
| Board / RAM | ASUS X99-A, 46 GiB |
| OS | Debian sid, gcc 16.2.0, CUDA 13.4 |

The OEM 3050 came in prebuilt desktops and is a different configuration from the retail RTX 3050 8 GB. The host is a 2014-era X99 board; with every layer on the card, the CPU barely matters.

---

#### Step 1 — Build llama.cpp for the Card

```shell
export PATH=/usr/local/cuda/bin:$PATH
make build
```

The target runs `cmake` with `GGML_CUDA=ON`, `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86` and `GGML_NATIVE=ON`, then builds `llama-server` and `llama-bench`. It printed the commit, `77c4540ce`, which goes into `tpu.env` as `LLAMA_CPP_COMMIT`. The build took 10 minutes 24 seconds at `-j10`.

---

#### Step 2 — Download the Exact QAT GGUF

```shell
make download
```

The target downloads the file and checks it against `MODEL_SHA256` in `tpu.env`. The file is `xbill9/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-exact-gguf`, SHA-256 `419db9a6bf3bc15d770c85ccf9216827aa88c64fe8f3d72fbe5674f48efe2dc8`. It is Google's quantization-aware-trained (QAT) Gemma 4 E2B with every trained 4-bit value packed into Q4_0 exactly. On the 1650 Ti it measured 32x closer to bf16 by KL divergence than Google's own GGUF, and faster.

---

#### Step 3 — Configure the Server

`tpu.env` is the rig's configuration, and every value in it carries the measurement that set it:

```shell
N_GPU_LAYERS=99
CONTEXT_SIZE=131072
KV_CACHE_TYPE=f16
FLASH_ATTENTION=1
THREADS=6
PARALLEL_SLOTS=1
REASONING=off
OVERRIDE_TENSORS=per_layer_token_embd\.weight=CUDA0
```

| Setting | Why |
| :--- | :--- |
| `-ngl 99` | every layer on the card |
| `-c 131072` | the model's trained maximum; Step 8 |
| `-fa 1` | flash attention: 1.133x prefill, 1.071x decode |
| `-ctk f16 -ctv f16` | `q8_0` costs 7.4% of decode |
| `-ot per_layer_token_embd…=CUDA0` | the per-layer embedding table on the card; Step 7 |
| `--reasoning off` | answers start at once; a request can still ask for thinking |

---

#### Step 4 — Start It and Check What Is Serving

```shell
make serve
nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,process_name,used_memory --format=csv
```

```text
pid, process_name, used_gpu_memory [MiB]
47321, /home/xbill/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server, 1510 MiB
```

That is the first-light configuration: 8,192 tokens of context and the per-layer table left in host memory. The MCP server's attestation reads the device from the running process, since a CPU-only build would answer on the same port:

```text
device=gpu · pid=47321 · -ngl 99 · mapped: ggml-cuda, libcublas, libcuda, libcudart · /home/xbill/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server
mismatch: None
```

One chat request at temperature 0, "In one sentence, what is a TPU?":

```text
A TPU, or Tensor Processing Unit, is a specialized hardware accelerator designed to significantly speed up the training and inference of machine learning models, particularly those involving deep learning.
```

The server's own timings for that request: 34 tokens at 102.56 tokens per second.

---

#### Step 5 — Measure Single-User Speed

`llama-bench`, a 512-token prompt and 128 generated tokens, five repetitions per cell, the card cooled to 40 °C before each cell:

```text
fa1-f16-t6 pp512=3859.96±111.73 tg128=116.14±0.25 77c4540ce
fa0-f16-t6 pp512=3408.19±110.65 tg128=108.46±0.22 77c4540ce
fa1-q8-t6 pp512=3708.48±118.09 tg128=107.57±0.23 77c4540ce
fa1-f16-t4 pp512=3838.78±111.16 tg128=115.87±0.22 77c4540ce
fa1-f16-t6-rep pp512=3835.54±102.85 tg128=115.90±0.22 77c4540ce
```

**116.14 tokens per second generated, 3,860 tokens per second of prompt read.** The repeated last cell lands within 0.6% of the first, and the card held 1890 to 1905 MHz without passing 44 °C.

On the 1650 Ti the same file generates at about 81.7 tokens per second and reads prompts at about 345. That makes this card about 1.42x faster at generating and 11x faster at reading. Generating one token reads every weight once, so it follows memory speed, where the two cards are closer. Reading a prompt is matrix work, which this card runs on tensor cores and the 1650 Ti has none of.

---

#### Step 6 — Keep the Defaults That Measure Faster

| Setting | Prompt | Generate | Kept |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | :--- |
| flash attention off | 0.883x | 0.934x | ❌ on |
| `q8_0` KV cache | 0.961x | 0.926x | ❌ f16 |
| 4 CPU threads in place of 6 | 0.995x | 0.998x | ⚠️ either |

The KV cache for E2B is small, so quantizing it saves memory the card has plenty of and costs speed. Thread count makes no difference because the CPU does no model work.

---

#### Step 7 — Move the Per-Layer Embedding Table onto the Card

The `E` in E2B is a per-layer embedding table, `per_layer_token_embd`, 1.32 GB and 51% of the file. llama.cpp leaves it memory-mapped in host RAM by default and reads one row per token. With 6 GB of the card unused, the rig moves it with `-ot`. Card against host, mean of two passes each, order host, card, card, host:

| test | host | card | card / host |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| pp512 | 3845.18 | 3982.67 | 1.036 |
| pp2048 | 3759.36 | 3848.42 | 1.024 |
| tg128 | 115.91 | 115.98 | 1.001 |

A 2.4 to 3.6% gain on prompts, nothing on generation, for 1,260 MiB. Both card passes beat both host passes at both prompt lengths. The 1650 Ti measured no gain from the same move: this card reads prompts 11x faster, so fetching rows from host memory is a bigger share of its work.

---

#### Step 8 — Serve the Full 131k Context

Gemma 4 E2B was trained to 131,072 tokens. Only its 3 full-attention layers keep a cache that grows with context; the 12 sliding-window layers stay at 1,024 cells.

| `-c` | KV, full-attention | KV, sliding | process on the card |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8,192 | 48 MiB | 12 MiB | 2770 MiB |
| 32,768 | 192 MiB | 12 MiB | 2938 MiB |
| 131,072 | 768 MiB | 12 MiB | **3610 MiB** |

The full context costs 840 MiB over 8,192 and leaves 4.5 GB of the card free. Short chats do not notice: 256 generated tokens ran at 108.30 tokens per second at 8,192 and 107.99 at 131,072.

Long conversations do slow down, because every new token attends to everything before it:

| tokens already in the conversation | prompt t/s | generate tok/s | vs empty |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0 | 3959.63 | 116.02 | 1.000 |
| 8,192 | 2898.48 | 107.06 | 0.923 |
| 32,768 | 1690.19 | 90.68 | 0.782 |
| 65,536 | 1079.92 | 75.02 | 0.647 |
| 120,000 | 669.25 | 58.14 | 0.501 |

Generation stays over 100 tokens per second to about 8k tokens of conversation and halves by 120k.

---

#### Step 9 — Serve Many Users at Once

For the concurrency sweep the server ran 64 slots of 1,024 tokens (`-c 65536 --parallel 64`), 2612 MiB on the card. `sweep.py` sent 1 to 64 simultaneous requests, each with a unique prompt, five repeats per level, median reported:

```text
c=1      93.28 tok/s aggregate  TTFT    212.7 ms  TPOT   9.34 ms  per-stream 107.03
c=4     196.09 tok/s aggregate  TTFT    669.1 ms  TPOT  15.64 ms  per-stream  63.95
c=16    316.07 tok/s aggregate  TTFT   2702.4 ms  TPOT  30.12 ms  per-stream  33.20
c=64    358.05 tok/s aggregate  TTFT   8516.4 ms  TPOT 113.20 ms  per-stream   8.84
```

That is 512 tokens in and 128 out. With 128 in and 512 out, chat-shaped traffic:

```text
c=1     104.74 tok/s aggregate  TTFT    134.9 ms  TPOT   9.34 ms  per-stream 107.02
c=4     259.73 tok/s aggregate  TTFT    330.3 ms  TPOT  14.74 ms  per-stream  67.83
c=16    505.42 tok/s aggregate  TTFT   1114.3 ms  TPOT  29.32 ms  per-stream  34.10
c=64    618.12 tok/s aggregate  TTFT   3890.0 ms  TPOT  95.33 ms  per-stream  10.49
```

**3.84x and 5.90x the single-user output at 64 users.** Past 16 users the gain flattens while each user's speed keeps falling, so 16 is the practical ceiling: 34 tokens per second each, faster than anyone reads.

llama.cpp still reads prompts one request at a time, so time to first token about doubles with each doubling of users. The 1650 Ti ran into that wall: at 512 in and 128 out its output reached only 1.47x single-user. This card reads prompts fast enough that batched generation shows through anyway.

The card drew at most 110.93 W of its 120 W limit, held 1890 MHz in every busy sample and peaked at 68 °C. The server's prompt cache answered 0 tokens, so every prompt was read in full.

---

#### Step 10 — Bring Up E4B on the Same Card

`local-llamacpp-3050oem-4b-q4_0` is the E4B sister rig: same card, binary and flags, with the exact Q4_0 E4B file (SHA-256 `5462cc10…`, 4.20 GB).

| at 131,072 context | E2B | E4B |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Process on the card | 3610 MiB | 6430 MiB |
| KV cache | 780 MiB | 2,088 MiB |
| Generate, empty context | 116.02 tok/s | 60.41 tok/s |
| Prompt, empty context | 3959.63 t/s | 2230.50 t/s |
| Generate, 120k in context | 58.14 tok/s | 30.04 tok/s |

E4B generates at 0.52x E2B at every conversation length and fits with 1.7 GB to spare. The two rigs share port 8080 and do not fit on the card together. On the 1650 Ti, E4B fits at 8,192 context with the per-layer table in host memory and generates at about 39.8 tokens per second; this card runs it 1.52x faster with 16x the context.

---

#### Step 11 — Measure Answer Quality

Both files served one at a time with identical flags, no drafter, and three task sets: a 13-subset classification suite (3,880 questions), GSM8K math (1,319 problems) and BFCL simple tool calling (400 records), all greedy.

| task | E2B | E4B | E4B − E2B | 95% range |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | :--- |
| Classification suite | 0.683 | **0.730** 🥇 | +0.048 | +0.035 to +0.061 |
| GSM8K | 0.898 | **0.933** 🥇 | +0.035 | +0.020 to +0.050 |
| BFCL simple | **0.925** | 0.910 | −0.015 | −0.043 to +0.013 |

E4B is better at reading comprehension and math, and level on tool calling, where the range includes zero. Both 4-bit files score within the error ranges of their bf16 references measured on Cloud TPU: E2B suite 0.683 against bf16's 0.683, E4B suite level with its bf16 run. The quantization costs nothing measurable; the gap between the two is the model.

The whole suite took 6.4 minutes for E2B and 11.2 for E4B on this card.

---

#### 🔎 Tip: Spend the Spare Memory on Context

On an 8 GB card E2B leaves more than half the memory free even at full context. Spend it on the 131k context and on the per-layer table, both measured gains or free. Quantizing the KV cache to `q8_0` saves memory the card does not need and costs 7.4% of generation.

---

#### 🔎 Tip: Size `--parallel` Against `-c`

llama.cpp splits `--ctx-size` across `--parallel` slots. `-c 131072 --parallel 16` gives each user 8,192 tokens; `-c 16384 --parallel 16` gives each 1,024. Set both together, from what each user needs.

---

#### Compare and Contrast: Local Hardware

Gemma 4 E2B, the same exact Q4_0 file on every row except the last two, single user, `llama-bench` generation speed:

| Machine | Device | Generate tok/s | vs 3050 |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Desktop, RTX 3050 OEM 8 GB | GPU, 120 W limit | **116.14** 🥇 | 1.00x |
| Lenovo Yoga 9, GTX 1650 Ti Max-Q 4 GB | GPU, 40 W limit | 81.75 🥈 | 0.70x |
| Lenovo Yoga 9, i7-10750H | CPU, 6 threads | 18.84 🥉 | 0.16x |
| Samsung Galaxy Book Go, Snapdragon 7c Gen 2 | CPU, 2 cores | 8.33 | 0.07x |
| Lenovo Yoga C630, Snapdragon 850 | CPU, 4 cores | 5.00 | 0.04x |

| Capability | RTX 3050 OEM | GTX 1650 Ti |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Prompt read, 512 tokens | 3,860 t/s 🥇 | about 345 t/s |
| Full 131k context, E2B | 🟢 3.6 GB of 8 | ⚠️ not measured |
| E4B | 🟢 131k context, 60 tok/s | ⚠️ 8k context, 40 tok/s |
| 512 in / 128 out, best aggregate | 🟢 358 tok/s, 3.84x | ❌ 1.47x single user |
| Power under load | 110.93 W peak | 40 W cap |

---

#### Compare and Contrast: Cloud

The two cheapest cloud deployments of Gemma 4 E2B measured in this repository serve bf16 weights through vLLM: an AWS `g4dn.xlarge` with a T4, and one Google Cloud TPU v5e chip.

| Operating point | RTX 3050 OEM | T4, `g4dn.xlarge` | TPU v5e-1 |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| One user, output tok/s | 93.28 🥈 | 42.36 🥉 | 120 🥇 |
| 8 users, 512 in / 128 out | 224.18 | 242.47 | — |
| Best aggregate measured | 618.12 🥈 | 243.93 🥉 | 1,382 🥇 |
| Price | $179.97 once | $0.526/hour | $0.5779/hour, spot |

The one-user row compares like shapes for the 3050 and T4 (512 in, 128 out); the TPU figure is 128 in, 128 out. The TPU is faster at every point and serves 2.2x the 3050's best aggregate. The 3050 generates 2.2x the T4's speed for one user and lands within 8% of it at 8 users.

---

#### And Price/Performance?

All of this is arithmetic from the measured speeds, the cloud rates recorded in those runs, a used-card listing captured on 2026-10-14, and the US Energy Information Administration's 2026 residential electricity forecast of 18.2 cents per kWh.

**The card pays for itself in two to three weeks of continuous rental.**

| Against | Rate | Hours to $179.97 | Days |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| TPU v5e-1, spot | $0.5779/h | 311 | 13.0 |
| T4 `g4dn.xlarge`, on-demand | $0.526/h | 342 | 14.3 |
| T4 `g4dn.xlarge`, spot | $0.3559/h | 506 | 21.1 |

**Running it costs about two cents an hour.** At 110.93 W, the most the card drew in any sample, electricity is $0.0202 per hour against $0.526 for the T4.

| Per million output tokens | Cost |
| :--- | ---: |
| RTX 3050, 64 users, 128 in / 512 out, electricity at peak draw | **$0.009** 🥇 |
| RTX 3050, 8 users, 512 in / 128 out, electricity at peak draw | $0.025 🥈 |
| RTX 3050, one user, electricity at 80 W | $0.039 🥉 |
| TPU v5e-1, 64 users, spot | $0.116 |
| T4, 8 users, on-demand | $0.603 |
| TPU v5e-1, one user, spot | $1.338 |
| T4, one user, on-demand | $3.449 |

The local rows leave out the card's purchase and the host it sits in; the cloud rows leave out storage and data transfer. A card already paid for wins by an order of magnitude on running cost. The TPU is the faster machine and the better buy only for a burst of work too big for one 3050, or for anyone without a desktop to put the card in.

---

#### So, Which One?

For a single person or a small team running Gemma 4 E2B or E4B all day, the used RTX 3050 OEM. It is the only local card here with tensor cores and 8 GB, and both together are what it takes: E4B at full context fits, prompts read at thousands of tokens per second, and 16 users each still get 34 tokens per second.

The 1650 Ti laptop remains the right answer for one user who already owns it. The ARM laptops serve E2B, slowly. Rent the TPU for bursts of work.

Between the two models, E4B buys 4.8 points on the classification suite and 3.5 on math for half the generation speed. For tool calling, E2B is level and twice as fast.

---

#### Summary

The goal of this article was to bring Gemma 4 E2B and E4B up on a used RTX 3050 OEM and to measure what it delivers for the money against the other local and cloud deployments in this repository. The key to the solution was the exact Q4_0 QAT files, which leave enough of the 8 GB card free for the full context and for many users at once. The measured results were:

- 🟢 **116.14 tok/s generated and 3,860 t/s of prompt read** for one user, E2B, 1.42x and 11x the 1650 Ti.
- 🟢 **The full 131,072-token context in 3610 MiB** for E2B and 6430 MiB for E4B, with no cost to short chats.
- 🟢 **618.12 tok/s aggregate at 64 users** (128 in / 512 out) and 358.05 at 512 in / 128 out; 34 tok/s per user at 16.
- 🟢 **4-bit quality matches bf16**: E2B suite 0.683 against 0.683; E4B 0.730.
- 🟢 **Pays for itself in 311 to 506 hours** against the cheapest cloud options, and runs for about $0.02 an hour in electricity (arithmetic).
- ⚠️ **E4B generates at 0.52x E2B** for +4.8 suite and +3.5 GSM8K points.
- ⚠️ **Long conversations halve generation speed** by 120k tokens of context.
- ❌ **A `q8_0` KV cache and flash attention off are both slower** on this card.

Scope: one RTX 3050 OEM in an i7-5820K desktop, llama.cpp `77c4540ce` with CUDA 13.4, measured 2026-10-13, without speculative decoding. The 1650 Ti, i7-10750H and Snapdragon figures come from other hosts, llama.cpp commits and days with the same model file; the T4 and TPU figures come from vLLM serving bf16 weights under a different benchmark tool; so every cross-machine ratio is indicative. The card price is one used listing's asking price on 2026-10-14, and the electricity figures use the highest power draw sampled or the single-user benchmark's end-of-run reading.

The strategy for running Gemma 4 locally on a used RTX 3050 OEM was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

text:
The Model Is the Easy Part

We spent the past few months on a question that sounds simple: what does it actually take to move a coding workload off a frontier API and onto open-weight models you run yourself?

We picked coding agents deliberately. They are long-horizon, they are messy, and they are the workload most organisations would move first, because that is where the token bill is growing fastest. We ran a fixed set of real software engineering tasks across a range of open-weight models, each paired with hardware capable of serving it properly, and varied the agent harness on top. Then we measured what came out: tasks resolved, time taken, users served in parallel.

Three things surprised us.

## Capability is priced in steps, it’s not linear

The intuition going in was that better models cost proportionally more to run. They don’t. Quality improves gradually across the open-weight field, but the hardware underneath moves in jumps, because what matters is whether the weights fit in the memory of the box you already have. Cross that line and you are not paying for a few billion more parameters, you are paying for the next machine.

So some models are badly priced for what they give you and others are a bargain, and which is which has little to do with where they sit on a leaderboard. One mid-sized model in our set cost 4 times more to serve than a smaller one while barely improving the application performance with 2%. A much larger one cost only marginally more than the tier below while solving substantially more. The useful question is not which model is best, but which model lands just inside a hardware tier, measured per resolved task rather than per token.

## Concurrency is the variable nobody budgets for

Behind an API, concurrency is someone else’s problem. You get a reasonably predictable response time and you stop thinking about it.

If you manage your own stack, it becomes the binding constraint. Every user brings a context, every context has to fit in memory, and latency stops being acceptable long before the hardware stops working. How many developers a box can comfortably carry varied enormously across our setups, and not in the direction the spec sheets suggest. The largest, most capable configuration served the fewest people at once.

This is where most self-hosting business cases quietly fall apart. The break-even utilisation for the weaker configurations we tested sits far above what enterprises actually achieve. Reported utilisation in real deployments is low, and well-run estates are not dramatically better. If your case needs near-continuous saturation, it does not work.

## The harness changes the bill and only marginally influences application performance

We compared three widely used coding harnesses on identical hardware with identical inference settings, expecting the orchestration layer to matter a great deal. For resolve rate, it barely moved the needle. The spread across harnesses was a couple of tasks either way.

For cost, it mattered a lot. Same model, same hardware, same tasks resolved, and wall time differing by a factor of two depending on the pairing. When you are renting GPUs, wall time is what really defines your cost.

And when you settle on a harness, evals are key as things can easily break. In our experiments, one harness was the clear winner, until the next software release, made our performance collapse. The culprit was a small change in how prefix caching was handling. Suddenly, the caching mechanism broke entirely and the GPU rental cost skyrocketed with a factor 5. The key takeaway is: pick the harness your developers want to use, then instrument it, because a point release can move your costs more than a model swap.

## What we would tell you to do with this

The question is not whether self-hosting is cheaper. Asked that way it has no answer, because it depends on your workload, your peaks and your tolerance for slower agents.

The better question is what your real utilisation looks like, and what you cannot put on someone else’s API at any price. Data that is not allowed to leave the building, a stack nobody can rate-limit, prices that do not move under you mid-quarter. Those reasons survive contact with the spreadsheet. Cost alone usually does not.

text:
It's Not the Model, It's You

Every time a new frontier model comes out, we go through the same rituals: benchmarks get reported, leaderboards get reshuffled, and the social feeds fill up with a heady cocktail of vibes, hot takes, and everything we’ve found the new model can “one-shot.” Anyone watching from the sidelines could be forgiven for thinking that model performance is the single biggest factor driving AI transformation today.

But day to day, how much does the model really matter?

As part of my work at Jellyfish, I analyze and extract industry insights from our massive collection of software engineering workflow data, which tracks AI coding tool and agent telemetry across **300,000 developers from 1,300 companies**. And when you look at what actually happens inside real engineering teams after a new model drops, the picture is a lot more complicated than the launch-day discourse would suggest.

For example: this summer, Cursor changed its defaults after SpaceX announced it was acquiring the platform. New chats started opening on its in-house Grok models, Auto mode began routing to Grok, and free users were locked into using it. Within a few months, Grok went from essentially zero Cursor requests to nearly half, while Claude, GPT, and other models fell from about half to under a quarter. This wasn’t just free users: among paying customers Grok reached nearly 40%, and a third of engineers who had been using Claude or GPT were mostly on Grok by September. A huge share of Cursor traffic switched models because the defaults changed, not because engineers went looking for something new.

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/8yq0nnt5pohlgbkco8ma.png)

## So what happened?

If the model matters as much as we love to argue that it does, there should have been some meaningful change in coding output, right?

**There wasn’t.**

Comparing the engineers who moved the most onto Grok with colleagues at their own companies who barely touched it (more than 12,000 engineers at 222 companies), there was essentially no difference in output.

If you dig deeper, it turns out this isn’t a quirk of one particular model or vendor. When we look at the same engineers switching between major frontier models and families, **none of the switches made a measurable difference.**

## What does matter, then?

We’ve done large-scale analyses across our data to measure which factors explain the differences in how much engineers ship, and by how much.

- **Less than 1%:** The tool itself (model and harness together).
- **About 9%:** The volume of AI that engineers use.
- **About 12%:** Their company, team, and culture.
- **More than 75%:** The individual engineer: their role, their track record, their habits, and everything else that separates today’s great AI engineers from those still figuring it out.

To be clear about the scope, this isn't saying models don't matter. Better models raise the ceiling for everyone, and the frontier is a big part of why any of this works. But among the frontier models engineers are actually choosing between today, the specific one they happen to use explains almost none of the difference in what they ship.

Put another way, for the most elite runners, there might be some small difference between two different carbon-plated racing shoes (Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI GPT-6 Astra), and they’re certainly a lot faster than a pair of old boots. (Opus 4 maybe?) But at the end of the day, the difference between an Olympic marathoner and an amateur dry heaving on the side of the course is their physique and training, not their footwear.

## What this means for engineering leaders

For engineering leaders and practitioners this is ultimately good news, if slightly inconvenient.

The model is the most accessible lever you have, because it’s a dropdown, a router setting, or a procurement decision (and as the Cursor example showed, sometimes it’s not even your choice). But it’s also the one that moves the needle least.

The levers that matter more are slower and more challenging: getting people from occasional to deep use, building the practices and environments that let teams get good at working with AI, and investing in the people themselves.

The pace of frontier models is out of most of our hands. **These other things are squarely within our control.**

So the next time a model drops, don’t hesitate to try it out, and by all means share your vibes and one-shots with the world. (Otherwise I’d lose 90% of the content on my X feed.)

But if you're trying to understand why some of your teams get so much more out of AI than others, **the answer is much more likely to be found in your organization than in the model picker.**

text:
Are You Smarter Than a Fruit Fly?

Google [mapped the complete male fruit fly brain](https://research.google/blog/a-connectomics-milestone-mapping-the-complete-male-fruit-fly-brain/), and my first question to an agent was “Can this run on a laptop?” The simulation has 176,422 neurons and runs on a laptop CPU.

My second question was “Is there something ridiculous that we can do with it, though? That’s engineering-focused: make it do a code review or clear context or something.”

The fly can’t read code, so Jev, a TypeSafe model, answers thirty yes/no questions about each change and the answers become a smell. I tried to train the fly on the codebase by using mutation testing to identify good and bad parts of the code and then train the fly to have memories based on that. On 301 changes it had never seen, it agreed with the tests 290 times. A logistic regression on the same thirty answers got 298.

If a fruit fly can do code review moderately well, then why are humans still doing it?

Reviewing code is the bottleneck. Humans aren’t involved in writing it anymore, and the functionality is what matters. Models are getting good, which means the code quality is getting good and we’re at the precipice of starting to let go of that control.

It’s a big trust issue for humans. Feels like giving up a lot of control but I think that humans are just as capable of slop as agents are. Agents are able to be persistent and review, given the right set of tools and the right context on the outcome.

I want evidence and a receipt that it tested the results and that what it’s proposing to ship actually solves the problem or adds the feature or addresses the issue in the way that’s intended. I want:

- Videos
- Screenshots
- Test results
- Command output
- Smoke tests
- An easy way for me to replicate it myself

On the last agent PR I approved, I looked at the most important bits. The part that made it most important was just where the core business logic was. Agents can verify that it’s logically correct, but we need to make sure that it makes sense for the use case or the application.

Humans should understand why code is changed and why the way that it’s changed matters, but at a higher level, not necessarily line for line. They should just have an understanding of what the code is doing and why, and specifically why not other methods.
