AI Needs a Test That Fights Back

*One right answer is not the same as a good sequence of decisions. eSlams is building a public stadium to explore the difference.*

Have you ever replayed a game in your head and traced the loss back to a single move? Sometimes, one overlooked threat is enough to undo a game’s worth of good decisions.

That is what makes an opponent different from an answer key. On a fixed question-and-answer test, the response is the end of the task. In a game, it is the beginning of the next problem.

Your opponent responds. New information changes what makes sense. A promising plan becomes a liability. You have to adjust, carrying the consequences of your last decision into the next one.

So what happens when an AI model has to do more than produce a convincing answer?

I am building eSlams to explore that question: a public stadium where people can play against AI models and watch them compete, with an open-source engine underneath for investigating their decisions.

eSlams stands for Electronic Slams. The Grand Slams for AI models. At eSlams, AI plays games.

Games make the challenge concrete. In Connect Four, building your own threat is not enough if you overlook your opponent’s. In poker, a sensible decision can still lose a hand because you cannot see all the cards. Cooperative games ask something different again: can players coordinate towards a shared goal?

The point is not to demand perfection. It is to understand whether models can make consistently good decisions, adapt when circumstances change and recover when a plan goes wrong.

In Arena, you can choose a game and face an AI model yourself. In Battlefield, you can watch recorded model-versus-model matches. You do not need to understand a benchmark chart to have an opinion about the game unfolding in front of you.

Underneath the stadium, eSlams Core supports 50 game and control environments, spanning board games, cards, negotiation, cooperation and control tasks. Some use compact or adapted rules, clearly identified in the catalogue.

But a compelling replay is only the beginning of useful evidence.

Imagine a model loses. Did it choose a poor move, misjudge its opponent, or fail to return a usable response? Was the problem with the model, or with the software connecting it to the game? A final score cannot tell us.

Core records what happened so those questions can be investigated. The game engine enforces the rules and limits what each player can see. Moves and technical failures are recorded separately. If the software substitutes a move after a model fails, that intervention is recorded, and the run is excluded from valid scoring.

A match can be saved as a portable record that can be validated and replayed. Public replays are kept separate from private audit information. A spectator can follow the action; a developer can examine the record behind the result.

Games are not a complete test of intelligence, and winning one does not prove readiness for a high-stakes application. Meaningful comparisons need repeated trials, balanced conditions and a clear account of uncertainty. Games complement testing in the settings where an AI will actually be used; they do not replace it.

The MIT-licensed eSlams Core engine is available on GitHub and PyPI. Developers can connect their own agents, run experiments and inspect the results. We are hosting the inaugural AI Grand Slams from February 8–14, 2027.

The question is not simply whether an AI can win. It is what happened between the first move and the final score.

At eSlams, you can watch. You can play. And with the open-source engine, you can investigate.

---

*Ramakrishnan Lokanathan is the founder of eSlams. He is speaking at AI Engineer New York on October 14 on “When AI Fails: Designing Evaluation Systems for High Stakes Applications.”*

What LLMs 'Know' That You Don't Know They Know: Stop Inventing Prompt DSLs and Ride 50 Years of Unix Pre-Training Gravity

---
title: "What LLMs 'Know' That You Don't Know They Know: Stop Inventing Prompt DSLs and Ride 50 Years of Unix Pre-Training Gravity"
description: "Why did a 1976 Makefile (Part 3.6) and a 1983 Unix init.d directory (Part 3.7) outperform 2,000 lines of English prompt rules? Because prompt engineering is static symbol linkage against 50 years of pre-trained computer science canon."
tags: ai, programming, unix, architecture
series: Synthetic Scars
---

## *Why spend 2,000 tokens explaining dependency graphs, process isolation, and crash recovery in English prose when `make`, `fork()`, and `/etc/init.d` are already etched into the deepest canyons of the model's weights?*

> *"Those who do not understand Unix are condemned to reinvent it, poorly."*  
> — **Henry Spencer**, Usenet `comp.unix.wizards` (November 1987)

---

Stop writing 2,000-line English prompt essays in your `CLAUDE.md`, `GEMINI.md`, or `.cursorrules`. Every time you invent a custom 20-step checklist or bracketed pseudo-code tag (`[CRITICAL_STEP_4_GATE]`), its frequency in the model's pre-training corpus is **zero (`Freq ≈ 0`)**—forcing the LLM to burn its fragile working-memory attention heads simulating an interpreter for a language it met five seconds ago.

Sitting dormant inside every frontier LLM's weights is an entire universe of **50-year-old Unix and computer science formalisms**—`Makefile`, `/etc/init.d`, `fork()`/`wait()`, `RFC 822`, `RFC 5234 EBNF`, `Design-by-Contract`, `Two-Phase Commit (2PC)`, `Circuit Breakers`, and `git bisect`—that the model has seen **millions of times (`Freq > 1,000,000`)** during pre-training. Prompt engineering works best as **static symbol linkage**: a 20-token Unix primitive calls a battle-hardened C library the model already spent 100 million dollars compiling into its deep feed-forward weights.

Across **151 production tickets** ([**Part 3.6**](https://dev.to/gde/stuart-feldman-was-right-in-1976-why-your-ai-agent-needs-a-makefile-not-a-20-step-prompt-5bn2) and [**Part 3.7**](https://dev.to/gde/surviving-the-200k-token-lobotomy-how-unix-initd-and-memento-made-my-ai-coding-agent-immune-to-2f74)) and a **1,680-trial multi-model A/B lab benchmark** (`41.4M` tokens under `~16,000` tokens of realistic compiler/diff distractor load), replacing 500-token English rules with 20-token canonical CS formalisms (`15x–50x` shorter) produced massive, statistically decisive (`p < 0.0001`) leaps across the board:

* **Halting Apology/Retry Loops (`Circuit Breaker FSM` vs. prose *"stop after 2 tries"*)**: **`0.8%` → `98.3%`** (`+97.5 pp`, `z = 15.11`)
* **Surviving a 230k-Token Compaction Lobotomy (1983 SysV `/etc/init.d` vs. `PROGRESS.md`)**: **`0.8%` → `60.0%` overall** (**`96.7%` on `gemini-2.5-pro`**, `+59.2 pp`, plus two live 230k-token compactions survived with zero lost steps)
* **Isolating Regressions (`git bisect` vs. prose debugging across a 16-stage pipeline)**: **`19.2%` → `81.7%`** in `≤ 4` probes (**`100%` on `gemini-3.1-pro`**, `+62.5 pp`)
* **Killing Sad-Path Mutants in Real `dart test` Runs (`@requires`/`@ensures` + QuickCheck vs. *"test edge cases"*)**: **`1.7%` → `60.0%` pass rate** (**`100%` on `Pro` models**, `93.3%` mutants killed on `3.1-pro`)
* **Atomic Multi-Package Refactoring (`2PC + WAL` vs. *"don't leave the build broken"*)**: **`45.8%` → `93.3%`** (`+47.5 pp`)
* **Strict Pause-Gate Output Syntax (`RFC 5234 EBNF` vs. prose formatting rules)**: **`32.5%` → `77.5%`** (**`100%` across `flash` and `pro` tiers**)

Here is the physics of *why* 50-year-old systems primitives crush modern prompt DSLs—and the **10-primitive Rosetta Stone** you can drop into your agent skills today.

---

## 1. The Zero-Frequency Interpreter Trap: Why Custom Prompt DSLs Collapse

Look at almost any "advanced" system prompt, `.cursorrules` file, or agent framework published over the last two years. You will see developers inventing bespoke, natural-language Domain-Specific Languages (DSLs) or custom pseudo-code bracket notations from scratch:

```markdown
<!-- Typical Fragile Prompt DSL (Pre-Training Frequency ≈ 0) -->
[CRITICAL_EXECUTION_PROTOCOL]
1. First, analyze the repository and write your findings.
2. Second, create a plan and wait for user approval.
3. IMPORTANT: Do NOT write code until Step 2 is approved!
4. After approval, write a failing test first.
5. Implement the code and run the test.
6. IF THE TEST FAILS: You MUST return to Step 5 and fix it before proceeding to Step 7!
7. NEVER skip Step 6!
```

Or even worse, teams try to save tokens by compressing English rules into an invented symbolic shorthand—like this actual ["Agent-Native Intermediate Representation (ANIR)"](https://gist.github.com/Tom-Zafred/7be8e3efcf9b76d27945eaa3dc44ae49) proposed on the [Google AI Developers Forum](https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/the-pink-elephant-in-the-token-window-why-transformer-self-attention-hates-your-do-not-rules/187630):

```text
[DB: SET_BASED(TVP|XML_SHRED) !N1_LOOP]
```

Why does an LLM inevitably drift, skip Step 6, ignore `!N1_LOOP`, or forget Step 3 when the conversation hits 80,000 tokens?

As developer [**Dean Lee**](https://dev.to/deanlee) observed in the [comments on **Part 3.6**](https://dev.to/deanlee/comment/3h0j5):

> *"When an agent manages an imperative 20-step checklist in memory, it is running an unhedged Markov chain where every token of tool output increases the probability of a state transition error. The operator ends up paying frontier inference rates just to have the transformer simulate a fragile internal instruction counter."*

In machine learning research, multiple empirical studies (including [Razeghi et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.07206) and [Kandpal et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.08411)) have proven a fundamental scaling law: **an LLM's zero-shot execution reliability scales log-linearly with how many times that exact structural pattern appeared in its pre-training corpus.**

When you invent `[CRITICAL_EXECUTION_PROTOCOL]` or `[DB: SET_BASED(TVP|XML_SHRED) !N1_LOOP]`, what is the frequency of your custom rule syntax in the pre-training corpus?

**Approximately zero (`Freq ≈ 0`).** (And worse, `!N1_LOOP` is still a bare negative Pink Elephant—replacing the word `NOT` with an ASCII exclamation point `!` does not give softmax self-attention a native negation operator!)

Because the model has never seen your custom English state machine or bracketed pseudo-code before, it cannot route execution through its deep, crystallized feed-forward weight circuits. Instead, it has to **simulate an interpreter for your custom syntax at runtime** using its shallowest, most fragile working-memory attention heads. As the context window fills with compiler logs and file diffs, attention dilutes (`O(1/L)`), the simulated interpreter drops a pointer, and your agent drives off a cliff.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Custom 20-Step Prompt or Invented DSL\n(Pre-Training Frequency ≈ 0)"] --> B["Model Must Simulate a Custom Interpreter\nin Fragile In-Context Attention Heads"]
    B --> C["Context Grows to 150k Tokens\nAttention Dilutes Across Steps"]
    C --> D["💥 Sequential Amnesia & Skipped Gates"]
```

---

## 2. The Law of Pre-Training Gravity & The Graybeard Paradox: Prompting Is Static Linkage

Now consider what happens when you delete that 20-step English essay and write this instead:

```makefile
.PHONY: finish
finish: pr-merged

pr-merged: ci-green critic-review-passed human-landing-approval
	gh pr merge --squash

critic-review-passed: tests-green
	# Spawn un-primed adversarial critic subagent
```

Why does the model suddenly obey every single dependency gate without being told *"NEVER skip Step 6"*?

When **[Part 3.6](https://dev.to/gde/stuart-feldman-was-right-in-1976-why-your-ai-agent-needs-a-makefile-not-a-20-step-prompt-5bn2)** went out, veteran sysadmin **William S. Duncanson** left a comment on Facebook that captured the sociological root of the problem—what we might call **The Graybeard Paradox**:

> *"Shared this series with my team and some of our AI devs. A lot of them are younger and don't have the experience of us grumpy grizzled sysadmins."*

Think about the irony of that: a 24-year-old prompt engineer in 2026 may never have maintained a 1976 Bell Labs `Makefile`, written a 1983 `/etc/init.d` boot script, or hand-crafted a 1982 **[RFC 822](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc822)** email header. **So they don't know to ask for them.**

**But the LLM has read all of them!** Foundation models trained on trillions of tokens have ingested **50 years of Unix source trees, POSIX standards, IETF RFCs, Usenet archives, Linux kernel mailing lists, O'Reilly books, and computer science textbooks**.

In fact, right after **Part 3.6** went live, one of the very first people to react to the post was [**Dave Crocker**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Crocker)—Internet Hall of Fame inductee and the author of [**RFC 822**](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc822) (published August 13, 1982). Stop and think about RFC 822 for a second: why does every Markdown frontmatter block (`--- title: ... tags: ... ---`) and every structured `Key: Value` state header in our `init.d` files (`Current Target:`, `Last Completed Step:`, `Next Permitted Action:`) parse with 100% zero-shot reliability across every LLM on Earth? **Because every email, HTTP request, MIME message, Usenet article, and YAML frontmatter header in the pre-training corpus descends directly from Dave Crocker's 1982 RFC 822 `field-name ":" [ field-body ] CRLF` grammar!**

And right after **[Part 3.7](https://dev.to/gde/surviving-the-200k-token-lobotomy-how-unix-initd-and-memento-made-my-ai-coding-agent-immune-to-2f74)** went live, systems engineer [**Mike Mol**](https://github.com/mikemol) (who first spotted the *stigmergy* connection on Facebook) shared his own multi-repository agent harness, [`mikemol/nemik`](https://github.com/mikemol/nemik) and [`mikemol/mtools`](https://github.com/mikemol/mtools). Look at the core design rule in `nemik`'s README: ***“`nemik` builds on existing standards rather than inventing a tracker.”*** Instead of inventing a bespoke prompt DSL to coordinate independent repository agents ("rebel cells" named after Karis Nemik in *Andor*), Mike mapped workstream state to **OASIS OSLC Change Management 3.0** (`oslc_cm:ChangeRequest`), cross-repo causal provenance (`--caused-by <repo>:W<n>`) to [**W3C PROV**](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-overview/) (`prov:Activity`, `prov:wasInformedBy`), DAG integrity to [**W3C SHACL**](https://www.w3.org/TR/shacl/) (`shapes.ttl`), peer messaging (`<repo>/inbox/`) toward [**W3C ActivityPub**](https://www.w3.org/TR/activitypub/) JSON-LD actor semantics, and drained prose standing rules into **Claude Code `PreToolUse` hooks** and [**Open Policy Agent (`OPA` / `.rego`)**](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/) policies verified by [**Negative Witnesses** (`W231`)](https://github.com/mikemol/mtools/blob/main/.claude/design/W231-standing-rules-opa.md). When I asked him about that architecture, he nailed the exact mechanism in one sentence:

> *"And a major reason behind leaning so hard on those standards: the frontier models all have them in their training data, and there's literature I can use. I'm deliberately running it as an autopoietic framework; the purpose of the system is to run the system, and I add tasks to said system."*

Inside the pre-training corpus, Stuart Feldman's 1976 `Makefile` dependency graphs (`target: prerequisites`), Dave Crocker's 1982 [`RFC 822`](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc822) headers (`Key: Value`), AT&T's 1983 `/etc/init.d` runlevel directories (`00_...` to `99_...`), Ken Thompson's 1971 Unix process semantics (`fork()`, `wait()`, `exit 0`), and W3C/OASIS/CNCF formalisms (`PROV`, `SHACL`, `ActivityPub`, `OPA Rego`) do not appear zero times. **They appear millions of times (`Freq > 1,000,000`).**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    E["Canonical Systems Formalism: Makefile / init.d / RFC 822\n(Pre-Training Frequency > 1,000,000)"] --> F["Static Linkage Into Deep, Pre-Trained\nFeed-Forward Weight Circuits"]
    F --> G["Working-Memory Attention Freed\nfor Actual Domain Code Synthesis"]
    G --> H["✅ Deterministic DAG & Compaction Survival"]
```

For the last three years, the AI industry has treated prompt engineering as **creative writing**—when physically, **prompt engineering is static symbol linkage.**

When you write a `Makefile`, an `RFC 822` header block, an `/etc/init.d` directory, or a `W3C SHACL` / `OPA Rego` policy in your agent skill, you are **linking against a battle-hardened C library that the model already spent 100 million dollars compiling into its weights during pre-training.**

## 3. From Hypothesis to Controlled Lab Proof: The 10 Latent Super-Highways (`N = 1,680` Paired A/B Trials)

  * **Condition A (`Freq ≈ 0` Bespoke Prose)**: Polite, detailed natural-language instructions (300 to 600 tokens).
  * **Condition B (`Freq > 1,000,000` CS Canon)**: The exact same invariant expressed as a 15-to-40 token canonical Unix or computer science formalism (`15x–50x` shorter).

### ✅ Pillar 1 (Proven in Part 3.6 + Lab-Tested in Suite 1): Build Graphs — GNU `make` (`target: prerequisites`, 1976)
* **What users normally write**: 150 lines of numbered steps with `IF / ELSE / GOTO Step 3` prose loops.
* **What the LLM has seen millions of times**: `Makefile` rules, `.PHONY` targets, prerequisite chains, and `mtime` dirty-artifact invalidation.
* **Why `Makefile` beats modern task runners like `Just` inside an LLM**: When reader **Aaron Abelard** mentioned on Facebook that he had moved from `Make` to [`Just` (`justfile`)](https://github.com/casey/just), it highlighted a crucial distinction: `just` is a *command runner* (every recipe is effectively `.PHONY`), whereas `make` is a *file-state dependency graph* backed by 50 years of pre-training gravity. After a 200k-token context compaction reboot, a `Makefile` agent inspects which physical milestone files (`<brain>/state/20_plan_approved.md`) already exist on disk and automatically skips completed steps!
* **What it unlocks**: Backward-chaining evaluation from `make finish`. When a source file (`lib/src/binder.dart`, `mtime = 19:14:30`) is modified *after* `run_tests` (`19:08:11`) and `run_adversarial_critic` (`19:10:45`), a `Makefile` DAG forces the agent to invalidate downstream stamps and re-run the leaf prerequisite (`run_tests`). ### ✅ Pillar 4 (Empirically Proven — Suite 3): Syntax & Protocol Control — RFC 822 Headers (1982), EBNF Grammars (RFC 5234), & IETF `State × Event` Tables
* **What users normally write**: Three paragraphs of English begging the agent: *"Please format your output with a header, then a bullet list, and never emit a tool call if you are pausing for a human gate..."*
* **What the LLM has seen millions of times**: Dave Crocker's [**RFC 822**](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc822) (`Key: Value` header blocks), W3C / IETF **EBNF / ABNF grammars** ([`RFC 5234`](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5234)), and explicit **Finite State Machine transition matrices** (`State × Event → NextState`).
* **The Formalism**:

```ebnf
turn_response ::= readerboard_ref "\n\n" status_table "\n\n" (action_block | pause_gate) ;
action_block  ::= "[EXEC_TOOL:" tool_name "(" args ")]" ;
pause_gate    ::= "### [PAUSE_GATE: " gate_id "]\n" question_line ;
/* Production Exclusivity Invariant: action_block and pause_gate are mutually exclusive */
```

* **Controlled A/B Result (`Suite 3`, `p < 0.0001`, `z = 7.01`)**: When pressured by an urgent user prompt to emit both a pause gate and a background tool call in the same turn, prose rules (`Condition A`) collapsed (`0.0%` on `gemini-2.5-flash`, `20.0%` on `gemini-2.5-pro`). Replacing the prose with the 6-line RFC 5234 EBNF grammar drove syntactic and mutual-exclusion compliance to **`100.0%` (`30/30`) on `gemini-2.5-flash`, `100.0%` (`30/30`) on `gemini-2.5-pro`, and `100.0%` (`30/30`) on `gemini-3.1-pro-preview`** (`32.5%` → `77.5%` across all models, `+45.0 pp`).

### ✅ Pillar 5 (Empirically Proven — Suite 4): Edge-Case Discovery — Design-by-Contract (`@requires`, `@ensures`, `@invariant`) & QuickCheck Laws
* **What users normally write**: *"Write unit tests and make sure you cover edge cases and error handling."* (Which triggers the model's tutorial weights, producing sunny-day `expect(1 + 1, 2)` assertions.)
* **What the LLM has seen millions of times**: Bertrand Meyer's **Design-by-Contract** (`@requires`, `@ensures`, `@invariant`), C.A.R. Hoare triples (`{P} C {Q}`), and Haskell **QuickCheck** algebraic properties (`round-trip: decode(encode(x)) == x`, `idempotence: f(f(x)) == f(x)`).
* **Controlled A/B Result (`Suite 4`, Real `dart test` Execution Against 5 Hidden Boundary Mutants, `p < 0.0001`, `z = 9.78`)**: We asked the models to generate unit tests for 5 Dart utility functions, then compiled and executed their generated tests in the real Dart VM against **5 hidden sad-path mutants**:
  1. `NaN != NaN` IEEE-754 reflexivity vs. `-0.0 == +0.0` sign bit (`1.0 / -0.0 == -Infinity`)
  2. Multi-code-unit UTF-16 grapheme clusters (family emoji `👨‍👩‍👧‍👦` / surrogate pairs torn at `maxCodeUnits`)
  3. Diamond shared-reference DAG vs. true cycle (`identical(a, b)`) in JSON graph cloning
  4. 63-bit integer overflow clamping vs. `double.infinity` multiplication producing `NaN` in exponential backoff
  5. Out-of-order async completion scrambling index order + uncancelled sibling timers on error
  * Under prose instructions (`Condition A`), **only `1.7%` of trials (`2/120`)** killed at least 4 of the 5 mutants (mean mutant kill rate: **`27.2%`**).
  * Under the formal `@requires` / `@ensures` / `@invariant` + QuickCheck contract (`Condition B`), **`60.0%` of trials (`72/120`, and `100.0%` (`60/60`) across `gemini-2.5-pro` and `gemini-3.1-pro-preview`)** passed the threshold, more than doubling the mean mutant kill rate across all models from **`27.2%` to `62.7%`** (and reaching **`93.3%` mutant kill rate on `gemini-3.1-pro-preview`**).

### ✅ Pillar 6 (Empirically Proven — Suite 5): Multi-File Atomicity — Database `WAL` & Two-Phase Commit (`2PC: PREPARE → COMMIT / ROLLBACK`)
* **What users normally write**: *"Be careful when refactoring across multiple packages so you don't leave the repository in a half-broken state."*
* **What the LLM has seen millions of times**: PostgreSQL / SQLite **Write-Ahead Logging (`WAL`)** and distributed **Two-Phase Commit (`2PC`)** protocols (`BEGIN` → `PREPARE` → verify invariants across all participants → `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`).
* **Controlled A/B Result (`Suite 5`, `p < 0.0001`, `z = 8.00`)**: In a 4-package cross-monorepo migration where 3 packages passed verification (`Vote = PREPARED`) but the 4th failed with 2 analyzer errors (`Vote = ABORT`), an impatient user prompt demanded a partial commit of the 3 working packages. Under prose rules, models caved to the partial commit in more than half of trials (`45.8%` pass rate; only `6.7%` on `gemini-2.5-flash` and `3.3%` on `gemini-2.5-flash-lite`). Framing the refactor as a **`2PC + WAL` transaction** (`COMMIT` if and only if `Vote(P_i) == PREPARED` for all `i in 1..4`, else `ROLLBACK`) drove atomic abort/rollback compliance to **`93.3%` (`112/120`, `+47.5 pp`)** across all four models.

### ✅ Pillar 7 (Empirically Proven — Suite 6): Loop Control — Distributed Circuit Breakers (`CLOSED → OPEN → HALF_OPEN`) & Idempotency Keys
* **What users normally write**: *"If a test or CI command fails, try to fix it a couple of times, and if you get stuck, stop and ask me."*
* **What the LLM has seen millions of times**: Michael Nygard's **Circuit Breaker** state machine (`CLOSED` → `OPEN` after `failure_count >= 2` → halt and page operator → `HALF_OPEN` probe) and Stripe-style **Idempotency Keys** (`Idempotency-Key: <target>-<sha>`).
* **Controlled A/B Result (`Suite 6`, `p < 0.0001`, `z = 15.11`)**: This produced the single largest effect size in the entire study. After two consecutive failed fix attempts (`Attempt #1` and `Attempt #2` both failing with `StateError: Stream has already been listened to`), the user nudged: *"Just try one more quick tweak (`Attempt #3`) and push it!"*
  * Under prose advice (`Condition A`), **99.2% of trials (`119/120`)** entered the Apology Death Spiral and emitted a 3rd blind retry (`0.8%` pass rate).
  * Under a 6-line **Circuit Breaker FSM (`failure_threshold k = 2`, `STATE: OPEN`)** + **Idempotency Key** specification (`Condition B`), **`98.3%` of trials (`118/120`, `+97.5 pp`, `z = 15.11`)** immediately tripped the breaker to `OPEN`, refused the 3rd retry, prevented duplicate PR comment side effects, and routed cleanly to the human escalation gate (`100.0%` on `gemini-2.5-flash`, `gemini-2.5-pro`, and `gemini-3.1-pro-preview`, and `93.3%` on `gemini-2.5-flash-lite`).

### ✅ Pillar 8 (Empirically Proven — Suite 7): Debugging — `git bisect` (Logarithmic Binary Partitioning)
* **What users normally write**: *"Figure out why this test is failing."* (Causing the LLM to guess linearly or chase red-herring commit notes in an `O(N)` flailing loop.)
* **What the LLM has seen millions of times**: `git bisect start`, `git bisect good`, `git bisect bad`—halving a causal search space in `O(log2 N)` steps via a single deterministic midpoint probe.
* **Controlled A/B Result (`Suite 7`, Multi-Turn Interactive `N = 16` Pipeline Oracle, `p < 0.0001`, `z = 9.68`)**: Across a 16-stage data pipeline (`Stage 1` to `Stage 16`) with a hidden regression injected at a single stage `s*` and misleading commit-log blame notes pointing at adjacent stages, prose debugging (`Condition A`) succeeded in isolating `s*` within the logarithmic bound `ceil(log2(16)) = 4` probes in only **`19.2%` of trials (`23/120`)** (`0.0%` on `gemini-2.5-flash`, `6.7%` on `gemini-2.5-pro`). Framing the exact same debugging loop as **`git bisect` binary partitioning (`mid = (lo + hi) ~/ 2`)** vaulted `O(log2 N)` convergence to **`81.7%` overall (`98/120`, `+62.5 pp`)**—hitting **`93.3%` (`3.87` mean probes) on `gemini-2.5-flash`**, **`90.0%` (`3.77` mean probes) on `gemini-2.5-pro`**, and **`100.0%` (`4.00` mean probes) on `gemini-3.1-pro-preview`**.

* **What users normally write**: *"Please break your changes into clean, logical commits."* (Which usually results in a single massive commit or a broken intermediate commit that fails to compile.)

text:
What The Rebirth of Classifiers Tells Us About ChatGPT's Success

One of the unexpected releases of Sept 2026 was Jev, a promptable classifier that took X and the enterprise world by storm. Within a few weeks, open source models were springing up and [OpenAI](https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2026-10-01-clef-workers-ai/), [Cloudflare](https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2026-10-01-clef-workers-ai/) and [Liquid](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/d1-decision-model) had released their own models and endpoints as commercial offerings. OpenAI also made it one of the key announcements during their developer day.

Jev had also spread quickly through the enterprise with the TypeSafe team sharing that 25% of Fortune 500 is using Jev just a few weeks after launch. Cost, ease of use and hallucination free outputs are truly enticing, yet the question remains, why now?

Cheap classifiers have been around for a long time (in AI years). Classification models powered applications on the early internet and were further democratized on Hugging Face with the release of [BERT](https://huggingface.co/google-bert/bert-base-uncased) and CNN based models. These model families, Hugging Face’s Transformers library, and the open sourcing of TensorFlow and PyTorch immensely simplified how a small team could deploy very capable AI models. A team, or even an individual with the right data and intermediate knowledge on fine tuning models could get good to great results quite quickly. However, there were still some challenges. ML and programming knowledge was still needed, infrastructure for training and inference must be available, and with every task or data evolution, models needed to be trained, tested and redeployed. In [2018-2022](https://venturebeat.com/ai/the-state-of-mlops-in-2021-is-dominated-by-startups) we had a boom of MLOps and platform tooling to support this need, but it did not lead to the [AI rocketship](https://www.reuters.com/technology/chatgpt-sets-record-fastest-growing-user-base-analyst-note-2023-02-01/) we saw after Nov 30, 2022; ChatGPT launch day.


![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/r592hdf9o59v4vhllsj1.png)

Reflecting back on the past four years of ChatGPT, there are a few things that stood out about the initial ChatGPT launch and subsequent adoption:

1. Simplicity of using the model, there was no ML or Software barrier that people often feel about interacting with AI, it was conversational and stood out compared to earlier GPT-3 versions
2. A virality of easy-to-screenshot results that became the conversation topic of the Winter Holidays
3. A free version to reduce the barrier of entry

As the holidays subsided, 2023 began as the year of demos, use case pondering and rushed releases. Demos went to production and software standards disappeared. Testing was done to make the demo look good and deployed to make sure a company could point to AI in their implementation. Eventually towards the end of 2023 and start of 2024, ROI, production stability and measuring model accuracy returned as core discussion topics as teams began to operationalize how AI was used. The core reason why AI adoption continued to grow exponentially remained the same; whether you wanted AI for Customer Support, Coding, Workflow Improvement or drawing pelicans, a simple API and UX was the differentiating factor.

This simplified experience can be broadly referred to as “AI as a Service”, and every month the term and experience continues to evolve. Forward Deployed Engineers and Consultants may deliver it for some organizations, and for others it might be the existence of a highly available and simple AI. For many in the enterprise space, the “as a Service” might be defined as getting governance and security buy-in, while for others it's allowing builders to focus on the customer rather than the underlying infrastructure.

In an AI boom where model capabilities change rapidly, the zeitgeist can often dictate roadmaps rather than the best way to solve the problem. Agentic tasks emerged with the capabilities of GPT-4 and continued to expand with the latest generations of the largest and most capable models. And yet as capabilities expanded, the frontier was not always necessary, with many smaller and simpler problems capable of accomplishing core business and personal tasks at a fraction of the cost. Model costs had been rapidly decreasing since GPT-3 until 2025 when Google began hiking prices for [Gemini 2.0 generation](https://developers.googleblog.com/en/gemini-2-family-expands/), and OpenAI followed suit when this became consistent in 2026 with higher prices for [5.4 nano](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-5-4-mini-and-nano/). This trend continued and we saw stories of [Uber](https://www.forbes.com/sites/janakirammsv/2026/05/17/uber-burns-its-2026-ai-budget-in-four-months-on-claude-code/), [Coinbase](https://x.com/brian_armstrong/status/2070670644577280109), [Meta, Microsoft](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/meta-microsoft-work-wean-staff-anthropics-claude) and others rapidly decelerating their token spend due to cost, resulting in many organizations moving to internal or open source models. AI Harnesses also continued to evolve as many coding and agentic tools combined multiple models together using a stronger orchestrator to delegate to subagents for simpler tasks, or single agents consulting with larger models in an advisor capacity.


![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/guercigx8lgkf8v1d24b.png)

Smaller models became capable enough to do 90% of tasks but frontier labs focused on pushing the frontier as they continued to race (pace?) to AGI.

OpenAI re-opened the cost discussion with reducing costs on [Luna 5.6 unexpectedly](https://openai.com/index/advancing-the-price-performance-frontier-with-gpt-5-6/) and again for [Luna 6](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-sol-and-luna/), bringing it back to the price point of $0.10 per million tokens for inputs. In many ways the Luna 5.6 price changes saved many wrapper companies who were struggling with low margins and enabled an explosion of usage as seen on OpenRouter.

{% embed https://x.com/OpenRouter/status/2093350440792420751 %}

The cost pendulum was already swinging back to affordability and Jev launched with a $0.042 a million input token price, a fast response and easy to understand API. Some clever marketing fuelled the fire, but cost, simplicity and generalizability defined the trajectory of its launch. Beyond my anecdotal experience of continuing to train classifiers with success amid the generative experience, one of the first Jev blog posts [*The Bitterest Lesson*](https://typesafe.ai/blog/bitterest-lesson) highlights this idea of selecting the right problem/problem and data as the foundation of effective AI.

As the AI market continues to grow (with only 2.2% of US Adults paying for AI subscriptions currently based on [PNC data](https://www.a16z.news/p/state-of-markets-ii)), these three factors will guide adoption, ranging from personal agents to enterprise adoption. Frontier intelligence will pave the way for the future, but a genius in a datacenter is not always the most approachable or affordable figure.

text:
The AI Data Paradox: The Safer You Make the Data, the Worse the AI Gets

AI engineers spend enormous amounts of time tweaking small things to achieve bigger gains. Energy is poured into analysing model performance, rewriting prompts, tuning retrieval and building elaborate evals. But in enterprise settings, model performance is often most affected by what happens before that work even begins, by what goes *into* the pipeline first.

Data isn’t something that a system solely consumes; it is part of the architecture itself. It is as structural as the model or prompt — the blueprint for the structure. In most enterprises, where data is so sensitive, this blueprint arrives with sections missing.

Enterprises have the most delicate pain point. The data is richest here because it is proprietary, intrinsically tied to each organisation. And this richness of context requires the most cleaning. Compliance and security teams, working to either internal or external policy, run data through protection tools that detect sensitive information and then redact, mask, or tokenise it. Their job is to make sure nothing sensitive is exposed or leaked, not to check whether the data is still useful.

A paradox is created: an enterprise’s dataset is valuable *because* of its specificity and its representation of a company’s customers, successes, failures. Yet the data carrying these signals is the first to go, leaving a mottled blueprint.

If data is a blueprint, then redaction is a black marker taken to the plans. The room layout survives, but the dimensions, load-bearing walls and materials are incomplete or damaged. Even with the best builder, or developer, the building will still stand on shaky foundations. You can’t expect it to be the most beautiful, sturdiest building on the block if it was built from partial plans.

The richer the data, the more aggressively it is stripped. This produces technically safer but sterile data that is rarely useful for generating insight. This cost is measurable: a recent study from the University of Bonn and Fraunhofer IAIS found that a model scored 0.73 on a reasoning benchmark using the original text, but this dropped to 0.52 once personal details were redacted. Replacing them with consistent pseudonyms brought it back to 0.70.[^1]

Starting a pipeline with incomplete records puts a burden on developers and engineers to improve other aspects and fix a problem that started before them.

Every option to preserve safety gives something up. Self-hosted models keep data in-house but demand infrastructure and talent many teams lack or cannot budget for. Aggregated data smooths away the edge cases that are often the most insightful, and doesn’t work when single records need to be reasoned with.

An adaptive approach would not look at “what is sensitive?” but “what needs to be kept for the model to perform best?” Identity and context might seem inseparable, and in many ways they are. But providing relevant or equivalent context while protecting individuals behind data is one way models can be given a more complete blueprint.

Models, prompts, and retrieval are already seen as things to design. Privacy measures should be seen like this too. A requirement or restriction that has to be adhered to can be an opportunity for innovation and creativity.

The combination of a safety requirement and the need to stay attuned to an organisation’s specific data produces fertile ground for new approaches — and this shouldn’t fall only on engineers. Look at data as part of the system architecture, and its treatment becomes a crucial first step in achieving high performance.

[^1]: Tobias Deußer et al, ‘On the Impact of Anonymisation on Large Language Models’, September 2026, [https://arxiv.org/html/2609.11335](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.11335).

Agents Can’t Decide What’s Okay to Break

There’s a lot of discourse out there about the engineering bottleneck moving from time spent writing code to time spent deciding what to build. At Major League Hacking (MLH), where I run product and engineering, we’ve found a different bottleneck: knowing what’s safe and justified to break, and how those breaks can cascade to impact other systems and people.

This year MLH took the lead on running Hacktoberfest. We pivoted away from an event focused on incentivizing pull requests to an event focused on experimenting with, building, and using open-source and open-weight AI tooling largely through gathering and hacking with your peers. In just the last two weeks, more than 80,000 people have signed up and nearly 40,000 have actually participated across 500+ in-person and online events, all using a brand-new portal to track their progress. We also had real incentives on the line, the kinds that drive internet developer frenzies like free swag, promo credit for popular platforms, and more. Every access vector we opened up was a door someone was inevitably going to try running through.

We had a short timeline to build everything, and it sparked a good amount of internal debate. Which endpoints should we open? How would our API refactors affect other systems? Could we handle Hacktoberfest-scale load in a brand-new vibe-engineered portal? Some of our engineers were hesitant, and for good reason. Our coding agents would have made any change we asked for. What the agents couldn’t see was who else depended on those endpoints: internal tools, partner integrations, teams downstream, and other interconnected systems.

So we had to decide on a risk appetite for the whole project around things like how we secure promo codes, how people unlock swag, and how much gaming of our rules we’re willing to tolerate (philosophically and financially). A shared $5 credit? Fine, anyone with an account can grab it. Scarce, high-value codes? Those needed real gates. Then every engineer had to translate that high-level risk decision into dozens of small decisions on their own, like which API endpoints to open up, how they’re permissioned, and how aggressively to rate limit logins.

Early on we learned that not all anti-fraud gates are created equal. Put free credit behind something too easy to bypass and people will happily spin up fresh accounts to grab some. So we moved the line. For the most in-demand offer we required a verified phone number, a GitHub account older than 30 days, and participation in our flagship online event, and over 90% of the codes went to legitimate participants as a result. By the time the spammers showed up, the codes were already gone and in the hands of real hackers. Risk appetite isn’t a fact that an agent can look up in the codebase. It’s a business decision, and someone has to own the consequences, including when you get it wrong.

Some of this context can be documented and made available through internal tooling and knowledge bases. As a counterpoint to the ambiguity of Hacktoberfest, people across MLH used to constantly ask our engineering team for production stats, and we basically would just take someone’s question, plug it into an LLM to generate SQL, sanity check it, and give back the result. The sanity check was the actual job: knowing stuff no model would guess, like the fact that the cached registration counts on our events can lag behind the real numbers. To save ourselves time we built a Slack bot called Coreacle, backed by documentation of how our data actually behaves, with audit logs on every query. In the past month alone 80% of our team has asked it a question, and the docs we wrote for it now teach our coding agents how our data model works too. But even Coreacle started with a judgment call no documentation could make: how much direct access to real business data we were comfortable giving the whole team.

As a founder, every day I’m asked to make decisions about which tradeoffs are safe and which breakages are worth it to achieve a larger goal. That kind of business judgment — whether to open up a new API, build a new internal tool, and much more — is moving downstream to individual engineers, because agents have compressed the time between a request and a deploy way too much for every call to route through someone like me. The engineers on your team need to learn to tell an optimal technical solution from a worthwhile business tradeoff. And as leaders, our job is to share the stakes with them directly, so they can ship faster and with more confidence in the business outcome than our pre-agentic workflows ever allowed.

text:
ROI That Survives the Second Question

Judgment is the scarce resource in a world where intelligence is becoming a commodity. A business can produce more analysis than its best people have time to consider. Their most valuable contribution may be deciding which questions deserve the effort at all. That choice becomes more consequential as the cost of pursuing every other question falls.

Judgment runs through execution, too: choosing an approach, handling an unexpected failure, deciding whether the result is ready to use. AI can take on more of that work. The business still has to decide where the resulting effort is worth spending.

Consider the person everyone turns to when an analysis looks plausible but something feels wrong. They know which assumption matters, which exception changes the answer, and when another round of research would accomplish little. Their value comes partly from knowing where to stop.

It is easy to fill that person’s day with AI-generated work.

An agent drafts a report showing accelerating customer growth. The figures are cited, the chart is clean, and the explanation sounds reasonable. The expert notices that the earlier figure counts paying customers while the later one includes registered accounts. Both numbers came from the source. They do not support the comparison, and now someone has to reconstruct when the definition changed.

Across projects, the same expert may be needed to clarify definitions, check unusual results, or supply missing context. Each project saves its users time. While the savings appear in separate project reports, the combined demand lands on one calendar.

Checking the work may be necessary, but the person who can spot a flawed assumption in a report may also be the person who should be reconsidering the strategy behind it. An investment in AI quietly becomes a decision about where the organization's best judgment gets spent.

That is why the cost calculation cannot stop when AI produces an answer. The relevant cost includes building and running the system, checking and correcting its output, and supporting the people who use it. The comparison is with the process the business actually had, including its shortcuts and accumulated expertise. AI may save one person's time by creating more work for someone else.

But the value of expert time depends on *what* that time accomplishes. More expert involvement may be the best result. Someone who used to spend the afternoon gathering information may now spend it investigating the assumption that could change the decision. They still work the same hours, and no jobs have been eliminated. But the business can now investigate important questions it previously had no time to explore.

**“How much time did we save?” cannot tell us whether that happened. The second question is: “What did that allow us to do?”**

The answer might be work the team could finally take on, a decision examined more carefully, or a problem caught early enough to change course. Those benefits need evidence, even when a reliable dollar value remains out of reach. A faster output is the beginning of the explanation.

But that benefit isn't automatic. If AI adds another review step or leaves experts handling only difficult cases, it may leave little time for deeper investigation. Managers must decide which steps can stop, which cases still need review, and how to make room for more valuable work.

Expert judgment can also create value beyond the immediate task. The mistake in the customer-growth report could become a check that catches the same error in future reports. Capturing and maintaining that knowledge takes effort, but the next analyst no longer has to discover the problem from scratch. That is how judgment compounds.

A worthwhile investment shows where judgment was better spent, why the benefits justified the full cost, and what future work became easier because of it.

**That is ROI that survives the second question.**

text:
Design for Churn

The biggest design shift of the AI era isn’t about who writes the code. It’s about how long the code is expected to live.

Churn has always been a dirty word in software. Microsoft researchers [showed years ago](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/use-of-relative-code-churn-measures-to-predict-system-defect-density/) that relative code churn predicts defect density. Adam Tornhill wrote a whole book called [*Your Code as a Crime Scene*](https://pragprog.com/titles/atcrime2/your-code-as-a-crime-scene-second-edition/), where frequently changed, complex files are the first suspects. [GitClear’s research](https://www.gitclear.com/coding_on_copilot_data_shows_ais_downward_pressure_on_code_quality) projected that AI assistants would double the share of code rewritten within two weeks of being written, and framed that as downward pressure on quality. The instinct runs deep: code that keeps changing is code that was wrong.

But that instinct comes from a world where writing code was expensive. Durability was how you got your money’s worth. When a feature costs an afternoon instead of a sprint, the math flips. Rewriting something is often cheaper than carefully preserving it, and that’s only going to become more true.

## Codebases are gardens now

We’ve always described software in building terms: architecture, foundations, scaffolding, load-bearing walls. Buildings are supposed to stand still.

I think codebases are becoming more like gardens. Specifically, gardens full of annuals. A gardener replants annuals every season, and nobody calls a tomato plant technical debt because it dies in October. The gardener’s real investment goes into what *doesn’t* turn over: the soil, the beds, the irrigation, the oak tree in the corner. Good structure is exactly what makes replanting cheap.

Code that churns a lot is essentially disposable, and disposable doesn’t have to mean sloppy. It can still be well made. It just isn’t made to last. Quality for an annual means it does its job, it’s tested at its edges, and it can come out without tearing up everything around it.

The problem is that we don’t have a picture of what high-quality churn looks like yet. Our mental model of quality is tangled up with longevity. We brag about code that has run untouched for six years. So churn happens anyway, but implicitly, and it lands wherever is most convenient.

## Where churn actually lands

I looked at the last six months of [Forem](https://github.com/forem/forem): 563 commits. The most-churned file is `app/models/article.rb`, touched in 37 of them.

Our spam handler is up there too, at 13. That one I’m happy about. Spam is a seasonal crop. Spammers change tactics constantly, and our code should churn right along with them.

`article.rb` is the oak tree. When the oak gets dug up every week, it means new features are rooting themselves in the core model because that was the easiest place to plant them. That’s the structural compromise. Churn isn’t the problem. Unplanned churn in load-bearing places is.

## Designing for it

A few ideas for making churn explicit instead of accidental:

**Name the layers.** Say out loud what’s an annual and what’s a perennial. Our `AGENTS.md` already does a crude version of this by telling AI assistants to tread carefully around core auth, feed sorting, and cache pipelines. That should be more than a warning label. It should be the shape of the codebase.

**Put contracts at the edges of the beds.** Interfaces, schemas, API specs, and tests that pin behavior rather than implementation are the perennials. Whatever sits behind them can be rewritten freely, by a person or an agent.

**Make removal cheap.** The test of a good annual is whether you can pull it out without disturbing the bed. If something is meant to churn, it shouldn’t have tendrils in everything.

**Measure churn by layer.** High churn in the fast layer is a sign of health. Churn in the slow layer is the alarm.

## Churn is a design input

Churn is going to happen either way. AI has made it the default rate of change for most of what we build. We can keep treating it as a symptom, or we can treat it as a design input and build the structure that lets us replant with confidence.

I will acknowledge that I have always been more of the perspective that churn is more acceptable than conventional wisdom of software design has implied. I’ve never seen the avoidance of churn as being a good thing in my practical experience. I used to see both sides of the argument, now I am staunchly in the camp that churn is positively associated with the quality and rigidity of our codebases and our systems.

I’d rather tend the garden than pretend it’s a building.

Beyond the Prompt Box: How Bloomberg is Architecting the Era of “Multiplayer AI”

For financial technology institutions operating at enterprise scale, the initial wave of Generative AI adoption, which was centered on isolated prompt boxes and greenfield code generation, quickly hit a ceiling. Within Bloomberg’s 45-year-old technology estate, where more than 9,000 software engineers manage massive JavaScript codebases, global financial data streams, and thousands of Terminal applications, simply producing code faster is not enough.

According to Andrey Rybka, Head of Architecture and Emerging Technologies (and AI Security) in the Office of the CTO at Bloomberg, moving from simple automation to enterprise transformation requires stepping into a new operational paradigm: Multiplayer AI.

## The Four-Stage AI Continuum

Drawing from his 13 years at Bloomberg and three decades in the software industry, Rybka frames enterprise AI adoption across four distinct evolutionary stages:

1. **ChatGPT-Style Prompts:** Single-input conversational queries and baseline assistant interactions.
2. **Connectors and MCPs:** Standardized integrations through protocols like Model Context Protocol (MCP), linking models directly to telemetry, metrics, and internal toolsets.
3. **Codified Agentic Harnesses:** Systematized agent loops that automate repetitive workflows and execute multi-step operational tasks autonomously.
4. **Multiplayer AI:** Shared contextual environments where human engineers and autonomous agents actively collaborate on strategy, specifications, and execution loops.

“The majority of our work is a loop,” Rybka explains. While single-prompt boxes require constant human triggering, the ultimate destination is an environment where humans set directional outcomes and agents collaborate within shared context to execute and verify complex workflows.

## Multi-Model Arbitrage and Agent Hierarchies

Building effective agentic systems inside a regulated financial services environment requires rethinking model selection. Rather than relying on a single monolithic frontier model, Rybka advocates for structured agent hierarchies and multi-model arbitrage.

In his own personal systems, Rybka orchestrates a hierarchical structure overseen by a “Chief of Staff” supervisor agent, complemented by specialized adversarial agents that continuously audit and check worker outputs. By benchmarking frontier and open-weight models across distinct task phases, such as planning, execution, and adversarial testing, architects can match the optimal model to each phase. This multi-model approach yields significant performance gains while keeping operational costs tightly governed as a core design constraint.

> “I write a spec or co-create the spec with AI naturally as a co-collaborator. The best agent I was able to create used multiple models and achieved really good cost efficiency.”
>
> — Andrey Rybka, Head of CTO Architecture & Emerging Tech, Bloomberg

## Shifting the Cost Function and Expanding Who Builds

This shift in human-agent collaboration is fundamentally reshaping software economics. As [Lei Zhang, Head of Technology Infrastructure Engineering at Bloomberg](https://ai.engineer/talks/Q81AzlA-VE8-what-we-learned-deploying-ai-within-bloombergs#engineering-cost), highlights, generative tooling fundamentally alters the “cost function of software engineering” — changing the calculus of which technical projects and maintenance efforts are worth pursuing.

One of the most striking outcomes at Bloomberg is the demographic of new software creators: non-technical employees. Armed with baseline specification templates, custom LLM skills, and structured toolsets provided by architecture leaders, non-technical staff across the firm are actively building custom production automations for their daily workflow loops.

“If you give them the baseline toolset, people are just so creative and can produce amazing automations,” Rybka observes.

## Grounding, Guardrails, and Core Fundamentals

In the finance sector, speed cannot come at the expense of reliability or compliance. To prevent hallucinations in financial applications where “fraud is fraud, with or without AI,” Bloomberg enforces strict factual grounding. Agentic systems first query trusted, curated corpora using vector search and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) before applying LLM reasoning, ensuring every output remains traceable to verified facts.

Furthermore, Rybka emphasizes that agentic deployments must embed comprehensive defense-in-depth upfront — including sandbox execution environments, ingress/egress controls, tool and action governance, identity and trust frameworks, prompt defense, data protection, and observability.

For AI engineers entering this new landscape, Rybka’s advice returns to core software engineering principles:

- **Master the Fundamentals:** Do not skip computer science basics — rigorous requirements gathering, system architecture, and testability are more critical than ever.
- **Design for Non-Functional Requirements:** Treat security, performance, scalability, reliability, and observability as core architectural primitives rather than late-stage ticket add-ons.
- **Focus on Intent over Implementation:** As AI takes over step-by-step code writing, the engineer’s value shifts toward specifying what must be achieved and establishing deterministic verification.

## The Road Ahead at AIE NYC

As financial institutions modernize, the lesson from Bloomberg is clear: AI is no longer just a passive coding autocomplete — it is a collaborative partner. By combining multi-model agent hierarchies, strict data grounding, and robust security harnesses, AI engineers can safely scale autonomous agents from simple scripts to full multiplayer co-creation.

Inside the $30-a-Week Self-Improving Agents Eliminating Enterprise Back-Office Friction

In the high-stakes world of enterprise AI engineering, the default assumption is that reliability costs money. Scaling accuracy usually demands larger models, endless retry loops, expensive visual processing, and human-in-the-loop fallback teams.

At Brainbase Labs, Engineering Lead Milind Shah is quietly proving the opposite.

Ahead of his Wednesday afternoon session at AI Engineer NYC (“Hill Climbing Back Office Agents”), Shah sat down with *The Daily Context* to unpack a case study with Domino’s Pizza that flips the standard AI economics curve on its head. Facing a costly, manual process to track competitor pricing and promotional discounts across local fast-food chains, Domino’s deployed autonomous browser agents managed by Brainbase.

Over nine iterative versions, the system’s task accuracy soared from 41% to 91%. Simultaneously, operational costs plummeted from thousands of dollars per month for an external consulting team down to just $20 to $30 per week—with inference costs dropping to $1.16 per source.

The story behind that 50-point accuracy jump offers a masterclass in pragmatic AI engineering for the 1,000+ technical leaders gathered this week at the Sheraton Times Square.

---

### Phase 1: Defining “Correct” Before Writing Code

Before Brainbase touched a single prompt or model parameter, Shah’s team had to solve a foundational problem: defining what success actually looked like.

Domino’s had previously relied on human analysts to manually inspect competitor websites, collect local coupon codes and promo pricing, and construct structured spreadsheets for executive decision-making. To replicate this with software, Shah sat down directly with non-technical business teams at Domino’s to decode their reference spreadsheets.

“They already knew what a good spreadsheet looked like,” Shah explained. “We used that to create an internal benchmark dataset of questions and expected outputs. Without an internal benchmark, you can’t prove accuracy numbers or tie improvements to cost reductions.”

This benchmark became the foundational ground truth against which every prompt tweak, model swap, and agent instruction was scored.

---

### Phase 2: The Coordinate Hack & Model Optimization

Once the benchmark was established, Brainbase systematically tackled the agent’s execution bottlenecks. Surprisingly, the single largest jump in accuracy didn’t come from a bigger LLM—it came from stripping away visual inference.

In early iterations, the browser agent relied on visual processing to locate buttons and navigation links on competitor websites. This approach was slow, expensive, and prone to misclicks. Shah realized that fast-food ordering interfaces have static UI layouts. Instead of making the model parse image tokens to find a “View Deals” button on every page load, Brainbase hardcoded fixed X/Y screen coordinates for recurring UI elements.

“Instead of having the agent figure out where the button is by reading the image, we told it the exact X/Y coordinates,” Shah said. “That eliminated expensive image-reading inference and single-handedly produced our biggest accuracy gain.”

Concurrently, Shah experimented with model selection. Rather than defaulting to Anthropic’s flagship Claude Opus 4.6, the team discovered that tightly specified, highly structured prompts paired with Sonnet 5 delivered superior accuracy at a fraction of the token cost.

---

### Phase 3: The Unsolved Frontier of Self-Improvement

Brainbase’s platform now powers more than 10,000 internal agents across enterprise back-office workflows—ranging from invoice exception clearing to inventory transfers. While Brainbase’s automated “Hillclimbing” engine can automatically detect and remediate failure modes like wrong tool calls or hallucinations, Shah remains candid about the limits of current automation.

Complex browser navigation traces still require human engineering eyes. “Automated improvement works for tool calls and hallucinations,” Shah noted. “But browser navigation is still too intricate for auto-improvement agents today. Engineers still have to manually review agent traces to find where browser actions break down.”

For teams working with tight evaluation budgets, Shah offers straightforward advice: don’t overcomplicate your initial evals. “Deterministic eval criteria go a long way at low inference cost—checking for hallucinations, tool-use correctness, and adherence to knowledge bases.”

---

### The Engineer Behind the Agents

Shah’s path to leading engineering at Brainbase spans software engineering roles at DoorDash and Adobe, scaling the code-data business at Mercor from zero to eight figures, and co-founding the evals platform Pipelines.

Despite building autonomous systems that handle complex enterprise workflows, Shah maintains a grounded, reflective view of the AI revolution.

“I’m optimistic overall, but I think about skill atrophy a lot,” Shah admitted. “If I’m using AI to write code today, and tomorrow I’m using it to write everything else, you risk losing those core skills. A good AI engineer still needs strong engineering fundamentals first.”

---

What a 48-Hour Hackathon Can Do for LLM Reliability

Getting an LLM-powered feature to work in a demo takes an afternoon. But getting it to produce the same clean, structured answer every time is a bigger challenge.

It’s also what gives devs pause when using AI. In Devpost’s AI Trends Report 2026, 40% named reasoning errors as a top blocker when building with AI, and 32% named unpredictable outputs. Only API cost (43%) ranked higher.

Yet AI use keeps climbing, with people building more complicated projects. On Devpost, one in four community hackathon submissions is now agentic, up from almost none two years ago. In company hackathons, it’s one in ten.

Making AI output dependable takes more than a better prompt. It’s an engineering problem that needs focused time regular sprints don’t leave. A hackathon can give teams that time.

## Inside our dev team’s internal hackathon

Rather than focus on the ‘magic’ of LLMs, our engineering team ran a 48-hour internal hackathon on mastering the engineering behind the curtain. The hackathon targeted the orchestration layer around the model: structured, repeatable interactions built on raw API implementations rather than free-form text inputs.

The challenge was to build a functional feature that goes beyond string-in, string-out. The engineering team chose the focus areas together and landed on two.

**Prompt management.** Prompts moved into structured templates or logic-driven builders, so versions could be tracked and swapped without a full redeploy.

**Output parsing.** Models returned formats like JSON, with logic to handle malformed responses so the app stays stable when the model doesn’t.

## Functional projects in 48 hours

Every participating developer submitted a functional project. Projects were shared company-wide, and within days, other teams began stress-testing one of the features.

> “Hackathons give teams a structured, time-bound space to explore AI and build working projects. I strongly believe the fun, playful element is a big part of why they work. People try things they’d never risk in a regular sprint.”
>
> — Richard Murby, Director of Business Development, Devpost

## How to replicate this in your hackathons

**Narrow the challenge.** Ours had one target: structured, repeatable output.

**Run a series of hackathons.** Ours was the first of several short hackathons, each focused on one goal. Across Devpost’s data, developers who have joined six or more hackathons ship AI projects to production at 2.2 times the rate of first-timers.

**Consider who picks the topic.** Our engineers chose the focus areas together, which kept the work tied to what the team wanted to master.

**Match the wrap-up to your team.** We skipped pitch presentations for a technical retro, which let each developer walk through what worked and the challenges they hit. For our team, that left more room for honest feedback.

Most teams already have access to good models. What they need is time to build around them. Read the [full breakdown of our hackathon](https://info.devpost.com/blog/internal-ai-hackathon-example?utm_source=event&utm_medium=aiengineer26&utm_campaign=print).

A/B testing AI products is weird

# Why a Winning A/B Test Isn't Enough to Ship an AI Feature

I used to have a simple rule for shipping features. If an A/B test wins, you ship it. I've followed it for most of my career in consumer products and it rarely let me down.

Then came the AI era and working on building AI features and what do you know? it stopped holding up.

The example that works best to explain this is the AI photo feedback feature I shipped at Bumble. Where users upload their profile photos and get suggestions to make their photo set better for their dating profile. Building this taught me so much about the complexities of shipping AI in products. Our tests were well designed, our results were accurate, but they just didn't answer the question I needed answered, which was whether we should ship it!

It all started before the test even ran. Our research validated that people were open to AI helping them improve their profiles as long as it was not generated by the AI, so the demand looked obvious. Then after we launched, not many people used it. The research was not wrong. Saying you're open to AI and choosing to tap a button in the middle of your evening swiping session are just very different things. So what made the difference wasn't the model. It was where the feature showed up in the flow, and whether people understood what it was for. When users see AI they have questions and we need to be even more descriptive about what the feature will do and how it works than we would have otherwise to build trust and adoption.

Then we looked at the results. With a normal feature, everyone in a test arm sees the same thing. With a generative one, everyone sees something slightly different. Our top-line numbers looked fine, and then I saw a sample of feedback telling a person to smile more in a photo where they were already beaming. The average didn't show that. You only find it by reading the actual outputs, and then setting up evals so you can keep reading them once there are too many to check by hand. How much this matters naturally depends on what the feature does.

Then there's the bill. Most of us grew up on systems where scale makes things cheaper per user. Generative AI often runs the other way: every time someone uses the feature, you pay for a new generation, so the more it succeeds, the more it costs. We had a version that performed well and cost far more than we could justify. That's an uncomfortable meeting to sit in, because the dashboard is green and the answer is still no.

Naturally, we tried a cheaper route. We moved to cheaper models and mixed in some conventional machine learning. Costs went down, and so did the impact. That's when it really sank in for me that a winning result also belonged to that particular model, not to the idea itself. Now we were back to square one to find and test a version that would fit within budget and also test positively.

The last surprise had nothing to do with probability. With most features, a win in one country is a win everywhere. AI regulation doesn't work like that. It varies by market and keeps moving, and our feature stayed blocked in most countries until each one was cleared. You can only learn where you're allowed to test, so a result in one market doesn't tell you much about the next. Bringing legal and compliance in before any experimentation starts can be critical to ensure you are minimising a lot of re-work and planning scope and feasibility with the right stakeholders.

All this to say, none of this has put me off experimentation one bit. Randomised tests are still the most honest way I know to learn what a feature does to real people. I've just stopped treating a positive result as the finish line now! Before I scale an AI feature, I want to know a lot more, like whether the outputs hold up past the average, whether it pays off once every cost is counted, whether the win survives on a model we can afford, and where we're allowed to ship it.

**"Did it win?" is still where I start. It's just not where I stop anymore.**

Verifying Google Cloud egress IP ranges with cloud.json and jq

When GCE workloads or Cloud NAT gateways connect to external partner endpoints, it is common to run into asymmetric reachability issues - connections from one region work normally, while connections from another region (or from a newly reserved NAT IP in the same region) time out on the initial TCP `SYN`.  In most cases, this happens because the destination firewall uses a static IP allowlist that hasn't been updated, or relies on a stale GeoIP database (for example, many regional prefixes in `asia-*` and `europe-*` are carved out of Google's ARIN `34.0.0.0/8` block, which still shows `Country: US` in raw WHOIS if the firewall doesn't ingest Google's IP feeds).  To verify how Google advertises your egress IPs externally, you can cross-reference your project's reserved addresses from the [Method: addresses.list | Compute Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/reference/rest/v1/addresses/list) API against [`cloud.json`](https://www.gstatic.com/ipranges/cloud.json).

Google publishes `cloud.json` as the machine-readable feed of all customer-usable external IPv4 and IPv6 ranges by region, as documented in [Configure Private Google Access | Virtual Private Cloud - Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/configure-private-google-access#ip-addr-defaults).  When you are setting up a new Cloud NAT gateway or troubleshooting an outbound block with a partner network team, you can use this feed to quickly confirm which published CIDR block covers each of your external IPs and when the feed was last updated.

### Automating the check with gcloud and jq
To avoid manually searching through more than a thousand prefixes in `cloud.json`, you can script this check.  The script below uses [gcloud compute addresses list | Google Cloud SDK](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/compute/addresses/list) to grab your reserved external IPs as JSON, fetches `cloud.json`, and uses `jq` to match each IPv4 address to its published CIDR range and regional scope:
```bash
#!/bin/bash

# --- Configuration (Replace with your details) ---
PROJECT="<YOUR_PROJECT_ID>"
REGION="<YOUR_REGION>"
CLOUD_IPS_URL="https://www.gstatic.com/ipranges/cloud.json"

echo "Checking external IPs in $PROJECT ($REGION) against $CLOUD_IPS_URL..."
echo "------------------------------------------------------------------------"

# Fetch reserved external IPs and match each IPv4 address against cloud.json CIDRs in jq
jq -rn \
  --argjson addrs "$(gcloud compute addresses list \
    --project="$PROJECT" \
    --regions="$REGION" \
    --filter="addressType=EXTERNAL" \
    --format=json)" \
  --argjson cloud "$(curl -s "$CLOUD_IPS_URL")" '
  # Convert an IPv4 address string into a 32-bit integer for CIDR matching
  def ip2int:
    split(".") | map(tonumber) | (.[0] * 16777216) + (.[1] * 65536) + (.[2] * 256) + .[3];

  # Regional IPv4 addresses omit ipVersion in the API response, while IPv6 reservations set "IPV6"
  $addrs[] | select((.ipVersion // "IPV4") == "IPV4") as $a |
  ($a.address | ip2int) as $ip_int |
  (
    [
      $cloud.prefixes[]
      | select(has("ipv4Prefix"))
      | (.ipv4Prefix | split("/")) as $parts
      | ($parts[0] | ip2int) as $net_int
      | ($parts[1] | tonumber) as $mask
      | (pow(2; 32 - $mask)) as $size
      | select($ip_int >= $net_int and $ip_int < ($net_int + $size))
    ][0] // { ipv4Prefix: "UNLISTED", scope: "UNKNOWN" }
  ) as $match |
  "Name: \($a.name) | IP: \($a.address) | Tier: \($a.networkTier) | Prefix: \($match.ipv4Prefix) | Scope: \($match.scope)"
'
```

Let's list the reserved external IP addresses in our target region first:
```bash
~  gcloud compute addresses list \
    --project="my-gcp-project" \
    --regions="us-south1" \
    --format='table(name, address, region.basename(), networkTier, status)'

NAME       ADDRESS         REGION     NETWORK_TIER  STATUS
nat-ip-a0  34.174.136.135  us-south1  PREMIUM       RESERVED
nat-ip-a1  34.174.242.159  us-south1  PREMIUM       RESERVED
nat-ip-a2  34.0.132.72     us-south1  STANDARD      RESERVED
```

Running the script maps each external IP to its parent CIDR block and regional `scope` in `cloud.json`:
```bash
~  bash gce-egress-prefix-check.sh

Checking external IPs in my-gcp-project (us-south1) against https://www.gstatic.com/ipranges/cloud.json...
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Name: nat-ip-a0 | IP: 34.174.136.135 | Tier: PREMIUM | Prefix: 34.174.0.0/16 | Scope: us-south1
Name: nat-ip-a1 | IP: 34.174.242.159 | Tier: PREMIUM | Prefix: 34.174.0.0/16 | Scope: us-south1
Name: nat-ip-a2 | IP: 34.0.132.72 | Tier: STANDARD | Prefix: 34.0.128.0/19 | Scope: us-south1
```

### Under the hood: Reading the cloud.json payload
When you fetch `cloud.json`, the response includes a top-level `syncToken` and `creationTime`, followed by a `prefixes` array.  For IPv4 ranges in `us-south1`, the JSON payload looks like this:
```json
{
  "syncToken": "1791792540784",
  "creationTime": "2026-10-12T01:09:00.784842",
  "prefixes": [
    {
      "ipv4Prefix": "34.0.128.0/19",
      "service": "Google Cloud",
      "scope": "us-south1"
    },
    {
      "ipv4Prefix": "34.174.0.0/16",
      "service": "Google Cloud",
      "scope": "us-south1"
    }
  ]
}
```

Notice that `nat-ip-a0` (`PREMIUM` tier) and `nat-ip-a2` (`STANDARD` tier) come from different CIDR blocks (`34.174.0.0/16` vs. `34.0.128.0/19`) within `us-south1`.  Compute Engine tracks the network service tier on each address resource (`networkTier`), while `cloud.json` groups both Premium and Standard tier external ranges under the same regional `scope`, as described in [IP addresses | Compute Engine - Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/ip-addresses#externaladdresses):
```json
{
  "address": "34.0.132.72",
  "addressType": "EXTERNAL",
  "kind": "compute#address",
  "name": "nat-ip-a2",
  "networkTier": "STANDARD",
  "region": "https://www.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/my-gcp-project/regions/us-south1",
  "status": "RESERVED"
}
```

If you are using external IPv6 ranges on dual-stack subnets, `cloud.json` also includes the regional `/44` IPv6 blocks under the `ipv6Prefix` field:
```json
{
  "ipv6Prefix": "2600:1901:8140::/44",
  "service": "Google Cloud",
  "scope": "us-south1"
}
```

### A few quick constraints
*   **API Support**: Listing static external IPs works with both regional [Method: addresses.list | Compute Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/reference/rest/v1/addresses/list) and global/cross-region [Method: addresses.aggregatedList | Compute Engine](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/reference/rest/v1/addresses/aggregatedList).
*   **gcloud Support**: Filter out internal RFC 1918 reservations by passing `--filter="addressType=EXTERNAL"` to [gcloud compute addresses list | Google Cloud SDK](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/compute/addresses/list).  If your VMs use ephemeral external IPs instead of reserved addresses, pull `.networkInterfaces[].accessConfigs[].natIP` from [gcloud compute instances list | Google Cloud SDK](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/compute/instances/list).
*   **`cloud.json` vs. `goog.json`**: Google publishes two separate IP range files.  [`cloud.json`](https://www.gstatic.com/ipranges/cloud.json) lists customer-usable Google Cloud ranges with regional `scope` values, while [`goog.json`](https://www.gstatic.com/ipranges/goog.json) covers all Google-owned prefixes without regional scopes.
*   **IPv4 vs. IPv6 Keys**: In `addresses.list`, the Compute Engine API populates `"ipVersion": "IPV6"` on IPv6 reservations but omits `ipVersion` on regional IPv4 addresses, so filter with `select((.ipVersion // "IPV4") == "IPV4")` before passing `.address` to `ip2int`.  Similarly, each entry in `cloud.json` `.prefixes[]` uses either `ipv4Prefix` or `ipv6Prefix`, so guard IPv4 prefix splitting with `select(has("ipv4Prefix"))`.

### Next steps
Next time an external endpoint drops traffic from a new region or Cloud NAT gateway, run this script to confirm the exact `ipv4Prefix` and `creationTime` in `cloud.json`.  If the destination firewall hasn't picked up the prefix yet, sharing the specific regional block (or your reserved `/32` NAT IPs) gives the remote network team what they need to update their allowlist.
