One Weekend: 3,000 Open-Source AI Projects

Every October for the past twelve years, developers around the world have taken part in Hacktoberfest, a month-long celebration of open-source software: code that anyone can use, inspect, and improve. For most of that history, the rules were simple: Contribute a set number of pull requests and earn a T-shirt. **Thousands of people made their first contribution to open source because of Hacktoberfest.**

**This year, we changed the format.** Hacktoberfest 2026 is focused on open-weight models and open-source artificial intelligence: models and tools that anyone can download, run and modify. Participants are learning how these systems work, building their own AI tooling, and adapting existing open models for new uses.

When we announced this year’s theme in August, we had hoped to support 300 in-person gatherings. **There are now more than 500 Fests planned in over 60 countries**, ranging from university hackathons to small groups of developers meeting at their local library or office. In the first week alone, participants in-person and online submitted more than 3,000 projects.

On Oct. 1, the first day of the event, students at COMSATS University in Abbottabad, Pakistan, gathered for a Hack Day. By evening, they had built a locally hosted hospital-management platform, a multimodal companion for visually impaired users, and a tool that helps newcomers make their first open-source contribution. The group photo they sent us afterward says more than any statistic I could share: a group of people who chose to spend their day learning to build something together.

For many people, AI is something experienced alone: typing into a chat window, using a tool built by someone else and governed by someone else's pricing and policies. What I'm seeing this month is a clear appetite for something different. People want to sit next to each other, run a model on their own machine, take it apart, and understand how it works.

That is why we built this year's Hacktoberfest around open innovation. Open source has always worked because nobody owns the tools. Anyone can look under the hood, and anyone can pull up a chair. We believe AI should work the same way: shaped by people building in public in India and Ireland, Peru and the Philippines, all over the world.

[Hacktoberfest](https://hacktoberfest.com) runs through Oct. 31. When it ends, I don’t expect its impact to be measured solely in code. It will show up in mentorships that started at a folding table, in local tech communities meeting for the first time, and in people who walked in unsure what an AI model was and walked out having built something with one.

Code is abundant. Confidence is a formula.

*AI can make code creation abundant. The harder challenge is building confidence in what gets shipped.*

AI has changed the economics of software creation. A task that once required hours of implementation can now begin with an agent producing an initial solution in minutes. As agents take on broader assignments like changing code across a repository, refactoring services, writing tests, and preparing pull requests, the volume of output will continue to rise.

That is an extraordinary opportunity, and it’s also why the next challenge for engineering organizations is not generating more code but creating confidence in the code that reaches production. In the agentic software factory, agents write, test, and propose changes faster than people can review them line by line.

Code creation is becoming abundant; code confidence is not.

This distinction matters because a completed pull request is not the same as a dependable outcome. The code may compile and pass a narrow test suite while still violating an architectural convention, introducing a security weakness, duplicating existing functionality, or creating maintenance costs that surface much later. The faster an organization generates changes, the less feasible it becomes to rely on heroics and manual review alone to catch every issue.

The way forward is to treat code confidence as something that can be designed into the software delivery system. A useful formula is **Intent × Guiderails × Verification × Evidence**. And yes, the multiplication sign here is deliberate. Each of these four pieces are crucial. Strength in three cannot make up for weakness in the fourth.

Clear intent without verification does not prevent mistakes. Strong verification without evidence does not create accountability. Guiderails without clear intent merely automate ambiguity. Evidence without independent verification is only a record of what an agent claimed.

Here is what each part of the formula means in practice.

## Intent: Make the standard explicit

Agents are remarkably capable at pursuing a stated objective. But “build a payments feature” or “modernize this service” is not a sufficient objective for a production codebase. An organization’s definition of good software includes much more, such as business logic, security expectations, design patterns, performance needs, dependencies, and conventions accumulated through years of engineering.

Intent is the discipline of making those expectations explicit. It means defining the goal of a change and the standards it must meet before an agent begins work. The better the context, the fewer cycles agents spend producing plausible but unsuitable answers, and the less rework falls to developers later.

## Guiderails: Shape the work before it creates risk

Guiderails translate intent into boundaries that guide how agents operate. They may define which repositories, dependencies, data, or actions are permitted; where human approval is required; and what policies apply to a given class of code.

The purpose is not to constrain every useful action. It’s to give agents enough structure to operate productively and predictably. A well-designed guiderail lets teams safely grant more autonomy because everyone understands the conditions under which that autonomy applies.

The result is repeatable autonomy. Rather than treating every agent-driven change as a one-off experiment, teams can apply consistent boundaries and expand agentic development with confidence.

## Verification: Check every change independently

Verification is where confidence is tested. As agents generate code at increasing scale, every change needs consistent evaluation for the qualities that matter: correctness, reliability, security, maintainability, and compliance with the organization’s own standards.

Independence is essential. A model can assist in reviewing its own work, but an organization should not rely solely on the same probabilistic system that produced a change to determine whether that change is safe to ship. Repeatable, independent checks provide a common standard across models, agents, and toolchains. This is especially important when the AI tools themselves are evolving quickly.

Verification also needs to occur in the flow of work, not as a slow, final checkpoint. The goal is to identify and fix problems at the source, while the agent or developer still has the context needed to resolve them.

## Evidence: Make confidence visible and auditable

A change may be well-intentioned, carefully governed, and thoroughly checked. But engineering leaders, auditors, and the teams responsible for production still need to know what happened and why. Evidence is the durable record: what standards applied, what was checked, what was found, and how the issue was resolved.

This matters most in complex and regulated environments, but it’s valuable everywhere. Evidence makes quality measurable, allows teams to improve their practices over time, and gives organizations a defensible basis for moving quickly.

## Building the factory around confidence

The most promising vision for agentic software development is not one in which people disappear from the process. It’s one in which people, agents, and verification systems each contribute their strengths. Agents accelerate execution, and engineers provide judgment and direction. The delivery system supplies the standards, controls, and evidence that allow autonomy to scale.

The organizations that succeed will be the ones that build code confidence into every change, at any volume, and at agent speed.

That is the real work of the agentic software factory, producing software an organization has the confidence to stand behind.

Start with four questions the next time an agent opens a pull request:

* Did the agent know your standards before it started?
* What was it allowed to touch, and what needed a human decision?
* Did something other than the model that wrote the change check it?
* Can you show what was found and how it was resolved?

Wherever the answer is "no," that is where your confidence gap lives. Close it there first.

Kepler's Vinoo Ganesh on Building AI You Can Trust

Vinoo Ganesh is the CEO of Kepler, which builds AI for industries where accuracy matters, starting with finance. Before Kepler, he spent seven years at Palantir, built and sold an alt data company, and led business engineering at Citadel.

Ahead of his AIE New York sessions, including a fireside chat with Jack Woodroffe on Tuesday at 2:55 PM, he sat down with The Daily Context to talk about building AI people can trust, why Kepler's model never writes a number, and why he doesn't believe a bigger model is the answer.

*This interview has been edited for length and clarity.*

## The team, the talk, and New York

**The Daily Context:** Tell us a little about your background and about Kepler.

**Vinoo Ganesh:** I'm Vinoo, Kepler's CEO. I spent seven years at Palantir leading Spark and the compute side there. Then I built an alt data company, grew it, and it got acquired. After that, I was Head of Business Engineering at Citadel and really focused on how we build software products and data products for portfolio managers, which, ironically, is very similar to what Kepler is doing now.

It's a heavy ex-Palantir team. Sarah was one of the engineering leads for the Palantir Ontology. Chris was at Palantir for 15 years, doing a lot of optimization. We have folks from Meta, Reflection AI, Datavant, Goldman, Oddity, you name it. So, it's a team that has spent a lot of time building products in environments where the accuracy and fidelity of information and data matter.

**The Daily Context:** That's an incredible pedigree, but it's also hard to convince people to walk away from those companies. How do you approach recruiting?

**Vinoo Ganesh:** We've been very lucky in that there are people who trust us, who've worked with us before, and who feel very positive about joining us again. But honestly, I make Eddie's job very hard at times, because I'm always saying, "Let's recruit these insanely talented people."

Ultimately, it comes down to a few things. First, the problems we solve are super technically deep. In a world where there are things that look like ChatGPT wrappers, a very deep set of technical problems is super appealing to engineers who are motivated by that.

Second, we're really lucky that our problem space has a huge element of importance to humanity. Yes, we started in finance, but AI you can trust, or enterprise intelligence you can codify, is kind of the last remaining alpha-generating milestone. Kepler is really powerful in that sense: if everyone has the same access to the same tools, what alpha or uniqueness remains? It turns out that's an existential question for a lot of folks.

Third, talent compounds. We have a really strong pedigree team, and people like working with very strong engineers. We have an insanely high bar for talent; you can ask Adil about that. We try to be very fair in our interview process, but we do have people who are intimidated by the backgrounds. We've gotten that feedback: "Do I want to work for an ex-Palantir, ex-Citadel team? Sounds scary." I think we're approachable and reasonable.

**The Daily Context:** What is your personal relationship to AI?

**Vinoo Ganesh:** I think "cautious consumers" is probably the best way to describe us. AI is really helpful for vast synthesis of information, especially in non-deterministic ways. If I have a bunch of queries I just want to understand at a high level, or get a vibe for, AI has been very powerful for that.

The challenges come in when people use AI in ways it shouldn't be used, like deterministic work, or work where accuracy is materially important. AI is very positive in a number of ways, but it also agrees with the vast majority of things you say. It doesn't follow steps, even when you ask it to. And it's a moving target. When models are being released at a pace of roughly one a day, keeping up with that rapidly changing environment is super hard. So it's a powerful tool and accelerant when it's deployed in the right way.

**The Daily Context:** What is your AIE New York talk about?

**Vinoo Ganesh:** We see the promise of AI so clearly because we're deep in it every day. The simple reality, though, is that deep exposure to and deployment of AI is still in its infancy at most companies. Even the ones that think of themselves as super AI-forward are normally just throwing Copilot on a few queries, and that's it.

Our question is always: why? What's the blocker to getting to the level that we, our team, and our peers use AI at? It comes back to the question of trust. So the talk is about how you build trust in an AI system, and our view on it: to really trust an AI system, you can't just use AI by itself. You need infrastructure around it. That infrastructure uses AI for the right scenarios, uses other tools for the right scenarios, shows proof, and, finally, is deeply embedded in the systems you already work in. How we go from early adopters to people using it in depth, every day, in 95% of cases, is the exciting space we'll talk about and that we're working on in detail.

**The Daily Context:** Why New York over San Francisco?

**Vinoo Ganesh:** As a forward-deployed engineer, I've learned that being close to your customers, geographically and emotionally, matters a lot. Our initial customers happen to be based here in New York. Finance is predominantly here, but I also think the urgency and importance of this problem space are uniquely captured in New York, where the speed of development, the speed of technology adoption, being first, and being smarter all matter a lot. SF is really powerful in a number of ways, more on the research side, but at Kepler we're very focused on the applied side, even though we do a good chunk of research ourselves.

## How Kepler works

**The Daily Context:** My research suggested Kepler checks citations against sources in real time, while the output is streaming. How does that work?

**Vinoo Ganesh:** We actually don't do it while streaming or in real time. The way we operate is that there are certain things deterministic tools will always be better at. So we run massive preprocessing steps that extract what we call facts. Those can be numbers, entities, people, places, and things. We annotate those facts with metadata that describes each unique fact. That can be relationships, or, for a number, it can be magnitude, scale, whether it's dollars or pounds, and so on.

The second piece is that we persist all of this data with provenance records. As data flows through the Kepler platform, the platform and agents are architected so they're consistently writing to a provenance ledger that, at any given moment, holds effectively every previous step taken. So we can see every twist, every turn, every determination an LLM makes, and we can even see deterministic changes. If two numbers get added together, we persist that output. If two numbers are multiplied, we persist that product. And we can show you the chain of transformations the number went through.

So a lot of it comes down to very detailed preprocessing and very detailed engineering up front, which then compounds because we can switch between the deterministic and non-deterministic pieces.

**The Daily Context:** Walk me through Kepler's first public equities ontology. Why was it important to build?

**Vinoo Ganesh:** Great question. Humans don't think in terms of rows and columns in a database. If you think about your Facebook friends, you probably think in terms of relationships: I am this person's friend; I believe this person is this many years old. We think in these complex, relationship-driven ways.

What's interesting for us, especially in the finance ecosystem, is that being able to codify and entity-resolve even something as simple as company names is a really hard problem. For example, Palantir and PLTR obviously refer to the same thing, but most systems can't easily entity-resolve them. That problem compounds when it's a person saying something. If I'm the CFO of a company and I mention Palantir, and it's transcribed incorrectly, how do I do any kind of canonicalization or entity resolution?

What we realized is that LLMs are really good at thinking through how to solve things, but they're not necessarily as good at doing the solving themselves. Developing the ontology allowed us to do a few things. First, it let us give LLMs tooling to interact with that ontology, so the LLM can do what it does best and the tools can do what they do best.

It also lets us be very mindful from a cost perspective. We're in an era post token-maxing, where using as many tokens as possible is no longer the cool new thing to do. Getting the best ROI out of each dollar you spend on tokens becomes really important. Kepler is predicated on using the right tool for the job, and sometimes a deterministic system, like knowledge graph traversal over an ontology, is a much better solution than a potentially multi-trillion-parameter model trying to do anything and everything. So the ontology lets us represent the preprocessed data in a way that both LLMs and Kepler's own execution engine can traverse pretty easily.

**The Daily Context:** The applications to finance are super clear. What other industries are a good fit for Kepler?

**Vinoo Ganesh:** Any industry that's regulated, where material accuracy matters. I've jokingly called these the "non-vibes industries." Think of something like insurance claims adjustment. Insurance is a very interesting potential area of expansion for us. Manufacturing, too. Even legal. Legal is interesting because if you think about the data, like case briefs, there's an inherent structure to it. There's precedent; there are cases like A v. B; and there's a time-based nature to it: this happened before that, so this precedent overrides that one.

So any industry where the accuracy of data matters is a potential opportunity for Kepler. That's why we've positioned Kepler as more of an engine than a particular vertical SaaS play. We now have pull across a bunch of different industries. Defense has been an interesting, more recent area, and fund of funds as well. Any of those spaces.

**The Daily Context:** Part of Kepler's promise is that the model never writes a number. How does that work? And Kepler has a connector inside Claude. How do you make sure that promise holds when Claude is delivering the last mile?

**Vinoo Ganesh:** This is probably the best question I have ever gotten, because we are desperate to talk about it, and no one lets us.

A couple of things. Kepler having an MCP was actually a request from Anthropic themselves. It wasn't a deliberate strategic positioning for what Kepler wants to be, because you're right: if Kepler runs through an MCP, the model can still hallucinate. It can pull the wrong number, and a bunch of other things.

Here's how we solve that problem. Kepler in Claude ships with apps, so what you're seeing is a rendered application, not Claude giving you text-based output. That rendered application has full auditability and traceability. We're passing what is effectively a blob of code or a blob of visualization back to Claude, and all Claude does is output it. It's almost like an API call, and the apps feature in Claude renders the Kepler UI. That's what makes every number auditable and traceable.

How do we ensure the model doesn't produce numbers? It's because of the invariant we've built into the platform. By preprocessing data and information, we assign identifiers to facts. What the model knows how to do is use deterministic tools that retrieve those facts. Think of it almost like a getter or a setter: I can do a lookup from a table, and the model substitutes that lookup in.

Right now in finance, the facts we care about are things like company names and numbers. But in law, we could enforce that same idea for court cases, to make sure each case actually exists before the model can return it. So right now, if the model can't resolve its output against the lookup, it rejects it. It can't actually state that fact.

**The Daily Context:** What does it say when that happens?

**Vinoo Ganesh:** It isn't included in the output at all. In practice, it looks like facts disagreeing. Say someone from Google said on an earnings call that Google's earnings were $1 last year, and the 10-K reports $100. Those are conflicting facts. Rather than trying to pick one, the model realizes that, upon resolution, it can't identify that number appropriately. So it has to present it to the user and say it's getting conflicting information.

Sometimes that's alpha, and it's right. If someone is saying something different, you could have new sources of information, and that could be alpha in its own right. Sometimes it's actually a mistake.

## The state of the industry

**The Daily Context:** What else do you not get asked about that you really want to talk about?

**Vinoo Ganesh:** I have one that's more of a comment on the state of the industry. In tech as a whole, there are a lot of waves, and we've seen the first wave of companies raising a lot of capital very quickly. They're in the land grab right now. We're very much in the early innings.

A lot of people ask me who Kepler's competition is, and it's a somewhat challenging question to answer, because, at least to my knowledge, there isn't a set of people out there trying to build this harness or this product in this way. So our competition looks a lot like vertical SaaS companies that have to build the airplane while it's in flight. More importantly, we're still early enough that this is a thesis: here's how we would solve this problem in the data.

I think we'll see a lot of other approaches. There are labs trying to remove hallucination by throwing as many tokens at it as they possibly can. I inherently think that doesn't make sense. A probability machine will continue to be a probability machine, even if the hallucination rate is 0.0001%. Ultimately, we're an execution engine. We look more like a database than a vertical app company.

Other questions are around where we are in this AI cycle, and the desire to use LLMs for everything. I don't think a bigger, badder, more powerful model will result in better output, any more than driving a Hummer from your home to the grocery store gets you to the grocery store in a better way. It doesn't make sense to me.

The last thing people don't seem to care about as much is that a lot of people are very okay sending private information to the labs. That's the weirdest thing to me, because coming from Palantir, data security was the most important thing. I've had meetings with major financial institutions that said, "Well, we signed an agreement, so we're just going to send all the customer data out to the labs," which is mind-blowing to me.

So there's a big question around what the future looks like when everyone is using this technology, and when alpha is much harder to come by. Those are open questions right now. That's exactly what I want Jack and others to talk about, and that's where I think the opportunity really is.

**The Daily Context:** What do you recommend for companies that want to apply AI to sensitive data?

**Vinoo Ganesh:** Ultimately, the question is how you maintain your edge. That's the most important thing. My frustration is that a lot of these organizations are digging their own grave, and I don't understand why that's the path they want to go down. Your own data is your alpha.

**The Daily Context:** More tactically, is there a way for a financial company working with inherently sensitive data to use AI without sending that data to the labs?

**Vinoo Ganesh:** I would deploy on-prem. The crazy thing is that deploying a model seems like the most insane thing in the world. But you spend two seconds thinking about it and realize you can pretty easily run the model in your VPC and do any kind of editing of these agents on your own platform. It sounds really scary until you do it, and then you realize it's not insane in any way.

**The Daily Context:** If you were advising a 20- or 21-year-old recent college grad looking at engineering and AI engineering, what would you tell them?

**Vinoo Ganesh:** In any major technical shift, there's one big driving question. Here, it's whether AI is just another disruptive technology — not the harbinger of the end of the world, just another disruptive technology we all learn to live with. I think that framing makes people feel a lot less scared.

The Industrial Revolution was a huge technological shift. The dot-com era was a huge technological shift. There were a bunch of these material changes, and none of them ended the world. What I did was figure out how to adapt to the new way of doing things and the new set of processes.

My belief is that people in college right now have a very unique opportunity to rebuild the world through the lens of these new technologies. I wonder what the AI version of McKinsey will be. What's the AI version of Lazard? I'm not saying those companies will be gone. It's more that there's a huge opportunity to get very familiar with using a technology to fundamentally rewrite how industry works.

Personally, I'm really excited about medical use cases, if we can solve the accuracy problem. That, to me, is a huge opportunity. How many prescriptions are filled incorrectly because someone can't read a doctor's handwriting, and a patient gets 10x the dosage they should have? Those are all huge opportunities, and I think the next generation has a unique ability to build these future technologies.

*Apartment hunters, accessibility tools and debugging agents top a 12-hour build day in Manhattan*

By 9 a.m. Sunday, the room at 9th Avenue and 31st Street was already buzzing with excitement and anticipation. Laptops were open, coffee was poured, and the line for scallion pancake bacon egg and cheese wraps (catered by Win Son Bakery) snaked across the room. Twelve hours later, teams made from 150+ builders had their projects for science-fair demos at the inaugural [AI Engineer NYC Hackathon](https://luma.com/AIEngineerNYHackathon) in an unofficial kickoff for AI Engineer New York conference week.

Major League Hacking (MLH) presented the event with AI Engineer as co-host. It was free for anyone to join and bring their team, their idea, or just themselves and hunger to learn. Attendance at the hackathon exceeded capacity in the main 9th floor space, so an overflow room on the 6th floor was set up to accommodate the extra demand.

The crowd was not the usual hackathon mix of students. Many attendees build software for a living as engineers, founders, researchers and product people, and they chose to spend a Sunday building some more. If you haven’t been to a hackathon before, or in a while, the choice to spend more time “working” can feel strange. But nothing can replace the way it feels to get your hands on a keyboard and work through a problem side by side with other builders. At the AI Engineer NYC hackathon, this really came through. Conversations moved from "how does this API work" to "here's how we handle this in production." Teams that had met at the morning team-formation session were trading deployment tips and opinions on agent frameworks within an hour.

## Dumplings and Demos

The Nom Wah lunch spread, a nod to the Chinatown dim sum institution, did more for networking than any icebreaker. Builders carried plates of dumplings back to their tables and kept talking, and newly formed teams sat down together for the first time without a screen in front of them. Mentors circulated all afternoon, and in the evening the happy hour gave a final burst of energy before the demo deadline.

There was plenty of laughter, some groaning at stubborn bugs, and the occasional cheer when a demo worked on the first try. Many people who arrived alone left with teammates, collaborators and a few new friends.

## A Very New York Winner

First place overall went to **[Boroly](https://boroly.vercel.app/)**, which takes on one of the city's most familiar headaches: finding an apartment. Boroly compares listings side by side and adds neighborhood context like local grocers, restaurants, and laundromats. It scrapes this local data and uses Google's Gemini to summarize what it finds, so renters can see what living on a block is actually like, not just the square footage or the number of bedrooms. ([source](https://github.com/hakanero/boroly))

Second place went to **[Claude Code Ripple](https://github.com/nsodhi-cmu/claude-code-ripple)**, a tool for developers (a “Mod,” a new class of agentic plugins) who have changed one line of code and then watched something unrelated break. Ripple traces how a change spreads through a codebase, including renames, before it ships.

**[Resurface](https://resurface.thomasmann2001.workers.dev/)** took third. It turns forgotten bookmarks into animated reels and uses those saved links to build a profile of a user's interests that AI agents can draw on. ([source](https://github.com/AnalystTom/Major-League-Hacking-Hack-))

## Partner Prizes Spark Creative Builds

Partner challenges gave teams more ways to win. **[Public Palate](https://github.com/jzeng151/public-palate)** won Best Use of Nimble by combining restaurant inspection records with reviews, and the runner-up, **[Nibble](https://github.com/NandanHemanth/Nibble)**, finds the cheapest grocery prices in your area. **[Explorin](https://github.com/NicholasSutin/explorin)** won Best Use of Gemini API with experience-based personalization of travel recommendations. **[RetailScope AI](https://retailscope-ai-demo.onrender.com/)** took Best Use of Snowflake with a tool for finding commercial real estate deals. **[Zig Actions Runner](https://github.com/Lementknight/zig-actions-runner)** won Best Use of Tiger Data for a lightweight, local GitHub Actions runner. **[rezolution.si](https://github.com/harshpv07/bugbot)** won Best Use of Sentry with an agent that investigates bug reports and generates fixes. **[MyVision](https://github.com/SaltySandy/scene-companion)**, which helps visually impaired users detect nearby obstacles, won the Sentry raffle.

## Setting the Tone for the Week

The hackathon was planned as a lead-in to the conference, because many of the coding agents, data pipelines and context-aware assistants that builders engaged with on Sunday leverage the same workflows and tools that speakers will cover over the next few days. Attendees who missed Sunday can find these builders around the conference all week. They are the ones who look tired but happy, and many of them now have a new project and a new team.

AI Engineering Has Entered Its Audit Era

A conference agenda is a pretty decent dataset.

Between what is pitched and what is accepted, it's always an attempt to triangulate on the zeitgeist of the moment. So I dug through the roughly 140 sessions at [AI Engineer New York](https://ai.engineer/nyc/2026/schedule) and tried to get a sense of what themes exist at this event that might not have been so collectively front of mind six months ago.

The first finding is the obvious one: this is an agent conference now. Two in five sessions have "agent" in the name. That's table stakes; the interesting part is what people want to *do* about them.

It's also a finance conference by design, billed as "Where AI Engineering Meets Wall Street." That makes it more useful, not less. Finance is the stress test: an industry where "mostly right" is a liability, every decision needs a paper trail, and someone always asks *why*. Whatever worries this room now will worry the rest of us soon.

## "It works" is no longer the bar. "Prove it" is.

After agents, the biggest cluster is evaluation and verification: nearly 20 sessions, six with the word "trust" in the name. Generation is cheap now. Proving it's right is where the work is. Addy Osmani and Manish Kapur are asking [who verifies the software factory](https://ai.engineer/nyc/2026/schedule?view=list&session=11b98f47-dcc2-4524-8c06-d1f6c3ff044b), and other talks cover verification loops and agent fixes that quietly break something else.

Finance pushes past correctness into defensibility. One session asks whether you can [defend an agent's decision after it passed every eval](https://ai.engineer/nyc/2026/schedule?view=list&session=30afe596-abe2-417c-bd5a-313fa4bc54b3). That might be the sharpest question at the conference. Vinoo Ganesh is on three sessions, one of which boils down to a single instruction: don't let models invent numbers. Passing evals and earning trust are different things, and the gap between them is where many AI engineering careers will be made.

## Agents are becoming principals

About a dozen sessions deal with security, identity, permissions, or payments. We spent twenty years building that stack for humans. Now we're rebuilding it for software that acts on its own. The panel on [intent-based auth](https://ai.engineer/nyc/2026/schedule?view=list&session=e65f74f9-2174-406d-bd32-2d7073eb677d) includes Dick Hardt, who led the design of OAuth 2.0. Others cover agent permissions in regulated industries, financial accounts for agents, and the idea that your next user is an agent.

My favorite pairing: one talk asks why agents don't pay for things even though they can, and another walks through [six attacks on x402 agent payments](https://ai.engineer/nyc/2026/schedule?view=list&session=eaa39362-c0ec-4849-a90d-841f4825a5b3). That's the whole adoption curve in two talks. The rails exist; the trust doesn't yet. If you run an API, ask now what changes when the caller is an agent with a budget.

## Intelligence has a price tag

Cost is the other loud signal. There are sessions on tokenomics, the cost of intelligence, and the hidden costs of a faster model. Then Wall Street's own vocabulary shows up: compute markets, the dark pools of compute, and a session from the CEO of Compute Exchange. One of the speaker lounges is literally the Token Billionaires Lounge.

When people describe GPUs in the language of market structure, compute has become a commodity. AI engineers now have to think like CFOs: what does this call cost, and is the better model worth it?

## So what do we do with this?

Ryan Carson argues that your job is now [agent manager](https://ai.engineer/nyc/2026/schedule?view=list&session=f7204e6d-a47c-4535-804e-16b4db579b95). Laurie Voss is talking about the rise of the product engineer. I think they're right, with a caveat from another session: [stop turning your humans into APIs for your agents](https://ai.engineer/nyc/2026/schedule?view=list&session=ac709f86-ce51-4582-a680-70449c32d29c).

A conference like this, with fairly pragmatic outcomes center of mind, is able to cut through frontier model headlines and help us understand the themes we can apply more agency to. We're trying to do our job as AI Engineers by proving the output, scoping the authority, and paying the bill.

I got Jev to zero mistakes. I'm still using Flash-Lite.

*Jev is a brilliant decision model. Gemini Flash-Lite is the model nobody talks about, and it’s fast, accurate, and nearly free. Here's what we measured picking between them, and why the pair is the cheapest setup of all.*

![I got Jev to zero mistakes. I'm still using Flash-Lite.](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/sdtw0dybbdigc8vt6sr6.png)

Jev is the most hyped model right now. TypeSafe's decision model doesn't chat and doesn't write. It reads some text and a list of options and returns calibrated probabilities over those options. A few hundred milliseconds, for almost nothing. Every feed I read has a post about it.

We had a real job for exactly that kind of model, already running in production on something much less fashionable. So instead of reading about Jev, we put it on our own data, ran both models a few thousand times, and kept score.

I love Jev. I'm still using Gemini Flash-Lite. Here's why.

*This is the long version of a lightning talk I gave at AI Tinkerers NYC on October 7, 2026. The slides are on [Speaker Deck](https://speakerdeck.com/theycallmeswift).*

## The setup

A test that passes when the code is broken is worse than no test. With no test, you know you don't know. With a false green, you ship.

At Major League Hacking (MLH), we grade AI coding agents with [benchspec](https://github.com/theycallmeswift/benchspec), an open-source eval runner we built for the job. You write what an agent should have done as plain-English checks in a markdown file. benchspec runs the agent in a sandbox and grades every check, with and without the skill under test, so the difference is what the skill actually teaches. After a run, the checks look like this:

```plaintext
- ./.meta/index.md exists
- Exactly six files match ./.meta/templates/*.md
- The summary faithfully reflects the three key facts from the source
```

Each check gets verified one of two ways. **Cheap code**: does this path exist, how many files match this glob, does this file have a line matching a pattern. Free, instant, exact. Or an **LLM judge** reads the content for meaning. That costs money every run.

A classifier, the router, reads each check and picks a checker (`file_exists`, `glob_count`, `regex`, a few more) or defers to the judge.

![After each run we have a list of plain-English checks; an LLM classifies each as deterministic or defers it to a judge](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/ne09ujyg2knli8aa9323.png)

*The router's job: one check in, one checker out, or a deferral.*

The router's two mistakes aren't equal:

- Send something to the judge that code could have handled: **you lose a few cents.**
- Send something to code that code can't actually verify: a broken result reports green and nobody finds out. The person who trusted that green ships on it. **We lose a user's trust.** Cents come back. Trust doesn't.

![Being overly cautious costs a few cents. Being over confident costs our users' trust.](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/iqpixpk011e70burikw1.png)

So: when in doubt, defer.

## The secret

The router I actually run is [Gemini Flash-Lite](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/models/gemini-3.5-flash-lite), the smallest of Google's three Gemini tiers. Pro is the frontier model. Flash is the everyday one. Flash-Lite is the one Google itself describes as built for "high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks like translation and classification".

Flash-Lite has the same million-token context window as its bigger siblings, an answer in well under a second, and $0.30 per million input tokens. The current version, 3.5, shipped in July. It got a line in the release notes and no keynote. Nobody hypes it, but they should be.

![99% of my monthly LLM calls are for Gemini Flash-Lite. It's my most used model by orders of magnitude.](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/s3235akq8uztnd27z5xj.png)

99% of my monthly LLM calls go to Flash-Lite. That number comes from my own AI Studio usage page, across every project I have. Pro got nothing. Flash, almost nothing. And the calls are long in, short out: the shape of classification work.

Then Jev showed up. Text in, probabilities over a fixed set of options out, nothing written, by design. $0.042 per million input tokens, output free, a few hundred milliseconds. For a router, that's a perfect pitch.

## Round 1: the mistake you can't afford

The experiment is simple. Our router is a single call with one job: read a check, pick a checker or defer. We swapped Flash-Lite out of that slot, put Jev in, and ran the same checks through both. Each model got its own prompt and nothing else changed.

Here are eight real ones. ✓ is safe, ~ is over-cautious (deferred when code could have done it), ✗ is dangerous:

![Out of the box, Jev made 3 mistakes we can't afford. Flash-Lite made none.](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/f95xwoplfy449zuq1btc.png)

Jev made three dangerous *(false positive)* calls. Two checks need the content read for meaning, and Jev sent them to `regex`. A regex can find a `source:` line. It can't tell you whether that line names the right move. The third: "no `.DS_Store` anywhere" is about the whole tree, and Jev picked a checker that looks at one path. It passes on a repo full of `.DS_Store` files.

Flash-Lite: zero false positives. Over-cautious twice, which costs cents *(not trust!)*.

## Make No Mistakes

Jev reads literally. TypeSafe's own docs say it answers the question you wrote, not the one you meant. So I rewrote the question. I expected worked examples to do the heavy lifting, because that's what works for chat models. They didn't. What worked was one sentence:

![Imagine the checker runs and passes. Could the check still be false? If yes, that checker is wrong: defer.](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/04uoxsgx2f8gqfwtihn6.png)

Read quickly, it's the equivalent of writing "make no mistakes" when prompt-engineering. Here's why it isn't that, and why it worked on Jev specifically.

**It's a test, not a plea.** "Be careful" gives the model nothing to do. "Imagine this checker passed. Could the check still be false?" is a procedure it can run once per option. Take "the log entry has a `source:` line naming the move". Imagine `regex` passes. A `source:` line exists. Could it still name the wrong move? Yes. So `regex` is out. Take "no `.DS_Store` anywhere". Imagine `not_file_exists` passes on `./.DS_Store`. Could there still be one in a subfolder? Yes. Out. Every checker gets a mechanical answer, and the mechanical answer is the routing decision.

**It asks about the checker's blind spot, not the check's shape.** The original prompt asked "can this be verified mechanically?" That's a question about the check, and `regex` looks mechanical. The rewrite asks "what does this checker fail to see?" That's a question about the tool. Same information, opposite direction. Jev answers exactly what you ask, so it gives a different answer.

**The criteria changed to match.** The old criteria described what a check should look like: `regex` is for "a named file has a line matching a stated pattern." The new ones describe what the checker *mechanically does and cannot see*:

| Checker | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `regex` | The assertion says a named file has a line matching a stated pattern or literal prefix. | Tests whether one named file has a line matching a pattern. **It cannot tell what the matched text means or refers to.** |
| `not_file_exists` | The assertion says a single path is gone or never existed. | Tests one exact path for non-existence. **It looks at that path and nowhere else.** |
| `skill_invoked` | A bare activation line: skill X was invoked. | Tests whether the named skill was invoked. **It sees nothing about what the skill did.** |

**Examples made it worse.** I folded our worked examples into Jev's original prompt and its dangerous checks doubled. Examples teach pattern-matching: "a line that says X" looks like the `regex` examples, so `regex` it is. The test teaches the failure mode instead.

![Weak prompt: Flash-Lite still zero. Jev: not zero until the rewrite. Examples made Jev worse.](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/kuizwxre195j0m6mg6mi.png)

*Checks that must go to the judge but were sent to code. Flash-Lite got to zero on Jev's weak prompt too.*

With the rewrite, Jev went to zero on the eight, and on every check we have. Zero dangerous, zero wrong checkers, run after run. Tuned on half, zero on the half it never saw.

The one sentence fixed Jev. It didn't fix Flash-Lite. We wrote a fresh batch of whole-tree checks neither model had seen, like "nothing named draft.md exists in any subfolder".

Both models made false positive calls on them. With the rewrite, Jev went from 35 false positive runs to 0. Flash-Lite barely moved. The difference is how each one failed. Jev got the same checks wrong run after run: a blind spot. Flash-Lite got a check wrong about one run in five and right the other four: a flip. Jev obeys a precise criterion literally, so a better criterion fixes it. Flash-Lite forgives a sloppy criterion but doesn't fully obey a precise one. A blind spot is a prompt bug you fix. A flip is sampling noise you measure for.

## Does a smarter model mask a weak prompt?

If the prompt is the biggest variable, does a better model make it stop mattering? Same phrasings, Jev's bare prompt, three models.

![Does a more powerful model mask a weak prompt? Yes!](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/9j3jb0vgg8nvuuncfzdg.png)

Yes. Flash-Lite was still wrong about one run in five. Gemini 3.8 Flash and Opus 5.5 were never wrong. A stronger model masks a weaker prompt.

It doesn't make the prompt stop mattering. The same prompt change that fixed Jev pushed both bigger models toward deferring. It cut Opus's right answers by more than half and 3.8 Flash's to none. The prompt is still the single largest variable; the model decides how expensive your mistakes are. And the mask costs an order of magnitude more in both price and latency.

## Beyond our data

Our checks come from one project. So we ran the same experiment on a slice of the [Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/leaderboard.html). The task: pick the right function and write its arguments, or say none fits. "None fits" is that benchmark's version of defer. Calling a function that doesn't fit is the dangerous direction.

The first thing we learned had nothing to do with either model. Flash-Lite kept calling a function on items the answer key said had none, and every time I marked it wrong.

After the fourth or fifth failure, I read the item. "Who won the World Series in 2020?" with one candidate function, `get_champion(event, year)`. The function answers the question. The key said it didn't. So I checked every "none fits" item in our sample. Seven items matched. Flash-Lite had flagged all seven by disagreeing with the key. We score without them and list them in the repo. A cheap model with a real job found a bug in a public benchmark.

![BFCL: Jev 94.6% label accuracy, 1.1% false positives, no arguments, 261 ms, $0.025 per 1,000. Flash-Lite 96.9%, 4.3%, writes arguments 93.3%, 800 ms, $0.257. Jev + Flash-Lite 96.4%, 1.1%, 92.0%, 689 ms, $0.101.](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/4y9rrvl3bcdirvovla36.png)

*Jev's false-positive rate is at a 0.8 probability bar: call the function only if Jev is at least 80% sure.*

Neither model is at zero. With its top label, Jev called a function on about one in thirteen items where nothing fit. Flash-Lite, about one in twenty-five. But Jev has a knob. Raise the bar to 0.8 and its false positives drop to 1%, at the price of deferring twice as often. Flash-Lite has no knob, but it writes the arguments, and gets them fully right over nine times in ten.

The third card, Jev + Flash-Lite, gets Jev's false-positive rate and Flash-Lite's arguments for well under half the one-call price. That combination is where this ends up, so the rest of the post is about it.

## The call you don't need

Take the `_Last updated` check. Jev returns `regex` with a probability distribution. And stops. Which file? What pattern? That takes a second model. Flash-Lite, one call, returns the label, the arguments, and a reason, because it can write.

![Cost table: Jev → Opus 5.5 $1.18, Jev → Fable 5.1 $2.33, Jev → GPT-5 $2.42, Jev → Flash-Lite $0.10, Flash-Lite only $0.52 per 1,000.](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/bqfp19j1pm3rn25idbg3.png)

*Measured, billed through OpenRouter. Time is mean milliseconds; cost is per 1,000 checks.*

Now look at the fourth row: **Jev → Flash-Lite, $0.10.** Cheaper than Flash-Lite on its own, at $0.52. How does adding a model make it five times cheaper?

## How Jev + Flash-Lite saves the money

Nothing clever. Two multipliers, both on Flash-Lite's bill.

**1. The second call only runs when there's something to write.** A check that goes to the judge has no arguments. Jev defers it and Flash-Lite never sees it. On our full set that's most checks: fewer than four in ten have anything for Flash-Lite to do.

**2. The second call uses a shorter prompt.** The one-call prompt is long, with worked examples, because that's what keeps Flash-Lite safe on the routing decision. And it goes out on every check. In the pair, Jev has already made the routing decision. The second prompt only has to say: here's the check, here's the checker that was chosen, write its arguments. That's about a seventh of the tokens.

```plaintext
An eval assertion has already been routed to a deterministic checker. Write that checker's arguments.

Assertion: {check}
Checker already chosen: {label}

Arguments needed per checker:
- file_exists / not_file_exists: "path"
- glob_count: "glob" and "count"
- regex: "path" and "pattern"
...
Reply with one JSON object holding only the arguments and nothing else.
```

Jev itself costs about three cents per thousand checks. Rounding error.

![Where does the money go? Flash-Lite only is $0.52 per 1,000 checks, almost all of it input tokens; Jev → Flash-Lite is $0.10](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/mruhdt34d4nj7lfax5wk.png)

*Blue is Flash-Lite input, yellow is Flash-Lite output, coral is Jev.*

Put the multipliers together: a call on about half the checks, with a prompt a seventh the size, plus a near-free first hop. Measured, $0.52 becomes $0.10 per 1,000. On the production mix it'd be lower still.

The same thing happens on public data. On BFCL the pair costs less than half of one Flash-Lite call. The second hop runs on about half the items and reads one function's schema instead of every candidate's.

What you pay for it: one more round trip, about a quarter of a second on average. And you inherit Jev's routing, not Flash-Lite's. On BFCL that means Jev's false-positive rate and Jev's knob.

## The takeaways

1. **Flash-Lite is Google's best-kept secret.** For most classification work it's the right balance of fast and cheap. It's smart enough to forgive a sloppy prompt and to generate. It gave us zero dangerous calls on Jev's bare prompt and wrote the label and the arguments in one call.

2. **Prompts are your single biggest variable.** One sentence took Jev from 35 dangerous runs to 0, and examples made it worse. Smarter models soften the problem. They don't remove it: the same prompt change still pushed Opus from mostly answering to mostly deferring.

3. **Private evals separate real from hype.** We didn't have to take anyone's word for Jev, including TypeSafe's. We had real checks from a real product. So we ran the hyped model against the one we already use and found out. What's true: fast, cheap, zero once you ask the right question. What isn't: examples help, a smarter model makes prompting irrelevant. What nobody was saying: the cheapest setup is both of them.

To go deeper, start with the [practical getting-started guide to Jev](https://dev.to/charlie_chen_d661f49e69cb/what-is-jev-ai-a-practical-getting-started-guide-to-typesafes-decision-model-2gaf). Google's [Gemini 3.6 Flash & 3.5 Flash-Lite developer guide](https://dev.to/googleai/gemini-36-flash-35-flash-lite-developer-guide-268i) covers the model.

Happy Hacking!

Building AI Analysts for Wall Street: A Q&A with Compound Co-Founder Yijia Liang

# Building AI Analysts for Wall Street: A Q&A with Compound Co-Founder Yijia Liang

*Ahead of AI Engineer New York, The Daily Context spoke with Yijia Liang, co-founder of Compound, about building autonomous financial analysts, why general-purpose AI falls short in finance, and what it takes to earn the trust of high-stakes users.*

**The Daily Context: Tell us about yourself and Compound.**

**Yijia Liang:** I'm EJ, one of the co-founders at Compound. We're building AI for Wall Street and finance, specifically private equity. We're building long-running autonomous analysts that behave and perform tasks the same way they would if you delegated the work to a human.

Previously, I was a vice president on a private markets team, investing in late-stage companies like Rippling, Databricks, and ClickHouse. Before that, I was an investor at Y Combinator's growth team, and I began my career at Bain in its private equity group.

I've spent a lot of time in buy-side finance, and I've found that the most interesting parts of the job aren't where people spend most of their time.

What's exciting about dealmaking is understanding a company, determining whether it's a good investment, and deciding whether to invest. But people spend most of their time building Excel models, PowerPoints, and Word memos, along with all the research and orchestration that goes into a deal.

That's what Compound is intended to help with. We're building much higher-quality outputs than you'd normally get from Claude or ChatGPT off the shelf, specifically for financial services.

**The Daily Context: What will you be talking about at AI Engineer New York?**

**Yijia:** The talk is about long-running autonomous analysts for finance and how we've approached that problem.

Recently, we've seen personal agents reach a kind of takeoff velocity because they've crossed a certain threshold of quality and productivity. But in finance, a lot of people in private equity and banking are still using AI as a chatbot. They're using ChatGPT or Claude to answer questions, or as plugins in Excel and PowerPoint.

That's very different from saying, "I'm going to delegate an entire workstream to you and come back 12 hours later."

That's what we're focused on building. The talk will walk through the technical details of how we're approaching that problem.

**The Daily Context: When you set out to build an AI system that actually does financial analysis, rather than another general-purpose agent, what fundamentally broke?**

**Yijia:** From day one, our focus was on how we could credibly produce ROI for the end user. In our eyes, that was the analyst or associate doing the grunt work. ROI means getting hours back in your day. Instead of you doing the Excel model or PowerPoint, Compound does it for you in exactly the same way you would have done it.

Initially, the models weren't good enough. We spent a lot of time figuring out how to get o3 or Sonnet 3.7 to work better with Excel. The models improved, but we realized three other things were broken.

First, the tools themselves. Excel, PowerPoint, and Word are built for humans, not agents, and certainly not cloud-based agents running hundreds of parallel processes.

Second, collaboration. So much of finance happens in small teams, with multiple people providing opinions and feedback. But AI has been so single-player. Even if you're giving an individual a few hours back, you're not solving the bigger problem of how to give hours back to the team or firm.

Third, context. Even with skills, memory, and dreaming, off-the-shelf models aren't perfect for finance because of the sheer number of unstructured files involved. Code is largely characters and Markdown files. Finance involves PDFs, Excel spreadsheets, and PowerPoints, which are much richer in information.

**The Daily Context: What does good actually look like? Is it getting to the right number, showing the steps, or something more?**

**Yijia:** There are two ways I think about good.

The first is reaching this almost magical threshold where someone looks at your output and says, "Yeah, that's what I would've done," and gives it a checkmark.

We're already seeing that in coding. Basically every software engineer I know is using AI to drive their coding. They look at the result, decide it looks good, and check it off. If we can produce financial models and PowerPoints that reach that same bar, that's great.

The second is whether AI passes the sniff test for judgment and critical thinking. That's where I don't think we're there yet.

Evaluating deals requires creativity, judgment, and self-iteration. When you work with an incredible human analyst, they often have next steps and follow-ups ready, even without being asked. They'll proactively address issues before you raise them.

AI isn't there yet. It produces something, and the implicit understanding is that there isn't necessarily a follow-up or next step.

When you work with a really good human analyst, they've usually already anticipated the three comments you're going to have. That's the level of quality we aspire to.

**The Daily Context: Fast-forward five years. Will AI remain embedded in Excel, or will the entire interface for financial analysis change?**

**Yijia:** Excel has survived for 40 years for two reasons. It's an incredible piece of software, and it functions as both a calculator and a canvas for financial firms to express ideas.

Some firms have 40 years of financial history stored in Excel. Unless you figure out how to map that information into a structured database, it's going to be difficult to move away from it.

Five years from now, I think Excel will still exist. But most firms will have moved toward having a data warehouse and will be migrating firm-level information out of Excel.

I think we'll see people relying more on HTML or another type of artifact that isn't Excel.

But people will still want auditability and traceability. How do you step into calculations and fully trust that a number is correct?

That's what Excel is great at. You can see the math, and the engine is deterministic. Whatever replaces it needs to offer that same trust.

**The Daily Context: Do you think vertical AI is the future, or will general-purpose models eventually serve specialized industries like finance?**

**Yijia:** I think about AI in terms of how it augments what differentiates one firm from another. For some firms, that's their human capital, the history of deals they've done, their relationships, or their platform.

You can accomplish that by building your own AI, using general-purpose tools, or using domain-specific solutions.

I strongly believe there will be vertical-specific solutions in finance, and multiple winners, because the category is so massive.

The reason is the unique nature of the data. Look at the most successful financial businesses before AI: Bloomberg, Capital IQ, and FactSet. They're built around supplying data to customers.

But what's becoming more interesting isn't just the data you provide, which will become increasingly commoditized. It's how you help firms harness their own data.

I think every firm will eventually have a data warehouse, a data lakehouse, and an ontological layer. I call it a "company brain."

The big winner will be someone who can operate that brain and become a real partner as firms deploy AI across their businesses.

**The Daily Context: Financial services companies handle enormous amounts of sensitive information. How should they think about sharing data with AI models?**

**Yijia:** Zero data retention needs to be table stakes. Model companies should not train on your data. That's our stance.

We have zero data retention agreements with every one of our model providers. We've chosen not to roll out new models if they don't have that protection available.

The next question is how you build valuable systems on top of that data. Firms will want to own those systems themselves.

You have to start with the most stringent version of security. Start from least privilege rather than most privilege.

**The Daily Context: What's your advice for AI engineers building tools for high-stakes users?**

**Yijia:** Two things.

First, you get one or two shots on goal before finance users form an opinion of your product. And that opinion is basically set in stone for a long time.

When Claude came out with its plugins and Opus 4.5, the narrative on Wall Street became that Anthropic had won the enterprise. Even when newer models came out from competitors, that narrative didn't change much.

Finance users treat AI products almost the same way they treat human analysts. They have incredibly high expectations. If you can't deliver the first or second time, they're going to write you off.

Second, you have to constantly reinvent. There's creative destruction happening in product development because AI is moving so fast.

Every week or month, we reevaluate what we've built. Is there an opportunity to rewrite it, make it better, make it faster, or even start from scratch because of how much AI has improved?

**The Daily Context: What's something you wish more people would ask you about?**

**Yijia:** I don't think people talk enough about eval construction in finance.

We're focused on the outputs that move the needle for customers. Our evals focus on entire workflows, from information ingestion and research gathering to writing and grading the outputs.

A lot of benchmarks evaluate whether the answer is correct, rather than evaluating the entire body of work.

But in finance, the body of work is actually the most important thing people evaluate.

We focus on high-quality outputs because that's what drives ROI for customers. How realistic our evals are compared with others in the market is a real differentiator for us.

**The Daily Context: Is there anything else you want to highlight?**

**Yijia:** We talked earlier about multiple people working with AI at the same time. I think that's going to be a big part of the future, especially for deal teams.

With our new product version, we've built that in natively. It's almost like a shared Slack channel where multiple people can talk with AI together.

Our belief is that you have to unify where people collaborate with the outputs they're working on.

That might mean multiple people talking in a channel about a financial model or leaving comments on a PowerPoint for the agent to incorporate.

It's a much more natural way of working. From an engineering perspective, it's also difficult to build a system that works well when taking feedback from five different people at once.

I think multiplayer and collaborative AI will be a major next frontier.

Welcome to AI Engineer New York

Welcome to New York City. Whether you came from a few blocks away or flew in from the other side of the world, you're in for a life-changing experience.

**New York is AI Engineer’s second home in the United States.** Some of our best talks ever and most memorable summits happened here last year. There’s a reason we keep coming back: this city takes new ideas and puts them to work at a scale few places can match. Frontier AI leaders from the West Coast come to meet centuries-old global financial institutions here, but also the people building in fashion, media, real estate, insurance, and every corner of the city’s economy. We moved dates: Fall is a beautiful time to visit, and I hope you get to enjoy New York beyond the conference too.

**This one is personal for me: In some ways, the last 20 years of my life have led to this.** I studied finance on the East Coast, then traded currency derivatives in Singapore, London, Dubai, Taiwan, and New York. I saw how much of a business moving billions of dollars in options, swaps, and futures still depended on making sense of language, and I built NLP programs (in Haskell!!) that rapidly powered our entire options desk — as both a trader and a technologist, I could finally see how being fluent in both creates far more impact than either individually.

Later, as a "quantamental" analyst at a hedge fund, I built trading and data pipelines and worked with alternative data, managing a >$1B portfolio in an era before Airflow, Modal, or Temporal. I saw how formalizing our PM's investing rules made us better at decision-making and scaled our small team to do far more than in the history of finance. Not everything was roses... I also saw how badly machines can go wrong, and why human judgment still matters, ESPECIALLY in key places. New York is where I REALLY learned to code, where I first became an engineer at Two Sigma, and also where I started my blogging career because [DEV](https://dev.to) sponsored a conference exactly like this one. 10 years of writing and speaking later, we now have Latent.Space and AI Engineer.

The world is also bigger than finance. We offer you 5 tracks across finance (named for Jim Simons of RenTech), engineering (named for Claude Shannon, founder of information theory), leadership (named for Richard Sutton, the king of scale), evals (named for Alan Turing), and AI (named for John McCarthy, who led the 1955 Dartmouth workshop that created the field). **We want to build the best AI conference New York City has to offer**, and **the best AI in finance conference anywhere**. We humbly ask for your help to make us a lasting and positive fixture in the NYC landscape.

Over the next three days, I hope you find ideas, connections, and tools you can bring to your team tomorrow. I also hope you wander into a session outside your field, meet someone you disagree with, and discover an opportunity you hadn’t considered. Some of the smartest people working in AI are in New York this week. Take the time to learn from each other.

**Thank you for being here. Welcome to AI Engineer New York!**
