I Write on a 2006 iMac and Code on a $200 Laptop

![imac](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/lsf20ka9puiwh88jxt8g.jpg)

I've always loved the idea of reusing old hardware, especially when it's still more than capable of the job you need it for. Planned obsolescence aside, a lot of machines can still do what we need them to do. They just stopped getting OS and security updates.

My main coding machine is a $200 laptop from 2020. Most of my writing happens on a 2006 iMac. Both were hand-me-downs from family members, so I didn't pay for either one.

They each have their own job, and that's on purpose. I try to separate tasks across my devices. Here's what each one does, what it can't do, and why I keep using them.

## Yes, I have a gaming PC

![mainpc](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/uiwu57vb9osvmlym6ctp.jpeg)


Before anyone asks: I do have a gaming PC. I code on it too, and it doubles as my dev workstation. It mostly gets used for experimenting with local models, heavy multitasking, or, most recently, debugging Oniria.

But most of my time nowadays is spent studying, and gaming in my free time. My laptop really comes in handy when I get an idea on the go or I'm traveling, or when I just straight up don't want to get distracted by my growing Steam backlog.

## The laptop: Random budget HP, 2020

This gal is ole reliable. When I was given her, I immediately uninstalled Windows, installed Fedora Linux, and stripped out a few bloated apps and repos. Now she's my minimalist coding machine for when I want to focus. I usually find myself using this little machine for most of my coding, more than my dual-monitor workstation. I don't know, there's just something about its simplicity that's alluring to me.

![gal](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/s0pdquud6650cur80d2s.jpeg)

![olereliabe](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/e41tstk9br181yz725i5.png)

Here's what it's working with. I ran fastfetch with the logo and the hostname line turned off, so it's just the parts that matter:

```bash
fastfetch -c none -l none -s os:host:cpu:gpu:memory:disk
```

- **OS:** Fedora Linux 44 (Workstation Edition)
- **Host:** HP Laptop 15-dy2xxx
- **CPU:** 11th Gen Intel Core i3-1125G4 (4 cores, 8 threads)
- **GPU:** Intel UHD Graphics, integrated
- **Memory:** 8 GB
- **Storage:** 256 GB

None of that is impressive in 2026, and I'm fine with that. Eight gigs of RAM doesn't leave room for a dozen open apps, so I don't open a dozen apps. I keep her lean and she keeps up.

And since she runs Fedora, she still gets regular updates. That's more than I can say for the iMac.

## The iMac: 2006, Mac OS X Tiger

My writing machine is a 2006 Intel iMac with 2 GB of memory, running Mac OS X Tiger. It runs FocusWriter, and that's about it. It gets used for writing. Just writing.

It's also not connected to the internet. Tiger hasn't gotten a security update in well over a decade, so keeping it offline is the safe call. Honestly, that's the whole point too. There's no browser to wander into, no notifications, no "let me just check one thing real quick." When I sit down at it, the only thing it can do is the thing I sat down to do. All finished work is then transferred from a USB stick onto my laptop or main PC 

## Limitations are kind of the point

I think limitations get a bad rap. When a machine can do everything, I end up doing a little bit of everything: a tab here, a settings tweak there, a "quick" round of something from the backlog. When a machine can only do one or two things, I stop fiddling with my setup and actually make stuff.

That's what minimalism comes down to for me: fewer decisions. I don't have to decide whether to open Discord on the iMac, because I can't. Every option I take away is one less thing pulling at my attention, and those add up fast.

Constraints also push me to get creative with what I've got. When the tool can't do the fancy thing, I have to figure out the simple version. A lot of the time, the simple version is the one worth shipping anyway.

## If you've got an old machine in a closet

Don't write it off just because it can't keep up with everything anymore. Give it one job. Put Linux on it, take it offline, make it your writing machine or your focus-coding machine. Strip it down to the one thing you keep meaning to do more of.

Neither of my machines is new, and neither was expensive. They're still the ones I reach for the most when I actually want to get something done.

So, what's your old-machine setup? I'd love to hear what you've given a second life. 💻

text:
Llama Village: a virtual world powered by local AI with llamadart

![Animated gameplay showing llamas conversing in the village while Dash flies nearby.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leehack/llama-village/main/docs/media/header.gif)

*Llama Village in motion. The characters’ dialogue is generated by an on-device model.*

[Watch the full trailer on GitHub](https://github.com/leehack/llama-village/releases/tag/v0.1.0-preview)

I wanted to try building a 3D game with `flutter_scene`. I was already working on llamadart, so I thought it would be fun to use local AI in the game too. My starting idea was fairly loose: make it look good, keep it simple, and put Dash, the Flutter mascot, in a scene with some llamas.

I wanted to show different kinds of AI working together, including multiple characters acting on their own. But I did not have a game concept I liked yet.

## Finding a reason for the AI

I spent quite a while on the visuals. I tried a hand-drawn look, asked for something closer to Borderlands, and eventually switched to a softer film style because the earlier renders kept looking glitchy. Meanwhile, we tried several game ideas. I was not happy with how they played.

These were two of my messages in the Claude Code session:

> “Btw the game isn't fun.”

> “What's the point of ai?”

Eventually I asked for a village where the llamas would live and interact on their own. I wanted to give them personalities, see their thoughts and conversations, and control Dash to interact with them. That was the idea we went ahead with.

![An overhead view of the colourful huts, bakery, paths and pond at golden hour.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leehack/llama-village/main/docs/media/01_village_golden_hour.jpg)

*The village at golden hour, with the bakery in the centre and the festival stage in the foreground.*

## Who lives here?

Pip, Mo, June, Bramble, and Clover each have a personality, needs, relationships, goals, and things they know. They make plans, walk around the village, and stop to talk. A missing scarf, a bread rumour, a secret crush, and the upcoming Berry Festival give them things to care about.

![June says “Oh, real poems now. Tell me more about them.” while talking with Bramble.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leehack/llama-village/main/docs/media/02_conversation.jpg)

*June and Bramble talking. Each line is written from the speaker’s situation and the conversation so far.*

They do not all know the same things. In the inspector below, June knows that Mo knocked Pip’s scarf into the pond because she heard it from Mo. Other entries are things she saw herself. The game keeps track of both the information and how she got it.

This is what I mean by a multi-agent system in this game. Each llama has its own knowledge, goals, and relationships. They use the same underlying language model, with different context for each character.

![June’s inspector lists facts and marks whether she saw them or heard them from another llama.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leehack/llama-village/main/docs/media/04_inspector.jpg)

*The inspector shows what June knows and who told her.*

## How a conversation changes the village

I wanted to try more than one kind of AI. The language model writes dialogue and thoughts. Embeddings help compare the meaning of the dialogue with facts the listener could have learned. An optional Laya decision model helps choose casual conversation topics from the options the game allows.

Movement, needs, knowledge tracking, and endings are handled in code. After a conversation, the model reports which facts were mentioned and suggests changes to mood and friendship. The game checks the fact claims before accepting them.

**A llama knows → they talk → the game checks → a neighbour learns.**

Secrets require explicit keyword evidence; embedding similarity alone is not enough.

For example, imagine one llama passing along news. The speaker needs to know it first. The model writes the exchange, and the game checks whether the words support transferring that information. If accepted, it becomes something the listener knows and may discuss later.

The llamas can keep walking and going about their day while the model is busy writing.

## Enter Dash

You play as Dash. Click a llama and he flies over to visit. The game generates four things he could say while he is on the way. I specifically wanted selectable options here, so you can play without stopping to type a message.

![Dash visits Pip beside the pond. Four choices offer teasing, news, a compliment and gossip.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leehack/llama-village/main/docs/media/03_dash_choices.jpg)

*Dash can tell Pip the bread rumour is false, or start another rumour about Mo.*

The game chooses the available intentions and facts; the model words the options for the character. You can encourage someone, help them, pass along news, or stir up gossip. The llama’s reaction and the resulting changes to trust or mood are governed by rules, while the model gives the reply its voice.

Passing along a correction can help. Gossip can leave a llama believing something false. Those changes carry into later interactions and count toward the ending.

## Making the village in 3D

I had a lot of fun building this with `flutter_scene`. I kept asking for changes to the characters, especially making the llamas look different from one another and getting Dash’s face right. Then came the weather, animals, music, and cutscenes for skipping the night.

![Fireflies glow around a pond with ducks, a small boat and warm lamps at night.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leehack/llama-village/main/docs/media/05_night_fireflies.jpg)

*Fireflies and lamps around the pond at night.*

![Clover and Bramble run along a village path in the rain.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leehack/llama-village/main/docs/media/06_storm.jpg)

*Clover and Bramble heading home during the storm.*

The models and the 3D renderer share the same machine, which makes performance a concern. The scene needs to keep running while text is generated. Some work can happen ahead of time, like writing Dash’s options during his flight.

Llamadart provides the cross-platform local AI foundation. The game shown here is the macOS preview, running inference locally with the model files already on the machine. Bringing the same experience to other devices still requires working through their memory, inference, and rendering budgets.

When I started thinking about mobile, I even asked whether we could make a version without an LLM. That is still an open design question. Generating everything live has a cost, and I would want to reconsider how much of it a mobile version needs.

## A festival, then a storybook

I also wanted the game to have a goal and different endings based on what Dash did. The Berry Festival gives the week a destination. The llamas perform, a winner is chosen, and the ending reflects the relationships, rumours, and trust built up during play. The winner and ending are determined by game rules.

![Mo stands in a warm spotlight beneath the Golden Bell, with June and Pip on stage.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leehack/llama-village/main/docs/media/07_festival_spotlight.jpg)

*Mo wins the Golden Bell in this recorded playthrough.*

Afterward, the game turns the week into a picture book. A journal records notable events, conversations, rumours, and Dash’s visits. The model uses a digest of those events to write the pages, alongside pictures captured during play.

![An open picture book titled The First Day, with a village image and a narrative about the day.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leehack/llama-village/main/docs/media/08_storybook.jpg)

*The first day, retold using the game’s journal and a picture captured during play.*

This was something I asked for after the game had taken shape: a fairy-tale book about what happened during the run. It is a nice way to look back at conversations and events you may have missed while following Dash.

## Where I would take it next

I would like to try a lighter version that works well on more devices. Llamadart’s cross-platform support gives me a starting point, but this game still needs its own performance work and testing on each platform.

For this version, I got to build the experiment I wanted: several characters talking and acting in the same world, with local models doing different jobs. I also spent far more time adjusting llama faces and village lighting than the original idea suggested.

If you try it, I would be interested to hear whether you prefer watching the llamas or getting involved as Dash.

[Explore Llama Village on GitHub](https://github.com/leehack/llama-village) · [Watch the preview trailer](https://github.com/leehack/llama-village/releases/tag/v0.1.0-preview) · [Explore llamadart](https://github.com/leehack/llamadart)

Writing assistance: this article was drafted with AI assistance using my development notes and project documentation. Gameplay images and animation are from Llama Village.

text:
You Should Know About System One Models

Production AI usually looks like this: stuff context into a prompt, ask a large language model a yes-or-no question, beg it to answer in JSON, then parse whatever comes back and hope.

The punchline is that it actually is incredibly useful to use LLMs for their judgment instead of their writing: is this spam, where does this belong, is this comment actually helpful? LLMs were the best tool for the job, even if they were the wrong tool for the job. The inherent inefficiencies of this idea made scaling an incredibly delicate balancing act of quality, token waste, intelligence and pseudo-determinism.

Then [Jev](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev) came along, and it seems like the missing piece.

## Judgment as a primitive

Jev, from TypeSafe, is a "System One" model. It doesn't generate text. You hand it some state (a comment, a profile, some JSON) and a set of questions, and it returns typed answers with probabilities. There are three shapes: yes/no, pick one from a list, or place it on a scale.

That sounds limiting until you notice how much of our LLM usage fits those three boxes. No parsing, no "respond with only one word." Just a decision your code can branch on, plus a probability that tells it when to act and when to escalate.

## How we use it in Forem

In [Forem](https://github.com/forem/forem), the open source software that powers [DEV](https://dev.to/), Jev plays two roles.

The first is **decision maker**. It labels new posts for anti-spam moderation, checks whether a post meets a badge's criteria, picks a highlighting language for unlabeled code blocks, and suggests tags for untagged posts.

The second, my favorite, is **traffic cop**. Our spam escalation check is a cheap Jev pass that asks a few questions in parallel: is this spam, is it pushing readers to a Telegram or WhatsApp contact, is it promoting something unrelated to this community? It never flags anything itself. It just decides what deserves a closer look from the full check.

Jev is orders of magnitude cheaper than LLMs, and along with lower latency, allows us to inject a layer of intelligence into parts of the system which had to be strictly algorithmic before.

## Where this is really headed

These decisions don't need a frontier data center. They need to be fast, consistent, and close to where things happen.

Think about a smart home. Was that a request to turn off the lights, or just a mention of them? Is this motion event worth waking me up for? Those are rigid, reactive, latency-sensitive calls. They should happen locally, without your living room phoning a server farm.

That's why I'm rooting for projects like [Laya](https://github.com/receptron/laya), an open source take on the idea that you can run yourself. It may not be there yet, but someone will make local judgment models work, and when they do, this whole class of AI moves onto the device.

## Practical problem solving

Many production AI use cases wind up as a solution looking for a problem, or simply lack scaled cost-effective usefulness. This tool complements frontier AI intelligence beautifully to maximize the practical roll-out ready usefulness of our systems.

I see the release of Jev as not just a usefulness-first AI innovation, but an articulation for how we should be designing tiered intelligence systems to control for costs and provide algorithmic-like control of our outcomes.

text:
Operational intelligence is sociotechnical

A scan of the Slack channels for a recent private equity deployment of Clonal ([our operational intelligence platform](https://clonal.io/)) might confuse you at first. There is far less talk of dbt models, evals, or Monte Carlo simulations than you would expect, and far more about “human factors,” “emotional resonance,” and endless conversations about how to facilitate alignment. The human kind, not the AI model kind.

Creating software is increasingly the easy part of our job. The harder part is building systems that people trust, use, and improve as they work with them. In financial services that matters a great deal. On the day we deploy Clonal, it is inert. Even once data is flowing, connecting sources and generating summaries does not create value on its own. Value shows up when better context changes front-line work: how analysts prepare, how ICs decide, how BD coordinates, and how the firm acts on an investment.

Our PE work shows this. Neither our clients nor we want another place to go look things up. We want the firm’s own history available to the person making a call, when they are making it. Part of that is an engineering problem. The rest is social. It takes careful system design and iteration, and it takes what we call human motions: the recurring things people do around the system, like walkthroughs, reviews, and deciding who owns what.

## Workflow even over feature

Consider how a deal lead prepares for a banker conversation meant to generate dealflow. Their questions are simple: What have we discussed before? Which companies are coming to market? What did we pass on, and why? What should we ask next?

A technically impressive platform can make that preparation *harder* if the answers are scattered across overlapping screens, abstract scores, and unfamiliar categories.

Early on, we built these as fully realized features, with visuals and styling. John Cutler, our product lead, noticed that this collapsed several mental models into one. The client was reacting to the data, the logic behind it, and the presentation all at once, so we could not tell which of those their feedback was about, and we rarely got a clear read on the actual state of the graph data. Now we start by understanding the question and writing sample queries, then sit with the client and walk through what the data surfaces. It’s a bit like paper-prototyping the insight.

## The operating model lives inside the architecture

In ontology design (we call it “topology”), small distinctions carry large consequences.

A `company` is not a `deal`. One company can have multiple `transaction processes` over time. An internal decision to pass may not be the same as communicating that decision externally. A fund passing does not mean the company is no longer in market. A missing interaction record does not prove a relationship has gone cold. We hit these constantly. They are the everyday semantics of the business.

If the platform collapses those distinctions, it can present a clean interface that misrepresents reality. Forward-deployed engineers and product managers work through system design with the client so the distinctions show up in the data model, workflow ownership, permissions, and visible action states. Without that regular contact, we build things that *function* but don’t *work*.

## Closing workflow loops and learning loops

Forward-deployed work keeps paying off after implementation.

Engineers and product leaders working alongside users see the gap between a requested capability and a usable routine. They watch someone navigate a real deal, investigate an unexpected comparable, or struggle to find the next action. That proximity exposes problems a requirements document rarely captures. Cheap code lets us compress those cycles a lot, but design and interaction with real people doing real work is the most important kind of HITL we do.

We are borrowing heavily from DDD and service design to make these sessions useful: short walkthroughs, focused wargaming, testing against real records, visible feedback tracking. All of it helps clarify what “good” means. Sometimes we can gather that from the environment. When we step into judgment-heavy work like deal evaluation, we have to find ways to turn intuition into evaluation.

## Trust is designed through restraint

In investment work, an attractive black-box score is usually less useful than a dated note with a clear source. A label like “cooling relationship” sounds intelligent, but it backfires when the professional knows they have had several recent conversations. “No recorded interaction since this date” claims less, and the reader can act on it.

The same applies to automation. An elapsed deadline can prompt a review, but it should not declare a process dead on its own. A queued update should not appear completed. Unknown data should stay unknown instead of becoming a confident-looking zero. None of this is hard to express in software, even hand-written code. It is easy to overlook in design.

## The deliverable is a repeatable capability

Our goal is for clients not to need our deployment teams. We aim to leave behind an organization with clearer ownership, reusable context, reliable decision pathways, and the ability to keep improving its own system.

The software we build and configure provides the machinery, and the human motions around it make it operational.

text:
Deploying LiteLLM: An Open-Source AI Gateway

[LiteLLM](https://litellm.ai) is an open-source AI gateway that provides a unified, OpenAI-compatible API for over 100 large language model (LLM) providers, removing the need to integrate with each provider's SDK and authentication scheme. In production, teams use LiteLLM to issue virtual keys with budget limits, track token usage and spend across providers, and configure centralized access control and routing. This guide walks through deploying LiteLLM on a Linux server using Docker Compose with PostgreSQL for persistent storage, Prometheus for metrics collection, and Traefik as the reverse proxy for HTTPS access. By the end, you'll have a fully functional, OpenAI-compatible AI gateway accessible over a custom domain, with virtual key management, spend tracking, and provider routing configured.

Before you begin, you need a Linux-based server with at least 4 CPU cores and 8 GB of RAM as a non-root user with sudo privileges, Docker and Docker Compose installed, a DNS A record (such as `litellm.example.com`) pointing to your server's IP address, and an API key from at least one [supported LLM provider](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/providers).

---

## 1. Set Up the Directory Structure, Configuration, and Environment Variables

LiteLLM requires a configuration file to define model providers and routing rules, a Prometheus configuration file for metrics scraping, and environment variables for secrets and database credentials.

**1. Create the project directory with subdirectories for persistent data:**

```console
$ mkdir -p ~/litellm/{letsencrypt,postgres,prometheus}
```

`letsencrypt` stores SSL/TLS certificates, `postgres` persists PostgreSQL database files, and `prometheus` persists Prometheus metrics data.

**2. Navigate to the project directory:**

```console
$ cd ~/litellm
```

**3. Set matching ownership on the Prometheus host directory (Prometheus runs as UID 65534 inside the container):**

```console
$ sudo chown -R 65534:65534 prometheus
```

**4. Generate a master key and salt key for LiteLLM. Run this command twice to produce two separate values:**

```console
$ openssl rand -hex 32
```

Save both values for the `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` and `LITELLM_SALT_KEY` fields in the next step.

**5. Create the `.env` file to store credentials and secrets:**

```console
$ nano .env
```

**6. Add the following values:**

```ini
DOMAIN=litellm.example.com
LETSENCRYPT_EMAIL=admin@example.com
LITELLM_MASTER_KEY=sk-YOUR_MASTER_KEY
LITELLM_SALT_KEY=sk-YOUR_SALT_KEY
LLM_PROVIDER_API_KEY=YOUR_LLM_PROVIDER_API_KEY
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=STRONG_DATABASE_PASSWORD
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://llmproxy:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@db:5432/litellm
UI_USERNAME=admin
UI_PASSWORD=YOUR_UI_PASSWORD
```

Replace the placeholders with your own values: `litellm.example.com` is the domain pointing to your server's IP address; `admin@example.com` is the email address for Let's Encrypt notifications; `sk-YOUR_MASTER_KEY` is the admin key used to authenticate with the LiteLLM API (replace `YOUR_MASTER_KEY` with the first generated value and keep the `sk-` prefix); `sk-YOUR_SALT_KEY` encrypts provider credentials stored in PostgreSQL and cannot be changed after the first model is added; `YOUR_LLM_PROVIDER_API_KEY` is the API key for the provider configured in `config.yaml`; `STRONG_DATABASE_PASSWORD` is the PostgreSQL password used by both the database container and the connection string; `admin`/`YOUR_UI_PASSWORD` are the LiteLLM dashboard credentials.

**7. Create the LiteLLM configuration file:**

```console
$ nano config.yaml
```

**8. Add the following contents:**

```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: my-model
    litellm_params:
      model: provider/model
      api_key: os.environ/LLM_PROVIDER_API_KEY

litellm_settings:
  callbacks:
    - prometheus
  require_auth_for_metrics_endpoint: true

general_settings:
  master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY
```

Replace `my-model` with a name of your choice to identify this model within LiteLLM, and `provider/model` with the LiteLLM provider prefix followed by the model identifier (for example, `anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5`). The `os.environ/` prefix tells LiteLLM to read the value from an environment variable at runtime rather than hardcoding it. The `litellm_settings` block enables Prometheus metrics via the `callbacks` field, and `require_auth_for_metrics_endpoint: true` restricts the `/metrics` endpoint to authenticated requests, so only Prometheus (sending the master key as a Bearer token) can scrape metrics successfully. The `general_settings` block defines the master key LiteLLM uses to authenticate admin API requests and virtual key management operations.

**9. Create the Prometheus configuration file:**

```console
$ nano prometheus.yml
```

**10. Add the following contents:**

```yaml
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s
  evaluation_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "litellm"
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["litellm:4000"]
    bearer_token: "sk-YOUR_MASTER_KEY"
```

Replace `sk-YOUR_MASTER_KEY` with the value of `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` from your `.env` file. Prometheus uses this token to authenticate its scrape requests against the protected `/metrics` endpoint.

## 2. Deploy with Docker Compose

The deployment stack runs LiteLLM behind Traefik, which handles TLS termination and automatic certificate provisioning through Let's Encrypt. PostgreSQL provides persistent storage for virtual keys, spend data, and usage logs. Prometheus collects gateway metrics by scraping the LiteLLM `/metrics` endpoint every 15 seconds over the internal Docker network.

**1. Add your user account to the Docker group:**

```console
$ sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
```

**2. Apply the new group membership:**

```console
$ newgrp docker
```

**3. Create the Docker Compose manifest file:**

```console
$ nano docker-compose.yaml
```

**4. Add the following contents:**

```yaml
services:
  traefik:
    image: traefik:v3.6
    container_name: traefik
    restart: always
    command:
      - "--providers.docker=true"
      - "--providers.docker.exposedbydefault=false"
      - "--entrypoints.web.address=:80"
      - "--entrypoints.websecure.address=:443"
      - "--entrypoints.web.http.redirections.entrypoint.to=websecure"
      - "--entrypoints.web.http.redirections.entrypoint.scheme=https"
      - "--certificatesresolvers.le.acme.httpchallenge=true"
      - "--certificatesresolvers.le.acme.httpchallenge.entrypoint=web"
      - "--certificatesresolvers.le.acme.email=${LETSENCRYPT_EMAIL}"
      - "--certificatesresolvers.le.acme.storage=/letsencrypt/acme.json"
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro
      - ./letsencrypt:/letsencrypt

  litellm:
    image: docker.litellm.ai/berriai/litellm:v1.89.1
    container_name: litellm
    restart: always
    volumes:
      - ./config.yaml:/app/config.yaml
    command:
      - "--config=/app/config.yaml"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: ${DATABASE_URL}
      STORE_MODEL_IN_DB: "True"
    env_file:
      - .env
    expose:
      - "4000"
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test:
        - CMD-SHELL
        - python3 -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:4000/health/liveliness')"
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 40s
    labels:
      - "traefik.enable=true"
      - "traefik.http.routers.litellm.rule=Host(`${DOMAIN}`)"
      - "traefik.http.routers.litellm.entrypoints=websecure"
      - "traefik.http.routers.litellm.tls=true"
      - "traefik.http.routers.litellm.tls.certresolver=le"
      - "traefik.http.services.litellm.loadbalancer.server.port=4000"

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    container_name: litellm_db
    restart: always
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: litellm
      POSTGRES_USER: llmproxy
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - ./postgres:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    expose:
      - "5432"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -d litellm -U llmproxy"]
      interval: 1s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10

  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus
    container_name: litellm_prometheus
    restart: always
    volumes:
      - ./prometheus:/prometheus
      - ./prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
    expose:
      - "9090"
    command:
      - "--config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml"
      - "--storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus"
      - "--storage.tsdb.retention.time=15d"

```

This configuration deploys four services behind a single HTTPS endpoint: `traefik` acts as the reverse proxy and TLS terminator, redirecting HTTP to HTTPS via Let's Encrypt; `litellm` runs the proxy image pinned to a specific release tag, mounts `config.yaml`, and waits for PostgreSQL to become healthy before starting; `db` runs PostgreSQL 16 as the persistent backend for virtual keys, spend data, and usage logs; `prometheus` scrapes LiteLLM metrics every 15 seconds with a 15-day retention window. The named volumes for `db` and `prometheus` ensure their data survives container removal or recreation.

### Verify the Docker Image with Cosign

LiteLLM Docker images are signed with [Cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/quickstart/quickstart-cosign/). Verifying the image signature before deployment confirms the image has not been tampered with since it was published by the LiteLLM team.

**1. Download and install the Cosign binary:**

```console
$ curl -O -L "https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/releases/latest/download/cosign-linux-amd64"
```

**2. Move the binary into your system path:**

```console
$ sudo mv cosign-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/cosign
```

**3. Make the binary executable:**

```console
$ sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/cosign
```

**4. Verify the installation:**

```console
$ cosign version
```

**5. Verify the LiteLLM image signature using the pinned public key.** This checks the same release tag deployed in the Docker Compose file. LiteLLM publishes signatures for the `ghcr.io` registry specifically, so this confirms the `v1.89.1` release itself, not the `docker.litellm.ai` mirror byte-for-byte.

```console
$ cosign verify \
    --key https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/0112e53046018d726492c814b3644b7d376029d0/cosign.pub \
    ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.89.1
```

A successful verification outputs a JSON payload confirming the image was signed with the LiteLLM public key.

### Start the Stack

**1. Start the services:**

```console
$ docker compose up -d
```

**2. Verify all containers are running:**

```console
$ docker compose ps
```

Verify that all four containers show an `Up` status, with `litellm` and `db` marked `(healthy)` and `traefik` listing ports 80 and 443 under `PORTS`.

## 3. Access and Configure LiteLLM

LiteLLM exposes a web-based admin dashboard at the `/ui` path of your configured domain, with visibility into model configuration, virtual keys, usage, and spend tracking.

1. Open your web browser and navigate to `https://litellm.example.com/ui`, replacing `litellm.example.com` with your configured domain.
2. Log in using the credentials from your `.env` file — the value of `UI_USERNAME` in the **Username** field and `UI_PASSWORD` in the **Password** field, then click **Login**. Verify that the dashboard loads and displays the main navigation panels.
3. Click **Models + Endpoints** in the left sidebar to verify the configured model providers. The model defined in `config.yaml` appears in the list with its alias and underlying provider model. The left sidebar also provides access to **Virtual Keys** for managing scoped access credentials, **Usage** for per-model and per-key request tracking, and **Logs** for spend and cost breakdowns by model, key, and team.

## 4. Test the Gateway and Create a Virtual Key

LiteLLM exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, so any application built for the OpenAI SDK works with LiteLLM by pointing `base_url` at the gateway. Virtual keys provide scoped, credential-isolated access without exposing the master key.

**1. Install the Python virtual environment package:**

```console
$ sudo apt install -y python3-venv
```

**2. Create a Python virtual environment:**

```console
$ python3 -m venv litellm-env
```

**3. Activate the virtual environment:**

```console
$ source litellm-env/bin/activate
```

**4. Install the OpenAI Python SDK:**

```console
$ pip install openai
```

**5. Export your master key as an environment variable, replacing `sk-YOUR_MASTER_KEY` with the `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` value from your `.env` file:**

```console
$ export LITELLM_MASTER_KEY="sk-YOUR_MASTER_KEY"
```

**6. Export your gateway domain as an environment variable, replacing `litellm.example.com` with your configured domain:**

```console
$ export LITELLM_DOMAIN="litellm.example.com"
```

**7. Create the test script:**

```console
$ nano test_litellm.py
```

**8. Add the following contents, replacing `my-model` with the model name you set in `config.yaml`:**

```python
import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["LITELLM_MASTER_KEY"],
    base_url=f"https://{os.environ['LITELLM_DOMAIN']}",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="my-model",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is an AI gateway?"}],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

**9. Run the script:**

```console
$ python3 test_litellm.py
```

The script returns a response from the configured LLM provider, confirming the gateway is routing requests correctly.

**10. Create a virtual key using the LiteLLM API, replacing `my-model` with the model name you set in `config.yaml`:**

```console
$ curl -X POST "https://${LITELLM_DOMAIN}/key/generate" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer ${LITELLM_MASTER_KEY}" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"key_alias": "test-app-key", "models": ["my-model"], "max_budget": 5.00}' \
    | python3 -c "import sys, json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['key'])"
```

The command prints the generated virtual key, similar to `sk-M9M0_aUDLi7AuhXtOAw6uw`. Each key can have its own model access list, budget limit, and rate limit.

**11. Export the virtual key returned in the previous step, replacing `sk-your-virtual-key` with the full key string printed:**

```console
$ export LITELLM_VIRTUAL_KEY="sk-your-virtual-key"
```

**12. Send a request using the virtual key, replacing `my-model` with the model name you set in `config.yaml`:**

```console
$ curl -X POST "https://${LITELLM_DOMAIN}/v1/chat/completions" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer ${LITELLM_VIRTUAL_KEY}" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{
      "model": "my-model",
      "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello from a virtual key!"}]
    }'
```

The gateway authenticates the virtual key, routes the request to the configured provider, and returns the model response.

**13. Return to the dashboard at `https://litellm.example.com/ui` and click Logs in the left sidebar.** Each entry shows the model alias, key alias, token count, and estimated cost for requests sent through both the master key and the virtual key.

## Next Steps

- Add more models to `config.yaml` and issue per-team or per-application virtual keys with distinct budget limits.
- Build Grafana dashboards on top of the Prometheus metrics for gateway observability.
- Set up alerting on budget thresholds and failed provider requests.
- Rotate the master key and salt key periodically and re-verify Docker image signatures on every upgrade.

For the full guide with additional tips, visit the original article on **[Vultr Docs](https://docs.vultr.com/how-to-deploy-litellm-open-source-ai-gateway)**.

Your Guide to AI Engineer New York 2026

AI Engineer New York is here! This conference built for Wall Street. Banking, hedge funds, fintech, insurance, asset management are top of mind, and we expect more than 1,000 engineers and technical leaders plus more than 100 speakers. You'll hear from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind, and from Two Sigma, Bridgewater, Citadel Securities, JPMorganChase, Vanguard, Ramp, and Coinbase.

## Three Tips

- RSVP early.
- Front-load the Expo.
- Budget time for Midtown.

## The Week Started Sunday

AI Engineer and Major League Hacking kicked things off with the AI Engineer New York Hackathon yesterday. A free day of building, with mentors, demos, and prizes. AI Engineer Kids Day ran the same afternoon for builders ages 9 to 15.

## Today, Monday: Workshop Day

Today is for building. Workshops are 9:00 to 12:00 and 1:15 to 4:30 covering managed agents, eval basics, and how to cut the AI bill. Pick one or two and stay put. Room-hopping a workshop gets nobody anywhere. The Expo opens at 4:00, and the welcome reception is from 5:00 to 7:00.

## The Main Event: Keynotes and Breakouts

Tuesday and Wednesday our keynotes start at 9:00, then breakouts through late morning and afternoon. Each room has a track. Engineering in Shannon. Leadership in Sutton. Evals in Turing, and McCarthy is curated. Sponsor Expo sessions join after lunch, and the Expo floor is open 10:30 to 4:30.

Five rooms at once can mean missing things. Don't worry. AI Engineer streams and posts talks to its YouTube channel.

## What Everyone Is Talking About

Trust, mostly. Evals, verification loops, deployment gates, and AI code review take up more space than anything else, They all try to answer the question of whether an agent's decision holds up in front of a regulator. Agent identity and auth is a close second. Agents with their own accounts and payment rails are the new arrival.

The open question is still about people. If AI writes the code, someone still has to know if it's good. That judgment comes from building real things, which is why started with a hackathon.

## Who Will You See?

CTOs, CEOs, and founders make up nearly half of attendees, and about a third work at companies with more than 10,000 people. Another third work on teams of fewer than ten. Bank architects and three-person startups, all in the same lunch line.

Join the conversation in the comments!

Where to Spend Your Week at AI Engineer New York

AI Engineer New York has 137 sessions on the schedule and up to five running at any given moment. Choices have to be made. Here is a look at the sessions and evenings you might build your day around.

## Today, Monday: Workshop Day

Pick the workshop that matches a problem already on your desk and stay for the whole thing. The **Claude Managed Agents Workshop** with CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall opens Sutton at 9:00. Teams still figuring out how to measure agent quality belong in Turing, where Laurie Voss kicks off with **Evaluations with Phoenix 101**.

A big opportunity is at 1:15 in Sutton. Nick Nisi and Zack Proser’s **Beyond “Done”: Building Verification Loops for AI Agents** takes on the question hanging over the rest of the week. How does a team trust what an agent hands back? The Expo opens at 4:00, and the welcome reception runs from 5:00 to 7:00.

## Tuesday: Trust, Money, and Agents That Pay

Show up early for keynotes. Max Kanat-Alexander asks **“Does Code Quality Even Matter?”** at 9:54. Aparna Dhinakaran follows at 10:12 with **“What does an AI engineer do?”** Two big questions, both before 10:30. Freddy Lecue follows at 10:40 with the Wells Fargo foundation model that handles fraud detection at scale.

Later, the evals room has a great morning on the schedule. **“Your Financial Agent Passed Every Eval. Can You Defend Its Decision?”** at 11:30 and **“Lies, Damned Lies, and Evals”** at 11:55 both ask how much a good benchmark score is worth once regulators start asking questions.

Anyone tracking agentic payments should catch Jan Curn’s **“Agents can pay. So why don’t they?”** (12:20, Shannon) and Ishween Kaur’s **“Your Agent Just Paid for Nothing (6 Attacks on x402 Payments)”** (2:55, Turing). Banks and card networks spent the last few weeks pushing agent payments past the pilot stage.

For everyone security-minded, the **Intent Based Auth panel** at 11:30 in Simons puts Dick Hardt, Allie Howe, Ian Livingstone, and Michael Davis on one stage to sort out who an agent is and what it gets to touch.

Tuesday night will be fun! Table Stakes, a ping-pong happy hour from Arize, Modal, Google DeepMind, and more, runs from 5:30 to 8:30. Keycard, Braintrust, and Socket bring demos and drinks to the Elsie Rooftop. Optiver’s Think Fast! trivia night at M Social goes until 10:00. RSVPs required across the board.

## Wednesday: Can AI Do the Job?

Day Two makes room for the skeptics. At 11:05 in Shannon, Ryan Stevens explains why giving a finance agent more context made it worse. Over in McCarthy, **“Can AI run Goldman Sachs?”** (11:30) and **“Agents Can Rewrite Compilers. Why Can’t They Pick Stocks?”** (12:20) take the hype straight at finance’s hardest problems. Stick around McCarthy at 11:55 for Maty Bohacek’s **“Two Ways to Rob an AI-Native Bank.”** You won’t want to miss it.

Thinking about careers? Catch Addy Osmani and Manish Kapur on **“Who verifies the software factory?”** (11:30, Sutton), then Laurie Voss on **“The Rise of the Product Engineer”** (12:20, Shannon). Runway CEO Cristóbal Valenzuela closes the keynote stage at 5:06 with **“Everything will be Simulated”**. Big title. Good closer.

## Thursday: Still Going

Don’t miss the final few events: Prior Labs and Mistral host The Next Frontier of AI Agents in Midtown Thursday night while Sonar runs an afternoon session at Convene on Madison Avenue about building an agentic software factory.

**Times and rooms can still move. Check the live schedule before committing.**

LangChainJS and Gemini 4 Argon: What's here and what's coming?

Google has released the latest version in the Gemini family, Gemini 4 Argon, and I was fortunate enough to be able to preview and test it.

The first thing I did was try it against the LangChainJS test suite - and it passed with flying colors.

However, if you're looking to use LangChainJS with Gemini 4 Argon today, there are a few things you need to keep in mind. And if you have some big future plans with Argon - there are a few things we're working on to make them working together better. This is a quick note to help let you know where we are and what we're working on.

![An incomplete sketch of a parrot, two stars, and the Roman numeral IV, generated by Gemini / Nano-Banana](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/ktyqax1va2i9n7t26zzy.jpeg)

## Gemini 4 Argon works today!

You can use LangChainJS with Gemini 4 Argon using either the Google AI (gai) or Google Enterprise / Vertex (gcp) platforms. No changes or new libraries necessary. Just use the model name "gemini-4-argon" and you're all set to go!

There are two things to keep in mind, however:
* The "minimal" thinking level (and a thinking budget of 0) aren't supported, but LangChainJS doesn't turn this into "low" like it does for other models where "minimal" isn't supported. A fix for this is coming shortly.
* "maxOutputTokens" has a 64k limit. Although Gemini 4 Argon supports up to 1M output tokens using a feature called Long Decode, but this requires some additional work. More about this below.

If you're using either "maxReasoningTokens" or "thinkingBudget", we'll continue to support these parameters for backwards compatibility, mapping them to Google's "thinkingLevel" values.

## Exciting new updates soon.

First, if you're not already using the "@langchain/google" library, this might be a great time for you to do so. This is where we're focusing all new work.

As mentioned above, some changes to fix the thinking level will be available soon. Follow [issue 11940](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchainjs/issues/11940) to learn more.

Long Decode allows for output up to 1M tokens, the most of any of the frontier models. But this required some internal changes in Google's API. There are two ways to address this, and we'll be adding support for both:

- Currently we support Google's "Generate Content" API. Google has added a "continuationToken" parameter which will let you read the response in 64k chunks.
- Google also has the "Interactions" API, which allows for many new features. We have just started the first phase of a project to make the Interactions API available through LangChainJS in a transparent way.

We'll be adding support for the "continuationToken", which will allow you to read the Long Decode responses one chunk at a time. This is, however, only meant as a stop-gap solution while we work on a better approach.

The Interactions API supports Long Decode directly when in "background" mode. We'll be implementing support for the Interactions API as quickly as we can, and "background" mode will be one of the initial features supported. We even hope to make it transparent in some cases, so the only thing you'll need to do is set "maxOutputTokens" to more than 64k and things should "just work".

Both of these require [issue 11879](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchainjs/issues/11879) to be completed first - and our focus is on getting that released ASAP so we can begin work on the other components. We'll also be adding a chunk of new tests to make sure the features work as expected and that everything works as smoothly as it always has.

## Our objectives

I've always tried to make LangChainJS as easy for developers to use, and continue using, as possible. You shouldn't have to make sure your parameters match the complex rules that Google enforces - the LangChainJS library should handle that for you.

The changes we are working on for Argon support are no different.

Your help and support for this project are, as always, appreciated.

My thanks, again, to the teams at Google who gave me early access to begin testing and work with Argon. And my thanks to family and friends who have always been there. Working on this project is one way I choose to help the community - and I hope you are contributing to the communities that are important to you.

I Turned DEV.to Into a Walkable 3D Library — Debugging It Has Been a Nightmare

![Dev](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/ml4bwi8tisl8l886vkkg.png)

![earlyversion](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/lt28umo8d5y3wd1u6e19.png)



DEV Library is my idea of first-person 3D reimagining of DEV.to. Not a themed scene with some article cards floating around, but the actual live catalogue, pulled from the Forem API, rendered as a walkable archive. Shelves. Rooms. Districts. Real cover images on real book spines. You move through it with WASD instead of scrolling a feed.

The idea sounds fun in a sentence. Building it has mostly been a long series of things breaking in ways I didn't expect, followed by me figuring out why.

This whole thing started as vibe coding, almost entirely for the Sanity x Dev.to Hackathon. I described what I wanted, and it appeared — cinematic lighting, spatial audio, entire systems I hadn't fully thought through myself.

That works great right up until the project gets big enough that things start breaking in ways a regenerated response can't actually fix. Once the catalogue was real and the scene had to survive thousands of live articles streaming in instead of a dozen mocked ones, I stopped being able to just describe my way out of problems. I had to open the animation loop, trace refs, and actually understand what was happening under the hood — not because I wanted to, but because "try again" stopped working. This post is mostly about that part.

## The stack

This is built on Next.js and Three.js — no game engine, no visual scene editor, nothing with a viewport where you drag an object and watch it move. Three.js is a JavaScript library for rendering 3D graphics in the browser using WebGL, and everything in it is code. There's no inspector panel with X/Y/Z fields you can nudge with arrow keys. If a shelf is floating six units too high, you don't drag it down — you find the line of code that sets its position and change the number.

That sounds like a minor inconvenience until you're trying to place hundreds of shelves relative to a curving, procedurally generated hallway. In something like Unity or Unreal, you'd see the mismatch instantly and drag things into place. In Three.js, you're reasoning about coordinates blind — changing a number, waiting for the scene to rebuild, walking into it with WASD to see if it's right, and doing that loop again if it isn't. Every position, rotation, and offset in this project exists only as a number in a function somewhere, not as something you can see and grab.

That's the actual reason so many of the bugs below are about where things are rather than what things look like. Coordinate math doesn't forgive vibe coding the way visual styling does — a color that's slightly off still looks fine, but a shelf position that's slightly off either clips through a wall or floats in the void, and you won't know which until you physically walk there.

## It didn't start here

![books!](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/5b3j85iv2ezya61jnqhq.webp)

This began as Oniria, Oni for short. — a first-person 3D dream journal. Memories as glowing orbs, relationship tethers between them you could physically fly along. It grew fast: cinematic lighting, spatial audio, recursive dream-diving, memory decay, an "Observatory" mode to zoom out and see your whole dream history at once. By the time I stopped to look around, I was 197 commits ahead of main and thirteen thousand lines deep, and I had to ask the obvious question: is this too much for a hackathon?

The answer reframed the problem instead of shrinking it:

> "The scope is too big for a hackathon if we keep treating every idea as equally important. But that doesn't mean Oniria itself is 'too much.' The problem is now product focus, not ambition."

So I picked one 90-second experience and froze everything else behind it. Somewhere in that process I looked at what I'd actually built — first-person flight through a graph of linked, related things — and asked a different question: what if this wasn't about dreams at all?

A codebase explorer idea came first (folders as worlds, imports as hallways). It never shipped, but it cracked something open: the engine wasn't really about dreams, it was a way to turn any linked, browsable structure into a place. So I asked for something stranger — import the entire DEV.to website into the engine. Literally surf the web.

## Issue #1: the first version was a conspiracy board

![dev library](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/rqkxmmqw6oloyz0gik98.png)

It technically worked. Articles, profiles, tags, search results, all floating in space simultaneously. Technically impressive. Completely unnavigable — you'd spawn into a cloud of unrelated nodes with no sense of where to look first.

This wasn't really a bug so much as a design failure, but it set the tone for everything after it: the fix wasn't a new feature, it was a metaphor. A library. Rooms as topics. Shelves as feeds. Books as articles. People get their own rooms. One idea did more for usability than every rendering improvement I'd made up to that point, because architecture can tell you where to go in a way floating labels never could.

## Issue #2: the library rearranged itself while I was standing in it

![dev2](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/wq9lnilwnof016gbq6mw.png)

![dev](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/gtgdrt1p33snmnnjlsyp.png)

Once real DEV articles started streaming in instead of a handful of mocked ones, the library needed hundreds, then thousands of shelves. That's when navigation quietly broke.

The cause: shelves had been positioning themselves relative to each other. Reasonable-sounding, until you realize it means navigation was an emergent side effect of layout instead of something the world actually guaranteed. Every time another page of articles streamed in, shelf positions could shift underneath the player. On a normal website, rerendering a list is boring. In a first-person space, it can teleport the person standing inside it.

This is the architectural decision the whole project ended up hanging off of:
> The path is authoritative. Everything else decorates the path.

One deterministic causeway became the coordinate system for the entire library — a function called archivePathPoint(bay) that converts a logical "bay" index into a world-space position. Shelves, fog, skyline, energy lanes, camera clamping — all of it now samples from that same fixed route instead of improvising its own position. Shelf placement itself moved to a seeded deterministic function, taking stable inputs (shelf ID, approximate bay, side of the path, jitter) so the world could still look organic without shelves jumping to new spots every time React state updated.

That single rule fixed an entire category of bugs at once. Streaming in more of the catalogue stopped being dangerous the moment shelves stopped being the thing defining the world.

## Issue #3: zoneRef.current is not a function

This is the one that actually made me sit down and trace code line by line instead of just asking for another pass. It's also the clearest example of that shift I mentioned up top — the point where vibe coding stopped being enough on its own.

```javascript
Runtime TypeError
zoneRef.current is not a function

900 |  if (nearestSection !== currentSection) {
901 |    currentSection = nearestSection
902 |    zoneRef.current(nearestSection)
```

zoneRef.current being called like a function meant it wasn't holding one. I went into the animation loop and traced where zoneRef actually got assigned — it was set inside a useEffect with a dependency on currentSection, but the animation loop was already running before that effect fired for the first time. A stale-closure timing problem: the ref existed, just not yet, relative to when the render loop reached for it.

This is the part nobody quite prepares you for with AI-assisted building. It can hand you cinematic rendering, spatial audio, and a fully explorable 3D library shockingly fast. It cannot hand you the fifteen minutes of "wait, when does this effect actually run relative to the render loop" that fixing this required. That part you still have to do yourself.

## Where it's at right now

![Reading Dev Book](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/30gn86wqs77rfabvt1sg.gif)

The catalogue streams in bounded pages instead of one blocking request. Shelves are seeded deterministically so they don't reshuffle as more content loads. The camera survives scene rebuilds. Districts organize themselves by real article tags instead of a fixed taxonomy. Nearby shelves react — brightening, waking their covers — while distant ones dim, which turned out to matter more than I expected: in 2D, hierarchy comes from typography and layout; inside a 3D archive with dozens of shelves visible at once, distance and brightness are the only hierarchy you get.

It's not done. I'm still working out how much of the catalogue can stay loaded before distant shelves start costing more frame time than they're worth. The skyline and haze systems are tuned but not perf-verified across a weaker GPU. And I'm sure there's at least one more zoneRef-shaped bug waiting somewhere in there that I haven't walked into yet.

But for the first time, it actually behaves like the thing I set out to build: not a DEV.to-themed scene, but an attempt to make the whole living catalogue into somewhere you can actually walk — one broken ref, one flickering cover, and one screen-eating book at a time.

More soon, including when this turns into my actual Sanity Challenge submission — where the CMS side of this story gets to be the main character instead of a supporting one.

## This week's theme: Side Hustle

**Build something with open-weight models or open-source AI that someone would actually pay for.**

Think small, specific, and useful. The best builds here solve a real problem for a real person, whether that's a freelancer, a small business owner, a niche hobby community, or your friend who keeps complaining about the same tedious task. A few ideas to get you going:

- An invoice and receipt sorter for freelancers that runs locally, so client data never leaves their laptop
- A listing writer for Etsy or eBay sellers that turns a few product photos into a polished description
- A menu translator for a local restaurant that handles their specific dishes better than a generic tool

Safe Autonomy in Kubernetes: Building AI Troubleshooting Agents with Google Cloud and Human-in-the-Loop Controls

Kubernetes troubleshooting often requires engineers to correlate pod events, container logs, resource metrics, deployment configurations, and application dependencies before identifying the root cause of an incident. While traditional automation can execute predefined recovery steps, Agentic AI introduces a more adaptive approach: investigating failures, testing hypotheses, gathering evidence, and recommending context-aware actions.

This blog explores how to build an AI-powered Kubernetes troubleshooting agent using **Google Cloud**, **Gemini**, and **Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)**. The agent follows a structured investigation workflow, collects operational evidence through controlled tools, identifies probable root causes, and proposes remediation actions with supporting evidence.

The central focus is **safe autonomy**. Instead of granting an AI agent unrestricted cluster access, the architecture incorporates least-privilege IAM and Kubernetes RBAC, policy-driven action boundaries, human approval gates for sensitive operations, and comprehensive audit logging. Read-only diagnostics are the default, while changes to workloads or cluster configurations require explicit authorization and validation.

Through practical scenarios such as `**CrashLoopBackOff**`, `**ImagePullBackOff**`, and failed Kubernetes deployments, the blog demonstrates how organizations can move from manual incident investigation toward AI-assisted, auditable, and controlled autonomous operations.

The goal is not to replace SRE engineers, but to help them resolve incidents faster while retaining control over production environments.



**The core problem: autonomy versus blast radius**


![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/zgcjjmd942vusmojm2vz.png)



Every agent design trades speed for risk, and the trade is set by what the agent can do, not by how smart the model is. Three failure modes show up repeatedly in Kubernetes:

• Confident misdiagnosis. The model reads a transient error as the root cause and proposes a fix for the wrong problem.

• Over-broad action. A reasonable fix such as restarting a pod becomes a bad one when applied to every pod in a namespace.

• Prompt injection through data. Logs, events and annotations are untrusted text. A crafted log line can try to steer the agent into running a command.

You cannot prompt your way out of these. A system prompt that says "never do anything destructive" is a request, not a control. The controls have to live outside the model: in identity, permissions, policy and a human approval step. The rule of thumb for this post is simple: the model proposes, the platform disposes.

**Reference architecture on Google Cloud**




![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/ndtb7c7l8jw8g9j9wuis.png)


Alerts reach the agent, which investigates through read-only telemetry. Every action passes through the executor, which checks scope and risk class and waits for a human before it uses the write identity. The agent can run on GKE itself or on Cloud Run, and the same pattern works with Google's Agent Development Kit, a Gemini function-calling loop, or an MCP server that exposes Kubernetes tools



**Autonomy tiers: earn trust one level at a time**




![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/5o17drznofhfts645jut.png)


**Designing the human-in-the-loop approval flow**


An approval step only protects you if the human can make a real decision in about thirty seconds. A bare "Approve? y/n" trains people to click yes. Design the request so the reviewer sees what they need:


1. **The exact action**. Show the literal command or API call, with namespace, resource name and arguments, not a paraphrase.
2. **The evidence**. Link the log lines, events and metrics that led the agent here, so the reviewer can check the reasoning.
3. **The blast radius**. State how many pods, services or users the action can affect.
4. **The rollback**. Say how to undo it, and whether the agent can do so automatically.
5. **An expiry**. An approval applies to one action on one object for a short window, say 15 minutes. It is never a standing permission.
Route the request to where responders already are. Chat tools, a ticket, or a pager acknowledgement all work. The key property is that the approval is recorded with the approver's identity and bound to the specific action, so the executor can verify it before running anything.


Two habits keep the loop healthy. First, require a different person than the one who triggered the agent for high-risk actions, the same four-eyes principle you use for production changes. Second, measure approval fatigue: if reviewers approve more than about 95% of requests in under five seconds, the gate has become decoration and the tier should be reviewed


**Guardrails that do not depend on the model**

The approval gate is one layer. Stack others underneath it so a bug in any one layer is not an incident.

• Separate identities for read and write. Run two Kubernetes ServiceAccounts: a read-only one for tier 0 and a narrowly scoped one used only by the executor after approval. The model never holds the write credential.

• Workload Identity Federation for GKE. Bind those ServiceAccounts to Google Cloud service accounts so the agent reaches Cloud Logging, Monitoring and Vertex AI without long-lived keys. Grant only roles such as log viewer and monitoring viewer to the read identity.

• Least-privilege RBAC. Use namespaced Roles, not ClusterRoles, and list verbs explicitly. Allow delete on pods, never on namespaces, persistentvolumeclaims or secrets.

• Admission policy. Use Policy Controller (Gatekeeper) or a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy to reject risky changes even if RBAC allows them, for example scaling a production deployment to zero or removing resource limits.

• Redact before the model sees data. Strip secrets, tokens and personal data from logs and manifests. Treat everything retrieved from the cluster as untrusted input, since log text can carry injected instructions.

• Rate and scope limits. Cap actions per incident and per hour, and restrict the agent to named namespaces and clusters.

• Audit everything. Cloud Audit Logs and Kubernetes audit logs record what the executor did. Also log the agent's prompts, tool calls and the approval record so an incident review can replay the reasoning.

A useful test: if the model were fully compromised, what is the worst thing the executor could do? Design until the answer is acceptable.


**Code walkthrough**: tools, risk classes and the approval gate
The pattern below is framework-agnostic.

 It works with Google's Agent Development Kit, a plain Gemini function-calling loop on Vertex AI, or an MCP server that exposes Kubernetes tools. Check the current ADK documentation for its built-in tool confirmation features before writing your own gate.


The key idea is that the model never calls kubectl directly. It calls tools, and each tool declares a risk class that the platform enforces.


```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum
import time, uuid

class Risk(Enum):
    READ = 0        # tier 0: runs immediately
    MUTATE = 1      # tier 2: needs human approval
    FORBIDDEN = 2   # never exposed to the model

@dataclass
class ToolSpec:
    name: str
    risk: Risk
    fn: callable

REGISTRY: dict[str, ToolSpec] = {}

def tool(risk: Risk):
    def wrap(fn):
        REGISTRY[fn.__name__] = ToolSpec(fn.__name__, risk, fn)
        return fn
    return wrap

@tool(Risk.READ)
def get_pod_logs(namespace: str, pod: str, tail: int = 200) -> str:
    # uses the READ-ONLY service account
    return k8s_read.logs(namespace, pod, tail=min(tail, 500))

@tool(Risk.READ)
def describe_pod(namespace: str, pod: str) -> str:
    return k8s_read.describe(namespace, pod)

@tool(Risk.MUTATE)
def rollout_restart(namespace: str, deployment: str) -> str:
    # uses the WRITE service account, only reachable via the executor
    return k8s_write.rollout_restart(namespace, deployment)
```
The executor sits between the model and the tools. Read tools run straight through. Mutating tools create a pending approval and stop.

```python
ALLOWED_NAMESPACES = {"checkout", "payments"}
APPROVAL_TTL_SECONDS = 900

class Executor:
    def __init__(self, approvals):
        self.approvals = approvals  # backed by Firestore or Cloud SQL

    def call(self, name: str, args: dict, incident_id: str):
        spec = REGISTRY.get(name)
        if spec is None or spec.risk is Risk.FORBIDDEN:
            raise PermissionError(f"tool not allowed: {name}")
        if args.get("namespace") not in ALLOWED_NAMESPACES:
            raise PermissionError("namespace out of scope")

        if spec.risk is Risk.READ:
            return spec.fn(**args)

        # MUTATE: request approval, do not run
        req = self.approvals.create(
            id=str(uuid.uuid4()),
            incident=incident_id,
            tool=name,
            args=args,
            expires=time.time() + APPROVAL_TTL_SECONDS,
        )
        notify_oncall(req)  # chat card with command, evidence, rollback
        return {"status": "pending_approval", "request_id": req.id}

    def execute_approved(self, request_id: str, approver: str):
        req = self.approvals.get(request_id)
        if req.expired() or req.used:
            raise PermissionError("approval expired or already used")
        if approver == req.requested_by:
            raise PermissionError("requester cannot self-approve")
        req.mark_used(approver)             # single use
        audit_log(req, approver)            # who, what, when
        return REGISTRY[req.tool].fn(**req.args)
```
Three details matter here. The args are validated and stored at request time, so the action that runs is exactly the action the human saw. The approval is single-use and expires. And the write credential is only loaded inside execute_approved, which the model cannot call.



An incident end to end: CrashLoopBackOff in checkout
Here is how the flow plays out for a realistic case. The scenario is illustrative.
1. Trigger. A Cloud Monitoring alert fires for the checkout-api deployment and opens an incident. The alert payload goes to the agent through Pub/Sub.
2. Observe (tier 0). The agent lists pods, sees three of four in CrashLoopBackOff, and pulls recent logs and events. The logs show a failed database connection, and the events show a ConfigMap changed twenty minutes earlier.
3. Correlate. The agent compares the new ConfigMap with the previous revision from the rollout history and finds a changed database host value that no longer resolves.
4. Recommend (tier 1). It posts a summary with evidence: the failing log lines, the config diff, and the timing. It does not guess beyond that evidence.
5. Request approval (tier 2). The best fix is a rollback of the last revision. The agent calls the rollback tool, and the executor sends a chat card showing the exact command, the single deployment affected, and the undo path.
6. Approve and execute. The on-call engineer checks the config diff, taps approve, and the executor runs the rollback using the write identity.
7. Verify and close. The agent watches pod readiness and error rate for ten minutes, posts the result, and attaches the full trace to the incident for the postmortem.
The human spent under a minute and still made the call. The agent did the slow part: reading logs, diffing config and checking recovery.



**Pitfalls and how to evaluate the agent**


Most failures come from the plumbing around the model, not the model itself.

• Overly broad tools. A generic run_kubectl(command) tool defeats every control above. Expose narrow, typed tools instead.
• Approval on summaries, not actions. If the card shows the agent's description rather than the real command, the human approves something other than what runs.
• Stale context. Cluster state changes during an incident. Re-read the object just before executing, and fail the approval if it has drifted.
• No kill switch. Provide one flag that drops the agent to tier 0 across every cluster.
• Skipping staging. Replay past incidents and run fault injection (bad image tag, missing ConfigMap, memory limits too low) in a test cluster before production.

**Conclusion and rollout checklist**


Safe autonomy is an engineering problem with a known shape: give the model narrow tools, keep credentials and policy outside it, put a well-designed human decision in front of every change, and widen its freedom only as the data justifies. Done well, the agent handles the tedious investigation and the human keeps the judgment.
