text:
I Built an AI Gardening App That Tells Me to Put the Laptop Down

*This is a submission for the [Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week1-2026-10-05)*

Coding is my thing. Gardening is a part of who I am.

I have hundreds of pots, and I know my plants through the little things they show me. I notice which ones respond well to buried banana peels, which seem happier with used tea granules or old buttermilk, and which need my lunch-box system instead of raw kitchen scraps buried around them. I watch their leaves, new growth and flowers.

I do not need an app to tell me how to care for my own plants. That understanding comes from spending time with them. But it made me think about how a tool could help someone who is still learning to notice these things.

For a long time coding and gardening lived in different corners of my day. I would code for hours, then walk away from the screen to be with my plants, and the two never really met. This challenge gave me a reason to put them in the same room. So first, thank you to the DEV team and everyone behind it. You gave me the opportunity to write code about the thing I love most, and I enjoyed every hour of it.

## The question I almost asked an AI

On 30 September I moved my marigold out of a shady, bright corner and into the open sun. The corner was there to keep the heavy rain off it. It grew from a cutting of a plant that came up by itself from last year's seeds, so it already feels a little like family.

On 5 October I counted about three open flowers and three buds. On 9 October I counted seven open flowers and five buds.

My first thought was to ask an AI why.

An answer would have been easy to get and easy to believe. But the sun, rain and time passing had all played a part, and I couldn't tell which one made the difference. Neither could an AI. So I asked a different question. Not "why is my plant doing this?" but "what should I look at before I change anything?"

That question became Garden Trials.

## What I Built

Garden Trials is a small app that runs entirely on your own computer. The whole idea fits in one line, which is look first, change one thing, let the garden answer.

I do not like screens near my plants. When I am with them I want my hands in the soil and my phone away. Sometimes a bloom looks so good that I click a photo, for myself and for other plant lovers. So I built the app the way I wish gardening tools worked. It talks to me before and after, and in the middle it asks me to put the laptop down and go and look.

1. I write a note about a plant and the day I saw it. A local Gemma model reads it into plain facts.
2. The app asks me to check one specific thing on the plant. Until I write down what I found, it will not suggest anything.
3. I either watch, or pick one change from a small fixed menu, ideally leaving a similar plant alone to compare.
4. I count and take a photo. The app shows me the last photo so I can match the angle.
5. I get a table, a chart, a verdict, an evidence level from 0 to 3, and one plain next step.

It is not a plant doctor. It never says what is wrong with a plant, and it never says what caused a result.

Garden Trials is for gardeners who are still learning to read their plants, and for anyone who wants to check their assumptions rather than jump to conclusions. It brings observations, follow-up checks, simple experiments and evidence tracking into one process. Instead of just recording what happened, it helps gardeners look at what changed, what else might have affected the result, and what their observations can actually tell them. It is not meant to replace the understanding that grows from spending time with plants, but to encourage closer observation.

![The Look First box asking me to go and check the plant before anything else](https://lfekpouqwpiysgtdelwd.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/public-assets/devto-images/garden-trials-look-first-question-petunia.png)

## Demo

{% embed https://youtu.be/Rm7X4btlZVk %}

The quickest way in is the sample garden. Tick "Try the illustrative sample garden" in the sidebar and you can walk through the whole loop with made-up plants. Nothing from it is ever saved to a real garden.

![The sample garden, clearly labelled as made up](https://lfekpouqwpiysgtdelwd.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/public-assets/devto-images/garden-trials-sample-garden-warning-screen.png)

## Code

{% embed https://github.com/shubhrapokhariya/garden-trials %}

Setup is in the README: Python 3.11 or newer, Ollama, `ollama pull gemma3:1b`, then `python -m streamlit run app.py`. The folder `examples/my-garden/` holds my real notes, counts and photos from this week. Start the app with `GARDEN_DIR=examples/my-garden` and you can read them without touching your own data.

## My real garden, this week

### Petunia

On 7 October I counted two open flowers, one spent flower, four buds and a lot of tiny buds forming. I took photos and counts on 7, 8, 9 and 10 October, but I only opened the app on the 10th, so I typed the first three days in afterwards. The app marks those entries as backfilled, which is exactly what they are. It is also why the trial says it started on 10 October.

When I saved the 7 October note, Gemma's reading dropped a number, so the app threw the reading away and kept my words exactly as I wrote them. Then Gemma's Look First question turned out to be about pests or disease, which I had never mentioned. The app blocked it and asked its own question instead:

> Count the open flowers and the buds right now. Do the newest shoots have buds?

![My note kept exactly as written. The app rejected Gemma's reading, so the line shown is my own words.](https://lfekpouqwpiysgtdelwd.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/public-assets/devto-images/garden-trials-gemma-reading-dropped-number-petunia.png)

I went and looked on the 10th. Four open flowers, two bright ones on top and two darker ones lower down that had just opened, and small buds at the tips of the shoots.

| Date | Open flowers | Buds | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 Oct | 2 | 4 | Front view. One spent flower not counted. |
| 8 Oct | 2 | 4 | Removed the spent flower. Photo from above. |
| 9 Oct | 2 | 4 | Buds clearly bigger and longer. |
| 10 Oct | 4 | 2 | Two buds opened. Bright sun, so the reds look brighter. |

![Petunia on 7 October (left) and 10 October (right)](https://lfekpouqwpiysgtdelwd.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/public-assets/devto-images/petunia-7-oct-and-10-oct-side-by%20side.png)

I removed one spent flower on the 8th. That was routine upkeep, not a test, but I want to say so. There was no comparison plant, and petunia buds open on their own anyway. The app gave this evidence level 0 and said it plainly. No change was made during these counts, so it shows what the plant did while I watched and says nothing about a cause.

![The petunia table and chart, with entries marked backfilled](https://lfekpouqwpiysgtdelwd.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/public-assets/devto-images/garden-trials-petunia-table-chart-2026-10-07-to-10.png)

The two new flowers opened darker and more velvety than the older ones. I read that a new petal is still small and tightly folded, so its colour is packed close together, and that as the flower opens fully and stretches out, the same colour spreads over a bigger petal and looks lighter. So I guess that is what I am seeing.

### Marigold

The 5 October photo was taken for myself, not for the trial. I clicked it just because the plant looked lovely, from the side, and only later decided to use it here. One bud is partly cut off at the edge. The 9 October photo is the one I took for the trial, from above, where every flower and bud can be seen. My first count may have missed buds I could not see from the side, so the jump from 3 to 7 open flowers is in my notes, but it is not a fair comparison. A few petals also looked flattened after some rain. The rain may be the reason, but that is a guess.

![Marigold on 5 October from the side (left) and on 9 October from above (right)](https://lfekpouqwpiysgtdelwd.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/public-assets/devto-images/marigold-side-by-side.png)

### Bougainvillea

Five cuttings, about a month and a half old, in the same soil and the same small black nursery bags on the same bench. One of them already has two pink flowers and the other four have none. Its mother plant is in full bloom, while my other bougainvilleas are only starting. My guess, not tested, is the variety or the time of year. The cuttings are different varieties, so "same soil, same bench" is not a fair test. A real test needs cuttings of the same variety, taken at the same time from different mother plants.

![Five bougainvillea cuttings, one with pink flowers](https://lfekpouqwpiysgtdelwd.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/public-assets/devto-images/bougainvillea-cutting-first-bloom-2026-10-10.jpg)

## How I Built It

The stack is small on purpose: [Streamlit](https://streamlit.io), one JSON file, and `gemma3:1b` running locally through [Ollama](https://ollama.com). I picked the 1B [Gemma](https://ai.google.dev/gemma) model to find out whether this idea works on an ordinary laptop with no cloud account. On a laptop CPU an answer can take up to a minute.

Gemma has three jobs. It reads my note into plain facts, suggests one thing to go and check, and picks one change from a short menu. Everything that has to be reliable lives in plain Python, because I treat the model's output the way I would treat any untrusted input.

- If a number from my note is missing in Gemma's reading, the reading is rejected and my exact words are kept.
- Details Gemma adds that I did not write are removed by a word-match check. It is a loose check, so it can miss some.
- The cause field is forced to "unknown" in code.
- Pest and disease questions are blocked unless I raised them first.
- Trials come from a fixed menu that is filtered per plant. "Water more" is never offered for bougainvillea, which likes to stay on the dry side.
- Verdicts and evidence levels are calculated by code, never by Gemma. Level 3 needs two finished trials of the same change, each with a comparison plant and nothing else changed, all pointing the same way.
- Saves go to a temporary file first and are then swapped in. A garden file that cannot be read is moved aside and never overwritten.

The tests replace Gemma with fake and deliberately bad answers, such as garbage, dropped numbers, invented pests, off-menu picks. A second set drives the real pages end to end. There are 85 tests, and none of them needs Ollama.

## What went wrong

The model did not behave in my own garden. Gemma's reading of all three of my notes was rejected by the number check, and one of its three questions was blocked.

![The sidebar panel showing three dropped numbers and one blocked question](https://lfekpouqwpiysgtdelwd.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/public-assets/devto-images/garden-trials-ai-output-guard-panel-counts.png)

The other two questions got through, and they were generic. "Is the plant's stem straight?" had nothing to do with what I was seeing, so I wrote down what I actually noticed. The guards block invented pests. They cannot make a small model's question a good one. They also only catch the failures I thought of, and the checks match English words, so notes in Hindi are not checked the same way. In my real garden Gemma only read my notes and wrote Look First questions. Both of my real trials were watch-only, so it never picked a trial there.

## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Gemma runs on my laptop through Ollama. There is no API key, no usage bill and no cloud AI call. My notes and photos sit in a folder on my own machine, and the photos are saved without their location data. Setup needs the internet once, to download the packages, Ollama and the model, and I switched off Streamlit's anonymous usage statistics.

Running Gemma locally let me build and test this idea without an API key and without paying for every request. I could try it as often as I liked, and if a better small model arrives, I change one setting (`OLLAMA_MODEL`) and the rest of the app stays as it is. The small model had clear limitations, which I describe above, but that was part of what I wanted to learn, which is how far an open model can take this idea on an ordinary laptop, with ordinary code checking its output. The experiment showed me both the value of running a model locally and the limits of relying on its answers.

## What I took away

The point of the app is what happens when I close the laptop. It asks me to go and look, and I stand there with the plant and nothing else. It cannot tell whether I really went outside, and I will not pretend it can. That pause is a promise I make to myself.

The AI can suggest what to look at. The garden gives the answer.

Thank you for reading, and thank you again to the DEV team for a challenge that let me bring the two things I love together.

## Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma

How I Built an Action Game with Godot During a Global Teen Hackathon with Prizes I had just recently completed a couple of medium-sized projects for Stardance, a global teen hackathon hosted by Hack Club, a global nonprofit organization for teen coders. To continue, I decided to follow a beginner mission that required just 5 hours of coding. I thought this project would be a quick and easy way to get a relatively small amount of digital currency for the Stardance shop, which allows you to purchase both physical and digital items. This digital currency is called Stardust.

**I decided to name the project CodeWare; more on that in a minute.** I went through the missions tutorial and finished in a decent amount of time. But I kept going back and making sure everything was perfect, squashing bugs before a real user would see them. But I thought to myself one thing. This one thing completely transformed the rest of the project (did you really think I ended it there?) The one thing I thought to myself was, **"Am I really going to just submit a simple project following a beginner tutorial?"** The answer to that question, and quite frankly the reason why I am making this article, is **an absolute, firm "no." I was not just going to turn in a simple beginner project following a simple beginner tutorial.** ![The Tyleruploads mountain range, which is the background of the title image for the CodeWare video game created by Tyleruploads](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/5x05vyx8jto8sz8agijj.webp) The title screen of the game is the Tyleruploads Mountain Range, which contains many mountains connected via land bridges. The suspension for those bridges is the game's logo turned into a bunch of small links. **Metaphysically, the game’s goal is to cross those bridges.** Based on the abstract nature of this game, it also has two very abstract endings: one for when you win, and one for when you lose all of your five lives. However, I am not going to explain exactly what happens in these endings, but I will explain their significance. They highlight **the eternity of coding in the realm of bureaucratic and automatic computer-generated code files.** When you take a deeper look into this seemingly elementary project, you may see a full world of possible interpretations. In the death scene, the user is said to be between the two sides of eternity, represented by the bicycle-looking infinity loop in the logo of the game. **The game is a collection of fast-paced, action-filled minigames.** Each minigame has a timer you can hear ticking throughout the game. If the timer strikes zero, you either lose one of your five lives and redo the minigame, or continue to the next one. The distinction depends on the minigame type. The two types are minigames in which you need to do something within a set time or survive until the time runs out. To set the record straight, before making this, **I had absolutely no experience in any sort of game development.** I didn't even have Godot—or any game engine, as a matter of fact—on my computer. I thought that Stardance Mission would be a **"gentle introduction to game development and Godot."** Originally. But it was more like **"ditch the mission and get actual game development skills."** Currently, I have invested **51 hours and 38 minutes of real (slightly underrepresented) coding time,** backed by a time tracker also provided by Hack Club. That was at least 5x larger than any project I had ever worked on before. The reason I was able to get in so many hours is because of **an unexpected plot twist.** That plot twist, something that may earn me a **Bambu Lab A1 Mini 3D Printer** (I don't know yet), is a **One-Month Extension**. I had joined the Stardance hackathon late in the summer, partly due to my one-month-long sleepaway camp that doesn't even allow certain MP3 players or any E-Readers—and definitely not any sort of personal computing device but a calculator. So, I was thinking **I will never have enough time to get a nice prize.** And while that could still possibly be true, at least now I have **a chance to have every single type of printer I could possibly think of** in my room. To be fair, that last sentence is actually **very anticlimactic**; the two types of printers I can think of are old HP printers with dirt-cheap generic toner cartridges and 3D printers. But what matters much more than what type of printer you have is how you use it. In the Stardance hackathon, your Stardust payout is determined with a very simple formula: `Multiplier * Hours Spent Coding = Stardust`. In case you didn't catch it in the first paragraph, Stardust is what you use to buy rewards (like a 3D printer) in the digital shop. The multiplier is a bit harder to explain. It is based on 12 reviews from other teenage coders around the world, and they rate it on the following topics: - **Originality:** "How distinct is the project from common projects?" - **Technicality:** "How much effort did the creator put into the implementation?" - **Usability:** "Did you like using it? Could you use it at all?" - **Storytelling:** "How well does the creator document the development journey through devlogs, documentation, commit messages, and READMEs?" I honestly think my project would get a pretty mediocre rating in terms of originality. It's just a video game. It could be boosted if the reviewers understand the philosophical aspects of the game, but they probably won't. For technicality, I really think this is where it'll shine. In the **51 hours and 38 minutes** I spent working on this project, I really think I made something spectacular. I went over it so many times until I was really sure it was perfect. As for usability, this has to be great. CodeWare is accessible on its own [Itch.io page](https://tyleruploads.itch.io/codeware) and [GitHub Pages site](https://tyleruploads.itch.io/codeware). It also has Linux, Windows, and even Web downloads available at its [GitHub Releases Page](https://github.com/tyleruploads/code-ware/releases/latest). I also think I did really well in storytelling. I made some very detailed devlogs (updates on what I code). Feel free to check out my game at the links a bit above here. You can also check out its [Stardance project page](https://stardance.hackclub.com/projects/57952). Right now, you are essentially stuck in the biggest cliffhanger ever: **Will Tyler get a 3D Printer?** Well, that is going to take until **November of this year** to find out. **SCROLL DOWN FOR IMPORTANT INFORMATION**

It turns out I did not need to wait until November! I did so well on this project that I got an **unimaginable payout of 1013 Stardust with a 16.45x out of 20x multiplier, with a 20% bonus for being "Blessed" because of my thoughtful voting.** With this unimaginable payout, I did not need to wait any longer to be able to purchase the 3D Printer! For perspective, it costs 802 Stardust. I am so happy with the awesome, thoughtful, and detailed reviews I got on my project! Here are some of them: > Review #1/12: > "This project is so cool. I really like how you used so many different pretty [colors on] the website and how you can watch gameplay videos because it is super confusing, **but after I watched the gameplay videos, I [understood] exactly what to do, so I will make sure to tell this project to all of my friends and family so they can play it too!!**" > Review #4/12: > "I really enjoyed the game. **It was really fun [to] play. At first the ticking was annoying, but you get used to it.** I liked **how simple, yet so [addictive] it was.** The levels are **creative** and match the game really well. No level was way too hard; they were just fine. Maybe [it] could be a bit harder. **Very good project!**" > Review #5/12: > "The game is **fun to play and difficult too.** I [tried] to beat level 1 but [wasn't] able to. **The mix of dodging, typing, and RGB matching gives CodeWare plenty of variety, and your detailed devlogs make the development journey easy to follow.** One useful code improvement would be making the orb-expiry timer in minigame 3 pause alongside the countdown by passing false to create_timer(). Well, overall, **the project is cool and fun to play.**" > Review #7/12: > "Hi, as an OG WII player, I gotta say that **the vibe fits perfectly [with] the meaning of "WarioWare-like game".** I bet it was **extremely fun to build** and it would be crazy good if you could play this with someone. Apart from my crazy and unrealistic ideas, **you did an amazing job!**" > Review: #10/12: > "**YOOO THIS PROJECT IS SOOOO GOOOD YOU SHOULD ADD MORE FEATURES LIKE A TUTORIAL.**" > Review: #12/12 (grammatical edits skipped to show full enthusiasm): > "**The art is really cool and homemade, all the games are intuitive to me. I know exactly what to do with those really helpful instructions at the bottom. I completed the game on my second try. Really fun.** > > None of the games seemed unfair in my opinion, but maybe make the games run for shorter time. > > **devlogs, communication is really good,** highlights what have done, challenges you faced, future plans and more. NICE! Your README is also very detailed and has lots of info, GOOD JOB > > **The extras page is really cool! Never seen that before. The gallery walk as well as credits! how unique. tuff** > > **lemme tell you something, lemme tell you something. YOU DO NOT NEED a licence for a simple WarioWare video game. RAAA** > > Something better, if can like leave the boring writing license stuff outside of the gameplay loop, like in the extras, that would be really appreciated!😁😁😁😁 > > One thing I experienced while playing is that you can actually pause the timer screen before the game starts, not sure if that's intentional but just FYI. maybe fix. > > **But overall you have put a lot of effort into this, this game is really fun, best WarioWare type-game i've seen so far.**"

I also happen to be **4th on the global leaderboard for hours shipped** on my team, which consists of approximately half of the Stardancers. But I know there are definitely some super large 200-hour projects from other people waiting to be submitted. I won't stand a chance a couple of days before it ends (actually, this time).

**I also got a beautiful certificate because of this project!**

--- ### What's Next? Thank you to everyone in the Hack Club community who played, reviewed, and supported **CodeWare!** I truly learnt so much about game development, Godot, and projects that take over 50 hours! Devlog: I Built a 3D Library in Three.js Without a Level Editor — So I Made My Own

#### Updated 3D Environment for Library


![New Dev Setting](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/ehgyzssnwaciwnu5r0yc.png)
#### Reading DEV Articles
![reading articles](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/907pwy8jw4kcizth5sno.gif)

A lot of you wonderful people enjoyed my last post on Oni, so heres an update on what I've been working on. 

I've been spending the last few days building the DEV Library inside Oniria, and somewhere along the way the project stopped feeling like "a cool Three.js scene" and started feeling like I was building my own tiny game-engine workflow.

The idea behind the library is pretty simple:

**DEV articles become physical books.**

Instead of opening DEV.to and scrolling through cards, you walk through rooms, browse shelves, pull out an article, read it, and return to the exact place you found it.

But actually constructing that space turned out to be one of the most interesting problems I've hit so far.

Earlier versions of Oniria leaned much harder into a cyber-world aesthetic: glowing structures, highways, towering architecture, and DEV articles scattered through something closer to a futuristic city. It looked interesting, but the more I built it, the more I realized the environment wasn't helping me _understand_ the information inside it.

![Old Design](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/tlzy0j3iol0b4gvx6ivl.png)

Articles were _technically_ spatial, but the space itself didn't explain why anything was where it was. Eventually I started asking a simpler question: if thousands of articles were going to become physical objects, what kind of place would naturally organize them? The answer was obvious — a library. That shift changed the project from decorating a cyber-world with content into designing an actual information architecture: rooms became categories, shelves became collections, books became articles, and the building itself could communicate how DEV is organized.

That decision also created a completely different engineering problem. I was no longer placing a handful of futuristic landmarks; I was trying to build an entire navigable library — rooms, shelves, paths, furniture, signs, lighting, and hundreds of precise spatial relationships — almost entirely through Three.js code, without a traditional live level editor.

That progression looked like this:

```plaintext
cyber city
    ↓
looked cool, but lacked informational meaning
    ↓
"what spatial metaphor actually fits articles?"
    ↓
library
    ↓
rooms = information architecture
    ↓
now we need to physically build it
    ↓
wait... we don't have a level editor
    ↓
build our own tools
```

## The problem: I wasn't using a level editor

Before building the in-world authoring tools, most object placement happened directly in Three.js. All by code. No 3D Editor. Ha, take that, purist!

I wrote a small helper that clones one of the loaded GLB assets, then applies its world position, scale, and rotation:

```typescript
const placeAsset = (
  template: THREE.Group,
  x: number,
  y: number,
  z: number,
  scale = 1,
  rotationY = 0,
  rotationX = 0,
) => {
  const instance = template.clone(true)

  instance.position.x += x
  instance.position.y += y
  instance.position.z += z

  instance.scale.multiplyScalar(scale)

  instance.rotation.y += rotationY
  instance.rotation.x += rotationX

  group.add(instance)

  return instance
}
```

That made placing something fairly straightforward:

```typescript
const table = placeAsset(
  readingTable,
  -16.2,   // x
  0.05,    // y
  -31.8,   // z
  1,       // scale
  Math.PI / 2,
)
```

But moving it still meant editing numbers:

```typescript
table.position.x += 0.8
table.position.z -= 1.2
table.rotation.y += Math.PI / 4
```

Or changing the original call:

```typescript
const table = placeAsset(
  readingTable,
  -15.4,
  0.05,
  -33.0,
  1,
  Math.PI * 0.75,
)
```

Then:

```plaintext
save
↓
reload
↓
walk back across the library
↓
look at it
↓
"nope"
↓
change the numbers again
```

That was basically my level editor. 😭 Below is an actual snippet of what I was working with:

![old level editor](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/vpxx2nvfbd4iu4x1hjwd.png)

And once the environment grew beyond a handful of props, it became painfully obvious that this wasn't going to scale.

With a normal interface, I can change some CSS, refresh the browser, and immediately see whether a card needs another 16px of margin.

In a 3D world, changing:

```plaintext
position: [-16.2, 0, -31.8]
```

might mean walking across an entire room just to discover that a table is clipping through a bookshelf.

![bugs](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/s86yz03fftoem9fjfi6w.png)

And at this point the library wasn't just a few props.

I was placing:

- walls and architectural pieces
- real and decorative bookshelves
- tables and chairs
- rugs
- plants
- pavilions
- signs
- room entrances
- shelf rows
- collision boundaries
- lights
- eventually, empty spaces reserved for shelves that don't even exist yet

The first version of my workflow was basically:

```plaintext
change coordinates
      ↓
save
      ↓
reload the world
      ↓
walk to the room
      ↓
inspect the object
      ↓
realize it's wrong
      ↓
repeat
```

It worked.

It was also slowly driving me insane.

The obvious answer would have been to move the whole project into a traditional level editor.

But I didn't really want another application to become the source of truth for the library.

The architecture was already deeply connected to code:

```plaintext
DEV data
   ↓
district
   ↓
room
   ↓
shelf slot
   ↓
Three.js placement
```

Also, the Three.js editor was really freaking annoying to use.

![three.js editor](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/totvhxcyqj40ztjdy4ns.png)

At this point I realized that moving assets this way would either take forever or it would never be perfect to my liking. There had to be an easier way — and then I had an idea. Why don't we make the location of each shelf predetermined by a layout I create? Essentially a blueprint — then have Codex place the individual assets at each coord/pin that I place. So that became my next goal.

## I needed to see coordinates inside the world

So instead I started building a tiny authoring system directly into Oniria.

The basic idea was simple:

> If I'm standing somewhere in the world and think, "this object should go here," I should be able to record it here.

I added an in-world layout marker tool.

Now I could walk into a room, find the location visually, and drop a pin.

A marker could store something like:

```json
{
  "label": "R1-P01",
  "roomSlot": 1,
  "districtId": "latest",
  "x": 16.154,
  "y": 0,
  "z": 5.369,
  "yaw": 1.57
}
```

Suddenly I wasn't trying to mentally convert a 3D room into numbers.

I could use the room itself to produce the numbers.

The workflow became:

```plaintext
walk through the space
        ↓
find the location visually
        ↓
drop a marker
        ↓
capture position + rotation
        ↓
turn the marker into real architecture
```

That sounds like a small change.

**It completely changed how I could build the library.**

![using an editor](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/ogrf4cnk87bc66x2lv2y.gif)

## The world became my editor

For example, when I wanted to add an object to a particular room, I could physically stand where it belonged and create a marker.

Then that surveyed position could go directly back into the scene:

```typescript
const surveyedPlacement = {
  x: 16.154,
  y: 0,
  z: 5.369,
  yaw: Math.PI / 2,
}

const instance = placeAsset(
  someLibraryAsset,
  surveyedPlacement.x,
  surveyedPlacement.y,
  surveyedPlacement.z,
  1,
  surveyedPlacement.yaw,
)
```

I started using the same workflow for things like:

```plaintext
"This shelf belongs here."

"This pavilion needs to move farther from the path."

"These two signs are colliding."

"This light needs to sit over this exact area."

"This decorative bookcase should sit between these DEV shelves."
```

![new layout yay](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/5u61hszdj2p1szxsss94.png)

## Persisting the layout

I also didn't want those markers to disappear every time the browser refreshed. So the markers became Sanity documents.

A marker now has a persistent identity:

```typescript
type LibraryLayoutMarker = {
  id: string
  label: string
  roomSlot: number
  districtId?: string

  x: number
  y: number
  z: number

  yaw?: number
  width?: number
  depth?: number
}
```

That means a layout session can survive reloads.

I can place several markers, come back later, and continue working from the same spatial notes.

I can also export them.

For example:

```json
{
  "format": "oniria-library-layout-pins-v1",
  "markers": [
    {
      "label": "R1-P01",
      "roomSlot": 1,
      "x": 16.154,
      "y": 0,
      "z": 5.369
    }
  ]
}
```

At this point I had accidentally built something halfway between a debugging tool, a survey tool, and a very small level editor.

And it solved a real problem immediately. Yay!

What started as a frustrating layout problem ended up teaching me something bigger about the project: if Oniria is going to treat the web as a place instead of a page, then the tools for building that place matter just as much as the content inside it. The DEV Library now has its own spatial logic, persistent layout markers, searchable shelves, dynamic slots, and an architecture that can evolve without losing its sense of place. I'm still building it room by room, but that's also the part I've started to enjoy most — every time the world gets difficult to work with, I end up building a new piece of the system that makes Oniria feel a little more real.

![oniria](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/hqkokxzpkmwnp2rdr0yx.png)

I'm an ER doctor. After decades without touching code, I built 3 websites with AI in one month — on my phone.

I've been an emergency doctor in Serbia for 12 years, Emergency medicine is intense, and burnout is real. This summer I started building websites out of pure curiosity, and as a way to switch off after shifts.

My coding background: a little BASIC and Pascal, a very long time ago,lol. Since then, nothing. Not a single line of code.

In one month I built three websites. Along the way I finally understood things that used to be just words to me: what PHP is and how it differs from WordPress, what SQL and a database actually do, what a website is made of and how all the pieces talk to each other. All three sites are live, and I built every one of them on my phone, in conversation with AI.

## The three sites

* [leaveittotheworld.com](https://leaveittotheworld.com/)
-an infinite wall where anyone can leave a short message to the world. You move around it like a map, zoom in and out, and new messages start near the center.

* [globalwallofgratitude.com](https://globalwallofgratitude.com/) 
-a place to publicly thank someone: your mother, a teacher, a neighbour, a stranger.

* [sendtothestars.com](https://sendtothestars.com/) 
-pick a real star, exoplanet or galaxy on an interactive sky and send it a message. You get a card with a live counter showing how far your message has travelled at the speed of light, save the card and it works even offline. Everything on the sky is meant to be scientifically accurate. Positions, distances and descriptions come from real astronomical catalogues: the HYG star database, the IAU lists of official star and exoplanet names, exoplanet.eu, OpenNGC for galaxies and nebulae, and published research catalogues for star clusters and black holes.

## How it actually works

I don't write the code. I explain what I want, we discuss it until the idea is clear, and only then does the AI write the code. I upload the files to my hosting, test on my phone and report back what's broken.

One rule I learned fast: **first agree, then code.** If you let AI write code while the idea is still vague, you end up rebuilding everything three times.

## Problems I didn't expect

- **Touch screens are hard.** On the message wall, tapping a card sometimes counted as dragging the wall. The fix was a bigger "drag threshold" for fingers than for a mouse. Pinch-to-zoom on the star map also jumped around until the touch handling was rewritten.
- **Big files and phones don't mix.** One page grew to 200 KB and my phone struggled to download and edit it. We split the data (thousands of stars) away from the code, and the file dropped to 22 KB.
- **WordPress plugins can bite.** One site runs on WordPress with code snippets. Importing a snippet silently created a duplicate, and the duplicate crashed the whole site. Now I always check for duplicates after an import.Not to mention the leftover plugins I tried at the beginning and then forgot about.

-$ About money

At first I thought: nice, maybe I can make a little money from this. I set up PayPal and got the whole payment flow working automatically: payment, server-side verification, the card appearing on the wall, the confirmation email. It worked with real payments.

Then I realised these are my first three "school" projects. They should be open to everyone, with no payment at all. So I switched payments off. All three sites are now completely free.

## What surprised me

A few weeks after launch, a message appeared on the wall from a complete stranger. Nobody I know, it just came from the internet. That felt better than any payment would have.

## What I'd tell another beginner

1. With AI, a complete beginner can get something real online, but you still have to understand what you're building. Ask "why" a lot.
2. Test everything on a real phone.
3. Security and privacy aren't optional. Ask the AI to review them, then ask again.
4. Launch before it's perfect, but not before it works.

## How I got here

The websites weren't the beginning. It all started last year, when I discovered AI.

First came posters. I had images in my head that I could never draw myself, and suddenly I could see them on the screen, looking exactly the way I imagined them.

Then I made three children's picture books.

Then I moved on to fashion. I designed a collection of dresses, and not just pretty pictures: complete designs, detailed enough to actually be sewn in real life.

Then came AI music, and that one still amazes me. You can make songs exactly the way you like them.

And finally, the websites.

Right now I'm making music videos for the songs I created. Some use AI animation, some are built in code, so that everything on screen follows the music: the beat, the mood, the moment.

Every step taught me something for the next one. A year ago I couldn't have imagined any of this. Now I can't imagine stopping.

I'm still an ER doctor. This is what I do between shifts, and it has been the best kind of therapy.

To be honest, none of my friends would really understand what I'm talking about. When I say "I moved the config file above public_html" or "the canvas was drawing the sky from the outside," I get polite nods. So I needed to share this story with people who actually get it. That's you.

Does any of this have a point? I don't know. But it made me happy, and maybe it will make someone else curious enough to try.

If you visit any of the sites, I'd love to hear what you think, especially what's confusing.

U zdravlje, everyone. That's Serbian for "to your health." Coming from a doctor, I mean it literally.

---

*This post was written with help from AI, of course , based on my own story.*

I built my husband a vim trainer with a Gemma coach that runs in the browser

*This is a submission for the [Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-weekend-2026-10-01)*

## What I Built

A lot of my friends build their own tools. They hit a problem and just make the thing they want. I wanted to build something for someone else this time, and the answer was sitting right next to me.

My husband has wanted to learn vim for a long time. He's tried a bunch of times, and it always ends the same way: he gives up. When I asked him why, it came down to two things. There are too many commands to memorize, and everything feels slow and awkward compared to what he's used to.

So I built **hjkl**, a browser app that teaches vim in tiny drills.

Each drill gives you a small buffer, a goal, and a keystroke "par" to beat. You solve it in a real vim editor, not a simulation. A few things I designed around his actual problems:

- **Only a few commands at a time.** Each lesson introduces a small set of commands, with a cheat sheet always on screen.
- **Every command shows the VS Code habit it replaces.** `dd` is Ctrl+Shift+K, `o` is Ctrl+Enter, `ciw` is roughly Ctrl+D and type. If there isn't a real equivalent (like `.` or `f`), it just says so.
- **Par instead of pass/fail.** You always finish the drill. If you took the long way, you see the shorter answer right there.
- **A Review list.** Any drill you solved over par goes into Review, worst first, and drops off once you hit par. Those are exactly the commands that haven't stuck yet.
- **A full Vim reference.** The lesson cheat sheet only shows what you're currently learning, but there's also an All Commands reference with everything covered in the app. You can search it by key, action, or the VS Code shortcut you're used to.
- **Plain names under weird keys.** `<CR>` shows "Enter" underneath and `<Esc>` shows "Escape". I added this after I had to ask what `<CR>` meant myself while testing.

Right now there are **17 lessons and 124 hand-written drills**, starting with basic movement and insert mode and working up through text objects, counts and combos, search, visual mode, substitutions, macros, registers, and more.

Then there's the AI part, which runs entirely in the browser.

When I handed it over to him, he actually sat there and worked through it for a while, which felt like a pretty good sign considering every previous attempt at learning vim had ended with him giving up. He liked the short drills and being able to see the more efficient answer when he took the long way. More importantly, he kept going without me having to convince him to.

## Demo

**Live:** https://hjkl.pinkpixel.dev

You'll want a desktop browser with a physical keyboard (vim on a phone keyboard is not a good time). The AI coach needs WebGPU.

## Code

{% github pinkpixel-dev/hjkl %}

## How I Built It

The app itself is Vite and plain TypeScript, no framework. The editor is CodeMirror 6 with `@replit/codemirror-vim`, so it's real vim behavior: motions, operators, text objects, dot-repeat, registers, search.

### Every drill is checked in real vim

Every drill has a reference solution, and par is just its length. The test suite runs every reference solution through the actual vim engine and checks that it really produces the goal. That turned out to matter a lot. My first pass had a few pars that couldn't be hit, and the tests caught them immediately. There are 182 tests now.

It also caught some fun bugs. My favorite: search drills worked fine on their own but broke after pressing Next. The vim plugin keeps search history and jump positions globally, so the second search tried to jump to a position from the previous, longer buffer and crashed. Now vim's global state resets for every drill.

### The coach: Gemma running on your GPU

The AI coach is optional and off by default. When you turn it on, it downloads **Gemma 4 E2B** once and runs it in a Web Worker on WebGPU with **Transformers.js**. Your keystrokes and prompts never leave the browser. The model files come from Hugging Face, and after that everything is local.

A few details:

- It loads Gemma 4 through the text-only path, so it only downloads the text model and skips the vision and audio encoders.
- It uses `q4f16` when the GPU supports fp16 shaders and falls back to `q4` otherwise.
- **Gemma 3 1B** is there as a lighter option you can switch to without turning the coach off.

On my machine, Gemma 4 E2B writes about 6 to 7 tokens a second, so a one-sentence explanation takes a few seconds. Gemma 3 1B is faster (about 10 tokens a second), but when I tested both on the same drills, 1B kept getting the commands wrong, and once it just greeted him instead of giving feedback. So Gemma 4 is the default.

The coach does two things:

1. **After an over-par solve**, it explains what the shorter answer does differently.
2. **The Hint button** nudges you toward the right command without giving away the whole sequence.

Getting the feedback accurate took some work. My first version sent the model the raw keystrokes, and after a drill solved with `x` seven times, it confidently told him he'd used `dd`. A small model reading `xxxxxxx` doesn't really see seven presses of one key.

The fix was to stop making the model parse vim. Before the keys go into the prompt, the app groups them the way vim reads them and labels each one:

```plaintext
x ×7 (delete character)
```

instead of `xxxxxxx`, and

```plaintext
cw (change to word end), typed "blue", <Esc> (back to normal mode)
```

instead of `cwblue<Esc>`. After that change, all of my test cases came back accurate, like: "`dw` deletes the word under the cursor, which is much faster than deleting each character individually."

### AI-generated drills

The part I'm happiest with is the **5 more** button on each lesson.

My first attempt let Gemma write whole drills: the text, the starting cursor, the solution keys. Only 2 of 12 drafts survived validation. The rest had missing cursor marks, keys that didn't do what the instruction said, or text glued onto other words. I kept adding filters and kept finding new kinds of mistakes.

So I split the job up based on what each side is good at:

- **Gemma writes a short snippet** of text (a SQL query, a shopping list, a CSS rule), plus a short instruction.
- **The app supplies the keys** by reusing the key patterns from that lesson's hand-written drills on the new text. Then it plays them in real vim to get the goal and par.
- **The instruction gets checked.** If Gemma's wording doesn't name what actually changes, the app swaps in a plain one like `Change "milk" to "eggs"`.

Now every batch keeps 5 out of 5, in about 15 seconds. Every generated drill is solvable at par, because the app played it before showing it.

### Deploying

It's a static site on Cloudflare Workers static assets. The only wrinkle was ONNX Runtime's wasm file, which is about 27 MB, over Cloudflare's 25 MiB per-file limit. Transformers.js already loads it from jsDelivr pinned to the exact version, so I just left it out of the build.

## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For this project it's pretty concrete. An open-weight model is the reason the coach can run in his browser at all.

With a closed API, every hint and every generated drill would be a paid request, plus a server and an API key to manage. For a gift that's supposed to stick around, that's a bad fit. Running Gemma locally means it costs nothing per use, it works without an account, and his keystrokes and mistakes stay on his machine.

It also means I could do things a hosted API would make awkward. I picked a model size that fits a laptop GPU, compared two Gemma models side by side on the same drills, and swapped between them with one click. The rest of the stack is open too: Transformers.js, ONNX Runtime Web, CodeMirror, and the vim plugin that made "use real vim" possible in the first place.

If I keep working on it, I’d like to add more lessons and keep improving the generated drills, but I also want to see what happens after he’s used it for a while. The whole point was to build something around the way one actual person was struggling to learn, so whether it really helps those commands stick is probably the best test I could give it.

## Prize Categories

**Gemma**: the coach and the AI drill generator both run Gemma 4 E2B locally in the browser through Transformers.js on WebGPU, with Gemma 3 1B as a lighter option.

text:
I Built a New Tab Extension for DEV

I spend a lot of time on DEV these days. Reading posts, finding interesting projects, participating in challenges, and occasionally writing something myself.

I also like daily.dev. Having a feed of developer content right there whenever I open a new tab is pretty convenient.

So naturally, I started thinking... what if I had something like that, but just for DEV?

And because apparently I can't have an idea without turning it into another project, I built one.

It's called **DEV Tab**, and it's a free, open-source browser extension that replaces your new tab page with a feed of posts from DEV.

It's now available on the Chrome Web Store.

**[Install DEV Tab for Chrome](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/dev-tab/mfhbilfjgklgebkclbkabohhkibomnop)**

Firefox support is built too, and the add-on is currently awaiting review. I'll update this post with the link once it's approved.

## A little more than just a feed

The original idea was pretty simple. Open a new tab, see what's happening on DEV, and click through to anything interesting.

But, as usual, I kept thinking of things to add.

![DEV Tab showing a grid of DEV posts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pinkpixel-dev/DEV-tab/main/screenshots/screenshot.png)

You can browse posts from Today, This Week, Rising, and Latest, along with dedicated sections for trends, events, podcasts, and videos.

There are also tag filters, so you can quickly jump between subjects you're interested in. You can save your favorite tags, hide tags you'd rather not see, and follow posts from specific DEV organizations.

A few other things I added:

- Search directly from the new tab page.
- Keyboard navigation using arrow keys and Enter.
- A compact view if you'd rather see more posts and fewer images.
- Reaction counts and previews of the three newest comments.
- A shortcut to create a new DEV post.
- Feed caching, so opening a new tab doesn't mean waiting for everything to load again.

Nothing particularly revolutionary here. I just wanted a convenient way to explore DEV without having to go looking for things.

## Then I decided it needed a dashboard

This part wasn't in my original plan, but I spend enough time writing on DEV that I thought having a better overview of my own activity would be useful.

If you add your DEV API key in the extension settings, you unlock some additional features, including a personal dashboard.

![DEV Tab dashboard with example statistics, charts, and post activity](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pinkpixel-dev/DEV-tab/main/screenshots/dashboard.png)

The dashboard includes your follower count, views, reactions, comments, and new followers, with options to look at the last 7, 30, or 90 days.

There's also a daily views chart, an activity heatmap that lets you browse previous years, and a list of your published posts and drafts.

You can see recent followers, top supporters, and where your readers are coming from, too.

I particularly like having the activity heatmap and post statistics together. It's interesting to look back and see when I was active and how different posts performed.

*The dashboard screenshot above uses fictional example data, by the way.*

## Connecting your DEV account is completely optional

You don't need an account or API key to use the extension. The public feeds, search, filters, and other browsing features work without one.

But if you do connect your DEV account, you also get access to your personal feed based on the tags you follow, your reading list, and semantic search.

You can generate an API key from your [DEV settings](https://dev.to/settings/extensions).

The extension doesn't have a backend, analytics, or tracking. Your API key stays in your browser's local extension storage and is only sent to DEV for authenticated API requests.

I wanted to keep it simple and avoid introducing a separate service just to display information DEV already makes available.

## A few limitations

There are a couple of things I would have liked to include but couldn't because of the DEV API.

For example, you can't directly react to posts, leave comments, or save articles to your reading list from the extension.

You can view reaction counts and preview comments, but interacting with a post opens it on DEV itself.

I'd love to have those actions directly in the feed someday, but for now, that's a limitation of what's available through the API.

## Built with WXT, React, and TypeScript

I used [WXT](https://wxt.dev/) for the extension framework, along with React and TypeScript.

This was my first time using WXT, and I really liked being able to build for Chrome and Firefox from the same codebase.

One thing I spent some time on was making sure the feed wouldn't constantly refetch everything whenever a new tab opened. The first page of each feed gets cached for ten minutes, and previously loaded posts can still appear if you're offline.

It's a small thing, but when you're replacing something as frequently used as the new tab page, I think it matters.

## Give it a try!

DEV Tab is open source, so you can take a look at the code, report bugs, suggest features, or contribute if you'd like.

**[Chrome Web Store](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/dev-tab/mfhbilfjgklgebkclbkabohhkibomnop)**

**[GitHub](https://github.com/pinkpixel-dev/DEV-tab)**

The Firefox version is currently awaiting approval, and I'll add the link here when it's published.

This started as one of those little "wouldn't it be nice if..." ideas, and somehow turned into a full browser extension with a personal analytics dashboard.

I guess that's what happens when you keep finding things you want to build.

If you use DEV regularly, I'd love to hear what you think! And if there's something you'd find useful in a future version, let me know.

Building a 512-LED wall that dances to my music: FFT, ESP32, and a custom serial protocol ## Context A while ago I decided my wall needed to react to music. The build is 512 WS2812B LEDs — eight 8×8 panels arranged as a 32×16 grid — driven by an ESP32. The design decision that shaped everything came early: the PC does all the analysis, and the ESP32 is a deliberately dumb display. The PC decodes the mp3, FFTs it into 32 frequency bands, builds a 16×32 RGB frame, packs it, and streams it over USB serial at 921600 baud. The ESP32 receives 1542-byte frames, applies a 25 A current limiter, and hands them to FastLED. The interesting engineering is in that split, the protocol between the two halves, and what I had to debug to make it not corrupt. ## Approach **The architecture: PC is the brain, ESP32 is the wall.** The PC already owns the audio stream, so doing the analysis there means zero duplicated state. `soundfile` decodes the mp3, numpy computes the FFT into 32 bands, a vectorized HSV→RGB frame builder renders a 16×32 image, and `pack.py` serializes it. The ESP32 firmware only parses frames, runs the current limiter, and calls `FastLED.show()`. Palette and geometry changes are Python edits — no firmware re-flash needed to tune the visuals. That split is why the whole project lives comfortably in two small codebases instead of one hairy one. **The protocol had to be engineered, not improvised.** Each frame is exactly 1542 bytes: 2-byte magic (`0xAA 0xAA`) + 2-byte length + 2-byte sequence number + 1536 raw GRB bytes (512 LEDs × 3). The numbers on the wire dictated everything else: | Quantity | Value | Why it matters | |---|---|---| | `FastLED.show()` | **15.86 ms** | Hardware floor: 512×24 bits × 1.25 µs. Cannot be improved in code. | | Frame on wire | **16.7 ms** | 1542 bytes × 10 bits ÷ 921600 baud | | **Frame ceiling** | **~31 fps** | receive + show are serialized; 32+ fps ⇒ RX overflow ⇒ corruption | | Current cap | **24 fps** | `SERIAL_MAX_FPS` — user-chosen; measured ceiling ~27 fps under lock-step | For context, 921600 baud is roughly 90 KB/s — nothing exotic by USB standards, but at that rate a 1542-byte frame takes 16.7 ms on the wire, which is the same order of magnitude as the render time. That's why the rate math matters: the three fps numbers (24 shipped / 27 measured under lock-step / 31 hard ceiling) sit in a deliberate ladder — I ship conservatively below the measured ceiling so the wall never brushes the corruption edge in normal use. The first version was fire-and-forget: the PC streamed frames and hoped. It didn't hold up — during `FastLED.show()` the ESP32 isn't reading the UART, and frames piled up and corrupted. The fix was **lock-step flow control**: the ESP32 sends an ACK byte (`0x01`) after every rendered frame, and the Python side holds the next frame until it arrives. Zero frames lost during LED update; a missed ACK degrades that one cycle to fire-and-forget instead of stalling the wall. **The rewrite that made it sample-synced.** The original stack was pygame/tkinter. I replaced it wholesale with sounddevice + numpy: playback position now comes from the audio callback counter, so the FFT is sample-synced by construction — there's no drift between what you hear and what the wall shows, ever. Every tunable lives in one `settings.py`. The frame builder is numpy-vectorized and locked by a golden reference test. ## Architecture ```mermaid graph LR A[MP3 folder] --> B[soundfile decode
libsndfile] B --> C[numpy FFT
32 bands] C --> D[vectorized HSV→RGB
16×32 frame] D --> E[pack: GRB + panel remap] E --> F[USB serial @ 921600
1542 B/frame @ 25 fps] F --> G[ESP32 UART RX
4096 B buffer] G --> H[magic / LEN / SEQ parse] H --> I[25 A current limiter
protects 30 A fuse] I --> J[FastLED.show()
15.86 ms floor] J --> K[8× WS2812B boards
512 LEDs] J -->|ACK 0x01| F ``` ## Evidence The wall playing "Slow Dancing in a Burning Room" by John Mayer — the 32×16 grid reacting to the vocal line and the guitar: [▶ Watch the live demo](https://youtu.be/Uu5eGVKEy94) The system was accepted on hardware in two tagged states: `v1-working` (the pygame/tkinter stack, preserved as a revert point) and `v2-headless` (the rewrite). The test suite is real: `8/8 test_pack.py`, `2/2 test_render.py`, `3/3 test_audio.py`, plus a passing end-to-end `pipeline_test`. The frame builder has a golden reference test — the packed bytes are asserted against a precomputed output, so a geometry change can't silently break the wire format. The git history reads as a debugging log, which is what it is: ```plaintext b192b92 feat: lock-step flow control — ESP32 ACKs each render, zero frame loss f2fbb6d perf: I2S DMA LED driver, numpy pack_frame, monitor_speed fix 0f20384 feat: acceptance hardening — seq=0 heartbeat resync, fps docs, diag off 0ef09f0 feat: 24fps acceptance — truthful counters, single pacing governor 8969187 feat: headless entry point (folder loop, synced FFT->serial) 70dd905 feat: numpy-vectorized frame builder with golden reference test ``` ## What went wrong **The 256-byte buffer that couldn't hold a 1542-byte frame.** The default ESP32 UART FIFO is 256 bytes. Frames are 1542. While `FastLED.show()` runs (15.86 ms of not-reading-the-UART at 921600 baud), the FIFO overflows and the stream corrupts. The fix is one line — `Serial.setRxBufferSize(4096)` *before* `begin()` — but it took real staring at garbage frames to find. The lesson: your buffer size is a protocol parameter, and the default will betray you exactly when the hardware is busy. **I lost 50–70% of sent frames and shipped it anyway.** Under lock-step, the ESP32 is busy in `show()` when frames arrive, so a large share of what the PC sends is dropped. This is now a *characterized* behavior, not a mystery: each delivered frame is still audio-synced, so the wall shows a slightly sparser but correct animation. I documented it as a known characteristic and accepted it rather than pretending I'd fixed it. **The first stack was throwaway.** pygame/tkinter worked but made the timing story fragile. The rewrite to sounddevice+numpy was the difference between "roughly synced" and "synced by construction." I should have started there. ## Known limitations - ~50–70% of sent frames are lost to `show()` RX-starvation windows; every delivered frame is still sample-accurate. - Hard ceiling ~31 fps because receive and render are serialized; shipped at 24 fps. - The UDP path is dormant — serial is the only live transport. - The 25 A limiter caps aggregate brightness: it scales all channels if Σ((R+G+B)/255)×20 mA exceeds 25 A, protecting a 30 A fuse at 30.7 A theoretical max draw. ## Lessons learned - A dumb-device/smart-host split keeps a hardware project small: re-tune visuals in Python, never re-flash. - Flow control beats fire-and-forget at 921600 baud. An ACK byte is cheaper than debugging corruption. - Measure the hardware floor before designing the protocol. 15.86 ms of `show()` time made the frame ceiling a math problem, not a guess. - Buffer size is a protocol decision, and the default is a trap. - Tests work on hardware projects too — the golden reference test means the wire format can't silently drift. ## Links - Repo: [Shaarkymoo/music-visualizer](https://github.com/Shaarkymoo/music-visualizer) — firmware (`src/main.cpp`), PC app (`python/`), full docs + parts list - [FastLED](https://github.com/FastLED/FastLED) — the LED driver library - [sounddevice](https://python-sounddevice.readthedocs.io/) / [soundfile](https://pysoundfile.readthedocs.io/) — the audio engine - [WS2812B datasheet](https://cdn-shop.adafruit.com/datasheets/WS2812B.pdf) — the LED in question

text: A solarpunk garden for your GitHub profile, generated daily from your contributions _solarpunk: soft colors, nature and gentle technology, the opposite of cyberpunk's dark neon_ I turned my GitHub contribution graph into an isometric garden. One tile per day, a plant that grows with the number of contributions, seasons that follow the calendar, and a small gardener walking around today's tile. It is a plain SVG with CSS and SMIL animations, regenerated every day by a GitHub Action. Python standard library only, no dependencies, MIT license: [Shagshag/garden-graph](https://github.com/Shagshag/garden-graph). I built it with Claude Code. I decided what the garden should look like and judged every render by eye. The assistant wrote most of the code and ran the command-line checks. ![The one-year view, light version on the upper right and dark version on the lower left](https://www.shagshag.net/medias/2026/10/garden-year-split.gif) > Note: You can see the animated SVG in the [README of the repository](https://github.com/Shagshag/garden-graph/blob/main/README.md), or open the raw files in the [assets folder](https://github.com/Shagshag/garden-graph/tree/main/assets). This article shows how to put the same garden on your own profile, and how to adapt it to where you live. ### 🌱 Where the idea came from I started from Giorgi Kobaidze's article [I turned my GitHub profile into a cyberpunk console, with a city built from my contributions](https://dev.to/georgekobaidze/i-turned-my-github-profile-into-a-cyberpunk-console-with-a-city-built-from-my-contributions-h4c). {% embed https://dev.to/georgekobaidze/i-turned-my-github-profile-into-a-cyberpunk-console-with-a-city-built-from-my-contributions-h4c %} I took the general shape of the project from it. A daily GitHub Action calls the GraphQL API, a Python script writes an SVG, the isometric view is drawn from the back to the front (no 3D engine), the animations are CSS inside the SVG, and the workflow commits only if the files changed. The article also explained that `contributionsCollection` covers one year per request (see the [GraphQL reference](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/users)), and that you ask for more with one aliased field per year. I do it slightly differently, see the annex. That inspiration was cyberpunk: a city, dark, neon. I wanted something fresher and more pleasant. I am also making a solarpunk restoration game, so the colors are soft and close to nature, and the wind turbines recall the gentle energy side of the theme. ### 🌳 What's in the garden Each day is a tile. The plant on it depends on how active that day was compared with your other active days (quartiles): bare soil for no contribution, then a sprout, a flower, a tree, and for the busiest quarter a wind turbine with a solar panel. Days that have not happened yet are packed earth. The season follows the date, and every file exists in a light and a dark version. Three views are generated: the current year folded in two half-years (big tiles, easy to read), an overview of the last five years, and a view made for phones. ![The five-year overview, light version on the upper right and dark version on the lower left](https://www.shagshag.net/medias/2026/10/garden-split.gif) ![The mobile view, light version on the upper right and dark version on the lower left](https://www.shagshag.net/medias/2026/10/mobile-garden-year-split.gif) ### 🪏 Setting it up on your profile 1. Get the files into your own repository: either fork it, or create `/` (the repository GitHub uses for your profile README) and copy the files in. Enable GitHub Actions. 2. Open `.github/workflows/garden.yml` and pick your climate and language: ```yaml env: GARDEN_CLIMATE: temperate-north # see the table below GARDEN_LANG: fr # fr (the default), en, ja or hi GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GH_STATS_TOKEN || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} ``` 3. Run the **Update garden** workflow once from the Actions tab. After that it runs every day at 05:17 UTC (`17 5 * * *`) and commits only when something changed. That makes one commit per day, and a run takes about 15 seconds. By default the garden is drawn for the owner of the repository, so a fork shows its own owner's garden, not mine. Set `GITHUB_LOGIN` only to show someone else's contributions. To also count your private contributions, add a secret `GH_STATS_TOKEN` (a token with `read:user`) and enable "Private contributions" in your profile settings. `GARDEN_YEARS` (5 by default) sets the number of years in the overview. ### 🏡 Adapting the garden to where you live A contribution graph does not know about seasons, and most people do not live in four neat ones. The first version was written for the northern hemisphere, so it was wrong in Australia. A six-month shift fixed that but only covered temperate climates, so I moved to a `GARDEN_CLIMATE` setting. I looked at where GitHub accounts are to decide which climates to offer. In the official [Octoverse 2025 post](https://github.blog/news-insights/octoverse/octoverse-a-new-developer-joins-github-every-second-as-ai-leads-typescript-to-1/), the United States comes first with 28 million developers, India second with 21.9 million, and Brazil is fourth with 6.89 million. China is also in the top ten. That gave seven climates: | `GARDEN_CLIMATE` | Seasons | For | | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- | | `temperate-north` | spring, summer, autumn, winter | North America, Europe | | `temperate-south` | the same, shifted by six months | southern Australia, New Zealand, Argentina, South Africa | | `monsoon` | cool, hot, monsoon, post-monsoon | India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal | | `tropical-south` | wet (Nov to Apr), dry (May to Oct) | central Brazil, Indonesia, southern Africa | | `tropical-north` | wet (May to Oct), dry (Nov to Apr) | the Sahel, Central America, mainland Southeast Asia | | `china-southeast` | mild winter, spring rains, humid summer and typhoons, clear autumn | Guangdong, Fujian, Hong Kong | | `japan` | sakura, spring, tsuyu, summer, autumn, winter | Honshu | The months are averages. A specific region (the east coast of India, Kerala) can have its rains at other dates, so a climate is an approximation. In Japan a month can be cut in two, because tsuyu runs until mid-July. If your region is not in the list, you add a climate in `render.py`: one entry in `CLIMATES` (which season each month belongs to, and the order of the legend) and one entry in `PALETTE` for each new season (ground color, leaves, flower colors, and whether the trees carry blossoms or fruit, or there are puddles or snow). For example, the two-season tropics of the northern hemisphere are: ```python "tropical-north": (_months(wet="5 6 7 8 9 10", dry="11 12 1 2 3 4"), ("wet", "dry")), ``` The drawing code does not test season names, it reads the palette, so nothing else has to change. ![The monsoon climate](https://www.shagshag.net/medias/2026/10/climate-monsoon-light.png) ![The japan climate](https://www.shagshag.net/medias/2026/10/climate-japan-light.png) The monsoon climate, then the japan climate. Languages work the same way. `GARDEN_LANG` takes `fr`, `en`, `ja` or `hi`. The texts in `i18n.py` are complete sentence templates with placeholders (`{login}`, `{total}`, `{first}`, `{last}`), not words glued together, because word order and punctuation change between languages. To add a language, copy an entry of `STRINGS` and translate it. Numbers follow local usage, including the Indian grouping (12,34,567). ### 🥗 Putting it in your README Embed the year view in your profile README with ``, which serves a light and a dark image. The switch with `` comes from Kera Cudmore's [GitHub README images based on prefers-color-scheme](https://dev.to/keracudmore/github-readme-images-based-on-prefers-color-scheme-5cp8) and from the "Adding an image to suit your visitors" section of the [GitHub quickstart for writing on GitHub](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/getting-started-with-writing-and-formatting-on-github/quickstart-for-writing-on-github). {% embed https://dev.to/keracudmore/github-readme-images-based-on-prefers-color-scheme-5cp8 %} ```html ``` The order matters, the first match wins. ### 📱 Three views, three sizes The part about phones is mine. Neither of the two sources above deals with it. On GitHub the 1000 px image is displayed a bit smaller, and the tiles of the five-year overview end up under 20 px wide, which is hard to read for a single day. That is why the one-year view exists, folded in two half-years so the tiles are about twice as big. On a phone it is worse: the image is shrunk to about a third of its size and the title falls to around 8 px. The third view, `garden-mobile-*.svg`, has a narrow canvas, a bigger text and the legend under the garden. The first two `` lines above pick it with a `max-width` media query combined with the color scheme. If you also embed the five-year overview, it is too fine for a phone. An `` cannot be hidden, so on a phone the repository replaces it with `blank.svg`, an SVG of one pixel. That is a workaround. The README of the repository does it with a second ``: ```html ``` ### 🐛 Problems along the way Two things broke along the way, and only one of them was a real bug. The wind turbines first turned with a CSS animation, which broke as soon as the plants were scaled. They now use SVG's own animation. Screenshots are frozen, so the movement was checked by advancing the virtual time of a headless browser. The gardener walks a few tiles around today's tile. The first version walked a fixed distance, so at the start and end of the year he left the field, since the first and last weeks can be partial. ![Wile E. Coyote falling](https://www.shagshag.net/medias/2026/10/wile-e-coyote-3018138172.gif) The walk is now limited to the tiles that exist on his row, and its duration follows the distance so the speed stays the same. It was checked on January 1st, January 10th, December 20th and December 31st. ### 🐞 Similar projects I am not the first to draw contributions as a garden. [a104437ana/sakura-garden](https://github.com/a104437ana/sakura-garden) draws them as flowers in an SVG for a README, and [qrstajalli/BranchOut](https://github.com/qrstajalli/BranchOut) turns the last year into a pixel-art garden. garden-graph differs by its isometric view, the seven climates, the four languages, and the phone view. ### 🐌 Limits and where it stands - The Japanese and Hindi texts have not been reviewed by a native speaker. - The fonts are not embedded in the SVG, so Japanese and Hindi need a matching font on the viewer's machine. - I tested on github.com (the repository page and my profile page), not in the GitHub mobile app and not on other sites. - On a phone, the combination of mobile and dark follows the system theme, not necessarily the theme chosen inside GitHub. - The tiles stay small on a phone, because the width is fixed. - The months of each climate are averages, so a climate is an approximation by region. Remaining work: a review of the Japanese and Hindi texts, embedded fonts, and a test in the GitHub mobile app. ### 🧮 Annex: fetching several years in one request Giorgi's article gets the list of active years with `contributionYears`, then builds one aliased field per year. garden-graph does the same with one difference: the number of years is fixed (`GARDEN_YEARS`, 5 by default), so there is no first query. `fetch.py` takes the current year and goes back from there, then sends a single request: ```python fields = "".join( f'y{y}: contributionsCollection(from: "{y}-01-01T00:00:00Z", to: "{y}-12-31T23:59:59Z") {{' "contributionCalendar { weeks { contributionDays { date contributionCount } } } } " for y in years ) ``` Each field asks for one calendar year, from January 1st to December 31st, so it stays under the limit of one year. The API refuses a longer range. A GitHub calendar is made of whole weeks. The first and last week of a year can hold days of the previous or the next year, so the same date can come back in two fields. The script keeps a date only if it belongs to the year of its field and is not in the future, and stores it by date: ```python for y in years: for week in user[f"y{y}"]["contributionCalendar"]["weeks"]: for d in week["contributionDays"]: if d["date"].startswith(str(y)) and d["date"] <= date.today().isoformat(): counts[d["date"]] = d["contributionCount"] ``` The result goes into `data/contributions.json`. If the API does not answer, the script prints a message and keeps the previous file, so the garden is still drawn from the last data it had. ### 🌻 Sources - Giorgi Kobaidze, [I turned my GitHub profile into a cyberpunk console, with a city built from my contributions](https://dev.to/georgekobaidze/i-turned-my-github-profile-into-a-cyberpunk-console-with-a-city-built-from-my-contributions-h4c) - Kera Cudmore, [GitHub README images based on prefers-color-scheme](https://dev.to/keracudmore/github-readme-images-based-on-prefers-color-scheme-5cp8) (July 2025) - GitHub Docs, [Quickstart for writing on GitHub](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/getting-started-with-writing-and-formatting-on-github/quickstart-for-writing-on-github) - GitHub Docs, [GraphQL reference, Users](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/users) (`contributionsCollection`) - GitHub, [Octoverse 2025](https://github.blog/news-insights/octoverse/octoverse-a-new-developer-joins-github-every-second-as-ai-leads-typescript-to-1/) - [a104437ana/sakura-garden](https://github.com/a104437ana/sakura-garden), [qrstajalli/BranchOut](https://github.com/qrstajalli/BranchOut) - [Shagshag/garden-graph](https://github.com/Shagshag/garden-graph) (MIT) --- What kind of theme would you want to see next? Drop a comment below if you end up adding a new climate or language!
