A System That Lets AI Work Directly With a Real Xbox — Now Open Source

---
title: A System That Lets AI Work Directly With a Real Xbox — Now Open Source
published: true
description: XCP turns one-shot code generation into a continuous software lifecycle: build, execute on Xbox, observe, correct, evolve, repeat.
tags: showdev, microsoft, ai, opensource
series: XcpStudio
---

XCP turns one-shot code generation into a continuous software lifecycle: create, execute on Xbox, observe, correct, evolve, repeat.

AI agents are getting very good at producing software.

What interested me was what happens after the code exists.

A generated project can compile and still be wrong. A port can launch while losing important behaviour. An agent can make a convincing change without knowing how that change actually behaves on the machine that has to run it.

I wanted the software project to continue beyond generation.

The same project should be able to change, run on a real Xbox Series X, produce evidence about what happened there, return that evidence to the development side, receive another correction, become a new version, and run again.

That eventually became XCP.

But it started somewhere much smaller: with a virtual machine inside the Xbox application sandbox.

The project should not disappear after generation

A lot of AI-assisted development still has an implicit shape:

prompt
  ↓
agent
  ↓
source files
  ↓
build
  ↓
done

I wanted a loop instead.

AI agent / developer
        ↓
     XCP project
        ↓
 create / modify / adapt
        ↓
    target candidate
        ↓
     XBOX SERIES
        ↓
 execute + observe
        ↓
 structured evidence
        ↓
 correct / evolve
        ↓
     next version
        ↺

The agent does not run unrestricted on the console.

It works from the PC side, where the project can be inspected and modified. Xbox executes the prepared candidate. XCP records what happened and brings that information back into the project lifecycle.

The next iteration can therefore start from real target behaviour, not only from what the agent expected the software to do.

That distinction became the core of XCP for me.

XCP turns an AI agent from a one-shot code generator into a participant in an ongoing software lifecycle.

The project survives the generation.

Its versions have identities. Executions belong to specific versions. Evidence belongs to specific executions.

That makes continued work possible without treating every new generation as an unrelated pile of files.

Create, adapt, and keep going

XCP currently enters that lifecycle in two main ways.

A project can start from an idea.

In the public creation programme, an AI-driven, human-directed workflow completed 28/28 lifecycle operations across an interactive project and a utility.

The interesting part was not that an AI produced code. We already know models can do that.

The interesting part was that the work continued through the wider lifecycle: project creation, preparation, execution and subsequent decisions.

The second path starts from existing authorized software.

That is substantially harder because a real project is more than source files. It has state, input behaviour, timing, scenes, persistence, assets, engine conventions and interactions between systems.

The first public real-source case uses Minilens, an authorized Godot 2 project.
![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/q0ytuv37yvl2my3daoja.png)

That case completed 14/14 lifecycle operations and 5/5 declared semantic acceptance checks on Xbox.

I am deliberately not describing that as “Godot compatibility”.

It is a narrower and more useful result: real source software crossed the full path from source observation to an Xbox execution and a measured decision.

And then the project can continue.

One of the public lifecycle sequences is:

1.0.0 → 1.1.0 → 1.0.0

A later version was produced, exercised, and the lifecycle retained the ability to return to the earlier known version.

That is a small example, but it captures an important idea: evolution is part of the system, not an afterthought.

The software is expected to be changed again.

The Xbox became part of the development loop

The Xbox is not only the place where the final result gets deployed.

It is an execution target inside the loop.

Consider a simple behavioural change.

An agent modifies movement. XCP prepares the next candidate. The candidate runs on Xbox. Target observations are recorded. Those observations are compared against the behaviour the project was supposed to preserve. The result becomes evidence attached to that version.

The next correction can then work from that result.

This pattern can repeat.

That is very different from asking a model to generate another implementation after someone manually reports that “movement feels wrong”.

The target itself contributes information to the next development step.

This is also why I became less interested in “AI-generated software” as a category.

Generation is one operation.

Maintaining an evidence-bearing relationship between an agent, a software project and a real execution target is a much larger problem.

The virtual machine that made this possible

The Xbox side began as a separate research problem.

I wanted programmable execution on a retail Xbox Series console while staying inside the public application environment.

That produced XVM, a deterministic virtual machine used by the current reference runtime.

XVM v2 currently has 26 admitted opcodes, 16 registers, typed memory, bounded control flow, static execution budgets, deterministic snapshot/resume, a canonical CPU path and GPU differential execution paths.

Those details deserve their own article.

For XCP, the more important property is simpler:

new bounded work can be submitted to the execution target without every new behaviour becoming a completely new native application.

The VM gives XCP a programmable target.

It also gives the target the ability to reject work that does not fit its current execution contract.

That is enough to keep a useful separation between the software producer and the machine executing what it produced.

XVM does not remove the Xbox sandbox.

It creates a programmable layer inside it.

Running the software was not enough

Once the VM worked, another problem became much more important.

Real software does not begin as VM instructions.

It begins as behaviour.

A player moves. A collision fires. A value survives a restart. An input changes some state. A scene transition happens.

The implementation of those behaviours can be completely different on another runtime.

This forced XCP to separate three things:

source behaviour
      ↓
semantic representation
      ↓
target implementation

The current reference source family is Godot, while Xbox/XVM is the first reference target.

Those environments do not share the same engine, scripting model, APIs, scene implementation or runtime assumptions.

So XCP cannot simply copy structure and call the result equivalent.

The source side has to expose enough meaning for the target side to reason about what can actually be preserved.

And then the result still has to be measured.

That produces another distinction which now runs through the project:

execution is not fidelity.

A candidate can launch successfully and still behave incorrectly.

A movement path may work while collision semantics changed. A scene may look right while persistence is broken. A playable subset can still contain behaviour that was never observed.

XCP therefore keeps operability, fidelity and stronger equivalence claims separate.

This is not mainly about being conservative with wording.

It makes the evidence useful to the next iteration.

If the system can say where behaviour diverged instead of merely returning “build succeeded”, an agent has something concrete to work on.

Xbox is the first target, not the definition of XCP

Today the concrete path looks like this:

Godot → XCP → Xbox / XVM

But that is not the architecture I want to stop at.

The source side and target side are being separated deliberately.

The future model is closer to:

Godot ─────┐
Unity ─────┤
Unreal ────┤
Custom ────┘
           ↓
          XCP
           ↓
      target contract
       ↙         ↘
 Xbox / XVM    other runtimes

Only the first path has public research evidence today. The other arrows are directions for the architecture, not current compatibility claims.

This is where XCP becomes much more interesting.

The long-term value is not moving one Godot project to one Xbox. It is making source systems and execution targets independently extensible.

If another developer can eventually write an adapter for a different engine without rewriting the core, that tests the semantic boundary.

If someone can implement another XVM runtime from the same contract, that tests the execution boundary.

If another target can consume XCP projects while preserving the evidence model, Xbox has done its job as the first forcing function rather than becoming a permanent limitation.

The next test is other developers

Most XCP development still lives in a large private research repository.

That repository is useful as a laboratory, but it is not what I want to publish as the platform.

It contains years of experiments, Xbox runtime work, product prototypes, operational tooling, evidence pipelines and branches that should not become accidental public APIs.

So I am preparing a clean open-source extraction instead.

The current model is roughly:

spec
runtime
semantic
adapters
evidence
conformance
sdk
examples

Godot would begin as the reference source adapter.

XVM would begin as the reference execution substrate.

Xbox Series would remain the first reference target.

XCP Studio is the product environment around that platform.

The experiment I care about after that is not another demo produced by me.

It is somebody else building the next adapter, runtime or verifier.

That will expose very quickly whether the abstractions are actually general.

From a VM on Xbox to a continuous software lifecycle

I originally wanted to see how far programmable execution could be pushed on Xbox.

That produced XVM.

XVM made repeated target execution possible.

Repeated execution made it possible to return structured information from the hardware.

That information made a continuous agent loop possible.

And that loop became XCP.

AI agent
    ↓
software project
    ↓
real execution
    ↓
evidence
    ↓
next decision
    ↺

The VM is still an important part of the system.

Xbox is still the first real target.

But the project is no longer mainly about either one.

It is about keeping software alive after the AI finishes writing the first version.

AI builds. Xbox executes. XCP verifies.

Then the project continues.

Current public work

XCP Studio: xcpstudio.com

XCP Research: github.com/Daniele-Cangi/XCP-Research

XCP-Research currently contains the architecture description, the public XVM model, selected bounded Xbox evidence and offline verification tooling. The implementation remains private while the active research branches are consolidated and the open-source platform boundary is extracted cleanly.

Writing note: I used AI as an editorial assistant to help restructure and edit this article. The project, experiments, technical claims and final publication decisions are mine.

text:
"we should go out this weekend": I built a Discord member that holds the clock until we're outside

*This is a submission for the [Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week1-2026-10-05)*

> **TL;DR.** Group plans don't die from disagreement. They die because nobody holds the clock. **Quorum** is a member of your Discord channel that does. Tell it what limits you, type `/plan`, and Gemma 4 drafts real places nearby that fit everyone. A Temporal workflow then runs the poll, locks the plan, re-checks the rain at 05:30 and sends the 06:00 reminder, even if my laptop crashes or the agent server is asleep. Total bill: $0.

---

## What I Built

The problem Quorum solves is older than any of that. You know how it goes. Someone says "we should go out this weekend." Three people agree. Nobody picks a place, nobody closes the poll, and on Sunday nobody is outside.

The villain here is **the missing clock**. Not disagreement. Not apathy. There is just nobody whose job it is to say "the poll closes at 22:00, I'll check the weather at 05:30, see you at 06:00."

**So I made that somebody a bot.**

For each friend, the whole interaction is a few taps in the channel they already use:

1. **`/join`**, then one line per limit: `/me no car`, `/me home by 11`, `/me knee hates long descents`.
2. Someone types **`/plan date:2026-10-17 people:4`**. Quorum replies with 2-3 real places near home, each with the limits that shaped it.
3. A **vote menu**. You pick every option you can make. When enough people can make the same one, it locks. If 22:00 the night before comes first, Quorum says so, and nobody feels guilty.
4. At **05:30** it re-checks the rain for the exact hours you'll be out. At **06:00** it posts the reminder, or the rain-proof switch. When you're back, it asks for one line about how it went and remembers it for next time.

![Split panel on a dark pine background. Left, labelled BEFORE the group chat: three messages from Sara, Omar and Lina saying we should go out this weekend, yes we should, and so are we going on Friday at 23:40, then red text reading Sunday: nobody went. Right, labelled AFTER Quorum in the channel: two Discord bot messages, a Locked plan for Kachnar Park at 08:00 and a 06:00 Good morning reminder](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ArqamWaheed/quorum/main/docs/images/before-after.png)

*The whole product. The left side is every group chat. The right side is the job nobody wanted.*

---

## Demo

{% embed https://youtu.be/VRqerFYBRGc %}

The 30-second demo is also in the repo: [docs/quorum-demo.mp4](https://github.com/ArqamWaheed/quorum/blob/main/docs/quorum-demo.mp4).

**Try it without joining any chat:** [quorum-y649.onrender.com/try](https://quorum-y649.onrender.com/try). Type a few made-up people with their limits, a city and a date. You get the same options the bot would post. It runs on Render's free tier, so the first load can take about a minute while it wakes. That nap turns out to matter below. On the live service, one draft for Islamabad took 72 s: two tool calls, Lake View Park and F-5 Park, zero invented places.

This is what `/plan` posts in the channel. Every option names the limits it was built around:

![Discord message from the quorum app listing three options for Islamabad: Morning walk at Kachnar Park at 08:00 for 2 hours, Visit Childrens Park at 07:30 for 2.5 hours, and Short outing to CDA Park at 08:30 for 1.5 hours, each with a line reading Shaped by no car and home by 11, and a vote menu below](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ArqamWaheed/quorum/main/docs/images/discord-options.png)

*Shaped by your limits, not by a generic "top 10 parks" list.*

The poll locks the moment enough people can make one option. Then nothing happens for hours, on purpose, until the reminder:

![Discord message from the quorum app at 06:00 reading Good morning. Today: Morning stroll at Kachnar Park. Kachnar Park, start 08:00, about 2 hours. Rain chance during the outing: up to 12%](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ArqamWaheed/quorum/main/docs/images/discord-reminder.png)

*The 06:00 message. This is the one that actually gets people out of bed.*

> **What's real and what isn't**
> - Real: every message and every number in this post comes from runs against the live services (Gemma 4 on the Gemini API, MongoDB Atlas, Discord, Open-Meteo, OpenStreetMap), copied from the plan's own event log.
> - Not real yet: a group outing. The real plan is for Saturday 17 October, which is after the deadline. What you see is a full rehearsal with the timers compressed to minutes, plus three failure drills.
> - Not live after publishing: the Discord bot and the Temporal worker run on my laptop. The Render pages stay up.

---

## Code

{% embed https://github.com/ArqamWaheed/quorum %}

Apache-2.0. Interesting files:

* `src/temporal/workflows.ts`: the whole outing as one function. Poll, quorum, 05:30, 06:00, recap.
* `src/temporal/activities.ts`: calls to the agent server with retries, and every Discord message.
* `src/mastra/agents/quorum.ts` and `src/mastra/draft.ts`: the Gemma 4 agent, its tools, and the check that throws out any place the tools didn't return.
* `src/bot/discord.ts`: slash commands, plus votes turned into workflow signals.
* `scripts/test-workflow.ts`: the whole workflow against a local Temporal server with fake activities, timers in seconds. 9 checks.

The heart of it is a vote that can wait for days and survive restarts:

```ts
const reached = await wf.condition(
  () => tally(votes, options.length).count >= p.quorum, // enough people for one option…
  until(p.pollCloseAt),                                 // …or 22:00 the night before
);
```

```bash
npm install && cp .env.example .env        # Gemini key, Atlas URI, Discord token
./scripts/run-local.sh                     # Temporal dev server, UI on :8233
npm run worker & npm run bot & npm run dev
```

---

## How I Built It

**Four owners, one job each.** Temporal owns time. Mastra and Gemma 4 own reasoning. MongoDB Atlas owns memory. Render owns the public page. The laptop holds only the clock and the bot token.

![System flow diagram titled Four owners, one job each. Three boxes left to right: Discord channel (join, me no car, plan, vote menu), Laptop running Temporal, worker and bot (wait for quorum or the deadline, sleep until 05:30 then 06:00, retry the agent server 5 s with x2 backoff and 12 attempts), and Render free running a Mastra agent on Gemma 4 26B (weather tool, places tool, plan page). Yellow request arrows labelled slash commands and HTTPS 45 s timeout, a dashed result arrow labelled options and weather verdict, and a bar along the bottom for MongoDB Atlas M0](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ArqamWaheed/quorum/main/docs/images/system-flow.png)

*The split. A workflow can't judge a knee. An LLM can't sleep until 05:30.*

**Why a workflow, not cron or `setTimeout`.** The outing is one Temporal workflow. Votes arrive as signals. `condition()` waits for quorum or the deadline. Then `sleep()` waits until 05:30 and 06:00. The bot does all the time math and hands the workflow absolute timestamps, so the workflow itself stays deterministic. A `setTimeout` on a free host that sleeps every 15 minutes would die before Friday. Temporal persists the timers, so a restart just resumes them.

I didn't want to take that on faith, so I tried to break it.

![Plate titled Three ways I tried to break it, from the 11 October compressed test run. Three columns. Crash mid-poll: kill -9 the worker and restart the Temporal server, the plan came back in the voting step and locked. Agent server asleep: four red failed attempt boxes and a yellow fifth box, with log lines 15:55:14 attempt 1 failed, 15:55:50 attempt 4 failed, 15:56:56 attempt 5 ok, 25.9 s. Rain: with the rain limit forced to 0%, the 06:00 reminder switched to Visit Childrens Park](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ArqamWaheed/quorum/main/docs/images/drills.png)

*Durable by design, not by luck. Every step is a timer or a retry that Temporal persisted.*

**Crash.** Mid-poll, I ran `kill -9` on the worker, then stopped the Temporal server itself and started it again on the same database file. The workflow came back in `voting`. My vote landed. The plan locked.

**A sleeping server is a test, not a bug.** The agent runs on Render's free tier, which sleeps after 15 idle minutes and takes about a minute to wake. So the 05:30 weather check will usually hit a sleeping server. The activity has a 45-second fetch timeout and a retry policy (5 s, doubling, 12 attempts). To prove it, I stopped the agent server right before the check:

![Temporal Web UI, Pending Activities tab for the plan workflow: activity recheckWeather, state Scheduled, attempt 5 of 12 with 7 remaining, next retry in 38 seconds, and the last failure JSON showing fetch failed caused by connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:4111](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ArqamWaheed/quorum/main/docs/images/temporal-pending-activity.jpg)

*Attempt 5 of 12. Temporal kept knocking until the server answered.*

Temporal doesn't write every retry into the event history. It keeps the attempt count and the last failure. So the activity also logs every attempt to the plan's own record, and the public plan page shows it:

![Quorum plan page timeline titled Where it stands: yellow blazes for Options drafted, Poll open, Plan locked, then a red blaze for Weather re-check reading Rain up to 12%. Switched to the backup plan, with four red log lines of failed attempts and a fifth reading attempt 5 ok in 25873 ms, then Morning reminder, Recap asked and Remembered for next time](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ArqamWaheed/quorum/main/docs/images/plan-page-retries.png)

*Four failures and one success, in public. The retry log is a feature, not a debug screen.*

**The rule is code. The alternative is Gemma.** At 05:30 the forecast is checked by plain code against a rain limit. Only if it fails does Gemma get 20 seconds to pick or adapt a rain-proof alternative. If it can't, code takes the option with the least rain in its window. For the drill I forced the limit to 0%:

![Discord message from the quorum app reading Good morning. Rain is likely on the original plan, so we're switching to: Visit Childrens Park. Childrens Park, start 07:30](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ArqamWaheed/quorum/main/docs/images/discord-rain-switch.png)

*Plan B, posted at 06:00. Nobody had to call a group vote at dawn.*

**Mastra reasons, and only reasons.** The agent has two tools, `weather` (Open-Meteo) and `places` (OpenStreetMap), plus memory, and returns structured options. Its instructions forbid any place the tools didn't return. The code checks anyway: an option whose place isn't in the tool's list gets dropped, and if fewer than two survive, code builds them from real places. Across 16 smoke-test drafts it dropped **0** invented places.

**Gemma 4, measured rather than assumed.** Gemma 4 has built-in function calling, but Mastra's model catalogue doesn't mark the Gemma 4 IDs as tool-capable. So before trusting it, I ran the same planning prompt with a fake 5-person roster, 8 times per model:

| Model (same agent, Gemini API free tier) | valid plans with tool calls | invented places | median time | Gemini errors retried |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`gemma-4-26b-a4b-it`** | **8/8** | **0** | **128 s** | **0** |
| `gemma-4-31b-it` | 7/8 | 0 | 202 s | 4 |

26B runs Quorum. The 31B returned "Internal error encountered" on about half its calls at first, so transient Gemini errors are now retried inside the draft call, then again by Temporal. I also tried having code fetch the weather and places and handing them to Gemma in the prompt. It was not faster (120-193 s), so the time goes into generation, not tool round trips.

**Atlas remembers what a context window forgets.** Your limits live in a plain `members` collection, so they never depend on the model deciding to call a "remember" tool. Everything said to the agent, recaps included, also goes into Mastra memory on Atlas with semantic recall over **Atlas Vector Search** (3072-dimension Gemini embeddings). So next week's draft can read last week's recap before it proposes anything.

Two honest concessions.

**It's slow.** About 2 minutes per draft on the free tier. That's fine for a plan that waits until Friday night. It was not fine for my own test: the first compressed poll closed **53 seconds** after the options appeared, because drafting ate most of a 3-minute window. I gave test polls 7 minutes. Real polls stay open for days.

**OpenStreetMap's public Overpass servers were down all weekend.** Every mirror returned 504s or timed out. Places now fall back to Nominatim, the same OpenStreetMap data ranked by importance, and the results are cached in Atlas. Around Islamabad that still gives Margalla Hills National Park, Shakarparian and Rawal Lake Viewpoint. It also gives a few parks named after sector numbers, which is accurate and a little sad.

Things I refused to do:

* Do not let the bot read the chat. It connects with only the `Guilds` intent, no Message Content, so it sees slash commands and taps on its own buttons, nothing else.
* Do not store people who didn't `/join`. `/forget` deletes your limits and recaps.
* Do not let Gemma invent a place. If the name isn't from OpenStreetMap, it doesn't reach the poll.
* Do not edit the workflow during a live run. I froze `workflows.ts` with a git tag before starting the real plan, because Temporal replays history against the code.

---

## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A group chat holds things people wouldn't put in an app: whose knee is bad, who's broke this month, whose parents set a curfew. That shaped three choices.

**Open weights mean a local option exists.** The same agent switches to `gemma4:e4b` on Ollama with one environment variable. I haven't benchmarked it yet, so I won't claim a number, but the switch is in the code, and with it nothing leaves the laptop. A closed API offers no such switch.

**Honest trade-off.** The runs above used Gemma 4 through the Gemini API's free tier, which says content may be used to improve Google's products. `/help` says so before anyone joins, and the bot only ever sees what you deliberately send it.

**Open infrastructure all the way down.** Temporal's open-source server made a durable, multi-day workflow possible at $0 on a laptop. Mastra is Apache-2.0. The places come from OpenStreetMap and the forecasts from Open-Meteo. Total bill: **$0**.

---

## My Agent Session

I built Quorum with Claude Code, with the [Entire CLI](https://docs.entire.io) capturing every session and linking it to the commit it produced. Every checkpoint is browsable on the [`entire/checkpoints/v1` branch](https://github.com/ArqamWaheed/quorum/tree/entire/checkpoints/v1).

The one I'd point at is the fix for the 53-second poll:

> ● Checkpoint 199ef0496889
> commits 68e95ec fix: longer test-run poll window; drafting alone takes ~2 min on the free tier

Inspect it with `entire checkpoint explain 68e95ec` in a clone. The decision, why test polls are 7 minutes and not 3, now lives next to the code it explains.

---

## What I Learned

* **Durability is a product feature, not infrastructure.** The 06:00 reminder is the only message that gets people out of bed. If it depends on a laptop not sleeping, it isn't a feature.
* **Measure the model before you trust the catalogue.** The catalogue left Gemma 4's tool column blank. 8 out of 8 says otherwise for 26B.
* **The weakness belongs in the UI.** The plan page shows every failed attempt. A tool that hides its retries is a tool you can't trust at 05:30.

---

## Prize Categories

* **Best Use of Temporal:** the whole outing is one workflow (`planOuting`): vote signals, `condition()` with a quorum deadline, durable timers to 05:30 and 06:00, and activity retry policies. Survived `kill -9` of the worker plus a server restart mid-poll, and retried a dead agent server 4 times before attempt 5 succeeded.
* **Best Use of Mastra:** an `Agent` over Gemma 4 with `createTool` tools (weather, places), `Memory` with semantic recall, and structured options that name the limits that shaped them, with code that drops any place the tools didn't return. 0 invented places in 16 drafts.
* **Best Use of MongoDB Atlas:** Atlas M0 is the agent's long-term memory (Mastra `MongoDBStore`) and retrieval layer (Atlas Vector Search via `MongoDBVector`, 3072-d, index READY). It also stores members, plans with every retry attempt, polls, recaps and the places cache.
* **Best Use of Render:** the agent API, the plan pages and `/try` run on one free web service from one `render.yaml`, live at [quorum-y649.onrender.com](https://quorum-y649.onrender.com). Its 15-minute sleep is designed for: the 45-second timeout plus Temporal retries turn a cold start into a few logged attempts.
* **Best Use of Gemma:** `gemma-4-26b-a4b-it` plans every outing with native tool calls through Mastra. Measured against 31B: 8/8 vs 7/8 valid, 0 invented places each, 128 s vs 202 s median.
* **Best Use of Entire:** every agent-written commit has an Entire checkpoint, browsable on the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch, and quoted above to explain why the code is the way it is.

---

Quorum closes the poll at 22:00 the night before and reminds at 06:00. **If you've ever organised a group outing: where would you put the clock? The night before, or 48 hours out, so the people who can't make it say so early?**

text: I turned my GitHub contribution graph into a Metro train My GitHub contribution graph is a metro train now. {% embed https://github.com/vineetjk %} ![Commit Metro: one long Namma Metro train on an elevated viaduct at night, its driver's cab at the Commit Street platform](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vineetjk/vineetjk/master/docs/screenshots/metro/rest-dark.png) A few days ago I [listed my GitHub profile on the stock market](https://dev.to/vineetjk/i-ipod-my-github-profile-you-can-buy-shares-in-me-2mio). The stock, $VJK, gets its value from my commits, but the commits themselves were still only a number in a panel. I wanted the contribution graph on the profile too, drawn as something other than green squares. Bengaluru's Namma Metro runs on long elevated viaducts across the city, so the graph became a metro line. ## How the graph becomes a train GitHub's graph is 53 columns by 7 rows: a column for every week, a square for every day. Turn it on its side and it's a train. - Every coach is a week. There are 53 of them. - Every coach has seven windows, Sunday to Saturday. - A window lights up with that day's commits. No commits, it stays dark. A busy day, it glows bright gold. - The oldest week rides at the tail. This week's coach is right behind the driver's cab, and today's window pulses. My busiest repos hang on sign gantries over the line, each one above the coach of the week I committed to it the most. The line ends at Commit Street, the interchange where the green line carries $VJK, with a small LED board showing the live price. ## The ride The panel loops every 90 seconds: 1. It rests on today, with the driver's cab at the Commit Street platform. 2. It fades, goes back a year, and picks up the tail of the train. 3. The train runs along the viaduct while the camera moves along it a little faster, from the oldest coach toward the newest. 4. Under each repo gantry the train slows down and the camera zooms in. Between gantries it speeds up and the camera zooms out. 5. It brakes into Commit Street, and the loop starts again. Passing under a gantry: ![The train slowing down as March passes under the vfd-explorer gantry, then speeding up toward tripppyyy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vineetjk/vineetjk/master/docs/screenshots/metro/gantry.gif) Arriving at Commit Street: ![The head of the train pulling into the Commit Street platform, next to the green line train and the $VJK price board](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vineetjk/vineetjk/master/docs/screenshots/metro/arrival.gif) Zoomed out at full speed, months of coaches go by: ![The camera zoomed out at full speed, with coaches from March to September on screen](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vineetjk/vineetjk/master/docs/screenshots/metro/full-speed.png) It follows your GitHub theme, so light mode gets a daytime version: ![Commit Metro in light mode](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vineetjk/vineetjk/master/docs/screenshots/metro/rest-light.png) ## It took a few tries The first version gave every week its own 7-coach train, with a coach for each day. The camera panned along a row of them, and they didn't move. It looked like a camera driving past parked trains. So I fixed the camera and let the trains run through. That looked better, but now the stations had nowhere to go, because a station can't move along with a train. The next version moved both, and that idea stayed: the camera moves faster than the trains, so they run forward while it overtakes them. Then I put gaps between the trains, because 53 trains nose to tail looked like one endless train. ![An earlier version: separate 7-coach trains, one per week, running on the same track](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vineetjk/vineetjk/master/docs/screenshots/metro/first-version.png) And then the obvious question: why are 53 trains sharing one track? One long train fixed that, and it maps more directly onto the graph too, one coach per week. The last change was the stations. A 53-coach train stopping with a coach from March at the platform looks wrong, because a real train stops with the driver at the front of the platform. So repos became sign gantries over the line, the train only slows down under them, and the one real stop is Commit Street. ## How it works ### It's still just an SVG GitHub doesn't run JavaScript in a README. Like everything else on my profile, Commit Metro is an SVG loaded through an `` tag and animated with CSS. A Node script redraws it from my contribution data every time the profile's GitHub Actions workflow runs, so new commits show up on their own. ### Keeping each gantry above the right coach The train and the camera move at different speeds, so how does a gantry end up exactly above the right coach? It's built there. If week `u` is the coach in focus, the camera looks at `world(u)`, and the train has moved `world(u) - centre(u)`: ```js const centre = (u) => coachX(u) + COACH / 2; // coach u, in the train's own coordinates const world = (u) => STRETCH * centre(u) + W; // where the camera looks const runAt = (u) => world(u) - centre(u); // how far the train has moved along the line ``` With `STRETCH = 3` the camera covers three times the distance the train does. The gantry for week `i` stands at `world(i)`, so whenever the camera reaches it, coach `i` is right underneath. ### Speeding up and slowing down without a jolt Each stretch between gantries is two CSS `cubic-bezier` curves, one that speeds up and one that slows down: ```js const EASE = { speedUp: (from) => `cubic-bezier(.3,${0.3 * from},.7,${1 - 0.3 * PEAK})`, slowDown: (to) => `cubic-bezier(.3,${0.3 * PEAK},.7,${1 - 0.3 * to})`, }; ``` The slope at each end of a cubic-bezier is the speed at that end. So the two halves meet at the same top speed in the middle, and a stretch arrives at a gantry at the same slow speed the next one leaves with. Every stretch takes time in proportion to its length, so they all share one average speed. I sampled the motion to check it: under a gantry the train runs at 0.44 of its average speed, and it peaks at 1.62. The zoom is one more keyframe animation with the same percentages and the same curves, zoomed in at the gantries and out where the train is fastest. Because every animated layer shares that timing, the camera, the train and the zoom stay in step. ### A first frame that makes sense Some places that show a README never play the animation, like screenshots and some apps, and people with reduced motion turned on don't get it either. So the resting frame, with the train at Commit Street, is also the starting state. Anything that doesn't animate still shows today. ### The driver's cab The nose is one cubic Bézier curve from the roof down to the tip, extended back into depth for the top of the nose. The rear cab uses the same curve, flipped. The front one also has a small horn on the roof and two headlights whose beams fade out down the track. ![Close-up of the driver's cab: a bullet-train nose with a horn on the roof and two headlight beams, behind this week's coach](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vineetjk/vineetjk/master/docs/screenshots/metro/driver-cab.png) ### Where the gantries come from GitHub's GraphQL API returns commits per repo per day: ```graphql contributionsCollection { commitContributionsByRepository(maxRepositories: 25) { repository { name isPrivate } contributions(first: 100) { nodes { occurredAt commitCount } } } } ``` I group each repo's commits by week and keep my six busiest public repos. Private repos are left out, so their names never show up. If two repos have the same busiest week, they share one gantry and its board lists both. ## Try it Commit Metro is at the top of [my profile](https://github.com/vineetjk). The code lives in the same repo, mostly in [`scripts/lib/render/metro.js`](https://github.com/vineetjk/vineetjk/blob/master/scripts/lib/render/metro.js), if you want a train of your own. If your graph has a lot of empty windows, like mine does in August, that's what it looks like on a train too.

Chat with client In -> Invoice Out

*This is a submission for the [Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week2-2026-10-12)*

## What I Built

Every freelancer knows this moment.

The client says *"Great work, can you send the invoice?"* and suddenly you're digging through 200 WhatsApp messages to find the rate, the hours, the email address, and that one message where the price changed from $250 to $300.

Then you open a template, retype everything, export a PDF, and email it. Ten minutes gone, for something that's already written down in the chat.

**Chat2Invoice** fixes that. You paste the conversation, and a local AI turns it into a ready-to-send invoice PDF.

1. **Paste** your WhatsApp, Slack, iMessage, or email conversation (optionally attach a contract, a receipt, or a mockup).
2. **Review** what the AI found. Anything missing gets flagged, and everything is editable.
3. **Send** a clean A4 PDF. Download it or email it straight to the client.

**Who would pay for this?** Anyone who gets paid directly, outside platforms that auto-generate invoices: freelance designers, developers, writers, consultants, and small agencies who negotiate in DMs and then have to turn those DMs into paperwork.

The best part is that the chat never has to leave your machine.

## Demo

<!-- Add your deployed link or video here -->

**Step 1: Paste the chat**

![Chat2Invoice step 1](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/c8fqrbwtazhicti1rutz.png)



**Step 2: Review what the AI found**

The AI shows what it extracted and highlights anything it couldn't find. Here it caught one field was not found in chat.

![Chat2Invoice step 2](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/m54xsbtfklvrqkvn8syl.png)



**Step 3: Preview, download, send**

![Chat2Invoice step 3](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/8o3saj6mca9tavb6zrom.png)

> ## Struggling to learn Git?
> Learn Git by solving problems on [GitMission.com](https://www.gitmission.com/)
>
> [![GitMission preview](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/qdfho36qojkbd4041kme.png)](https://www.gitmission.com/)


## Code

{% embed https://github.com/0shuvo0/chat2invoice %}

## How I Built It

**The open-source AI part:** [Gemma 3](https://ai.google.dev/gemma) running locally through [Ollama](https://ollama.com). No API key, no per-request bill, no server in the middle. The app talks to Ollama on `127.0.0.1:11434`, and that's where the "understanding" happens.

**The stack:**

- **Next.js 14** (App Router) + **TypeScript** + **Tailwind CSS**
- **jsPDF** to generate the invoice PDF in the browser
- **pdfjs-dist** to read text out of attached PDF contracts, also in the browser
- **Inter** font bundled locally, so nothing is fetched from a CDN
- **Resend** for the optional "Send via Email" feature

**The flow:**

1. **Input.** Paste the chat or hit "Paste Clipboard". An optional "Advanced & Attachments" section lets you add notes that *override* the chat (like "Net 15, apply 10% holiday discount"), plus PDF/TXT files and images. Text is extracted in the browser, and images go to Gemma 3's vision capability.
2. **Review.** Missing required fields appear under **Action Needed**, and found ones are shown as editable fields. Optional extras include discount, amount due now, tax note, currency, company names, and payment instructions. The invoice ID (like `INV-2026-OCT-13-JD2N`) and issue date are auto-generated, and "Due Now" defaults to amount minus discount.
3. **Ready.** Preview the invoice, download the PDF, or send it to the client with an editable message.

I intentionally put a human checkpoint in the middle. The AI proposes, and *you* approve. A small local model will occasionally misread a message, and an invoice is a document with money on it, so the review step is a feature rather than a limitation. Missing details get flagged and asked for instead of invented.

**Running it yourself** takes a minute. Pull a model with Ollama, then create `.env.local`:

```dotenv
OLLAMA_AI_MODEL=gemma3:latest
OLLAMA_HOST=http://127.0.0.1:11434

# Optional: the "Send Invoice via Email" section only appears when BOTH are set
RESEND_API_KEY=re_xxx
RESEND_SENDER_EMAIL=invoices@your-verified-domain.com
```

`RESEND_SENDER_EMAIL` must be on a domain verified in your Resend account. Skip these two lines and the app simply hides the email section, so everything else works fully offline.

## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Client chats are some of the most sensitive text a freelancer owns. They contain real names, email addresses, rates, project details, and sometimes things covered by an NDA. Pasting that into a closed cloud API just to get a PDF is a bad trade.

Open-weight models changed the deal:

- **Privacy by architecture.** The chat is processed by Gemma on your own machine. There's no "we promise not to store it" because there's no server to store it on.
- **Costs nothing to run.** No tokens, no subscription, no usage cap. A tool for a side hustle shouldn't eat into the side hustle's income.
- **Works offline.** Text extraction, AI, and PDF generation all happen locally. Only the optional email step needs internet.
- **No lock-in.** The model is one environment variable (`OLLAMA_AI_MODEL`). If a better open model shows up next month, swapping it in is a one-line change, with no pricing changes or deprecations to worry about.

A closed API could do the extraction, but it couldn't make the promise that matters most to the person using this tool: *your client's conversation never left your laptop.*


## My First User
My friend who is in final year in college and he is super busy trying to manage study and freelance work at the same time. So this will save him a few hours monthly.

## Prize Categories

- **Best Use of Gemma**: Gemma 3 runs locally via Ollama and handles both text extraction and image understanding for receipts and mockups.

My plugin passed every check. It still didn't work.

We built a WordPress plugin. The idea was simple: you publish a post on your blog, and a couple of minutes later an announcement goes out to your social networks automatically. Headline, image, link. About two thousand lines of code. A small project, I thought.

I should probably mention that I don't write the code myself. Claude does. My contribution is asking questions, testing things and occasionally refusing to accept an answer because something about it bothers me. This turned out to be one of those occasions.

Before submitting, we went through all the checks. `phpcs` against the [WordPress coding standards](https://github.com/WordPress/WordPress-Coding-Standards): zero errors, zero warnings. The official [Plugin Check](https://wordpress.org/plugins/plugin-check/): clean. WordPress directory review: approved. The plugin was published, and I was quite pleased with us.

Then I installed it on an actual WordPress site. It didn't work.

### The green checkmarks were checking the wrong thing

Here's the embarrassing part: before submitting, we'd never actually run the plugin in WordPress. We'd tried, but our local environment wouldn't start. WP-CLI kept crashing with the latest PHP version, and instead of sorting that out, we carried on with static checks.

The WordPress directory review checks whether a plugin follows the rules and meets security requirements. It doesn't mean somebody has tested whether your particular publishing workflow works. I understood this perfectly well in theory. In practice, I saw all those green checkmarks and decided we were finished.

Eventually, we got the plugin running in [WordPress Playground](https://wordpress.org/playground/), which runs WordPress through WebAssembly without needing a traditional local server. It took one command to start. On the first proper test, we found two bugs.

### Bug one: the Connect button led nowhere

You click Connect, expecting to reach the Publora sign-in page, and WordPress sends you straight back to the admin dashboard. No error, no warning. You're just back where you started.

The problem was [`wp_safe_redirect()`](https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/functions/wp_safe_redirect/). We'd used it because, well, it has *safe* in the name. Unfortunately, it also restricts redirects to approved hosts. Our sign-in page lives on another domain, so WordPress replaced the destination with the admin URL.

The function was doing exactly what it was supposed to do. We were the ones asking it to do the wrong thing.

The fix was to allow the Publora authentication host for that particular redirect:

```php
add_filter('allowed_redirect_hosts', [$this, 'allow_auth_host']);
wp_safe_redirect($url, 302, 'Publora');
```

Nothing here looked suspicious to the static analyzer. The code was valid, the redirect was safe, and the Connect button was completely useless.

### Bug two: the editor kept losing the image

The second problem was harder to spot. When publishing from Gutenberg, the social announcement sometimes went out without the featured image. It also ignored the post settings: whether to share the post at all, which networks to use, and so on.

We'd attached publishing to the `transition_post_status` hook. When a post changes to `publish`, send the announcement. That seemed reasonable.

Except Gutenberg doesn't necessarily save everything in one request. The post status can change before the featured image and some settings have finished saving. The old metabox can send its data separately too. Our hook fired, we read whatever was available at that moment, and sent it off to social. Which, often enough, was nothing.

The plugin wasn't losing the image. We were asking for it before it had arrived.

We moved the publishing logic to [`wp_after_insert_post`](https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/hooks/wp_after_insert_post/), where we could work with the saved post data, and added a check to avoid sending an announcement when an already-published post was updated:

```php
if ($post_before instanceof WP_Post && 'publish' === $post_before->post_status) return;
```

Neither bug had anything to do with syntax or coding standards. We needed to see how WordPress actually behaved: where it redirected users, when Gutenberg saved its data, and which hooks fired along the way.

### And now, how we dug them up in the first place

This is probably my favourite part of the story, although I wasn't enjoying it quite so much at the time.

When we discovered the plugin wasn't working, Claude suggested contacting WordPress directory support. They know the platform, they could help us investigate, and we'd already passed review. A reasonable suggestion.

I didn't want to do that yet.

Partly because I hate waiting for support replies, and partly because we hadn't even managed to run the thing properly ourselves. It seemed a little early to ask somebody else why it was broken.

So I asked Claude to go back through the documentation and help me set up a working test environment. We opened Playground and started trying things. Publish with an image. Publish without one. Disable sharing. Select Mastodon only. Try the classic editor. Watch what happens, check the logs, change something and try again.

By the end of the evening, we'd found both bugs and fixed them. No support tickets, no waiting for somebody to investigate. Just us, WordPress and a rather overdue first proper test.

I still can't read PHP nearly as well as Claude. When it shows me a function, I often need an explanation of what I'm looking at. But I can tell when we're trying to get around a problem instead of understanding it. And sometimes I can be sufficiently stubborn about that to make us investigate.

This was one of those times. Claude did the technical work, and I contributed a firm refusal to send an email. An unexpectedly useful division of labour.

### What I took from it

I knew static checks weren't the same as testing a working plugin. I really did. I just apparently needed to publish one before remembering.

The other thing that stayed with me was how close we came to asking support for help with two bugs we hadn't even tried to reproduce properly. There are plenty of problems where support is exactly what you need. This wasn't one of them.

And I'm glad I pushed back on Claude's suggestion. Not because Claude was wrong to offer it, but because I would have learned very little from sending that email and waiting for somebody else to find the problem.

If you're building a WordPress plugin, I'd recommend running it in Playground before submitting it. We spent longer getting our broken local environment to cooperate than it took to find both bugs once WordPress was actually running.

The plugin passed review. The Connect button still sent me back to the dashboard. I think I'll remember that particular combination for a while.

---

Anyone else had something pass every check and then fail the first time you actually used it?

text:
What If Bureaucracy Was a 16-Bit Boss Fight?

What if renewing a passport was a JRPG quest?

Not metaphorically.

I mean **six signatures, absurd procedures, arcade confrontations, collapsing institutions, political caricatures, and one exhausted citizen trying to get a document stamped**.

That became **Civic Nightmare**.

It is a small open-source browser RPG built in **Godot 4.6**, and you can play it right now.

🎮 **Play in browser:**  
https://daniele-cangi.github.io/civic-nightmare/

🕹️ **itch.io:**  
https://unityloop.itch.io/civic-nightmare

💻 **Source:**  
https://github.com/Daniele-Cangi/civic-nightmare

---

## The whole game started with one stupidly simple problem

You need to renew your passport.

That should be easy.

Instead, you are sent through a surreal administrative world where every signature belongs to another machine of power, another procedure, another interpretation of reality.

The result is part JRPG, part arcade game, part political satire, and part bureaucratic nightmare.

![Civic Nightmare gameplay inside Donald Trump’s Oval Studio encounter room](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/t4jt3gu5q9p74wwlhjrw.png)

You play as an ordinary citizen.

Not a president.

Not a billionaire.

Not a chosen hero.

Just somebody who needs a passport.

Unfortunately, the paperwork has other plans.

## Six signatures. Six different kinds of nonsense.

The main quest sends you across a hand-built overworld to collect six signatures.

Each authority has its own environment, personality and procedure.

Some encounters became actual minigames.

One turns negotiation into a strange blackjack match.

Another turns 27 approvals into a physical consensus machine.

One makes you stabilize inflation with something resembling monetary-policy pinball.

Another turns a “three-minute special operation” into an intentionally forgiving pseudo-3D administrative corridor.

![Civic Nightmare gameplay during the Three-Minute Special Operation encounter](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/k5cqrtyh03625q272i3x.png)

The joke is not only in the dialogue.

I wanted the **architecture itself** to tell you something before anybody speaks.

Rooms, machines, monuments, queues, checkpoints and interfaces are part of the satire.

The bureaucracy is the level design.

---

## It gets stranger from there

Civic Nightmare also contains optional areas that have almost nothing to do with obtaining the passport.

Which is probably why they belong in the game.

There is a quantum UFO.

A classified bunker.

An unstable AI demonstration.

A cybernetic fulfillment cathedral.

A Red Phone.

And several situations where the official explanation of what is happening becomes less reliable than what is physically happening on screen.

![Civic Nightmare arcade battle against cybernetic Jeff Bezos in the Fulfillment Cathedral](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/ha3mfh3nlo5ysubltluv.png)

I deliberately wanted the world to feel as if several genres had been forced into the same administrative form.

The result is something I started calling **civic surrealism**.

---

## The browser version is the real game

This is not a stripped-down demo page.

The current build runs directly in the browser.

It includes:

- the overworld,
- signature encounters,
- minigames,
- optional investigations,
- persistent progress,
- a versioned local dossier,
- contextual touch controls,
- the final determination,
- and the CRT/VHS presentation layer.

Progress is stored locally in the browser, so you can leave and come back.

The game also runs on desktop through Godot.

> **Play it here:**  
> https://daniele-cangi.github.io/civic-nightmare/

---

## Why I made it open source

Civic Nightmare was always more interesting to me as a complete experiment than as a commercial game.

It is small, strange and finished enough to have an identity.

But there is a lot of room for other people to push it somewhere I would not.

So the source is public.

And this is the part I would really like to expand now:

> **I want other people to add to the nightmare.**

Contributions can be technical, visual or completely absurd.

### Things that would be genuinely useful

- new minigames,
- new optional encounters,
- dialogue,
- translations,
- pixel art,
- accessibility improvements,
- browser compatibility,
- touch controls,
- sound,
- bug fixes,
- tests,
- tooling,
- strange administrative procedures I did not think of.

You do **not** need to understand the entire project before contributing.

There are already scoped areas where somebody can work without touching the whole game.

The repository includes a contribution guide and architecture documentation.

👉 **Contribute here:**  
https://github.com/Daniele-Cangi/civic-nightmare

The bureaucracy is accepting applications.

---

## A few things I learned while building it

The biggest one was that satire works better when it becomes **mechanics** instead of just dialogue.

It is easy to make an NPC say something absurd.

It is much more interesting when the player has to physically participate in the absurdity.

A consensus process becomes a machine.

Economic stability becomes pinball.

A political claim becomes a scoring rule.

Administrative delay becomes level structure.

That was the point where Civic Nightmare stopped feeling like a collection of jokes and started feeling like a game.

Another lesson was that a small game benefits enormously from being visually opinionated.

The project mixes:

- pixel-scale characters,
- large authored environments,
- CRT presentation,
- arcade encounters,
- exaggerated civic architecture.

It is not trying to look neutral.

That helped a lot.

{% details Click to see how the game is structured %}

Civic Nightmare is built in **Godot 4.6**.

The main composition root coordinates the overworld and larger story transitions, while focused modules handle things such as:

- dialogue,
- quest progression,
- behavioural evidence,
- save data,
- room transitions,
- touch input,
- encounters,
- authored presentation sequences.

The game also separates runtime assets from editable source material and keeps contribution boundaries documented.

The browser build uses Godot Web export and keeps persistence in browser-backed local storage.

The repository includes headless smoke tests covering major game flow, save/restore, signature progression, touch state and scene transitions.

{% enddetails %}

{% details Click to see some of the stranger systems inside it %}

A few examples:

### The Greatest Deal

A readable blackjack-like game runs first.

Then a separate official result decides who gets the point.

The arithmetic and the declaration are intentionally different systems.

### The Consensus Engine

Twenty-seven approvals become a physical machine of scanners, stamps, translations, documents and exceptions.

### The 2% Miracle

The player physically stabilizes an inflation indicator through a pinball-like system.

### The Observation Problem

Inside the UFO, the player has to deal with temporal echoes and several incompatible observations of the same citizen.

### Administrative Hold

The pause system itself is diegetic.

What it shows changes depending on what has happened in the case.

{% enddetails %}

---

## The game is already finding its way into open-source lists

Civic Nightmare is currently listed in:

- **OpenSourceVideoGames**
- **OpenSourceGames**
- **Up for Grabs**

That last one matters to me because I do not want the repository to be merely visible.

I want it to be **workable by other people**.

If someone adds a translation, improves a scene, builds a new minigame or finds a spectacular way to break the bureaucracy, that is exactly what I want the project to become.

---

## Play it before reading the source

Seriously.

The code makes more sense after you understand the tone.

🎮 **Browser:**  
https://daniele-cangi.github.io/civic-nightmare/

💻 **GitHub:**  
https://github.com/Daniele-Cangi/civic-nightmare

Source code is released under the **MIT License**.

Media and narrative assets have their own rights boundary documented in the repository.

If you want to contribute, start with `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

If you just want to play it, that is also perfectly valid.

After all, somebody still has to get the passport signed.

> **Your passport is valid. Your interpretation remains under review.**

text:
I shipped a linter for checks that cannot fail. It had four of them.

> **Where this landed, 9 October 2026.** This post opens with 40%. That number is not
> wrong so much as it is not the quantity you would take it for, and I only found that out
> by being argued with in the comments. It has taken a week of measuring to say what it
> should have been, and the tool has changed more than the number has. This block replaces
> the two corrections that were stacked here, because three corrections in a row is not
> honesty, it is sediment.
>
> **The sampling was measuring the wrong unit.** The samples behind every figure were
> stratified with a cap of two findings per repository, to stop one repo dominating. But
> the tool emits one finding per (job, upstream) pair, and the false positives cluster in
> jobs with many dependencies: one reporting job produced eleven by itself. The cap deletes
> exactly that clustering. Simulated against a population I later labelled completely, the
> capped sampler is an **unbiased estimator of the per-job rate and runs about 16 points
> low for the per-finding rate**. So every percentage in this post understates, all in the
> same direction. [@arhancanli](https://dev.to/arhancanli) called this in the thread before
> I measured it.
>
> **What the numbers are now, all hand-labelled, no estimate of an estimate.** Four
> detectors are two. D4 went on 0 defensible of 18 sampled, D2 on 0 true of 27 **censused**.
> Corpus output went 1986 findings to 1026.
>
> | | basis | false |
> |---|---|---|
> | D3, all 653 | complete census, every finding read | **36.1%** `[32.5, 39.9]` |
> | D1 | gated on `--repo`, and **0** findings with it | see below |
>
> **The severity tiers are gone, and that is the result I did not expect.** Censusing all
> three strata gave HIGH 30.9%, LOW 31.6%, MEDIUM 52.8%. HIGH's interval overlaps the
> merged rest. The only real separation is MEDIUM being *worse*, and it came from the
> severity function short-circuiting on whether the workflow runs on `pull_request` before
> it looked at the finding at all. **The axis measured the trigger, not correctness.** It
> hid the better findings behind `--all` and shouted the worse ones, so collapsing it
> raised the default output from 238 findings to 653 and *lowered* the false rate a reader
> sees, from 44.1% to 36.1%.
>
> **D1 is gated rather than removed, and the gate reports nothing.** Its text says a
> skipped upstream leaves the dependent running without it; [GitHub documents that the
> dependent is skipped too](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#jobsjob_idneeds).
> 68% of its findings are that case. So it now says nothing
> unless `--repo` confirms the job is a required check. Then I ran that against live branch
> protection for all 373 findings: 10 resolved to REQUIRED, all in one repository, and all
> 10 vanish on a complete checkout where the tool can read the script that job calls. **On
> 275 repositories, `--repo` has never reported a finding.** It is kept because the gate is
> correct, not because it is productive, and that distinction is the whole post in one line.
>
> **Three numbers I published and had to take back,** every one caught by checking my own
> claim rather than by anyone complaining. The "65% false" I quoted for D1 came from a
> census covering 12% of the population it was quoted against. The "37.0%, 245 of 662" in
> my own 0.3.0 release notes added a stratum censused at **153** to a population taken
> after a suppression had already removed 9 of them; every commit since emits 653. And the
> **54.9%** in the table that used to sit right here kept 3 findings labelled true from a
> sample taken *before* the insight that refutes them, which is holding both positions at
> once: I shipped a suppression on the grounds that `cmd | grep -q X` is not a defect
> while still counting three of those lines as defects. The arithmetic carries its own
> check, and I had not run it. The census was 68 true and 85 false of 153, so removing 9
> false findings has to leave true at 68, and 68 + 76 = 144. A correction is a new claim
> and needs verifying as hard as the original.
>
> The part of this post I would still defend is the part about taste: the corpus average
> hid the problem, and pointing the tool at two repositories I respected is what found it.
> The part I would not defend is any specific percentage in it. The working is in the
> comment thread, including the fixes measurement killed before they shipped. The latest
> was a filter that genuinely improved precision, 31% false down to 17%, and I deleted it
> anyway: it bought those 14 points by discarding two thirds of the **true** findings, and
> on that population it turned out to be a shape classifier wearing a semantic test.

Yesterday I published a tool called deadgate to PyPI. It reads GitHub Actions workflows and finds checks that cannot fail: a required gate satisfied by a skipped job, an exit status swallowed by a pipe, a fan-in job that never reads whether its upstream passed.

Then I pointed it at [Arize-ai/openinference](https://github.com/Arize-ai/openinference), 1.2k stars, 22 workflows. It reported 13 HIGH findings.

Twelve of them were false.

Not borderline. Not "technically true but low impact." Their CI was correct and my tool could not see it. The version doing the reporting had been on PyPI for about an hour.

## What it could not see

GitHub's documented way to ask "did anything upstream fail" is the wildcard form:

```yaml
if: always()
run: |
  if [[ "${{ contains(needs.*.result, 'failure') }}" == "true" ]]; then exit 1; fi
```

My detector tested for that with `needs\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]+\.(result|outputs)`, which cannot match `*`. So the one spelling the documentation recommends was the one spelling the tool was blind to, and every correctly written fan-in gate came back as a gate that cannot fail.

The finding's own message read "never reads needs.\*.result" while failing to match that exact string.

I fixed it, shipped 0.1.1, and pointed the fixed version at [astral-sh/ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff). Twenty-one HIGH findings. Eighteen false. Ruff writes its gate a third way:

```yaml
env:
  NEEDS_JSON: ${{ toJSON(needs) }}
run: |
  failing=$(echo "$NEEDS_JSON" | jq -r 'to_entries[]
    | select(.value.result != "success" and .value.result != "skipped")')
```

That reads every upstream at once and the word `result` never appears in any workflow expression. There is nothing for my pattern to match.

The fourth one was not a spelling at all. scikit-learn has a job that calls a reusable workflow, so it has `uses:` and no `steps:`, and it passes `needs.check-sdist.result` through job-level `with:`. That expression was one I already understood perfectly. It just lived somewhere I was not looking, because I scanned step-level `with` and not job-level `with`.

Four classes. The first two shipped to PyPI. I found the third and fourth only because I kept pointing the "fixed" version at new repositories instead of declaring victory.

## The part I think is actually generalizable

Here is the number that matters, measured on a 275 repository, 4543 file corpus with both versions reading identical bytes:

| version | findings | HIGH |
| --- | --- | --- |
| before | 4562 | 1104 |
| after | 2917 | 658 |

Forty percent of HIGH findings were false. That sounds bad, and it undersells it, because 40% is an average and the errors were not spread evenly.

Only 15 of those 275 repositories use the wildcard idiom at all. The false positives piled onto the repositories that write their gates carefully. On openinference the false rate was 92%. On ruff, 86%. On a repository with no fan-in gate at all, it was zero, because there was nothing to misread.

**My linter was least accurate on the best code.**

If a tool is noisy on bad code, the noise and the signal arrive together and you read both. If it is noisy specifically on good code, the people who did the work correctly are the ones punished, and the obvious response is to stop running it. A corpus average cannot surface that, because the corpus is mostly ordinary repositories where the tool happens to be right.

I had the corpus. I ran it. It said 40%, and I would have shipped that as the headline. What actually found this was pointing the tool at two repositories whose CI I respected.

## The mutation that survived

To stop reporting jobs whose failure a gate already catches, I walked the needs graph transitively: if a gate covers `ci`, and `ci` needs `changes`, then `changes` is covered too.

I mutation tested the fix, which for me means planting the defect each test claims to catch and checking that something goes red. One mutation survived: the one that **deleted** my transitive walk.

My first instinct was a missing test. It was not. The mutation survived because the walk was wrong: `needs.*.result` reports only direct needs, and a failed grandparent makes the parent *skip*, and skipped is not failure, so the gate never sees it. Walking transitively would have suppressed real findings.

A surviving mutant has two meanings and they are easy to confuse. Either a test is missing, or the code does nothing. If I had written a test to kill it, I would have pinned a bug in place and called it coverage.

## The small one that is somehow the worst

While fixing all this I noticed five of my repositories advertised a stale test count in the README. I corrected them by hand and added a CI check so they could not drift again.

The check went red immediately. On a count I had just "corrected."

I had changed agent-graph's README from 42 to 58 and written a public commit message saying the previous commit overstated the count at 67. CI collects 67. My local venv was missing an optional extra, and `tests/test_rag.py` opens with `pytest.importorskip`, so nine tests vanished at collection with no error, no warning, and no mention of the file. pytest said "58 tests collected" and meant it.

The original number was right. I corrected a correct claim, publicly, using a measurement from an environment that was not the real one.

The check I shipped an hour earlier had the same blind spot and agreed with 58. It now fails when any test file on disk contributes zero collected tests, because that is the only evidence an environment is incomplete.

## What I am not showing

The sweeps above are driven by my own harness, and the agent scaffolding, gate implementations and prompts behind it are not in the repository and are not going in it. deadgate itself is small and MIT and you can read all of it. The thing that pointed it at 275 repositories and classified the survivors is the part I am keeping.

## The question I actually have

I do not know how to test a linter for this class of error without a sample of good code, and "good code" is not a property I can detect automatically. A corpus gives you volume and volume gives you the average, which is exactly the statistic that hid this.

The only thing that worked was taste: picking two repositories I already believed were well engineered and reading the output by hand. That does not scale and it is not reproducible, and I would like to be talked out of it.

If you maintain a static analysis tool, how do you measure your false positive rate on the code that is *already correct*? I would rather hear that I am missing something obvious than keep doing it by hand.

deadgate is at [pypi.org/project/deadgate](https://pypi.org/project/deadgate/) and [github.com/egnaro9/deadgate](https://github.com/egnaro9/deadgate), MIT, no model in the loop.

I work on AI evaluation and testing, open to relocation above $120K, portfolio at [erikhill.dev](https://erikhill.dev).
