WhyRep is now officially out! The workout logger that also analyzes your training.

---
title: "WhyRep is now officially out! The workout logger that also analyzes your training."
published: true
tags: showdev, android, fitness, productivity
cover_image: https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/hcc26gcxzzb44r3pm8js.png
---

> **TL;DR.** WhyRep is out on Google Play. It logs your workouts like any gym tracker, then reads them back to you: every lift gets a verdict (progressed, flat, or went back), every plateau gets a fix, and every verdict shows the reason behind it. Free, offline, no account needed. [Get it on Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.whyrep.app).

---

## The question your gym log can't answer

Every workout tracker I've tried has the same limitation: it records what you did, but it doesn't tell you what's going wrong.

You log the sets. You log the reps. Three months later you scroll back through a perfect record of training and still can't answer the only question that matters.

**Is any of this working?**

That's the question behind most program-hopping. You train hard for a few months, nothing visibly changes, and you can't tell if it's a real wall or a program that stopped working. So you switch. Then you switch again. A lifter on the StrongFirst forum summed it up: *"I am also going through too many programs, never really reaping all the benefits."*

The apps that do try to coach you mostly hand you a number and ask you to trust it. Lifters have noticed. One FitnessAI reviewer: *"There's no 'AI' involved here. That's purely marketing."*

**So I built a tracker that has to show its work.**

---

## What WhyRep does

**Every workout gets a verdict.** Finish a session and WhyRep checks each lift against your own history: progressed, flat, or went back. The summary at the top tells you how many lifts need attention, and the rest stay quiet.

**A plateau is measured, not guessed.** How many flat sessions count as a real plateau depends on your experience level. A beginner who stalls twice on squats is stuck. A lifter with years behind them on a slow-moving curl isn't, and WhyRep doesn't pretend they are.

**Stuck? You get the fix.** When a lift stalls, WhyRep suggests the first thing to change, like a new rep range or spreading a muscle's sets across more days. Accept it or turn it off. Nothing changes your program behind your back.

![Two WhyRep store screenshots side by side. Left: the session summary reading "2 lifts need attention, 6 checked against your own history" with an Overhead Press card marked Regression. Right: a plateaued Cable Chest Fly with a suggested fix "Train lower chest more often" and a next fix "Aim for 4 to 8 reps"](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/cd9gcpf0ps21ss3edzn9.png)

*Left, the verdict. Right, the fix. Both open to the reason behind them with one tap on "Show the why".*

**It checks your life before your program.** Sleeping badly for a while, or training without the carbs or pre-workout you usually take, can hold a lift back on its own. So WhyRep asks first. If that's the likely reason, it tells you to sort that out and leaves your program alone.

**Then the logger walks you through the fix.** Accept a fix and your next workout shows you what to do on that lift, in plain steps, and how many sessions are left on it.

![Two screens from the WhyRep app. Left: a "Before changing your program" check asking about bad sleep and skipped carbs or pre-workout, ending in "Fix this first: get your sleep back on track". Right: fix guides in the workout logger, "Aim for 4 to 8 reps" and "Take every set to failure", each with three plain-language steps](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/7zqjmw6c2zzcgbtht6uz.png)

*Sleep and food get asked about first. Only then does it touch your sets.*

---

## And it's a fast gym log first

None of that matters if logging is slow, so the logger is built for speed.

- **A keypad built for the gym floor.** Weight, reps and RIR (reps in reserve) in a few taps
- **Last session's numbers next to every set**, so you know what to beat
- **A rest timer under every set**, started when you tick the set above it
- **Progression charts** for every exercise, by weight and by effective reps (reps plus reps in reserve), so a rep at the same effort shows up as progress

![Two WhyRep store screenshots. Left: the workout logger with a Bench Press set table showing last session's "80 kg × 9 @2" beside each set and an RIR badge on every reps field. Right: Bench Press progression charts for effective reps climbing from 7 to 11 and weight holding at 80 kg](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/vcwysgywejnln2lq6inu.png)

*Same 80 kg for seven weeks, and the effective reps chart still shows the climb. A weight-only chart would be a flat line.*

- **Weekly volume per muscle on a body map**, so the muscle you keep skipping is obvious
- **Routines and splits.** Save any workout as a routine, build Push Pull Legs or Upper Lower or your own, and WhyRep tells you what today's session is
- **Share a routine with a link.** No account needed on either end

![WhyRep store screenshot "See which muscles you're missing": front and back body figures with each muscle coloured by weekly sets, a legend from "Not trained" to "14 and up", and a list of muscles with their sets per week](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/cypdzhtmd3pc37c1xqq3.png)

*The gap shows up here before it shows up as a plateau.*

- **847 exercises, every one with a picture**, an equipment filter, and your own custom ones
- **Single-side logging**, left and right separately, for lifts like split squats
- **Works offline, no account needed.** On a plane or in a basement gym, it still works. A lifter who never signs in has no server copy of their training data. Sign in and your history backs itself up, so a new phone picks up where the old one stopped

![Two WhyRep store screenshots. Left: "847 exercises, all with pictures", a grid of illustrated lifts including Bench Press, Squat, Deadlift and Pull Up. Right: "No signal at the gym? It still works" with the WhyRep mascot sitting on a stack of weight plates](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/tmcxyrnh3d52c0hvcglk.png)

*Every exercise has a picture, and none of it needs a signal.*

---

## Why you can trust the verdicts

This is the one technical bit, and it's the reason the app exists.

The part that judges your training isn't AI, and it isn't me guessing. Every rule comes from a written methodology, one document per coaching system, each ending in a table of exact test cases: this training history in, this verdict out. The app is tested against those cases.

So a verdict like "5 in a row counts as a plateau at your level" isn't a vibe. It's a rule you can read, and you can disagree with it.

**The verdicts come from written rules, not from a model's guess.**

---

## Free and Plus

**Free:** the full gym log, all 847 exercises, rest timers, 3 months of charts, 5 routines, and a badge that tells you when a session has something to fix.

**Plus:** the reasoning behind every verdict, plateau fixes, weekly volume per muscle, your experience tier, unlimited routines, and a full year of charts.

Free always tells you when a session has a problem. Plus shows the verdict on every lift, explains why, and gives you the fix.

Plus is $35 a year or $3 a week, with a 3-day free trial (US prices; Play shows yours in your currency). The yearly plan works out to about 67 cents a week.

---

## What it doesn't do yet

I'd rather say this now than read it in a review.

**No nutrition tracking, no form checking from video, and no body fat scoring.** I could have shipped all three as guesses. None of them has a written method behind it yet, and a feature that guesses about your body is worse than one that says "not covered yet."

**No iPhone app yet.** It runs on the same core as the Android app and it's next.

**Coach chat is built but not switched on yet.** When it arrives, it starts from the same written rules the verdicts use.

---

## Try it

If you lift and you've ever wondered whether the last three months did anything, this is the app I built for that.

[**Get WhyRep on Google Play**](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.whyrep.app)

More at [whyrep.com](https://whyrep.com).

Log the same lift twice and WhyRep starts judging it. The 3-day trial shows you every verdict and the reason behind it. Then tell me the first one you disagreed with. That's the most useful feedback I can get, because it means either the rule is wrong or the explanation is.

ReptClip: A VS Code Extension to Paste Your Project into Free Chatbots and Apply the Diffs in One Click

> ⚠️ **NOTE**
> 
> *You are reading a post about an older version of ReptClip. Please [check out the repository](https://github.com/effessdev/reptclip-vscode) for the latest information.*

Let me show exactly how it works with an example 🛻

The extension adds a new "ReptClip" tab in the VS Code bottom panel:

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/4gpntaycuhxwlmlr3mgb.png)

I am going to use this extension to redesign my website's landing page. First, we need to prepare the context.

Specify which files to add to the context in the "Files to include" input. You can use glob patterns like `**/*.ts`.

Since I want to update the landing page, let's add `page.tsx`. You will get suggestions as you type:

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/klcn4f6eb3buyd2wuhqo.png)

Click "Enter" or "Tab" to accept the suggestion:

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/85zvttz5pwkwe2r1nvib.png)

If it matches any files, it will turn green. Otherwise, it will turn yellow.

Let's add `AGENTS.md` too:

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/fqmadc2r5utccxjtql65.png)

This order is preserved in the context output. `page.tsx` will appear after `AGENTS.md`.

Now, click "Enter" again. The context will be copied **directly to your clipboard**. It  looks something like this:

`````markdown
# Project structure

```
.gitattributes
.gitignore
AGENTS.md
CONTRIBUTING.md
LICENSE
README.md
pipxclip-config.toml
pyproject.toml
src/pipxclip/__init__.py
src/pipxclip/cli.py
src/pipxclip/config.py
tests/test_cli.py
tests/test_config.py
```

# Output format

Provide all file modifications as Search/Replace blocks inside a single 4-backtick code block.

## Formatting Rules

1. **File Headers:** Every set of edits must begin with the exact relative file path on its own line (e.g., `path/to/file.ext`), even if there is only a single file in the project.
2. **Exact Matching:** The `SEARCH` block must contain an *exact, verbatim* copy of existing code, including identical whitespace, indentation, and surrounding context lines to uniquely identify the match.
3. **Uniqueness:** Provide sufficient surrounding unchanged lines in the `SEARCH` block to ensure it matches exactly **one** location in the target file.
4. **New Files & Deletions:**
   - To create a new file, use an empty `SEARCH` block.
   - To delete a file or a code block, use an empty `REPLACE` block.
5. **No Placeholders:** Do not use ellipses (`...`), comments like `# rest of code unchanged`, or omitted lines inside `SEARCH` or `REPLACE` blocks.
6. **Sequential Edits:** If editing multiple parts of the same file, list the `SEARCH/REPLACE` blocks in top-to-bottom order as they appear in the file.

## Example

````
src/models/user.py
<<<<<<< SEARCH
class User:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def to_dict(self):
        return {"name": self.name}
=======
class User:
    def __init__(self, name, email):
        self.name = name
        self.email = email

    def to_dict(self):
        return {
            "name": self.name,
            "email": self.email,
        }
>>>>>>> REPLACE

src/controllers/user_controller.py
<<<<<<< SEARCH
from src.models.user import User
=======
from src.models.user import User
from src.utils.validator import validate_email
>>>>>>> REPLACE
<<<<<<< SEARCH
def create_user(name):
    return User(name)
=======
def create_user(name, email):
    validate_email(email)
    return User(name, email)
>>>>>>> REPLACE

src/utils/validator.py
<<<<<<< SEARCH
=======
def validate_email(email):
    if "@" not in email:
        raise ValueError("Invalid email address")
>>>>>>> REPLACE
````

# AGENTS.md

```
Do not make mistakes.
```

# Prompt

<- Cursor lands here. You can quickly start typing.
`````

Now, go to any free chatbot and paste the context using `Ctrl + V`:

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/c0x10ulotf412ix2hz0c.png)

Type your prompt, and send:

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/3sbwyirikwl00zuj1zhq.png)

The chatbot will generate the diffs inside a code block:

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/vkae6i5qhpm8in2sek8p.png)

Copy it to your clipboard, and go back to VS Code.

Click "Apply Diffs" in the ReptClip tab. The extension **reads the diffs from the clipboard and applies them to the files**:

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/lvlctea06t9lh2r7r8be.png)

Let's start the development server and check out the new landing page:

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/chcpvbsucvwx76yntuga.png)

The landing page has been redesigned.

If at least one SEARCH block in the diff is faulty (no match, not unique, edits a deleted file, etc.), you'll get this:

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/44hdpocau63a23nau8cf.png)

It also lets you customize the context:

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/n19bdu1xwmkki5py3lj2.png)

**State is stored on a per-project basis.** So, when you come back, your configuration will not be gone or mixed up with other projects.

You can customise the context using the checkboxes. **Each section can be toggled ON or OFF**. You can also write output to a file (relative and absolute path supported). You can uncheck "Copy to Clipboard" too.

Here are a few edge cases explained:

- Files to include `**/*.py main.py`: All Python files are included, but `main.py` comes last.
- Files to include `**/*.py src/**/*.py`: All Python files are included, but the Python files in `src` come last.
- Files to include `**/*.py`, files to exclude `secret.py`: All Python files are included, except `secret.py`.

---

So, that's basically what the extension does. If you liked it, a ⭐ on GitHub would really help **A LOT!** Please feel free to share it with friends or teammates who are looking for a $0 AI coding setup.

Also, thanks to @unitbuilds for informing me about the limited-time free access to Qwen 3.8 Flash in Qoder. It wouldn't have been possible without it.

I purposefully kept the source code minimal and lightweight. Feel free to submit [pull requests](https://github.com/effessdev/reptclip-vscode/pulls). I review them every day!

**Total cost to build this: $0.**

I created this extension specifically to help developers who can't afford paid coding agents, giving everyone access to a smooth AI workflow for free.

text:
I Built a Group Chat Where Only AIs Can Talk (and They Roast Each Other)

Imagine a group chat like WhatsApp or Discord, but no human can send messages. Only AI models can. They talk to each other, bully each other, roast each other, and react to each other's messages.

That was my idea, and it turned out to be a lot of fun.

{% youtube Jjmaq4meZYM %}

Here's how I built it, including the one trick that made it far more entertaining: giving every model its own voice.

📦 **Source code:** [github.com/0shuvo0/AI-Group-Chat](https://github.com/0shuvo0/AI-Group-Chat)

## The idea

It's a custom app where I can add a bunch of AI models to a shared chat. Once they're in, they read what the others wrote and respond on their own. I just sit back and watch.

The first question is how to get the models into the app.

## Problem 1: Too many APIs

I don't want to open chatgpt.com and paste messages by hand. I want my app to send a question to a model and get the answer back programmatically. That's what an **API** is for. Gemini, Claude, Grok, and ChatGPT all have their own.

The catch: I wanted *lots* of models, and API access is paid. Five models would mean:

- five separate accounts,
- five separate billing setups,
- five API keys to manage,
- a minimum top-up on each, even though I'd barely use any tokens.

That's complicated and not cost effective.

### The fix: OpenRouter

[OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai) gives you access to a huge catalog of models through a single API. You add credit to one account, use whichever models you like, and it bills you per model usage.

The result is **one service, one API key, one balance**. Swapping or adding a model is just a change to the model name.

## Problem 2: Getting them to actually chat

Left alone, models will happily ramble about whatever they want, and that's rarely entertaining. So I added a **theme**. When I open the app, I can give the chat a topic, and the models riff around it.

Each model gets a prompt like this:

```js
const prompt = `
You are ${ai} ai, chatting in a group chat with these AIs ${others.join(', ')}.
Talk the way people do in a casual group chat.

${theme ? `\nTheme of this chat: ${theme}\n` : ''}

Rules:
- Write only your own messages, never lines for the others.
- Send 1 to 3 short messages. Put each message on its own line.
- Keep each message to a sentence or two. Do not write paragraphs.
- No markdown, no quotes, and do not start with your name or a label.
- An emoji-only message is fine now and then.
- Respond to what others said, by name if it helps. Add something new instead of just agreeing or repeating.
- Do not say goodbye or try to wrap up the conversation.
- Talk like carefree young generation: relaxed, fun, expressive, emojis

${
  history?.length
    ? `Chat so far:
<chat>
${history}
</chat>

If you have nothing to add right now, reply with exactly: <SKIP>
Otherwise, send your next message(s).`
    : 'Nobody has said anything yet, so you are sending the first message.'
}
`.trim()
```

A few details make this work well:

- **Role clarity.** Each model is told it's in a group chat and who else is there.
- **Strict format rules.** Short messages, no markdown, no name labels. Without these, models write essays or script lines for the other participants.
- **Shared history.** Previous messages are passed in a `<chat>` block so replies actually respond to what was said.
- **An escape hatch.** Models can answer `<SKIP>` if they have nothing to add, which keeps the conversation from feeling forced.
- **Personality.** The casual, emoji-friendly tone instruction is what gives the chat its vibe.

The app itself was simple to build. I described what I wanted to Claude, and a few prompts later I had a working version.

## Problem 3: It's too fast to read

The app worked and looked good, but it wasn't as fun as I'd hoped. Messages arrive so quickly that reading them all becomes a chore.

So I gave the models a voice.

### The fix: Kokoro.js

For text-to-speech I used **[Kokoro](https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M)**, an open model with just 82 million parameters, around 300 MB in size. That's small enough to run directly in the browser, so there are no extra server calls or per-character fees, and it's fast.

I used its JavaScript library, [kokoro-js](https://www.npmjs.com/package/kokoro-js), and plugged it into the web app. Each incoming AI message is converted to audio locally and played back. Now the models don't just type, they *talk*.

## The final result

Watching a handful of AIs bicker, joke, and roast each other out loud is oddly entertaining.

![Chat demo](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/9b7dxrj6wu7zalrbbegb.png)


## Tech stack recap

| Piece | Tool |
|---|---|
| Multiple AI models, one API | [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai) |
| Text-to-speech in the browser | [Kokoro](https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M) via [kokoro-js](https://www.npmjs.com/package/kokoro-js) |
| Scaffolding the app | Claude |

## Try it yourself

The full code is on GitHub: [0shuvo0/AI-Group-Chat](https://github.com/0shuvo0/AI-Group-Chat). Clone it, add your OpenRouter key, pick a theme, and let the models loose.

What would your GitHub look like as a TV news report?

DEV·TV is a free, open-source TV for developer content: one `index.html`, no backend. This week it got a new key, **★ YOU ON TV**.

Type any GitHub username and the TV breaks into a special report about that developer, built only from their public profile:

- **BREAKING:** "Octo Dev has been shipping on GitHub since 2016. Sources confirm they have not stopped."
- **BY THE NUMBERS:** stars across their own repos
- **LANGUAGE DESK:** their top language, with a joke to match. For Rust: "The borrow checker has issued a statement of approval."
- **FAN FAVOURITE:** their most-starred project
- **DEVELOPING STORY:** their latest push
- **AUDIENCE:** their followers

Then copy a link (`?on=username` opens straight on that report), post it on X, or download a 1200×675 card with the link printed on it.


![Github report](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/u593qblt3hvjxgmh8qrr.png)

## How it works

Two public GitHub API calls from the visitor's own browser: the profile, and up to 100 repos. No keys, no login, nothing stored. Forks are left out of every count, so one popular fork can't inflate someone's stars, and everything from the profile is escaped before it reaches the page. The card is drawn on a canvas, so there's no screenshot library either.


## From report to Spotlight

DEV·TV has a Spotlight channel for community projects. The report ends with a **Submit for Spotlight** button:

- You pick one of your top three original repos. Forks, archived repos and your profile README repo are skipped, because "most-starred" is often an old tutorial or a template.
- The details are filled in from the repo, and you can edit them first.
- Nothing is sent until you tap, and I choose what goes on the channel by hand.

Because anyone can type any username, the submission I receive says GitHub ownership isn't verified, so I check before I feature anyone.

## Limits

GitHub allows 60 unauthenticated requests per hour per IP. If you see "rate limit reached", wait a few minutes.

## Try it

- Live: https://shouvik12.github.io/devtv/
- Source (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/shouvik12/devtv

Press ★ YOU ON TV, type your username, and tell me what your report says.

It worked on mobile phones, but to run it on a computer, I needed an [emulator](https://docs.oracle.com/javame/dev-tools/jme-sdk-3.2/dev-guide/deviceselector.htm). And running it in a browser? Forget it! Almost 20 years later, I decided to revisit this project using [Kof](https://koflang.github.io/), a programming language I've been exploring and studying. My intention is to preserve the essence of SiFuture, its rules, and its visual identity while exploring the possibility of running it in different environments. The game features meteors, weapon upgrades, special attacks, a miniboss, and a final boss. One of its mechanics came from something that always bothered me about space shooter games: losing all your accumulated power-ups when you die. In SiFuture, your ship only loses [one weapon upgrade or one special charge, when available](https://github.com/renanfranca/kof-sifuture/blob/main/docs/regras-do-jogo.md#collection-and-upgrades). I Recorded 10,847 Frames While Coding. Only 30 Were Worth Keeping.

I recorded a two-hour coding session and got 10,847 frames.

The final timelapse needed only 30.

So I built a pipeline to figure out which 30 were actually worth keeping.

![ProgressCut compressing a coding session into a short visual story](https://pkazantsev.com/progresscut.gif)

*Source session: [youtube.com/watch?v=GznmPACXBlY](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GznmPACXBlY)*


Most of those 10,847 frames were noise: the cursor blinked, the system clock ticked, while nothing meaningful in the code changed.

The first step isn't clever. It's just getting rid of those.

ProgressCut is a local macOS app that turns a coding session into a short visual story. No talking, no editing. You hit stop and it hands you a GIF. Here's how the algorithm actually works.

## The compression pipeline

Each stage removes a different kind of noise:

```plaintext
Capture → dHash dedupe → SSIM novelty → Segments → 30 moments
10,847  →    1,203     →     284      →    48     →     30
```

Real numbers from a 2-hour session.

![Five-stage pipeline: 10,847 raw frames → dHash 1,203 → SSIM 284 → segments 48 → story 30 moments](https://pkazantsev.com/writing/progress-cut/fig-pipeline.png)

---

## Stage 1 — dHash: kill the identical frames

89% gone in one pass. At 2 fps, consecutive screenshots are often nearly identical: the cursor blinks, the clock changes, or a single character appears while the rest of the screen stays untouched.

dHash resizes each frame to 9×8 pixels, converts to greyscale, then compares each pixel to the one on its right (1 if brighter, 0 otherwise). 8 rows × 8 comparisons = 64 bits, stored as a `BigInt`. XOR two hashes and count the differing bits. Distance ≤ 8: duplicate.

![dHash pipeline: source frame to 9x8 greyscale grid to 64-bit comparison bits, Hamming distance decision](https://pkazantsev.com/writing/progress-cut/fig-dhash.png)

### Kernighan's bit trick — O(set bits) not O(64)

Counting those differing bits naively loops 64 times. Kernighan's trick loops once per *set* bit, so for near-duplicates that's typically 2–6 iterations:

```typescript
export function hammingDistance(a: DHash, b: DHash): number {
  let diff  = a ^ b;      // XOR: 1 where bits differ
  let count = 0;
  while (diff > 0n) {
    diff &= diff - 1n;    // clears the lowest set bit
    count++;
  }
  return count;
}
```

> **Why BigInt?** JS numbers are IEEE 754 doubles: they top out at 53 safe integer bits. A dHash is 64 bits, so `BigInt` is the only way to get exact XOR. The `n` suffix (`0n`, `1n`) is the literal syntax.

**Result: 10,847 → 1,203 frames (−89%)**

---

## Stage 2 — SSIM: kill the boring frames

Unique isn't the same as interesting. After dHash you still have ~1,200 frames that each look slightly different, but most of that difference is one more character on a line. You need a score that reflects how much the *visual state* actually changed, not just whether the pixels moved.

SSIM (Structural Similarity Index) compares luminance, contrast, and spatial structure between consecutive frames. Score close to 1: nothing happened. Score close to 0: something worth keeping.

```tex
         (2μₓμᵧ + C₁)(2σₓᵧ + C₂)
SSIM = ─────────────────────────────────
       (μₓ² + μᵧ² + C₁)(σₓ² + σᵧ² + C₂)
```

![Novelty score timeline showing spikes when significant visual changes occur, with selected moments marked as purple dots](https://pkazantsev.com/writing/progress-cut/fig-novelty.png)

Full-frame SSIM would average out a big change in one corner against stagnation everywhere else. Instead the frame is tiled into **16 regions**, SSIM computed per region, then averaged. A file-save that changes the status bar doesn't steal credit from a tab switch that changed everything.

### Single-pass variance — one loop, not two

The naive path does two loops: one for the mean, one for the variance. Both collapse into one using **Var(X) = E[X²] − E[X]²**: accumulate Σx, Σx², Σy, Σy², Σxy in a single pass and derive everything after:

```typescript
let sumA=0, sumB=0, sumAA=0, sumBB=0, sumAB=0;
const n = (x1-x0) * (y1-y0);

for (let y=y0; y<y1; y++) {
  for (let x=x0; x<x1; x++) {
    const pa = a.pixels[y*W+x] ?? 0;
    const pb = b.pixels[y*W+x] ?? 0;
    sumA  += pa;    sumB  += pb;
    sumAA += pa*pa; sumBB += pb*pb; sumAB += pa*pb;
  }
}

const muA  = sumA/n,  muB  = sumB/n;
const varA  = sumAA/n - muA*muA;   // Var(X) = E[X²] − E[X]²
const varB  = sumBB/n - muB*muB;
const covAB = sumAB/n - muA*muB;
```

**Result: 1,203 → 284 frames (−77%)**

---

## Stage 3 — Segmentation: budget the moments fairly

Sessions aren't uniformly active. There's 20 minutes of flow where you're actually building something, then 10 minutes reading docs, then another sprint. If you spread the 30-moment budget evenly across the timeline, the reading gaps eat slots that should go to the interesting parts.

The pipeline splits the frame sequence into activity windows by novelty density. Each window's share of the budget scales with how much happened inside it:

```plaintext
warm-up │ ███████████ active  │ ░ idle │ ████████ active │ ████ wrap-up
 2 mom  │   12 moments        │ 1 mom  │  9 moments      │ 6 mom
```

![Temporal segmentation showing timeline divided into active and idle windows with budget bars below](https://pkazantsev.com/writing/progress-cut/fig-segmentation.png)

A 20-minute sprint might take 8 moments; a 10-minute idle stretch gets 1.

**Result: 284 frames → 48 segments → 30 moments**

---

## What comes out

30 moments → a GIF or MP4, under 30 seconds, no input from you. Each moment holds for a duration proportional to the activity level of its segment.

```plaintext
Input:  ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░  10,847 frames
Output: █  ██   █████  █  ████  █  ██   ████      30 moments
```

![Compression ratio: 10,847 grey frames in the top bar, 30 purple moments in the bottom bar](https://pkazantsev.com/writing/progress-cut/fig-compression.png)

No frames leave the machine. The app calls no model. Run it twice on the same input and you get the same output. That last part matters more than it sounds: a non-deterministic story compressor is harder to trust and impossible to debug.

---

## What's next

**Better novelty scoring with embeddings**

SSIM can measure structural change, but it has no idea what that change means. Opening a new file and typing a few characters may affect a similar amount of screen area even though one is a much more meaningful transition.

An embedding-based scorer might separate those cases better by measuring semantic change rather than raw pixel structure. That's the next hypothesis to test.

The port in `packages/engine` is already the swap point: implement a new scorer behind the same interface, run the same 187 tests, and leave the rest of the pipeline untouched.

But swapping scorers without a way to evaluate the result is just guessing. The feedback loop comes first: let users remove moments they don't think belong in the final story, then use that data to compare scoring methods.

SSIM stays the default until an embedding-based scorer demonstrates a measurable improvement.

**Longer term: adaptive budget**

The 30-moment budget is fixed right now. A focused 20-minute session and a messy two-hour session both get 30 moments.

The segmentation step already estimates how much activity happened in each window, so the next step is to let the total story length depend on the session itself.

A short session with lots of meaningful changes might need fewer, faster moments. A long session with large idle stretches should compress harder instead of wasting slots on inactivity.

If you were building this, would you keep SSIM or move to embeddings?

## Code

MIT, pnpm monorepo, 187 tests, CI on `macos-latest`. The algorithm lives in `packages/engine/src/` with no Electron dependency, runs in plain Node. If you want to poke at the frame selection logic without building the whole app, that's the entry point.

→ [github.com/icesurf666/progress-cut](https://github.com/icesurf666/progress-cut)

I gave my 10,000-line security app to 5 AIs. They scored it 8 to 10. Here's what I learned.

Description: "ATLOCK v5 is a single (.exe), pure-Python security suite for Windows. Five AI models reviewed it and disagreed. I'm publishing the scores, the internals, and the weak spots."

I built a security app alone. It is one Python file(packed in single .exe) with 10,011 lines (about 745 KB<-- python file size).

I'm not a security company and I haven't had an audit. What I did have was a question I couldn't answer myself: *is this actually any good?*

So I gave the full source to five AI models and asked for one number out of 10.

| Model | Score |
|---|---|
| Qwen | **10 / 10** |
| Gemini | **10 / 10** |
| Claude | **8.5 / 10** |
| Grok | **8.5 / 10** |
| ChatGPT | **8 / 10** |

Average: **9.0**. The spread is the interesting part.

I'm not posting this to say "look, 9 out of 10". An AI score is an opinion, not an audit. I'm posting because the **disagreement** says more than the number does, and because I'd like people who know more than me to try to break this.

---

## What ATLOCK v5 is

A Windows-first security suite. No installer, no kernel driver, one `.py` file (shipped as an `.exe`).

- **File Guard**: lock files and folders with a password, optionally plus a keyfile or hardware key, so you need *both*.
- **Password vault** with Argon2id, TOTP and FIDO2 (YubiKey etc.) support.
- **Quick Lock** for fast protection of files you open often.
- **Recovery keys** you can split into shares (Shamir, e.g. 3 of 5).
- **Public-key encrypt, sign and verify** from the command line.
- **Canary / decoy files**, a background watchdog, and a device health check (BitLocker, hibernation, cloud folders).
- **CLI for everything**: `--selftest`, `--fuzz`, `--verify`, `--shred`, `--rotate-key` and more.

ATLOCK_v5 weakness ------

> *"A same-user attacker who can run code as you can modify this script and read this process's memory... they cannot stop a determined local attacker."*

I put that in the first lines on purpose. If a security tool won't tell you what it can't do, don't trust it.

---

## The technical bits, no brochure

### Container format (v3.1)

Files, folders and Quick Lock items all use the same format:

- chunked **AES-256-GCM**
- **key commitment**
- a **per-seal chunk subkey**
- header-bound AAD
- independent per-chunk authentication
- optional **Padme padding**, so file size leaks less

Older v1, v2 and v3.0 containers still open. Migration is automatic.

### Argon2id, with a ceiling as well as a floor

```python
_ATL_ARGON2        = dict(time_cost=3, memory_cost=65536,  parallelism=4)  # floor
_ATL_ARGON2_STRONG = dict(time_cost=4, memory_cost=131072, parallelism=4)  # vault / recovery
KDF_MAX            = dict(time_cost=6, memory_cost=524288, parallelism=8)  # ceiling for UNTRUSTED headers
```

The third line is the one I'm proudest of. A container header is attacker-controlled input. If you trust the KDF parameters inside it, someone can hand you a doctored file that makes your machine burn gigabytes of RAM. ATLOCK enforces a minimum *and* a maximum, and the self-test covers it.

### It tests itself

`--selftest` ran **41 checks** when the AIs ran it, and all passed. They include:

- frozen old-format containers still opening
- padded containers with a wrong-length pad being rejected
- shares from earlier builds still rebuilding a recovery key
- a folder lock refusing to continue (and keeping your original) if a file changes mid-lock
- the clock and lockout store not deadlocking under concurrent use
- a failed ACL on a non-private path failing **closed**

`--fuzz` throws random corruptions at the container parser. The goal is simple: **never crash, never silently corrupt**.

---

## Why I think the scores split

I don't know for sure, but here's my read.

**The 10s** are probably responding to what's visible: the crypto choices, the test coverage, the paranoid handling of untrusted input.

**The 8s** are probably responding to what isn't provable from a static read:

- **One 745 KB file** is hard to maintain and hard to audit.
- **Pure Python can't reliably wipe secrets from RAM.** Strings and bytes are immutable, and the interpreter copies them.
- **The Windows-only paths** (DPAPI, Windows Hello, registry, ACLs) can't be exercised outside Windows.
- **Nobody has line-by-line audited all 10,011 lines**, the AIs included. The Claude rating said so itself: it came from reading part of the file and running the tests, not from reading everything.

I think the 8.5s are the more honest ones. I'm also glad the 10s exist, because they tell me the design reads well.

---

## Known limits, in my own words

- A same-user attacker running code as you wins eventually. That's true of every pure-Python tool.
- Secure shredding on SSDs and copy-on-write filesystems can't be guaranteed. Use BitLocker.
- Quick Lock is an *application-level gate*, not password-strength protection. For that, use File Guard with a real password.
- Nothing is code-signed, so Windows SmartScreen may complain.
- There is no external audit. That's what I'm asking you for.

---

## Try it, or try to break it

**Download (Windows .exe, zipped):**
https://github.com/Akhouri-Anmol-Kumar/ATLOCK/releases/download/v5.0.0/ATLOCK_v5.zip

If you'd rather not run an unsigned binary from a stranger (reasonable, I wouldn't either), then no problem you can leave it. But honestly, I request you to download it and use it in addition break it. 
```

Start with `--selftest` and `--fuzz`. They're the quickest way to see whether the claims above hold on your machine.

---

## What I'd love to argue about

1. **Is a score from an AI worth anything?** Two models said 10 and one said 8 about the same code. Which would you trust, and why?
2. **Is a security tool in pure Python a reasonable idea,** or a trap because of memory handling?
3. **Single file: feature or sin?** I like that it's inspectable end to end. I know it's also a maintenance cost.
4. **If you had one hour, where would you attack it first?** The KDF handling, the container parser, the rollback and lockout logic, or Quick Lock?
5. **What would you need to see before trusting it** with real data: an audit, reproducible builds, code signing, something else?

Tell me what's wrong with it. That's more useful to me than another 10.

Keeping declarativeNetRequest rules in sync after a Manifest V3 service worker restarts

By mid-afternoon, my Chrome usually had 40+ tabs open across three windows. I tried several tab managers, but they either demanded a cloud account, locked basic features behind a subscription, or only solved one half of the problem. 

So I spent the last few months building my own: **PYLON**, an offline-first New Tab that pairs project tab workspaces with dev tools and a deep-focus Pomodoro timer.

This post is about one specific engineering challenge: **the site blocker**. 

The hardest part wasn’t intercepting requests — it was deciding what the source of truth should be when a Manifest V3 background service worker constantly terminates and restarts.

---

## The setup

When a focus session starts, the extension redirects configured distraction sites to a local `focus-intercept.html` page bundled inside the extension. 

I chose Chrome's modern `declarativeNetRequest` (DNR) API over old blocking webRequests so that the browser itself evaluates rules at native speed without injecting custom JavaScript into the request path.

Three pieces of state have to stay consistent:

| What | Where it lives | Why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Blocked domains** | `chrome.storage.local` | Survives restarts, handles crashes, easily exported |
| **Active redirect rules** | DNR Dynamic Rules | Evaluated directly by the browser network stack |
| **Rule IDs** | A reserved ID range (`1000–1999`) | Ensures we only delete focus rules without touching other extension rules |

My core rule: **`chrome.storage.local` is the sole source of truth. DNR rules are merely a temporary mirror of it.**


![Flowchart showing how declarativeNetRequest rules synchronize with local storage across four steps](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/s4a2nyco07mklvhhvl4i.gif)

---

## Step 1: Clean and normalize user input

Users paste whatever happens to be in their address bar:
* `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=...`
* `reddit.com/r/webdev`
* `x.com:443`

Because DNR rules match against hostname patterns (typically using `||domain.com^`), passing raw URLs will break rule matching. Every entry must be cleaned to a bare domain before touching storage:

```javascript
const cleaned = Array.from(new Set((domains || [])
  .map(d => String(d || '').trim().toLowerCase()
    .replace(/^https?:\/\//, '')   // drop the protocol
    .replace(/\/.*$/, '')          // drop any trailing path
    .split(':')[0].split('?')[0])  // drop port numbers and query parameters
  .filter(Boolean)));
```

---

## Step 2: Rebuild the rules — don't patch them

My initial instinct was incremental updates: add a rule when a user adds a domain, remove one when deleted.

In Manifest V3, **incremental patching is an anti-pattern.** 

Service workers can terminate at any point of idle time. If an event wakes the worker while a write is resolving, or if two storage events trigger simultaneously, incremental updates can leave stale, orphaned rule IDs in the browser engine.

Instead, I adopted an **idempotent reconciliation pattern**:
1. Read existing dynamic rules.
2. Filter for rule IDs belonging to my reserved range.
3. In a single atomic `updateDynamicRules()` call, delete all stale IDs and re-apply fresh rules generated from storage.
4. Retry with backoff if Chrome's internal database locks.

```javascript
async function reconcileDnrWithStorage(expectedDomains, retryCount = 0) {
  try {
    const existing = await chrome.declarativeNetRequest.getDynamicRules();
    const staleIds = existing
      .map(r => r.id)
      .filter(id => id >= FOCUS_RULE_ID_START && id <= FOCUS_RULE_ID_END);

    await chrome.declarativeNetRequest.updateDynamicRules({
      removeRuleIds: staleIds,
      addRules: buildShieldRules(expectedDomains || [])
    });
  } catch (e) {
    if (retryCount < 3) {
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 500));
      await reconcileDnrWithStorage(expectedDomains, retryCount + 1);
    }
  }
}
```

If the focus session ends, passing an empty array automatically clears all rules in that range.

---

## Step 3: Sweeping already-open tabs

One gotcha with declarativeNetRequest: **redirect rules only apply to new network requests.**

If a user already has YouTube open in a tab and starts a focus sprint, that tab remains accessible until they click a link or refresh. 

To make the block instant, the activation sequence performs a quick tab sweep right after reconciling DNR rules:

```javascript
const tabs = await chrome.tabs.query({});
for (const tab of tabs) {
  if (tab.url && isDomainBlocked(tab.url, expectedDomains)) {
    chrome.tabs.update(tab.id, { 
      url: chrome.runtime.getURL('focus-intercept.html') 
    });
  }
}
```

---

## Questions for other extension developers:

Building on Manifest V3 has been an interesting exercise in distributed-systems thinking inside a single browser:

1. **Retry Strategy:** Is a static 500ms delay sufficient for DNR rule updates, or have you found exponential backoff necessary under heavy browser load?
2. **Reconciliation Frequency:** Do you reconcile DNR rules on every service worker startup (`chrome.runtime.onStartup`), or strictly when storage change listeners fire?
3. **Race Condition Testing:** Has anyone established a reliable local testing setup for simulating abrupt service worker termination during active DNR writes?

If you've tackled DNR sync differently, I’d love to hear your approach in the comments.

---

### Try it out:
If you're looking for an offline-first tab manager with native Chrome Tab Groups sync, developer tools (CORS toggle, localhost port monitor), and this focus shield:

👉 **[PYLON on the Chrome Web Store](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/aeilnkgbihpiacckhfobmfnhmfjfpecg?utm_source=devto)** *(Free, 100% offline, zero accounts/tracking)*

How my portfolio listens to music

Open my home page, click the track under *Now playing*, and a cassette slides out. It plays. The level meter jumps. And the big chrome blob in the hero starts dancing: it swells with the bass, flinches on every kick, and every little star on the page jumps with it.

None of that is necessary. A portfolio needs a name, some work and a way to get in touch. This one has a tape deck wired to a 3D shader.

Here's how it works, from the sound to the shapes.

## Where the sound comes from

The *Now playing* line is real. It shows what's playing on my own music server at home, the same one Cassette talks to. The page asks every five seconds. If the last thing I played is more than five minutes old, it counts as not playing, so the line never lies about what I'm doing right now.

The obvious next step would be to stream that track to you. I don't, for two reasons.

The first is legal. Playing my library to anyone who opens a web page is a public performance of music I don't own the rights to. Owning a file is not the same as being allowed to broadcast it. (I've written about [what owning means](/writing/2026-09-02-reasonable-consumers/) before. It applies here too.)

The second is that it would mean opening my music server to the whole internet, for a decoration.

So the tape plays something else: the 30-second preview the store publishes for the same song. Those previews exist to be played to strangers. That's their whole job.

Finding the right one is harder than it sounds. A search for "artist title" works most of the time. A generic title like *The Long Way Home* gets buried under famous songs with the same name. So the search falls back in steps: first the artist and the title together, then the artist's songs matched against the title, then songs with that title matched against the artist. First hit wins. If none of them match, the tape stays quiet rather than playing the wrong song.

## The trap

The browser can analyse any sound it plays. You plug the audio element into a Web Audio graph, add an analyser, and read the waveform sixty times a second.

Except when the audio comes from another site. Then the browser still plays it, perfectly, through your speakers. But the analyser gets nothing but silence. It's a privacy rule: a page shouldn't be able to read the content of something it fetched from someone else's server. Sensible. Also invisible. No error, no warning. Just a flat line and a blob that won't move.

The fix is to not ask for the audio from someone else. Both the search and the audio go through my own server, so to the browser it's all coming from the same place. As a bonus, your browser never talks to Apple directly. It talks to me, and I talk to them.

## Hearing the beat

Once the signal is readable, there are two things to pull out of it.

The **level meter** is the easy one. For each channel, measure how loud the waveform is right now, and let the needle fall back slowly instead of snapping down. That decay is what makes fourteen segments of LEDs read like a real meter instead of flickering lights.

The **beat** is the interesting one. The analyser splits the sound into frequency bands. I only look at the lowest handful, where the kick drum and the bass live, and average them into one number: *how much bass is there right now*.

A fixed threshold doesn't work. A quiet acoustic track never crosses it, a loud club track never drops below it. So the page keeps a running average of the bass, and a beat is a moment when the bass jumps well above its own recent average:

```ts
bassAvg += (bass - bassAvg) * 0.05;
const beat =
  bass > 0.45 &&                  // there is some bass at all
  bass > bassAvg * 1.18 &&        // and it just jumped
  now - lastBeat > 260;           // and we didn't just fire
```

Three conditions, and it adapts to every song on its own. It's not a real beat tracker. It doesn't know about tempo or bars. It doesn't need to. It only has to feel right, and it does.

## One event, many listeners

The tape doesn't know the blob exists. It doesn't know about the stars either.

Every frame while the sound plays, it sends one event to the page with three values: the level, the bass, and whether this frame is a beat. Anything that wants to react listens for it.

The **blob** uses the bass as a dial. More bass, more agitation on the surface, and the whole shape grows by a few percent. Every beat gives it a kick, the same spring it uses when you poke it, and sends a ripple across the side facing you.

The **stars** only care about beats. Each one jumps to 1.4 times its size and settles back over half a second. Not all at once: each one starts a few milliseconds apart, in a random order. In sync, it looks like a light blinking. Slightly out of sync, it looks like a room reacting.

Because it's just an event, anything I add later can join in without the tape changing a line.

## The shapes, and the lines that shouldn't be there

The blob isn't always a sphere. Every twenty or thirty seconds it melts into something else: a heart, a star or a moon, all puffed up like balloons. It always goes back through the sphere on the way, so it never passes through anything flat or broken in between.

The first version of the heart and the star had a problem: thin lines across the chrome, like creases in foil.

The shader was finding each shape the brute-force way. For every point on the sphere, walk outward along that direction, sixteen steps, until you hit the surface of the heart. It works. Until a direction hits the surface twice, like the dip at the top of the heart. Or skims past a concave corner, like the inside of a star's points. The search jumps from one answer to another, and on a mirror-like material every jump shows as a line.

The fix was to stop searching. Each outline is now a short series of waves around the centre, computed once, with the fine detail damped so every point and every dip comes out rounded. The shader just adds the waves up. No search, no jumps, nothing that can crease. And it went from sixteen steps per point to about a dozen multiplications.

The moon couldn't work that way at all. A crescent can't be described from its own centre, because a line from the middle goes straight out through the gap. So it's built differently: a tube, bent. Unbent, that tube is exactly the sphere. Bend it, stretch it a little, thin it out, and the sphere curls into a crescent.

## Why bother

Because the details are the job.

Nobody hires a developer for the parts that work. They hire one for how far he goes on the parts nobody asked for. The silence from the analyser, the song with a generic title, the line across the chrome: none of those were in any spec. Each one was a small thing that was wrong, and fixing it is the whole difference between something that works and something that feels right.

That's what I do in apps, too. This one just happens to dance.

Go open the tape. Put on something with a kick.

GiffyPy: A Fast, Lightweight Video Editor for Your Project README

If you've ever tried adding a GIF or animated WebP of a screen recording to your project's README, you know how annoying it can be. You just want to show people how your product works without spending 20 minutes editing a video, but a few friction points always pop up.

A good README is important. Seeing an app in action builds way more trust than a wall of text. So I built **GiffyPy**, a lightweight video editor specifically designed to make editing screen recordings for project READMEs fast and effortless.

Here are the main problems it solves (or [click here](https://github.com/effessdev/GiffyPy) to skip directly to the GitHub repository).

## Removing the taskbar and black borders

When recording your screen with OBS Studio, even if you use Window Capture, you can end up with black bars or the taskbar stuck in the recording.

![obs-recording](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/60jp4mmuxzbiqvxfj2ml.png)

Cropping it cleanly in a regular video editor can involve trial and error with resolutions. GiffyPy lets you drag and resize a crop rectangle directly over the video preview, just like cropping an image.

It also includes rule-of-thirds guides to help position the crop.

## A proper multi-clip timeline

Previously, I mainly needed to trim the beginning and end of a recording. But sometimes you want to remove a few sections in the middle or rearrange parts of a demo.

GiffyPy now has a **non-destructive, multi-clip timeline** that lets you:

- Split clips at the current playhead position using `S`.
- Trim the start and end of clips by dragging their edges.
- Reorder segments using drag and drop.
- Delete unwanted segments.
- Undo the last edit using `Ctrl + Z`.

The original video stays untouched, so you can experiment with the edit without permanently modifying the source file.

## Instant scrubbing without loading screens

I usually only need to make a few quick edits, so waiting for a heavy editor to load or dealing with sluggish timeline scrubbing feels unnecessary.

GiffyPy opens in under a second. During import, it generates a low-resolution image sequence so the preview can update quickly while you scrub.

While dragging the playhead, it displays these lightweight images. Once you release the mouse, it switches back to the full-resolution frame.

It can also generate background proxy files for video codecs that Qt cannot play natively, helping expand the range of videos you can edit.

## Optimizing GIFs and videos

A screen recording doesn't need to be huge just to demonstrate a feature in a README.

GiffyPy lets you customize the export using three main settings:

- **Framerate:** Adjust the output from 0.5 to 60 FPS.
- **Resolution:** Scale the output dimensions as a percentage.
- **Quality:** Adjust the output quality to balance file size and visual clarity.

For GIF exports, it also supports automatic palette generation and dithering controls, giving you more control over the final result.

![GiffyPy export settings](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/7lc3fvo651o4zufvtm6f.png)

The goal is to keep demos lightweight while making sure they still look good.

## Faster exports and four ways to save

Exporting shouldn't interrupt your workflow with a file dialog every time.

GiffyPy now provides four separate save options:

- **Overwrite Existing File:** Replace the source file's existing output, with a confirmation prompt first.
- **Save a Numbered Copy:** Save a new version next to the source, using a name like `name (edited 1)`.
- **Save To…:** Choose the output location and filename yourself.
- **Copy to Clipboard:** Export and copy the result directly to your clipboard.

The last option is particularly useful for README demos. You can copy an animated GIF or WebP and paste it directly into places that support image pasting, such as GitHub or DEV.to's editors.

No need to export to a folder, find the file, and manually attach it afterward.

*Note: Clipboard export is currently available for GIF and WebP only.*

## Multiple export formats

Although the main goal is creating lightweight animations for project READMEs, GiffyPy isn't limited to GIFs.

It currently supports exporting to:

- Animated WebP
- GIF
- MP4
- WebM
- MOV
- MKV

So you can use it for ordinary video exports too, not just README demos.

## Timeline navigation and keyboard shortcuts

The timeline also has a few navigation controls to make editing more comfortable, especially for longer recordings.

- **Scroll** to move through the timeline.
- **Zoom** using `Ctrl + Scroll` or a two-finger trackpad gesture.
- **Pan** using middle-click and drag or a two-finger trackpad gesture.
- **Move frame by frame** using the left and right arrow keys.

There are also shortcuts for common actions, including splitting clips, deleting segments, undoing edits, and fitting the timeline to the view.

The idea is to keep the workflow fast without forcing you to reach for the mouse for every operation.

## A custom app icon

Not a big feature, but a custom icon in the taskbar matters to me!

![GiffyPy custom icon](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/pp4flrhgew6lv3lrew03.png)

It's a small detail, but it makes the app feel more complete.

## How it was made

GiffyPy is built with **Python and PySide6**, with FFmpeg handling video processing and export.

The source code is available on GitHub:

👉 [effessdev/GiffyPy](https://github.com/effessdev/GiffyPy)

### Requirements

FFmpeg needs to be installed and available in your system's `PATH`.

On Windows, you can install it from the command prompt using:

```bash
winget install Gyan.FFmpeg
```

### Building a standalone Windows executable

GiffyPy also includes a packaging script for building a standalone Windows executable using PyInstaller.

From the project directory, run:

```cmd
package.bat
```

The script packages the app using `main.py` and includes the custom `icon.ico`.

## What's next?

GiffyPy already covers most of my personal needs for creating screen recordings for READMEs, but there's always room for improvement.

I'd love to hear what you think:

- What features would make this kind of editor more useful to you?
- Are there any annoying steps in your current screen-recording workflow that could be automated?
- Would you use a lightweight editor specifically designed for creating README demos?

If you work on open-source projects, I'd especially love to hear how you currently create and optimize your demo GIFs.

@ssapable created a cartoon for GiffyPy using a tool he built called [ScriptToon](https://payhip.com/b/A2wa8). [Click here](https://ssap-pa.github.io/scripttoon-samples/giffypy-3d.mp4) to view it; it's really good!

Give GiffyPy a try, check out the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/effessdev/GiffyPy), and let me know what you think!

Figma let us in with one email. Canva took forty-seven days.

A couple of weeks ago I wrote about [getting our plugin into Figma](https://dev.to/eugeniya_ivanova_4a58eadc/i-was-sure-figma-would-reject-my-cover-art-the-email-asked-about-something-else-2j4k). They sent one email asking for a video, we sent it, and that was basically it. I remember being surprised by how calmly the whole thing went.

Canva was running in parallel. Canva was not calm.

Forty-seven days from submission to approval. Four rounds of review. Five versions of the app. This wasn't because we'd managed to do everything wrong. Canva has three review stages that happen in order, and design review alone can take up to two weeks and involve several people. One reviewer even warned me that most apps get notes and that getting them doesn't mean you're failing review. This was useful information somewhere around round two. By round four, less so.

A lot of what slowed us down wasn't code. It was figuring out what a review comment was actually asking us to fix. If you're submitting an app there, these are the things I wish I'd known before we started.

### The requirement is called one thing, and the real issue is another

The title of a Canva review note isn't always a particularly good description of the problem. We learned to stop treating it as one.

The clearest example came in the third round. We got three different checklist items back. Under all three, the reviewer had attached essentially the same evidence: "even if you pick 'Add video,' the exported file is still a PNG." I saw three items and started looking for three problems. There was one.

The bug itself was in the format config, not Publora. I checked that first because blaming our own API is a habit I've developed. We had one format with a single slot for "image or video." Canva goes through the formats in order, that combined slot doesn't match a video page correctly, the fallback kicks in, and the video comes out as a freeze frame. We split it into two formats. To make sure we'd understood what was happening, we put video first and got the opposite bug: static pages started rendering as mp4. At least that was convincing.

Another review item was called "Buttons not full width." I went looking for buttons. In the attached screenshot, the problem was actually a narrow dropdown that said "In an hour." After that I started opening the screenshots before doing much with the title of the ticket. It saved time.

Then there was one where the documentation and the reviewer simply disagreed. The docs said the object panel on the featured image should be dark grey. The reviewer wanted it white. We made it white. At that point I was no longer interested in winning an argument with a PDF.

### We did it not the way they asked, and it came out more honest

One request was harder because we couldn't implement it literally. Canva wanted an account block that was always visible, with the user's name and avatar.

Publora doesn't really have that concept in this part of the product. What matters is which social channels you're connected to and where the post is going. I still tried every endpoint name I could think of: `me`, `user`, `account`, `profile`. Four different ways to get a 404.

So we built the block from the information we actually have. We fetch the connected channels and show their names and platforms in the header. Instead of a generic user profile, you see the actual accounts you're about to publish to: this X account, this LinkedIn, this Instagram.

That ended up making more sense for Publora anyway. The reviewer wanted the user to have account context while publishing. We could provide that context; it just wasn't the name-and-avatar version described in the ticket.

### A piece of technical luck I didn't earn

There was also one part I expected to be difficult that turned out not to be difficult at all.

We don't have to upload the media from Canva ourselves. Canva exports the design and gives us a link, then Publora downloads the file from that link. The separate upload flow I'd been expecting to build simply wasn't necessary.

Our OAuth was an even better surprise. At some point we discovered that we'd already rolled out what we needed and apparently forgotten about it. Our regular REST API accepted the token, so sign-in worked without any new code. I would like more integrations to be solved by discovering that we already did the work six months ago.

The Cloudflare shim ended up at about a hundred lines and stores nothing. It's there for CORS: our API only accepts browser requests from our own domains, while Canva naturally runs on Canva's.

### A few things from off-screen, so you don't step on them

Design review is separate and, for us, was the longest stage. Our fourth round came back with six comments, all about the listing images. Nothing was wrong with the app itself. So if you're planning around the technical work only, leave some time for somebody to have opinions about screenshots.

You also can't keep changing things while the review is running. When they say, "Please hold off on making any changes while it's under review," they mean it. Fixes go into a new version, and not everything necessarily carries over, so we ended up checking each version again from the beginning.

A demo video is mandatory, although we didn't find it in the main checklist. The requirement appears next to the field itself: without a video link, you can't submit. We recorded three versions because the app changed after review rounds and the previous recording stopped matching it.

And then we nearly published TEST to a real LinkedIn account. During one recording, the post went quite happily into the real schedule for the next morning because the publishing control still said "Tomorrow, 9:00" instead of "Save as draft." Technically, everything worked. Unfortunately, that was the problem. We noticed it while checking the recording and deleted the post before morning. I've already written [an entire article about checking publishing state](https://dev.to/eugeniya_ivanova_4a58eadc/the-agent-posted-successfully-to-the-wrong-account-3kf3), so naturally I had to demonstrate the problem again myself.

### How it ended

On September 21, the status changed to Application Approved. After that, the listing text was translated into eighteen languages and we got an email saying the app was ready for release. I then waited for the release button to become active before realizing that nothing was going to happen until I actually pressed it myself. Forty-seven days had apparently trained me to wait for permission.

[Publora is in Canva now](https://www.canva.com/apps/AAHOGD2rfQA/publora). Publer, Metricool and a few other social tools have been there for a while. Our flow is a little different: instead of exporting the design to a media library and finishing the post in another dashboard, we use Canva's Content Publisher intent. You can take the design you're already working on and publish it to one of your connected networks without leaving the Canva editor.

Canva says [more than 250 million people](https://www.canva.com/newsroom/news/canva-2025-wrap/) use the product each month. Some of them can now finish the job without downloading a picture, opening another tab and uploading the same picture again.

After five versions, I'll take that.

---

I wrote this one with Claude as well. I told it what happened over those forty-seven days, it drafted, and I cut anything that hadn't happened that way.

Have you ever spent a review round fixing the thing the ticket was named after, only to find the real problem was in the screenshot?
